articles.title: Netflix Treats GPU Reliability as a Distributed Systems Problem
articles.text:
Netflix has detailed how it is building a reliability platform for large-scale GPU training and inference, using layered health checks, automated remediation, and fault-tolerant training to keep jobs running despite hardware failures.
The problem is particularly acute for large AI training jobs. A model may run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs, with all workers operating in lockstep. A single failed GPU, degraded network adapter, or slow machine can therefore stop or significantly slow the entire workload. Netflix has built its GPU compute platform on Kubernetes and designed it to detect these failures, remove unhealthy capacity automatically, and allow long-running jobs to recover from machine loss.
The approach has produced measurable results: Netflix reports more than 99.95% GPU-node availability and an increase in job success from approximately 98% to more than 99.5%.
A conventional cloud health check can establish that a virtual machine is running and reachable, but that does not mean its GPUs are capable of running a distributed training workload.
Netflix found that a GPU can respond normally to a status query while failing once memory is allocated or sustained computation begins. Similarly, a network adapter may be present but have fewer links than expected, allowing collective operations to continue at severely reduced bandwidth.
Device-level checks use NVIDIA DCGM to monitor GPU errors, memory, interconnect, and thermal conditions, while networking checks inspect the state and number of high-speed Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces. A Kubernetes node agent converts these results into node conditions that controllers can act upon.
The checks are deliberately designed to fail closed. If a diagnostic tool hangs, its timeout marks the machine unhealthy rather than allowing a broken check to report success. Netflix also maintains fallback paths using kernel logs when the normal GPU diagnostic mechanism itself fails.
Detecting a fault is only half the problem. Netflix has built controllers that progressively respond to failures rather than immediately replacing an entire machine.
A transient problem can initially block new work while allowing existing workloads to continue. If the condition persists, the machine is drained, and its workloads are moved. Depending on the failure, remediation can range from killing a problematic job or resetting a GPU to rebooting the machine or replacing it entirely.
This approach integrates with Karpenter's node auto-repair capabilities, with Netflix adding policies that determine how long to tolerate different failures and how much of the cluster can be disrupted at once.
Netflix also accepts that hardware failures cannot be eliminated. Instead, its training platform makes them cheaper to recover from.
Large jobs use checkpointing and elastic workers, allowing training to resume from the last healthy checkpoint when a machine is lost. The platform can then automatically retry failures, while application failures are classified separately to avoid repeatedly restarting jobs with genuine software bugs.
Netflix also treats the training job itself as a distributed system. Rather than looking only for failed machines, it can identify a single slow rank that is holding the rest of the job back. This matters because a GPU does not have to fail to reduce the throughput of a synchronous workload.
Netflix is also using NVIDIA's Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) capabilities to allow smaller inference workloads to share GPUs while maintaining memory-level isolation between tenants.
This improves utilisation compared with dedicating an entire GPU to every workload. Netflix is also working towards Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), which should allow more expressive resource requests and topology-aware placement, including ensuring that GPUs, network adapters and CPUs are positioned appropriately within the machine.
Meta also uses extensive hardware diagnostics, automated remediation, checkpointing, and rapid recovery. Its recent work focuses heavily on detecting hardware faults, including difficult silent data corruption (SDCs), across extremely large AI clusters. Meta reports that hardware failures accounted for more than 66% of training interruptions in its Llama 3 experience.
Netflix's architecture places particularly strong emphasis on closing the operational loop: validate hardware before scheduling, monitor it during execution, identify the failure domain, remediate automatically, and measure the resulting goodput. Meta, meanwhile, has invested heavily in hardware-level fault detection and cluster maintenance as well as recovery.
Both approaches reflect the same underlying reality: at thousands of GPUs, reliability can no longer be treated as simply keeping individual machines available.

articles.title: Estos Galaxy Watch estarían a punto de quedarse sin nuevas funciones de Samsung
articles.text:
Samsung podría dejar sin actualizaciones a sus Galaxy Watch más antiguos. Una filtración asegura que la surcoreana está considerando no lanzar más actualizaciones de sistema para los relojes inteligentes más viejos, privándolos de nuevas funciones. El soporte para los Galaxy Watch antiguos estaría limitado a parches de seguridad, tal y como ocurre con los móviles.
La información proviene del conocido filtrador kro_roe, quien asegura que Samsung ya no lanzará nuevas versiones de Wear OS y One UI Watch para relojes antiguos. El reporte no menciona qué modelos entrarían en esta categoría ni cuáles serían los motivos de la decisión. Es probable que la medida afecte a los Galaxy Watch 4 y 5, que están a punto de alcanzar el número de actualizaciones prometido por el fabricante.
Que un dispositivo se quede sin soporte no es novedad. Samsung y otras compañías ofrecen algunos años de actualizaciones de sistema operativo y parches de seguridad. Una vez que se cumple el tiempo de vida útil, estos dispositivos ya no reciben nuevas funciones ni correcciones de errores. Aunque los relojes no dejarán de funcionar, los usuarios ya no podrán aprovechar las características más recientes del sistema operativo.
Los Galaxy Watch 4 y 5 se quedarían sin actualizaciones pronto
Los principales candidatos que encajan en este escenario son los Galaxy Watch 4 y Galaxy Watch 5, que ya llegaron al final del camino. El Watch 4 ya recibió las cuatro actualizaciones de sistema operativo conocido, por lo que cumple el compromiso de soporte de Samsung. En el caso del Galaxy Watch 5, el reloj está en la lista de dispositivos compatibles con One UI 9 Watch, que sería la última versión antes de ser discontinuado.
De confirmarse por el fabricante, estos relojes no quedarían abandonados de inmediato. Aquellos que tengan un Galaxy Watch 4 o Galaxy Watch 5 podrán utilizarlos sin problemas, ya que los dispositivos pasarán a la fase de mantenimiento. Las únicas descargas disponibles a partir de este punto serán las actualizaciones para corregir vulnerabilidades o mejorar la estabilidad del sistema.
La situación será distinta para generaciones más recientes como los Galaxy Watch 8 o el primer modelo Ultra, ya que estos todavía tienen garantizados más ciclos de soporte. En el caso de los recién lanzados Galaxy Watch 9 y Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, Samsung lanzó un programa más ambicioso que ofrece hasta cinco actualizaciones de sistema y cinco años de parches de seguridad.
Con el fin del soporte para los modelos viejos, los usuarios podrían buscar alternativas. La más evidente sería comprar un reloj más nuevo, pero si el tuyo funciona sin problemas y no tienes dinero, tal vez exista un truco para extender el soporte aún más. Muchos usuarios están usando la IA para eliminar funciones o devolver el soporte a dispositivos Samsung, sin depender de lo que tiene planeado la marca.

articles.title: Warren advierte que la salida a bolsa de Anthropic obligará a fondos de jubilación a comprar sus acciones
articles.text:
La senadora demócrata Elizabeth Warren advirtió en una carta a Anthropic que la salida a bolsa de la empresa obligará a los fondos indexados con ahorros de jubilación de los estadounidenses a comprar sus acciones, aunque el precio sea volátil o esté sobrevalorado. La carta se hizo pública el 28 de octubre.
Warren, la principal legisladora demócrata del Comité de Banca del Senado, dirigió el texto al director ejecutivo de Anthropic, Dario Amodei. Le pidió respuestas a diez preguntas antes del 3 de noviembre.
Según el comunicado de la senadora, los proveedores de índices bursátiles eliminaron este año los períodos de espera que retrasaban el ingreso de las empresas nuevas en los grandes índices. Por eso las acciones llegan más rápido a las cuentas de jubilación.
“Esto significa que los fondos indexados que invierten los ahorros de jubilación de los estadounidenses se verán obligados a comprar acciones de Anthropic aunque la acción sea volátil o esté sobrevalorada”, escribió Warren.
Dos riesgos: seguridad pública y estabilidad financiera
La carta cita pasajes del formulario S-1, el documento que Anthropic presentó ante la SEC, el regulador bursátil de Estados Unidos, el 26 de octubre. De sus más de 90 páginas de factores de riesgo, la senadora destacó que la empresa admite que sistemas de IA avanzados podrían representar “riesgos catastróficos o existenciales para la humanidad”.
Warren sostiene que una inyección masiva de capital público acelerará el desarrollo de esa tecnología en pleno debate sobre su seguridad. También afirma que, por su tamaño, las variaciones del precio de la acción podrían sacudir a los mercados desde el primer día.
La senadora cuestionó además que la empresa necesite “un flujo insaciable de capital” y planteó que eso no justifica exponer a los ahorristas comunes a sus riesgos. Según el diario The Wall Street Journal, que vio la carta, también pregunta por los vínculos con socios como Amazon y Broadcom y por cómo se justificaría una valuación cercana a los USD 2 billones.
Una pérdida de USD 80.748 millones, casi toda contable
El S-1 muestra ingresos de USD 16.286 millones en el primer semestre de 2026, frente a USD 1.163 millones en el mismo período de 2025. La pérdida neta fue de USD 80.748 millones, frente a USD 12.969 millones un año antes.
La revista Fortune precisó que USD 72.400 millones de esa pérdida responden a un cargo contable por el mayor valor de los bonos convertibles que la empresa emitió. La pérdida operativa fue de USD 693 millones, y la compañía informó que, con una medición ajustada, tuvo una ganancia operativa de USD 1.600 millones.
El formulario indica que Anthropic tenía USD 131.651 millones en efectivo e inversiones de corto plazo al 30 de junio. Planea cotizar en el mercado Nasdaq con el símbolo ANT.
Una valuación de hasta USD 2 billones, según la prensa
Medios como Fortune y CNBC informan que la empresa busca una valuación de entre USD 1,5 y 2 billones. Reuters, citado por TipRanks, indicó que los inversores habían hablado recientemente de unos USD 1,5 billones para una salida prevista a mediados de noviembre. La cifra superaría los USD 1,77 billones de SpaceX en su debut de junio.
Anthropic no respondió de inmediato a la consulta de Moneywise sobre la carta. La fecha límite que fijó Warren para recibir sus respuestas es el 3 de noviembre de 2026.

articles.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.
Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.
Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.
The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.
A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.
Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.
Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.
Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.
Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank.
It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.
These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

articles.title: India needs a digital goods marketplace and control of its distribution layer, say Indus Appstore and Eloelo
articles.text:
India needs a digital goods marketplace and control of its distribution layer, say Indus Appstore and Eloelo
Priya Narasimhan of Indus Appstore and Sagar Gaonkar of Eloelo Group argued that India’s next 500 million users will come through AI-ready, locally priced platforms, and that sovereignty must extend beyond chips and models to app distribution, billing and data.
India’s app-first economy still lacks a thriving marketplace for digital goods, and fixing that is as much a question of sovereignty as of technology, according to speakers at the 17th edition of YourStory’s TechSparks.
Speaking on a panel titled “India’s digital economy 2.0: Public tech, AI sovereignty, and the next 500 million”, Priya Narasimhan, Chief Business Officer at Indus Appstore, said the country’s mobile-first habits should have produced a large digital goods market, but have not. She blamed distribution monopolies held by Google and Apple and the economics of their 15% to 30% billing commissions, which make lower-priced digital products unviable. Web stores, the other route, suffer from user friction and low reach, she said.
Narasimhan argued that digital sovereignty is about how and where consumers meet technology. She named three layers India must control: discovery and distribution through app marketplaces, monetisation and billing, and a data trust and consent framework. She pointed to the Epic Games and Google dispute in the US as proof of what happens when developers depend on gatekeepers. She stressed, however, that sovereignty does not mean rebuilding every base layer. The aim, she said, is to plug into global technology on India’s terms.
Sagar Gaonkar, CTO of Eloelo Group, said India’s strengths lie in its data, its cultural variety and its creative and platform-building talent. Chips and large language models can be built upon, he said, with value added for India and then exported. He added that security cannot be an afterthought as more tools are hosted outside the country.
On AI, Gaonkar said it helps microdrama platforms decide what to greenlight before a frame is shot, and personalise what viewers see. He also pointed to stories that adapt to a viewer’s preferences. Narasimhan said app stores must become hybrid platforms: simple and familiar on the surface for most Indians, and addressable by AI agents at the back end, so that developers can scale whether users tap an icon or ask a chatbot.
Both speakers challenged the idea that Bharat is a low-spending audience. Narasimhan recalled that PhonePe’s gold category scaled only after it allowed purchases of Rs 10 a day. Gaonkar said Indian users are value-conscious rather than unwilling to pay, and need a softer landing to experience a product before paying. Narasimhan also urged founders to talk to users rather than rely only on analytics.
Responding to audience questions, Narasimhan said Indus aims to cut the commission burden on developers, and rejected the suggestion that Indians do not value digital goods, citing microdramas, OTT and gaming. She said platforms should not let discovery become purely pay-to-play. On fraudulent installs, she said vetting combines automated checks with human review and constant monitoring, but admitted that no system is foolproof.

articles.title: Opening a US Office From Australia: Phones, Power, Internet and Support in a New City - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Expanding Across the Pacific: Key Considerations
For Australian businesses eyeing expansion into the United States, establishing a physical office brings a multitude of logistical challenges and strategic opportunities. Successfully navigating this process requires a comprehensive understanding of the local environment, particularly when it comes to telecommunications, power infrastructure, internet connectivity, and technical support. Each of these elements plays a critical role in ensuring smooth daily operations and long-term growth in a new city.
This guide delves into the essential factors that Australian companies must consider when opening a US office, focusing on the practical aspects of phones, power, internet, and support services. By addressing these areas early in the planning process, businesses can avoid costly delays and position themselves for success in the competitive American market.
Navigating Communication: Phones in a New Market
One of the earliest hurdles in setting up a US office is establishing a reliable phone system tailored to local expectations. Unlike Australia, where telecom providers and numbering conventions are relatively consolidated, the US telecom landscape is vast and highly regionalized. Providers differ not only by state but often by city or neighborhood, making it essential to carefully select phone technologies and service plans that best fit the operational needs of the business.
Voice over IP (VoIP) has become the dominant choice for many companies due to its flexibility, cost-effectiveness, and integration capabilities. VoIP systems facilitate calls over the internet, often linking with customer relationship management (CRM) tools and enabling advanced call routing, analytics, and recording features. This integration enhances customer service and operational efficiency.
A crucial consideration is the use of local phone numbers. Research shows that 70% of customers are more likely to engage with a business that uses a local phone number, underscoring the importance of establishing a recognizable presence through localized communication. For example, a company opening an office in Philadelphia may want to leverage tech support in Philadelphia to ensure seamless integration and troubleshooting of their telephony systems. Having reliable, city-based tech support can quickly resolve any disruptions, minimizing downtime and maintaining customer trust.
Additionally, businesses should consider toll-free numbers for national reach, but these often lack the local familiarity that builds rapport. Combining local and toll-free numbers can provide a balanced communication strategy that supports both local clients and wider audiences.
Understanding Power Requirements and Standards
Power supply differences between Australia and the US are significant and must be carefully addressed to avoid equipment damage or operational interruptions. Australia operates on 230 volts at 50 Hz frequency, while the US standard is 120 volts at 60 Hz. This discrepancy means that most Australian office equipment, including computers, servers, and networking hardware, may require voltage converters or transformers to function correctly within a US office.
Beyond voltage differences, businesses must also plan for power reliability. The US electrical grid experiences regional variability; some cities are prone to frequent outages due to weather events, infrastructure age, or maintenance schedules. For example, cities in hurricane-prone areas or with older infrastructure may face more frequent disruptions.
To mitigate these risks, investing in uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and backup generators is critical for protecting sensitive electronics and maintaining business continuity. These systems bridge short-term outages and provide time to safely shut down equipment if necessary.
Compliance with local electrical codes and safety standards is another vital aspect. The US has strict regulations enforced by state and local authorities, and non-compliance can lead to costly fines or insurance issues. Partnering with licensed local contractors familiar with these codes ensures that office power installations meet all legal requirements and operate safely.
Securing High-Speed Internet Connectivity
Internet connectivity is the backbone of modern business operations, enabling communication, cloud computing, data transfers, and customer interactions. While the US has extensive broadband coverage, the quality, speed, and availability of internet service providers (ISPs) can differ widely depending on the city and even the specific neighborhood.
According to the Federal Communications Commission, approximately 94% of Americans have access to broadband internet, but actual speeds vary significantly, with rural and some urban areas experiencing slower connections. For a business, choosing an office location with robust internet infrastructure is paramount.
Fiber-optic connections are often the preferred choice due to their high bandwidth and low latency, supporting demanding applications such as video conferencing, large file transfers, and cloud-based services. Cable and DSL remain options in areas where fiber is unavailable, but they generally offer lower speeds and less reliability.
When expanding into a city like Cleveland, companies should consider Cleveland’s top IT support to access local expertise in IT infrastructure and internet management. Local IT professionals can assist in evaluating ISP options, negotiating service agreements, and optimizing network configurations to ensure maximum uptime and performance.
Additionally, businesses should plan for redundancy by having backup internet connections or failover systems to avoid costly downtime caused by ISP outages.
Leveraging Local IT Support for Smooth Operations
Opening an office in a new city means entering an unfamiliar technology landscape with different vendors, service standards, and regulatory requirements. Local IT support is invaluable for bridging these gaps and ensuring that technology infrastructure is set up, maintained, and secured effectively.
Engaging with established local IT providers accelerates the onboarding process and helps navigate city-specific issues such as network architecture, software licensing, and compliance with US data protection laws. Cybersecurity is a particularly critical area where local expertise is essential. The US enforces stringent regulations such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), depending on the industry. Local IT providers are well-versed in these requirements and can assist with security audits, risk assessments, and implementing robust security protocols.
Furthermore, local support teams can provide training for staff, ensuring that employees understand best practices and the proper use of new systems.
Addressing Additional Operational Considerations
Beyond the core infrastructure, several other factors influence the success of opening a US office from Australia. Office location within the city can impact accessibility, proximity to clients, and employee convenience. Choosing a location near transport hubs or business districts can enhance networking and operational efficiency.
Time zone differences between Australia and the US pose challenges for communication and scheduling. Australian companies may need to establish flexible working hours or hire dedicated local staff to maintain consistent customer service and internal collaboration.
Compliance with US employment laws, tax codes, and business regulations also requires attention. Working with legal and financial advisors familiar with cross-border operations can prevent regulatory pitfalls and optimize tax strategies.
Cultural differences in business practices and customer expectations should inform marketing, sales, and customer service approaches. Hiring local talent or consultants provides valuable insights into American consumer behavior and business etiquette, which can improve market penetration and brand reception.
Conclusion: Planning for Success Across Borders
Opening a US office from Australia is a complex but rewarding endeavor that demands careful preparation across multiple dimensions. Telecommunications, power infrastructure, internet connectivity, and local technical support form the foundation on which operational success is built.
By partnering with trusted local providers and understanding the nuances of regional infrastructure, Australian businesses can establish resilient offices that meet customer expectations and regulatory requirements. Strategic choices about phone systems, power compatibility, and internet services – coupled with access to expert local IT support – equip companies to overcome common challenges.
Selecting the right city and building relationships with local IT support services like and can provide a competitive advantage and operational stability. With thorough planning and investment, businesses can bridge the geographic divide seamlessly and thrive in the dynamic US market.

articles.title: SS7 and Diameter Attacks: How Signaling Flaws Expose Your Phone
articles.text:
SS7 and Diameter signaling attacks can track, intercept, and impersonate you. Here’s how they work and how to stop them.
Your phone can be tracked, your SMS two-factor codes can be intercepted, and your number can be impersonated, all without malware, a phishing link, or any access to your device.
The attacks happen inside the telecom network, in the carrier-to-carrier control protocols known as signaling, the automated descendants of the old telephone switchboard. Most users never see them, and most carriers can’t reliably stop them.
Signaling attacks aren’t new. Most recently, they made headlines when Iranian-linked actors reportedly exploited outdated network technology to locate the phones of US personnel in the Middle East during the Iran war.
But the vulnerability has been around for decades, and it’s been used for far more everyday crimes, like intercepting bank one-time passcodes. It has even been demonstrated by popular YouTubers: Veritasium hijacked a tech influencer’s calls and texts using only his phone number.
This keeps happening
- Criminals have reportedly exploited signaling protocols in attacks on bank accounts and global telecom infrastructure.
- Citizen Lab exposed two long-running commercial surveillance campaigns abusing SS7 and Diameter, with thousands of attacks against targets in dozens of countries.
- Congressman Ted Lieu’s phone was hacked on live TV via SS7 on 60 Minutes Australia
- Attackers have intercepted SMS one-time passcodes to drain victims’ bank accounts.
What is a signaling attack?
Every call, text, and mobile data session requires your carrier to verify you’re a paying customer and route your traffic to the right destination.
Carriers do this with signaling–background messages that identify your location and forward traffic accordingly. Signaling has been the connective tissue between global providers for decades, and it is one of the most overlooked attack surfaces in mobile security.
Two protocols do most of the work: SS7 (from the 1970s, used in 2G/3G) and Diameter (its successor, used in 4G and most 5G).
Both were designed when a small number of large operators could plug into the system, so they assume that traffic claiming to come from a legitimate operator really does. SS7 has essentially no process for authenticating the machine making a request.
Diameter supports stronger authentication on paper, but operators don’t always deploy basic protections like encryption, and many fall back on the same peer-to-peer trust model.
An attacker with access to the global signaling backbone, through a commercial leasing arrangement or a compromised operator, can send messages that carriers worldwide treat as trustworthy.
How does it work
Signaling lets an attacker ask your carrier questions and make claims on your behalf:
- Harvest your IMSI. Knowing your number, an attacker can request your International Mobile Subscriber ID (IMSI) under the pretense of routing a call or SMS. It can be reused for follow-on attacks for years.
- Locate you in real time. Queries can return the cell tower you last connected to. Others, normally reserved for emergency responders, can return the actual coordinates your phone reports.
- Intercept communications. The attacker claims you’ve roamed onto another network, so your calls and texts are redirected to them. Combined with a stolen username and password, this delivers your SMS second factor to the attacker instead of you.
- Impersonate or block you. With your IMSI, an attacker can place calls or send SMS as you. A false roaming claim can also cut off service to your phone.
- Disrupt networks. Deliberately misconfigured signaling messages can overwhelm provider systems.
None of this touches your device. It happens in automated transactions you can’t see and that leave no trace on your phone.
Why firewalls and velocity checks fall short
Carrier signaling firewalls reliably block messages sent to or from the wrong place. For correctly routed messages, they often run a velocity check to test whether you could physically have traveled from your last known location to the one now claimed. If you were in New York an hour ago and a Turkish carrier says you’re on its network, the request is denied.
The structural problem is that the firewall’s location data is often hours old. In research presented at the Wireless Security conference in 2025, Cape, the privacy-first mobile carrier, measured Diameter updates from a visited network arriving as infrequently as every two to ten hours.
For subscribers in the US and Germany, over 250 distinct networks are reachable within a single hour of travel time. An attacker with enough operator identities will eventually find one that looks plausible.
Citizen Lab’s report shows this in practice: the actor it calls STA1 repeatedly tried to track a user by rotating through eleven operator identities in nine countries to look like legitimate roaming traffic. They also pivoted between SS7 and Diameter, which most carriers defend with separate firewalls and little coordination.
Consider a target who boards a flight from Nashville to Berlin and powers off her phone. A message posing as China Mobile claiming she’s roaming there gets rejected, because it’s physically impossible.
A message from a carrier in nearby Nassau, Bahamas, looks plausible, and the home carrier can be fooled into routing her calls and SMS to the attacker.
Protect yourself with private cell service.
Cape is America's privacy-first mobile carrier providing unlimited talk, text, and 4G/5G data, built from the ground up with privacy and security at it's core.
Most carriers track everything: where you go, who you call, what you do. Cape collects the minimum amount of information required to provide you with service, deletes call and text metadata after 24 hours, rotates your network ID to prevent tracking, defends against SIM- and network-based attacks, and more.
Privacy shouldn't cost more. Switch today and get $29 off for life.
Learn More →
How Cape defends against signaling attacks
Cape is a privacy-first mobile carrier, whose approach is to assume the global telecom system is compromised and build protections that keep communications private anyway. There are four layers:
1. Daily IMSI rotation. Almost every targeted signaling attack starts with an IMSI, and once an attacker has yours, it stays useful for as long as you have it. A Citizen Lab report confirms this, with the same IMSIs being attacked across operations separated by months and years. On most carriers, your IMSI is permanent. You get one when you activate your SIM and you keep it forever. On Cape, your IMSI rotates daily. The databases of harvested IMSIs that surveillance vendors build up over the years are no longer useful against Cape subscribers.
2. No SS7. Cape doesn’t support SS7 at all, and there is no SS7 fallback in the network, so SS7-based attacks have nothing to land on. Many carriers still struggle to retire legacy SS7 infrastructure because some revenue-generating part of their network depends on it.
3. Network Lock. Instead of trusting a network’s idea of where you are, Cape asks your device. When a foreign network requests to attach to your phone, Network Lock queries the Cape app, which evaluates the claim locally at the country level and reports back whether it matches. If an attacker tries to attach your IMSI from another country while your phone is at home, the request is denied and you’re notified. Cape’s systems learn only whether the claim matches, not where you actually are, and Cape never collects or stores your precise location.
4. Continuous penetration testing. Most signaling firewalls are compliance tools tuned to GSMA baseline recommendations. Those recommendations are distributed to more than 1,200 member providers, so the same guidance is available to attackers who can send signaling messages. Cape has third-party firms that specialize in current signaling exploitation techniques to test its infrastructure, then hardens the network against what they find, especially anything affecting subscriber privacy.
| Attack | Other Carriers | Cape | 
| Real-time location tracking | Phone attaches whenever it gets service; velocity checks can be beaten by plausible spoofing | Network Lock verifies attach requests against your device | 
| IMSI harvesting and reuse | IMSI is permanent and stays useful indefinitely | Daily rotation makes previously harvested IMSIs useless | 
| SS7-based attacks | Attackers use several methods to evade SS7 firewalls | No SS7 support | 
| Diameter-based attacks | Firewalls rely on widely published GSMA baselines | Firewalls updated from penetration tests using current techniques | 
You can’t patch the telecom backbone, but you can choose your carrier
Following every best practice, such as using encrypted messaging, avoiding public Wi-Fi, and enabling 2FA, still leaves your device dependent on networks never built with security in mind.
For people who are targeted, such as journalists, executives, security staff, and anyone whose accounts rely on SMS verification, the carrier is part of the threat model.

articles.title: Si vous avez installé Popcorn Time il y a 10 ans, votre PC ou votre Mac a été sauvé par une équipe de chercheurs
articles.text:
Ancienne version de Popcorn Time : jusqu’à 3 millions de PC Windows et 350 000 Mac exposés par une faille majeure
Oubliée depuis des années sur des millions d’ordinateurs, une ancienne version de Popcorn Time expose Windows et macOS à une prise de contrôle totale.
Si vous avez installé Popcorn Time sur votre ordinateur il y a plusieurs années, il serait temps de vous pencher sur une désinstallation. Selon un rapport de la société de cybersécurité Eye Research, une variante non officielle très répandue, baptisée Time4Popcorn mais distribuée sous le nom original du célèbre logiciel de streaming illégal, a laissé derrière elle un redoutable piège. Même sans ouvrir l’application, un utilitaire invisible continuait de s’exécuter automatiquement à chaque démarrage sur des millions de machines pour vérifier la présence d’éventuelles mises à jour.
Un programme de mise à jour oublié qui ouvre la porte aux pirates sur Windows et macOS
Découvert lors d’une inspection de routine, un programme de mise à jour, nommé Updater.exe sous Windows et PT.updd sous macOS, a fait tiquer Eye Research, cherchant en permanence à contacter des noms de domaine abandonnés par les créateurs de Time4Popcorn. Pire encore, ces requêtes transitaient en HTTP non chiffré et l’utilitaire exécutait n’importe quel fichier reçu avec les privilèges administrateur maximaux, sans vérifier la moindre signature numérique.
En rachetant l’un de ces domaines expirés, popcorntimeupd.xyz, les chercheurs ont d’ailleurs constaté que 50 ordinateurs par seconde tentaient encore de s’y connecter automatiquement pour réclamer une mise à jour. Après analyse des identifiants matériels, Eye Research estime qu’entre 2,5 et 3 millions de PC Windows, ainsi que 250 000 à 350 000 Mac, étaient exposés dans le monde, y compris au sein d’entreprises privées mais aussi d’institutions gouvernementales et militaires.
Face au risque qu’un cybercriminel acquière l’une de ces adresses pour déployer un rançongiciel ou constituer un botnet géant, l’équipe a mené l’opération IXIM entre novembre 2025 et mars 2026. Faute d’éditeur officiel pour corriger cette faille référencée CVE-2026-30612, Eye Research a utilisé le mécanisme vulnérable lui-même afin d’envoyer une commande désactivant définitivement le service de mise à jour chez les utilisateurs concernés.
Plus de deux millions de correctifs ont ainsi été déployés à distance, faisant chuter le trafic de 98 % avant que les quinze domaines rachetés par les chercheurs ne soient confiés à l’organisation à but non lucratif Shadowserver Foundation. Cette dernière se charge donc désormais de neutraliser durablement ces adresses afin d’empêcher leur reprise par des pirates.
Si aucune exploitation malveillante antérieure n’a été détectée, le danger n’est pas totalement écarté. D’autres domaines liés à Time4Popcorn appartiennent toujours à des tiers et l’application principale, bâtie sur un moteur Chrome de 2014 non sécurisé, reste vulnérable. Les experts recommandent donc de désinstaller complètement le logiciel pour écarter tout risque.

articles.title: Motorola Signature 27 : la date de sortie se précise, mais attention au prix
articles.text:
Dévoilé en septembre dernier lors du Snapdragon Summit de Qualcomm (sans tarif ni date de sortie), le nouveau smartphone haut de gamme de Motorola, le Signature 27, va livrer ses derniers secrets le 5 novembre prochain, notamment autour de son prix, qui s’annonce encore plus salé que le Signature sorti en début d’année.
Un prix en fuite pour le Signature 27
Motorola donnera les dernières informations autour de son Signature 27 la semaine prochaine, mais le site MegaPC a déjà référencé le smartphone à 1 594,90 euros pour sa version équipée de 12 Go de RAM et de 512 Go de stockage. À titre de comparaison, le Motorola Signature a été lancé à 1299 € (ce qui était plus élevé que les 999 € annoncés lors de sa présentation au CES 2026).
 Now that’s a nice touch.
motorola signature 27: elegantly crafted for comfort.
See for yourself on November 5.
#MotorolaSignature #SignatureStatement https://t.co/hG9ZjNY08h
— motorola (@Moto) October 29, 2026
Ce prix est évidemment à prendre avec des pincettes dans la mesure où une boutique en ligne peut tout à fait publier un prix provisoire en attendant le tarif officiel du constructeur pour la commercialisation. La page en question présentait le coloris Pantone Coal Smoke et signalait le produit comme étant en rupture de stock, sans indiquer de date particulière.
Un smartphone clairement haut de gamme
Du côté des informations officielles dont nous disposons, le téléphone embarque le processeur Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, une puce gravée en 2 nanomètres qui intègre un nouveau système de refroidissement « ArcticMesh » qui combine un gel thermique et une chambre à vapeur plus grande. Cela pourrait résoudre les problèmes de chauffe que nous avions pointés sur le Motorola Signature. Pour la partie photo, le Signature 27 mise sur un capteur principal Sony Lytia 910 de 50 mégapixels et un téléobjectif périscopique avec un capteur de 200 mégapixels qui offre un zoom optique 5x.
Pour ce qui est du suivi logiciel, la marque promet sept mises à jour majeures d’Android et de sécurité. Enfin, le volet audio bénéficie pour la première fois de réglages signés Bang & Olufsen. Un partenariat qui vient remplacer le précédent partenariat avec Bose.

articles.title: 17 horas de maratón, concursos y merchandising: la espectacularización de las salas sigue queriendo camelarse a la Generación Z
articles.text:
Nueve días después de que la Fiesta del Cine rebajara momentáneamente la entrada de las salas a 3,50 euros, Cinesa encierra este sábado a cientos de personas en seis salas de toda España durante 17 horas. Algunas han pagado 60 euros por la experiencia VIP del evento. El reclamo es que no se repetirá nunca, aunque habrá otras similares en el futuro "para generar FOMO", como nos contaron en la presentación de esta serie de experiencias con las que Cinesa quiere atraer a la Generación Z de espectadores.
Avalancha de drops. Cinesa Room se organiza en drops: eventos con fecha, aforo y reglas propias que no se repiten. El primero arranca este sábado 31 de octubre a las 10:00 y termina a las 3:00 del domingo: 17 horas de cine de terror simultáneas en seis complejos. El núcleo de las actividades será en Príncipe Pío de Madrid: quien aguante la maratón y acierte las pruebas de Kahoot proyectadas en pantalla se lleva diez años de cine gratis. Entre película y película pasarán por allí Paco Plaza y las voces del podcast Terrores Nocturnos, y el resto de ciudades recibirá esos contenidos retransmitidos desde la capital.
Los precios. Las entradas cuestan, según el grado de privilegios que dan, 29 euros (Survivor), 40 (Hero) y 60 (Final Girl). De estas últimas hay solo 50 entradas disponibles en toda España, con una prenda diseñada por Tito Customs de regalo. Felicia Byrge, directora de marketing de Cinesa, aseguró en la presentación a prensa que Príncipe Pío se vendió entero en pocos días y que Barcelona tuvo que abrir una segunda sala.
En busca del FOMO. Cinesa es un conglomerado especialmente activo en la búsqueda de actividades que vayan más allá de la experiencia tradicional en las salas de cine: en 2017, cuando aún no era habitual en el sector, empezó a ofrecer merchandising y más variedad de comida, junto con los primeros eventos para empresas; en 2018 apareció el primer cine LUXE, con butacas reclinables y otras comodidades; en 2023, la tarifa plana Unlimited. Además, en 2020 Cinesa abrió a particulares el alquiler de salas para celebraciones, y en 2022 lo amplió a partidas de videoconsola en pantalla grande.
El coste de la mejora. Tomás Junquera, director de Relaciones Institucionales de Cinesa, dijo en su día que "hemos perdido un 50% de plazas en cines normales para poner asientos reclinables" en las salas LUXE. Es decir, se tiende a favorecer la mejora de la calidad de la experiencia para que esta sea más memorable y única, y los espectadores inviertan tanto en la propia sala como en el atractivo de la película. Con Cinesa Room, esa filosofía se lleva al extremo, con un modelo, el drop, que hereda su nombre de la música y la moda. Las salas ya habían probado ese ansia consumista que genera la escasez con fenómenos como los palomiteros coleccionables, pero ahora lo limitado es la propia entrada.
La espectacularización de las salas. Cinesa forma parte de Odeon Cinemas Group, la filial europea que AMC compró en 2016. Ya en 2023, AMC se convirtió en distribuidora exclusiva de la película-concierto de Taylor Swift 'The Eras Tour', una operación que la compañía describió en su momento como el primer paso de una nueva línea de negocio. Y llevamos un tiempo viendo cómo el cine podría seguir el camino de la música, que se refugió en el evento irrepetible de los conciertos cuando el formato físico dejó de sostener el negocio.
Otras maratones. La maratón, como formato, tampoco es nueva ni siquiera para Cinesa: en Halloween de 2020 encadenó siete horas de terror en cuatro cines de Madrid por 13 euros. Este sábado, Cines Palafox celebra en Zaragoza su segunda Maratón Halloween: cinco películas desde las 23:59. Lo que Cinesa suma con Room es el envoltorio: los curadores de prestigio, el concurso con Kahoot, el merchandising de edición limitada y la garantía de que no habrá segundas oportunidades para la experiencia.
Nuevas generaciones. Según cuenta Byrge, los jóvenes dedican el 60% de su gasto en ocio a planes no digitales y el 64% considera clave el encuentro presencial para crear comunidad, aunque, ante la pregunta de un periodista, reconoció que parte de la muestra llegaba hasta los 34 años. Fuera de España hay cifras que respaldan esa intuición: el informe de diciembre de 2025 de Cinema United, la mayor asociación de exhibidores del mundo, afirma que la generación Z estadounidense pasó de 4,9 a 6,1 visitas anuales al cine, un 25% más. Es la generación, claro, que convirtió en gamberro despliegue de interactividad mostrenca los pases de 'Una película de Minecraft'.
La espectacularización de la sala. Es un fenómeno que venía de antes: IMAX cerró 2025 con 1.280 millones de dólares de taquilla mundial, un 40% más que el año anterior y récord de la compañía. Ellos mismos definen el formato como "una plataforma para el entretenimiento y los eventos". Casos de éxito hay montones, pero 'La Odisea' de Christopher Nolan, por ejemplo, abrió la venta de las sesiones en IMAX 70 mm un año antes del estreno, y las entradas se agotaron en un día, con reventa llegando a 200 libras en Londres. Más pantalla, más alicientes, más espíritu de conciertos para resucitar la cada vez más alicaida taquilla internacional.

articles.title: Hubble a une chance sur deux de s'écraser d'ici 2033, alors la Nasa cherche un plan de sauvetage
articles.text:
Hubble travaille toujours, mais il y a un problème : le télescope descend. S’il n’est pas menacé à très court terme, l’observatoire spatial voit en revanche son horizon s’assombrir dans les années à venir. Une analyse datée de juillet 2026 évalue même le risque d’une chute vers la Terre à une chance sur dix en septembre 2032 et une sur deux avant décembre 2033.
Perdre Hubble ne serait pas seulement la mort d’un symbole de l’aventure spatiale, ce serait aussi une terrible perte pour la communauté scientifique. L’engin reçoit en effet sept fois plus de demandes d’observation qu’il ne peut en traiter, malgré son ancienneté notable. Le télescope a été lancé en 1990, soit plus de 35 ans.
C’est dans ce contexte que la question d’une mission d’assistance s’est de nouveau posée dernièrement. Le centre Goddard de la Nasa, qui s’occupe de l’observatoire, a publié une demande d’informations, c’est-à-dire un appel à idées, sans engagement. Objectif : recenser les industriels pouvant proposer une solution pour remonter Hubble en orbite.
Cette sollicitation a été repérée le 29 octobre par Irene Klotz, rédactrice au sein de la revue Aviation Week.
Pousser, réparer ou faire tomber proprement Hubble
Dans le document de la Nasa, trois pistes sont proposées : la première est la capture de Hubble pour le hisser au-delà de 600 kilomètres d’altitude ; la seconde est une mission d’entretien pour prolonger sa vie ; la troisième se présente sous la forme d’une rentrée atmosphérique contrôlée. Et, donc, de la fin du satellite.
Quel que soit le chemin retenu, le lancement doit avoir lieu d’ici 2032. Pour les deux premiers scénarios, il s’agira de ne pas abîmer le télescope, pour qu’il puisse encore opérer le temps imparti. Goddard fournira les données techniques. Le lanceur, le vaisseau et l’éventuel équipage restent à la charge de l’industriel.
Ce n’est évidemment pas si simple. On l’a vu avec la tentative de la mission LINK qui devait venir en aide au télescope Swift, qui lui aussi connaît une lente mais inexorable chute vers la Terre. Un petit robot aurait dû rejoindre Swift, s’agripper à lui et le remonter. Hélas, les choses ne se sont pas bien passées et Swift est désormais perdu.
L’idée d’une mission de sauvetage ne date pas d’hier.
En 2022, la Nasa et SpaceX avaient étudié une mission Crew Dragon. En juin 2024, l’agence l’a refusée, jugeant le risque trop élevé pour le télescope. Le 1er juin 2026, devant un comité consultatif, Shawn Domagal-Goldman, directeur de la division astrophysique de la Nasa, s’est dit ouvert à un rehaussement de l’orbite, à condition que les coûts de fonctionnement de Hubble baissent.
Cette demande d’informations ne vaut pas commande, mais cela donnera à la Nasa du grain à moudre pour la suite. La Nasa prévoit de lancer un appel d’offres formel une fois les réponses des industriels analysées. Il ne faudra cependant pas trop tarder, car la mise en route industrielle d’une telle mission prendra des mois.

articles.title: Google devra répondre en justice aux accusations d’IA vocale d’un ex‑présentateur de NPR
articles.text:
L’ancien animateur de NPR David Greene accuse Google d’avoir copié sa voix pour l’un des deux hôtes virtuels de NotebookLM. La justice californienne a rejeté chacune des objections de l’entreprise, et le procès peut donc avancer, sans que le tribunal ait encore dit si la voix vient bien de lui.
AI killed the radio star. NPR, pour National Public Radio, est la radio publique américaine. Ses journaux et magazines sont diffusés par plus d’un millier de stations locales à travers les États-Unis, dont Morning Edition, sa matinale d’information. David Greene a présenté cette émission pendant près de dix ans, puis le podcast quotidien Up First, après quatre années passées à suivre la Maison-Blanche pour la radio publique. Il anime aujourd’hui Left, Right & Center et d’autres podcasts. En janvier, il a porté plainte contre Google en Californie, convaincu que l’hôte masculin des résumés audio de NotebookLM parle avec une voix fabriquée à partir de ses enregistrements.
Les quatre griefs de David Greene maintenus par la justice
Après le dépôt de la plainte, le 23 janvier, devant la cour supérieure du comté de Santa Clara, Google a obtenu son transfert vers un tribunal fédéral. Un magistrat du district nord de la Californie a renvoyé l’affaire devant la justice de l’État le 23 juillet. David Greene invoque quatre fondements, dont le droit d’exploiter son nom, son image et sa voix prévu par l’article 3344 du Code civil californien, la concurrence déloyale et l’enrichissement sans cause. Il réclame des dommages et intérêts, la restitution des bénéfices tirés de sa voix et l’arrêt de son utilisation.
Google a tenté de faire écarter ces griefs avant tout examen sur le fond. Dans une ordonnance du 23 octobre, Shella Deen, magistrate de la cour supérieure du comté de Santa Clara, a rejeté sa demande sur chacun d’eux. D’après Google, le public connaissait le travail du journaliste, et non sa voix. La magistrate a écarté cet argument dans le cas d’un homme de radio. « Un animateur radio touche son public par sa voix », écrit-elle, avant de conclure qu’il est raisonnable de supposer cette voix largement connue.
Shella Deen a aussi refusé d’appliquer la loi fédérale sur le droit d’auteur, que Google opposait à la plainte. Une voix ne peut pas être protégée par le droit d’auteur, rappelle-t-elle, et David Greene conteste ce que produit NotebookLM, non les données utilisées pour entraîner l’outil. À ce stade de la procédure, le tribunal tient pour vrais les faits avancés par le plaignant, sans se prononcer sur leur véracité.
Pour Google, la voix de NotebookLM appartient à un comédien rémunéré
Depuis septembre 2024, les utilisateurs de NotebookLM peuvent transformer leurs documents en conversation façon podcast entre deux voix de synthèse, l’une masculine, l’autre féminine. Selon la plainte, Google commercialise l’outil par des abonnements, dont la formule Google One AI Premium à 19,99 dollars par mois, et s’est servi de cette voix masculine lors d’un partenariat avec Spotify en décembre 2024. Tout a commencé par l'e-mail d’un ancien collègue de David Greene, qui lui demandait s’il avait prêté sa voix à Google. Des auditeurs lui ont ensuite écrit que l’hôte virtuel avait exactement sa voix, et un cabinet d’expertise en reconnaissance vocale a trouvé un taux de correspondance compris entre 53 et 60 %.
Pour Google, ces accusations sont sans fondement. En février, son porte-parole José Castañeda a expliqué au Washington Post que l’entreprise avait engagé et rémunéré un comédien professionnel pour enregistrer la voix masculine de NotebookLM. Shella Deen voit dans l’origine de la voix une question de fait, à examiner lors du procès. Google a-t-il fabriqué son hôte virtuel à partir des enregistrements du journaliste, ou à partir d’une autre personne dont la voix ressemble à la sienne ? La magistrate reconnaît aussi appliquer à l’IA générative une loi californienne écrite bien avant son apparition.
Aux États-Unis, aucune loi fédérale ne protège encore la voix d’une personne contre sa copie numérique. Au Congrès, la proposition de loi NO FAKES Act, qui créerait un droit fédéral sur les copies numériques d’une voix, est bloquée depuis octobre, et aucun vote n’est attendu avant la reprise de la session, après les élections de mi-mandat. En France, les comédiens de doublage passent directement par les tribunaux pour défendre leur voix. On vous avait d’ailleurs déjà parlé de Richard Darbois et d’autres doubleurs français, qui ont assigné en justice deux plateformes de clonage vocal.

articles.title: Hinter Pluto entdeckt: Algorithmus findet neuen Zwergplaneten
articles.text:
Hinter Pluto entdeckt: Algorithmus findet neuen Zwergplaneten
Im Juni 2025 lieferte das Vera-C.-Rubin-Observatorium in Chile erste Aufnahmen des Weltalls. In den kommenden zehn Jahren soll das riesige Spiegelteleskop den südlichen Himmel systematisch erfassen und dabei erdnahe Asteroiden, Zwergplaneten oder andere Himmelsobjekte sowie -ereignisse wie Supernovae kartieren. Außerdem erhoffen sich die Astronom:innen Hinweise auf Dunkle Energie und Dunkle Materie.
2026 ED138 kreist jenseits von Pluto
Jetzt haben der Astrophysiker Matthew Holman vom Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics und der Astronom Mario Jurić von der University of Washington einen vielversprechenden Zwergplaneten-Kandidaten aufgespürt. Der jenseits von Pluto kreisende eisige Himmelskörper firmiert derzeit unter dem Namen 2026 ED138.
Wie es in einer entsprechenden Mitteilung heißt, handelt es sich bei 2026 ED138 um einen der größten Zwergplaneten-Kandidaten im transneptunischen Bereich. Er soll einen Durchmesser von 600 bis 1.500 Kilometern haben. Zur Einordnung: Pluto ist knapp 2.400 Kilometer groß. Sollte 2026 ED138 als Zwergplanet bestätigt werden, wäre er neben Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea und Makemake erst der sechste seiner Art.
Dabei war es gar nicht so einfach, den möglichen Zwergplaneten ausfindig zu machen. Holman ließ dabei einen eigens entwickelten Algorithmus über Aufnahmen des Rubin-Observatoriums schauen. Der Algorithmus sichtet dabei unterschiedliche Aufnahmen von Milliarden von Objekten, vergleicht diese und ihre möglichen Bewegungen und identifiziert dann jene, die sich tatsächlich bewegt haben.
Zwergplaneten-Kandidat schon 2016 zu sehen
Mit dieser Methode stieß Holman schließlich auf 2026 ED138, da das Objekt trotz seiner großen Entfernung eine große Helligkeit aufwies. Daher war klar, dass es sich um einen ungewöhnlich großen Himmelskörper handeln musste. Um einen Fehler auszuschließen, überprüfte Holmans Kollege Jurić weitere Aufnahmen. Dabei entdeckte er den Zwergplaneten-Kandidaten in weiteren Daten, darunter Aufnahmen aus dem Jahr 2016.
Aktuell befindet sich 2026 ED138 rund 46 astronomische Einheiten von der Sonne entfernt. Zum Vergleich: Pluto kreist im Abstand von 40 astronomischen Einheiten um die Sonne. Ein Objekt von der Größe des möglichen neuen Zwergplaneten zu finden, sei etwas, das „wahrscheinlich nur einmal in einer Generation“ vorkommt, so Jurić.

articles.title: Aboyeji-backed AI engineering talent platform Talent Nation raises pre-seed funding - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian AI engineering talent platform Talent Nation, co-founded by serial entrepreneur Iyinoluwa Aboyeji, has raised an undisclosed pre-seed funding round as it looks to train and deploy one million African AI engineers over the next decade.
Co-founded by Aboyeji, who was behind Andela, Flutterwave and Moove, and South Africa-born lawyer Kesiah Valkin, who previously co-founded London-based 01 Founders, Talent Nation trains, certifies and deploys AI engineers into organisations looking to build their own AI capability.
The startup is betting that AI will increase demand for engineering talent rather than reduce it. As AI models generate more code, it argues, businesses need more engineers who can review, test and integrate that code into reliable systems.
“Talent is the final constraint to super intelligence. Engineers who can implement AI solutions are some of the most expensive talent to recruit anywhere. Talent Nation puts certified AI engineering talent within the reach of any organisation for a fraction of the cost of frontier labs and traditional consulting firms,” said Aboyeji, who serves as executive chairman.
The undisclosed round of funding was co-led by Enza Capital and UK-based LocalGlobe, with participation from Future Africa, Kaleo Ventures, Ajim Capital, Solving.org and Accelerate Africa.
Talent Nation’s academy, Learn2Earn, has received more than 63,000 applications in 18 months, assessed over 32,000 people, and now has around 1,400 fellows training across nine campuses in six cities. Fewer than three per cent of applicants are admitted.
Applicants first complete an online test on their phones, before progressing to weekly in-person trials at the company’s centres across Nigeria. Experienced engineers who meet the startup’s standards move straight to deployment, while others go through three-, six- or 12-month training programmes that include internships and practical work experience. Training is peer-led and project-based, with intensive build-athons held across its campuses.
Training carries no upfront fees. Revenue from enterprise clients is reinvested into developing more engineers, who in turn contribute towards future cohorts once employed. Its engineers are already working with clients including IHS Towers, and organisations can engage them on defined projects, as direct hires, or in embedded teams.
“The benefits of AI should extend far beyond the companies with the resources to develop and deploy it today. But technological breakthroughs alone will not deliver widespread adoption. That requires a fundamental shift in the cost and availability of AI engineering talent,” said Valkin, who is CEO.
Sir John Lazar, general partner at Enza Capital and president of the Royal Academy of Engineering, said engineering talent was a crucial bedrock of innovation.
“Enza is proud to co-lead this investment into Talent Nation because we believe the company’s remarkable founders can identify this talent, build pathways for African engineers into valuable work, not just in Lagos but in London, and hold their engineers to a global standard of excellence,” he said.

articles.title: Credit Direct wants to bring loans closer to Nigerians
articles.text:
Credit Direct, the consumer lending subsidiary of FCMB Group, a Nigerian financial services group, is expanding beyond traditional lending into embedded finance as it seeks to make credit and other financial services more accessible to individuals and businesses.
Victoria Arinze, product marketing lead at Credit Direct, said at Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos that Credit Direct wants to use partnerships with businesses and merchants to bring credit closer to these transactions.
Embedded finance involves integrating financial services into platforms where customers already make payments or conduct other transactions, allowing them to access services such as loans without having to approach a financial institution separately.
The continent’s 50 million small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face a funding gap estimated at more than $330 billion. Credit Direct aims to close this by extending its lending expertise and integrating financing into the platforms that businesses and people use.
“We are primarily a credit organisation, and that has not changed and will never change. Credit is still the core of what we do,” Arinze said “What we’ve realised, however, is that credit really is not the end of how a person’s finances is built. When you give them credit, they then need to live their life, and living their life means being able to pay for things when they want to or when they have to.”
Founded in 2007, Credit Direct has spent nearly two decades lending to Nigerians, including customers in markets traditional lenders have often been reluctant to serve. Its 2025 Nigeria Credit Landscape Report, which draws on data from more than 300,000 borrowers, found that the average loan amount on its platform increased by 23.5% to ₦449,178 ($326.75) in 2025, with rent, medical bills, and school fees being the three leading reasons customers borrowed.
Credit Direct is also expanding into SME financing through CreditDirect Business, one of its newer products. The product offers general-purpose loans, invoice-backed financing, and loan purchase order (LPO) contract financing, with loans of up to ₦50 million ($37,130) available to eligible businesses. Loan amounts depend on factors including cash flow, existing obligations, and the nature of the business. Arinze said it is still relatively new and that the company is using customer feedback and engagement to determine how its products should evolve.
“We’re not really looking to outbank the banks or out-fintech the fintechs. It’s really the people at the end of the day, and getting to that strength to partner with the persons that we have to when we need to,” she said.
Arinze said the company is now exploring expansion into other West African markets, with discussions currently ongoing. It did not disclose specific countries or timelines.
