articles.title: InfoQ AI, ML and Data Engineering Trends Report - 2026
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Language models have shifted from large-sized models to the small language models. We are also seeing the rise of reasoning models that can think through math and logic problems before responding.
- AI Agents are moving from personal agents to the agents working with teams to companies using agents across entire organizations.
- System One models like TypeSafe AI’s Jev will see more adoption because of their deterministic and faster inference, in addition to their lower costs compared to the LLMs.
- AI Inference continues to be a useful and powerful trend and more and more companies will start doing this moving forward.
- AI evaluations have been getting a lot of attention this year. Evaluations are a way to help us to make sure that the agents do the right thing for the right tasks.
- Physical AI has seen significant developments in 2026. We are starting to connect the software intelligence to machines that can perceive and act in the physical world.
The InfoQ AI ML Annual Trends Reports offer InfoQ readers a comprehensive overview of emerging trends and technologies in the areas of AI, ML, and Data Engineering. This report summarizes the InfoQ editorial team’s podcast with external guests to discuss the trends in AI and ML technologies for the year 2026 and what to look out for in the next twelve months. In conjunction with the report and trends graph, our accompanying podcast features insightful discussions of all of these trends.
AI and ML Trends Adoption Graph
An important part of the annual trends report is the trends graph, which shows the trends, technologies and topics that have made it to the innovators category and which have been promoted to the early adopters and early majority categories. The categories are based on the book, Crossing the Chasm, by Geoffrey Moore. At InfoQ, we mostly focus on categories that have not yet crossed the chasm. Here is this year’s graph:
It has been almost four years since ChatGPT came out back in November 2022. It has also been two or three years since RAG Technologies started seeing enterprise adoption and autonomous LLM agents came out. The explosive growth of the last few years has continued in 2026 and AI technologies have seen significant innovations and developments since the InfoQ team discussed the trends report last year (see 2025 trends graph below).
For the details of 2025 AI ML technology trends, also check out last year’s trends report article.
This year’s trends article builds on what we discussed last year. It highlights the trends graph, which shows different phases of technology adoption and provides more details on individual technologies added or updated since last year’s trends report. We also discuss which technologies and trends have been promoted in the adoption graph. For this year’s updated adoption graph, the team has also added a few additional topics that we didn’t discuss in the podcast.
As you will notice, we have also done some major reorganizing of the topics where there is an overlap of the scope, and removed a few technologies that no longer need to be tracked on the adoption graph because of their mainstream adoption.
Here are some highlights of what has changed since last year’s report:
Innovators
The first category on our adoption graph, Innovators, has a few interesting new topics added this year. These topics are discussed in detail below.
Agent-to-Agent Protocols
As agentic AI systems become complex involving multiple different agents and domains, the communication between the individual agents as well as between multi-agent systems is crucial for these systems to be consistently safe, accurate, and reliable.
One of our panelists in the trends report podcast, Daniel Dominguez, spoke about agent communication protocols and the significance they have in the overall agentic AI solutions.
Daniel Dominguez: There is an architectural shift happening underneath all of this. For agents to become useful inside enterprises, they need to access tools, data, APIs, and talk to other agents. All the protocols like MCP or A2A are going to become more and more different. I think the question would be whether agent protocols become a new enterprise integration layer.
For example, today we connect applications to APIs. Tomorrow we may increase and have agent discovery capabilities that we see in task coordinating work on top of those APIs. I think all of these architectural layers are also changing the way that agents interact with each other.
Inference Engines (vLLM, SGLang, llm-d)
Another area that saw a significant development and transformation is the AI Inference. 2026 has been called the year of inference. The companies are shifting from training models to running AI inference in production. Inference is expected to account for around two-thirds of AI compute spending by the end of this year. Reasoning models, long context, and agents have turned it from a model-execution problem into a systems problem spanning compute, memory, networking, routing, and economics.
Hien Luu discussed this trend in detail in what he is seeing in terms of inference frameworks.
Hien Luu: The inference topic has exploded since the beginning of 2026. Obviously from one end, you have all these inference stacks from vLLM, SGLang, and so on that are helping the rest of us to spin up our own inference service in our own environment. At the same time, these open-weight models are becoming more and more capable. That space is initially not a whole lot of people how it works and how to operate it, but now there's a lot more information and resources out there about how to actually use these software, [and] how to optimize them. At the same time, some of the use cases we talk about are the financial companies where you have PIIs.
The ability to host these open-weight models internally for those kinds of specific use cases are very, very relevant. I believe that that's going to continue to grow, continue to be the case where a company will do more of this moving forward now that it's a lot more approachable, easier to do. There are some companies that because they want to save cost, they actually want to host internal open-weights models for coding, for example. For many reasons that inference is going to continue to be a very, very useful, very powerful topic and more and more companies will start doing this moving forward in my mind.
Harness Engineering
A relatively new area that has been seeing a lot of attention starting this year is Harness Engineering. Hien talked about the importance of this topic and how it supports the engineering capabilities like memory management and co-execution.
Hien Luu: I want to add [two things] to discussions of agents. One is harness engineering. I think that extensions of context engineering. But the thing that I see is quite interesting and relevant to a workshop that I'm going to be giving is that these agent SDKs start out with just helping us to write the loop. Now this SDK has been expanded to provide harness engineering capabilities, including memory management for context, including co-execution, including some of the out-of-the-box tools for doing into actual local file systems.
That’s another trend you can see that these agent SDK from LangChain or Anthropic or OpenAI; they all move in that direction of adding more capabilities as part of the harness engineering. As anyone building agents moving forward, that's something to look out [for] and leverage. There’s a whole other trend of managing these agents. These companies are providing a runtime environment for you to host your agent. Whether you want to do it or not, that's a separate question, but that's what they're seeing. "We are able to build, we are able to build it well, and then how do we operate and run it at scale?"
Spec-Driven Development and AI Software Factories
With AI technologies contributing to most of the coding in the software development process, we are seeing the developers starting to focus more on the requirements and specifications to take full advantage of automating the design and coding tasks in their applications.
This technology shift has given rise to trends like Spec-Driven Development and AI Software Factories. Some organizations are creating dedicated teams to create the software factory model where the development teams can use AI tools to automate the complete software development process. This model includes the specific SDLC steps like automatically compiling and analyzing the business domain and requirements of an existing software application, reviewing the new business requirements or systems enhancements, writing functional and non-functional (technical) specifications for those new requirements, generating the design and development tasks to implement the new requirements, and, finally, auto-generating the code and other artifacts of the updated software application.
Panelist Hien Luu shared his insights about Spec-Driven Development.
Hien Luu: This probably started maybe four or five years ago. The coding agent now is pretty powerful. But as you build a project, typically you want to have a plan in advance in terms of what you want, the capabilities and whatnot, and not jump to the coding agent immediately to build. It is borrowing what we know as a good practice to do, but now codified it in a form for the coding agent that you work with. If you build a brand new greenfield project, for example, you build a spec up, what is it about? What are the capabilities that you want?
Then you have a brainstorming session with your coding agent to provide a context that it needs before you actually go and build it. I think there's a lot of good practices there that people have built around this. I think most people recognize that's a good practice. I don't hear much more about it now because as people are actually practicing it and the AI factory is another that's probably in the last few months of really how to infuse AI into the various steps of your software development life cycle.
The typical use case is, "Hey, somebody raised a bug. How do you get AI to take that from beginning to end to actually take the PR, do an analysis, try to recreate the problem, come up with a fix, submit a PR, and then you go through the rest of the steps of review and testing and so on?" That is as we all have too many things to do, too many tasks. I think if we can help automate that, that will accelerate another dimension to accelerating the software development life cycle.
Physical AI / Embodied AI
Another area that continues to see more and more innovation is Physical AI. This is where we bring intelligence into the real world. An AI agent is a software system, how do we bring the same power into the hardware, whether they're robots or collaborative robots (cobots) or self-driving cars.
Daniel Dominguez talked about what's happening and what we should be paying attention to in the Physical AI world.
Daniel Dominguez: Basically it's saying, "How do we bring AI into the physical world?" Over the last few years we have spent the time putting intelligence into software. Now we're starting to connect that intelligence to machines that can perceive and act in a physical world. So what, you said, we are starting to see robotics, we're starting to see autonomous vehicles, drones, and industrial systems are now part of this transition. What I think makes physical AI fundamentally different from software agents is that mistakes have physical consequences on the physical AI.
One thing is that in software, an agent can make a mistake generating their own file, but a robot can move their own equator. It’s going to be a whole different level of mistakes. Reliability, simulations, safety, verification, [and] evaluations are going to become more and more important in the physical world. Based on that, all the foundation models for robots that are happening right now, another important shift is that robotics are starting to benefit from more of the same foundational model approach that transformed the language and vision.
We're going to start seeing things like [a] simulation for digital twins robots, all the things that are going to happen for open robotics, [and] all the things that are going to happen from AI agents to physical agents. All of this is just going to start moving faster and faster over the next year because right now the AI is here. Now we have to put it in our physical world.
Chip Huyen also discussed how robots and vision language models can work together.
Chip Huyen: It's the next frontier to get the models into the real world and we see a lot of progress. I think the only challenge is that there are several challenges. We keep saying that robotics are like cars, like LLM to say, "Okay, we know we have a lot of robots in the real world." We have Waymos everywhere. We have Zoox. We see a lot of robots in the real world.
One big difference between robotics, models, and LLMs, it's that the challenge of backtracking. For LLMs, when you're training on a virtual, on the computer, if it makes a mistake, you can run back. You can reset the state and continue. You can do a lot of explorations and pick the best state.
You can't really do [that] exactly [in] robotics. You can't get a robot, "Okay, there's a staircase that's there". The robot falls and it breaks. You can't just run it back and get the same robot as before. It makes exploration extremely, extremely hard. Another challenge is data. I have been looking into a lot of robotic setups. I think Janatics Robotics company – we have a bunch of companies like Generalist, Physical Intelligence, Sunday, Skild AI, which I'm very excited about.
Other trends in the Innovators category we have added or revised for this year include the following topics:
- Agent Security and Governance
- Voice Agents
- Specialized Decision Models (e.g., TypeSafeAI's Jev Model)
- AI Gateways
- GraphRAG
- LLMOps / GenAIOps
- Brain-Computer Interfaces
Early Adopters
In the Early Adopters category, we would like to highlight two main topics: Innovations in language models and RAG.
AI Agents / Agent Orchestration
Similar to last year, Agentic AI has again been the dominant topic this year. 2025 and prior years were all about how to learn and how to build AI agents. Now the organizations are trying to figure out how to operate the agents, how to deploy them to production, and how to scale them in production.
Daniel Dominguez discussed the recent developments in AI Agents area, in this year's podcast:
Daniel Dominguez: I think the biggest change in 2026 is that AI is moving from being something that we interact [with] to something that we delegate [to]. Like Hien was saying, I think most AI applications over the last few years were based on a simple interaction. You will just ask a question and the mobile gives you an answer. Right now we're starting this year, we are starting to see a system that can plan, can use tools, can execute actions, can do their own work and continue working for a much longer period of time. I think this year is less about another jump in the model intelligence and more about turning that intelligence into actual systems.
What I find interesting is that agents are moving through several levels very quickly. We started with personal agents helping one person, then we started seeing agents working with teams, and now companies are thinking about agents operating across entire organizations. I think the important change is that we're moving from beyond just a chatbot model. Instead, we are simply generating an answer. An agent can have goals, can use tools, can interact with software, can make decisions, [and] can keep working until the task is complete.
I think that changes AI from [an] interface into something closer to an execution layer. We can see this mainly in software development. Software development is probably where this transition is more visible. We moved from autocomplete to copilots and now we have coding agents. We have tools like Claude, Codex, Cursor, Replit, and others that can navigate repositories, can modify multiple files, can run comments, can execute tasks, can inspect failures, and can iterate on their own. The interesting question is no longer, can AI write code? We already know that AI can write code.
In the AI Agents space, more complex systems using multiple agents (multi-agent systems) are becoming more common because of the additional benefits they can bring to the table, compared to systems based on individual agents.
Panelist Arthur Casals spoke about the current research happening with multi-agent systems, how these multi-agent systems work, and what are the real-world use cases to leverage them.
Arthur Casals: When you think about multi-agent systems as a topic, it's been there for a few decades already before LLM agents. People from the academic community are seeing whatever comes with LLM agents and after transformers and is related to the entire multi-agent systems trying to reinvent things that were there in the past. My research area is on classical multi-agent systems, before LLM, which doesn't mean that it can't incorporate or use LLM systems as part of it. But these days I've been working on belief revision. This is a big part of solving two problems actually in the AI landscape, one related to hallucination and the second one related to information accuracy and provenance after being processed by the agent. It's between computer science and philosophy, a lot of formal logic, but yeah, it's really interesting. One thing that we've been working with, I think since the beginning of this year, and the end of last year, is a formal logic-based profile definition that could be used. It's similar to the concepts around Jev that we were discussing before. So [they] have a structure input, a structural output and how we can make the AI not the agents refrain from using agents, but actually working from here to there.
AI Evaluations for Models and Agents
This year, we have also seen more developments in the quality assurance space with the AI evaluations, guardrails and harness frameworks. The year 2026 has been dubbed as the year of AI Evaluations. There are a lot of different techniques that are gaining attention in this area. Testing harness frameworks are probably the most talked about topic this year. As AI tools are increasingly leveraged to write code and other components of software solutions, the need for formal, rigorous, consistent and reliable validation frameworks has never been more critical. How do we then measure AI effectiveness? What kind of metrics can help in the evaluation and validation steps with an end-to-end process that has proper checks and balances?
We asked the panelists to explain what they are seeing in the agentic AI evaluation space. Here are their observations.
Hien Luu: This is a very important topic for companies that are bringing their AI agents to production, particularly the one that for their customers, not so much about internal ones. If you look at an example from DoorDash, they build an AI assistant for ordering food. You have other companies that are building customer support agents for external users. We all know that LLMs are not deterministics and building agents, they can take the wrong turn, they can make the wrong tool calls and stuff like that. Evaluations are a way to help us to make sure that the agents do the right thing for the right tasks at the highest level.
Without evaluation, how would you know that it's gone rogue or does something that's unexpected, not according to your company's policies and all that stuff like that. Companies not only have to do this, but they have to incorporate this as one of their core steps in building AI agents. A lot of companies end up building something called an evaluation harness, which helps drive the whole evaluation flow from getting the data, running the evaluation or tests, as we all know tests – right? – and then assessing the quality at the end.
Daniel Dominguez: I completely agree with the idea that this year is becoming the year of evaluations for models and agents. Once an agent can perform an action, evaluating only the model is not enough. You have to evaluate the whole system, you have to evaluate the model, the tool, the context, the agent loop, the environment. Here is where the metrics changed as well.
It’s not only whether the answer was correct, it's whether the agent completed the task, how much it cost, how long it took, how many interventions were necessary, and whether it did something unsafe along the way. I think all these evaluations were just starting to see how we are going to evaluate all this workflow regarding agents and regarding LLMs and regarding the interactions that they do in our job.
Outside of these highlighted technology trends, there are a few entries that we are moving from Innovators into the Early Adopters category. All these technologies listed below have gone through extensive development and adoption and are now being used by many applications in various organizations.
AI technologies have, for the right reasons, started being leveraged in the DevOps and SRE areas of the production support, troubleshooting, maintenance, and upgrade operations.
- Agentic Coding / Autonomous Software Engineering
- Agent Observability
- Inference Optimization and Model Routing
- Small Language Models (SLMs)
- Reasoning Models
- Explainable AI
- Virtual Reality (eg VR/AR/MR/XR)
- Cognitive Services
- Edge AI Inference
- Model Context Protocol (MCP)
- Multi-modal AI
- AI DevOps/AI-powered SRE
Early Majority
We are moving the following topics to the Early Majority category as these technologies have become more mainstream and are being widely adopted by software development teams in various organizations.
Context Engineering
In the age of AI agents, Context Engineering topic continues to be important and evolving to be used in AI powered solutions. Arthur Casals spoke about this with emphasis on one of the challenges in Context Engineering, the Context Pollution.
Arthur Casals: Context pollution is actually the biggest problem, the problem worth emphasizing now, because we've seen the past year or so movements toward bigger context windows in general, but they don't really solve the issue if the system cannot distinguish what's useful, what's current, what's alternative information from irrelevant, stale, adversarial material. I'm bringing something from my own research here, but in general, more context can make an agent slower, more expensive, less reliable.
The practical question would be, if you have your context window, regardless of the size of it, what enters the context? From which source, with which permission, for what step of the workflow so you don't have this huge pollution. That talks about retrieval quality, source distribution, professions rules, context model in general, context compression. I mean, there's a huge, huge heap of problems underneath the word context. That's how I see it.
Also, compared to last year’s report, we have more topics as listed below, that we think are ready to move to Early Majority status.
- Generative AI/Large Language Models (LLMs)
- Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
- Knowledge Graphs
- MLOps
- Vector Databases
- Data Contracts
- Data Observability
- Graph Data Analytics
- Synthetic Data Generation
- Open Table Formats (OTFs)
Late Majority
Finally, in the last category in our adoption graph, the Late Majority, we have a few topics that have moved from the Early Majority category. These technologies are now fully adopted by teams and part of their core architecture and design patterns and development processes.
- Automated Machine Learning
- Image Recognition (Computer Vision)
- Digital Assistants
- Data Mesh
- Stream Processing and Analytics
- Recommendation Engines
- Lakehouses
- Spark
Topics Removed from Adoption Graph
We also want to note that in this edition of the AI ML Trends Report, we have removed some mature technologies that have been in use for several years now. These technologies have become very much part of the mainstream technologies and adoption, and don’t need to be tracked on our adoption graph for our readers.
Some of these topics include mature technologies like NLP and Deep Learning, NoSQL Databases, In-Memory Data Grids, and Big Data (Hadoop).
Conclusion
AI is a significant technology shift. As we all know by now, after almost four years, it is not a fad or some temporary blip on the technology radar. It is here to stay. It is one of the major technology waves in the last twenty-plus years. We should take advantage of this technology transformation, not be afraid of it. Find ways to use AI tools to automate any workflows in your day-to-day life, whether it is in the office projects or in your personal life.
Some of the team’s predictions for the next year include:
- We expect to see more innovations in US-based robotic companies.
- We will also see a lot of cheaper and faster models; the TypeSafe style of model would be very interesting.
- We're going to start seeing limitations on AI, in the areas of energy and AI infrastructure in terms of access for electricity, capacity, and cooling data center locations. For 2027, some of the biggest AI stories may actually happen outside the models themselves; it's going to be more about energy, the chips, the infrastructure, and the geopolitics.
- Every AI agent will incorporate some form of the Jev model.
- Increasingly, communications are going to be between agents, moving forward as we figure out how to build, operate and bring all these agents to production.
- We'll see a lot of things using smaller specialized agents for mixed models, for well-defined tasks. The big difference will be in the surrounding system.
- AI will be even a bigger part of our daily lives. We think the niche areas will be settled where AI will be really valuable and where human intelligence is still required.

articles.title: La Seguridad Social concede una pensión mínima de 888 euros a los trabajadores que hayan cotizado 15 años, pero a partir de 2027 tendrán que esperar hasta los 67 para jubilarse
articles.text:
Es necesario haber cotizado 15 años. Al menos dos de ellos deben estar dentro de los 15 años anteriores a la jubilación. Con esto se obtiene el 50 % de la base reguladora de la pensión (el dato de referencia que se obtiene de las cotizaciones del trabajador). Por cada año cotizado a partir del decimosexto, se incrementa un poco más hasta que se alcanza el 100 %. En 2026 hacen falta 36 años y medio. A partir de 2027 serán 37. Nosotros ya os hemos explicado por qué 15 años no son suficientes.
A partir de 2026 se tienen en cuenta dos métodos para calcular la base reguladora. La Seguridad Social utiliza el más favorable para el trabajador. Uno consiste en dividir la suma de las 300 últimas bases de cotización (25 años) entre 350. Otro es dividir la suma de las 302 bases más altas de los 304 últimos meses (esto permite descartar los dos peores) entre 352,33. En caso de que estos métodos den un resultado insuficiente, entra en juego la pensión mínima.
Los tres mínimos y el complemento
Este no es el único mínimo. El Real Decreto 241/2026 establece tres importes anuales para los mayores de 65 años. Divididos entre catorce pagas, resultan en: 1.256,60 euros (con cónyuge a cargo), 936,20 euros (unidad económica unipersonal, es decir, sin cónyuge) y 888,70 euros (con cónyuge que no depende económicamente del pensionista). Es el menor de los tres. Aquellos que no tienen cónyuge tienen un mínimo mayor de 47,50 euros.
Sin embargo, este no se obtiene por tener 15 años de cotización. Es un complemento que se añade por la Seguridad Social si el importe de la pensión es inferior (artículo 59 de la ley). El real decreto establece que debe residir en España. Además, los otros ingresos (excluyendo la pensión) no pueden superar los 9.442 euros al año. Esto incluye rendimientos del trabajo y del capital; actividades económicas y ganancias patrimoniales. Si tiene cónyuge a cargo, el límite es de 11.013 euros (sumando los ingresos de ambos).
Aquí está la grieta. De forma retroactiva, en el año natural en el que se constate que se han sobrepasado los límites de ingresos, se considerará que el complemento que se ha cobrado en dicho año es indebidamente percibido. Y aunque es obligatorio avisar a la Seguridad Social, en un mes no se puede evitar devolverlo. Tampoco es posible consolidarlo. Es un andamio que se retira de golpe cuando dejan de cumplirse las condiciones.
Para hacernos una idea, podemos realizar nosotros mismos un pequeño cálculo. Con 15 años justos se cobra la mitad de la base reguladora. Solo se supera el mínimo si esta es superior a 1.777,40 euros (con cónyuge no a cargo); 1.872,40 euros (no tiene cónyuge); 2.513,20 euros (tiene cónyuge a cargo). Por ejemplo, si la base es de 1.200 euros, la pensión es de 600. Si además cumple con los requisitos de ingresos (sin cónyuge), el complemento es de 336,20 euros.
La edad de jubilación y lo que pasa en 2027
También aumenta la edad. Los que se jubilen en 2026 con menos de 38 años y tres meses de cotización tienen que esperar a los 66 años y diez meses. A partir de 2027, para los que no tengan 38 años y seis meses de cotización, la edad ordinaria será de 67 años. Para los que tengan esos años, seguirá siendo de 65. Con 15 años de cotización, el de 67 años es el que toca a partir del 1 de enero de 2027 (disposición transitoria séptima de la ley).
La posibilidad de adelantar la jubilación no es solución a esta carrera corta. Para poder jubilarse de forma anticipada (voluntariamente), es necesario haber cotizado 35 años de manera efectiva (hasta dos años menos que la edad ordinaria). Además, es necesario que, después de aplicar la reducción (que va desde el 2,81 % hasta el 21 % en función de los meses de adelanto y los años de cotización), la pensión sea superior a la mínima que tendrían con 65 años.
Por otro lado, hay que saber qué valor tendrán estas cuantías en 2027. Las pensiones se revalorizan cada enero con la media de la inflación de los 12 meses anteriores a diciembre. Las mínimas también deben actualizarse con el mismo porcentaje. Sin embargo, en 2026 el Gobierno ha decidido subir las mínimas más (más del 7 %) que el resto (2,7 %) (Ministerio de Inclusión).
En septiembre la inflación anual fue del 4,9 % (INE, 14 de octubre de 2026). Sin embargo, esta media no se cierra hasta conocer el dato de noviembre. Además, está pendiente de aprobar la norma de 2027. Por otro lado, está fijado por ley el valor de la edad. El 67 no está relacionado con el IPC.

articles.title: Netflix Titus Adds Single-Tenant VM Isolation for Containers
articles.text:
Netflix has added single-tenant Titus, a mode that runs one task alone on its own right-sized EC2 instance. The Compute/Platform team still owns and patches the host, so application teams keep the same API and deployment path. First adopters include stateful, high-throughput streaming workloads. Here, a neighbor's interference can lead to minutes of checkpoint recovery.
Titus launches millions of containers a week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances and is multi-tenant by default. Netflix says that cgroups, seccomp, the iocost controller, and traffic shaping can’t split shared hardware. This includes resources like the last-level cache and memory bandwidth. Its HTB traffic shaper also takes a global lock. A container that floods the host with small packets can burn the kernel CPU and starve its neighbors. Predictive CPU pinning and eBPF-based detection helped, but Netflix concluded that shared-kernel tuning narrows the gap without closing it.
Netflix rejected the alternatives for specific reasons. MicroVMs such as Firecracker and Kata need bare-metal or nested virtualization, and nested virtualization was not ready on Netflix's instance types. They also meant running a hypervisor layer, added virtualization overhead, and lacked GPU support. gVisor added overhead on I/O-heavy paths, and a single vendor does most of its maintenance. Running containers on EC2 would hand host patching and fleet sizing back to application teams. Netflix argues that these workloads require performance isolation, not defense against hostile tenants.
The Titus federation layer does most of the work. An allowlist, maintained by the Compute/Platform team, controls eligibility and federation records, which instance families a task may use. The autoscaler launches the smallest instance that fits the task's CPU, memory, and GPU request. Pod anti-affinity, a non-preemptible priority class, and a node taint enforce one task per node. Netflix disables defragmentation, so nothing relocates the task. To measure isolation, Netflix runs a reference app alone, then beside a "havoc" container, and scores retained throughput and P99 latency. The post publishes no scores.
Launch latency is the main cost. A fresh instance needs tens of seconds to boot before the image pull begins. Warm pools help less than on the shared fleet, because right-sizing produces many instance shapes. Netflix keeps a small warm pool for the most latency-sensitive starts and limits the available sizes. It dropped metal instances for these pools. Disabling Kubernetes preemption removed a scheduling bottleneck that left new nodes idle. Lazy image pulling (stargz, SOCI) and CRIU checkpoint restore are longer-term fixes.
Efficiency can improve. Moving sensitive workloads off shared hosts removes the anti-affinity spreading and disruption budgets that left those hosts partly empty. Fixed overhead from sidecars and system services pulls the other way. Netflix says it can cost a small instance tens of percent of its resources, and the largest shapes only a couple of percent. Discrete EC2 sizes also leave bin-packing gaps on large shared hosts, which favored right-sizing in practice.
Early users include managed Apache Flink, streaming data connectors, and telemetry and logging pipelines. Then, there are some latency-sensitive GraphQL and edge services. The rollout continues. For the shared fleet, Netflix is working on eBPF-based Expected Departure Time shaping to replace HTB, plus cache and memory-bandwidth partitioning (Intel RDT, AMD PQoS), NVIDIA MIG, and the cgroup v2 IO controller. Its long-term goal is one Compute API that picks EC2 or Titus placement from declared intent.
Single-tenant Titus joins a broader set of approaches to the same problem. Instance-per-Pod Webhook, an open-source project from NTT’s Akihiro Suda, uses a Kubernetes admission webhook and the Cluster Autoscaler to create a tainted, dedicated instance for each pod. AWS Fargate makes the pod the unit of infrastructure, so customers do not create, patch, or scale worker nodes. GKE offers sole-tenant nodes, dedicated physical servers that run only a single project’s VMs, along with GKE Sandbox, which runs each pod in its own Kata Containers microVM. Azure’s Pod Sandboxing is also built on Kata and gives each pod its own lightweight VM, isolated from other pod VMs and the host kernel. Most of these target security isolation from untrusted code, while Netflix’s post focuses on performance isolation between trusted internal teams.
Teams running shared Kubernetes platforms can borrow the pattern: dedicated node pools with taints, anti-affinity, and repacking turned off. Netflix recommends it for large, long-running, disruption-sensitive workloads sized close to a node shape and not for small or bursty services. The allowlist keeps the mode from eroding multi-tenant density.

articles.title: Former esports commentator builds his own custom mouse shell generator for 3D printing that doesn’t use AI — Mausstudio automatically detects buttons, screwholes, and sensor locations
articles.text:
Former esports commentator builds his own custom mouse shell generator for 3D printing that doesn’t use AI — Mausstudio automatically detects buttons, screwholes, and sensor locations
Mausstudio lets you design a 3D-printable gaming mouse shell without learning CAD.
Bastian Recha, “Unskilledcast,” is a German former CS:GO commentator, tech reviewer, and 3D printing enthusiast. On October 28, he posted a demo of his “Mausstudio” project on X that generates a customizable mouse shell around an imported 3D model of a mouse PCB intended for 3D printing — all running locally and not generated using AI.
Bastian posted on X after six days of inactivity, stating that he’s been busy working on Mausstudio, his custom 3D-printed mouse shell generator. His post shows a video of him demonstrating the software, playing around with the ways users can customize their mouse.
Mausstudio works by importing an STL 3D file of a mouse PCB, like the Razer Viper V2 Pro and Zaunkoenig M2K PCBs in Bastian’s demo, from which the software detects the location of several key components: Mouse button switch locations, sensor location, scroll wheel location, and screw hole locations. It then generates a shell around those key components, placing stems to reach the switches, cutouts for the scroll wheel, buttons for the side switches, and base cutouts for the sensor.
Bastian’s demo also showed how users can adjust the width, length, and height of the mouse, including the location of the hump. Further customizations include weight-reducing cutouts for the upper and lower shell, with options to have a fully enclosed shell without the cutouts. To demonstrate the level of customizability, Bastian also showed a battery shelf option, allowing you to customize the location of the battery and the shelf’s size by inputting the battery’s dimensions — this feature, Bastian emphasizes, is lacking in many custom 3D-printed mice, and battery placement is treated as an afterthought, often just using hot glue or double-sided tape to adhere it.
Bastian also boasts that Mausstudio runs completely locally and without generative AI, just math and algorithms.
Bastian has not yet announced a release date for this project, nor has he announced whether this is paid or free, but he has posted an update on what has been changed since his demo, including being able to edit detected component assignments, more side button control, saving shell designs to be used on other PCBs, and cleaner geometry. We’re not sure if it can handle split PCBs like on the G Pro X Superlight, but support for that may come in the future as well.
This project looks to be a great way for users to create a mouse that’s closer to their ideal shape; good gaming mice are not cheap, and it’s a costly endeavor to buy many mice just to try out various shapes. This project may be able to let users experiment with more shapes more affordably with their existing mouse without needing CAD skills or hoping that someone has designed a mouse shell for their PCB that fits their needs. We will have to see how good the software is when it releases, and how it will improve and mature with future updates.

articles.title: Anatomy of a Business Email Scam: How Fake Invoices Slip Past Busy Bookkeepers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Understanding the Rising Threat of Business Email Scams
In today’s fast-paced business environment, email remains a primary communication tool, especially for financial transactions like invoicing and payments. However, this reliance has made businesses, particularly their finance teams and bookkeepers, prime targets for increasingly sophisticated email scams. One of the most prevalent tactics involves fake invoice scams, where cybercriminals impersonate legitimate vendors or partners to trick businesses into paying fraudulent invoices.
The scale of this threat is staggering. With 94% of malware delivered via email and phishing attacks accounting for over 90% of data breaches, email-based scams have become the favored method for cybercriminals aiming to exploit businesses. According to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, business email compromise (BEC) scams led to losses exceeding $2.4 billion in 2023 alone. These numbers reflect not only the monetary damage but also the operational disruptions and reputational harm businesses face.
As these scams evolve, understanding their anatomy is critical to strengthening defenses. This article delves into how fake invoices slip past busy bookkeepers, what makes these scams so effective, and crucially, how businesses can protect themselves.
How Fake Invoice Scams Operate
Fake invoice scams exploit human error and process vulnerabilities, targeting busy bookkeepers who manage a high volume of invoices daily. The scammers’ goal is to create a sense of urgency or familiarity that prompts quick payment without thorough verification. Here’s a breakdown of how these scams typically unfold:
- Reconnaissance and Vendor Impersonation
Attackers begin by gathering information about the target company’s vendors and usual payment processes. They may monitor email communications through compromised accounts or gather data from social media and business directories. Using this intelligence, they craft emails that appear to come from trusted vendors, complete with legitimate logos and invoice templates.
For businesses unsure about their email security, it’s advisable to reach out to NuView. Cybersecurity services can help detect and mitigate these types of threats before they reach the finance team.
- Crafting Convincing Fake Invoices
The fake invoices are designed to look as authentic as possible, often mimicking the style and formatting of previous legitimate invoices. They include plausible invoice numbers, payment terms, and bank details that redirect payments to the scammers’ accounts. The scammer’s email address might be a close variation of the real vendor’s domain, making quick glances insufficient for detection.
- Exploiting Internal Process Gaps
Many businesses lack robust verification processes for invoice approval, especially under time pressure. Scammers rely on this by sending fake invoices during busy periods or end-of-month closing when bookkeepers are overwhelmed. Without a mandatory step for vendor confirmation or a two-person approval system, fraudulent invoices can easily slip through.
Why Bookkeepers Are Vulnerable
Bookkeepers, while skilled, often juggle multiple responsibilities and tight deadlines. Their focus on accuracy and timely payments can make them targets for these scams. Several factors contribute to their vulnerability:
– Volume of Invoices: Large organizations process hundreds or thousands of invoices monthly, increasing the chance that a fake one gets overlooked.
– Email Overload: Employees may skim emails quickly, especially when dealing with repetitive tasks, leading to missed warning signs.
– Lack of Cybersecurity Training: Many finance staff are not regularly trained to identify phishing and social engineering tactics.
– Pressure to Avoid Payment Delays: Fear of vendor dissatisfaction or service interruption can push employees to approve payments rapidly.
To counter these challenges, businesses can engage with CSS’ experts in Tampa who specialize in IT support and cybersecurity in Tampa and beyond, helping to implement stronger email filtering and internal controls.
Statistical Insights on Email Fraud Targeting Finance Teams
Recent studies highlight the growing risk and impact of email-based financial fraud:
– A 2023 survey found that 76% of finance professionals reported receiving suspicious emails targeting payments or invoicing.
– Companies with automated invoice processing are 60% less likely to fall victim to fake invoice scams compared to those relying solely on manual processes.
– Additionally, businesses that implemented multi-factor authentication saw a 50% reduction in successful email compromise attempts within the first year of adoption.
These statistics underscore the importance of combining technology with staff awareness to reduce exposure.
Best Practices to Prevent Fake Invoice Scams
Businesses must adopt a multi-layered approach that addresses both technological defenses and human factors:
- Implement Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
Securing email accounts with MFA reduces the risk of account compromise, a common starting point for scammers to monitor communications and send fake invoices. MFA adds an extra layer of security by requiring users to verify their identity through multiple methods, making unauthorized access significantly harder.
- Establish Clear Verification Procedures
Mandate a process where bookkeepers or accounts payable teams verify invoices directly with vendors through known contact details before processing payments. Any changes in payment instructions should be confirmed verbally. This simple yet effective step can prevent scammers from redirecting funds to fraudulent accounts.
- Use Automated Invoice Processing Tools
Automation can flag discrepancies such as duplicate invoices or mismatched vendor details, reducing manual errors. Many solutions also incorporate AI to detect anomalies and unusual patterns in invoicing and payment requests. By integrating these tools, businesses can streamline workflows while enhancing fraud detection capabilities.
- Train Staff Regularly on Cybersecurity Awareness
Continuous education helps finance teams recognize phishing attempts and social engineering tactics. Simulated phishing exercises can reinforce learning by exposing employees to realistic scenarios in a controlled environment. Training should be updated regularly to address emerging threats and evolving scam techniques.
- Monitor and Audit Payment Processes
Regular audits and real-time monitoring of payments can detect unusual transactions early. Setting payment limits and requiring multiple approvals for large payments adds extra security. These controls not only deter fraud but also provide an audit trail for accountability.
Enhancing Organizational Culture to Combat Scams
Beyond technical controls and verification processes, fostering a culture of vigilance is vital. Encouraging open communication where employees feel comfortable reporting suspicious emails or irregularities without fear of reprimand can help catch scams early. Leadership should emphasize the importance of cybersecurity as a shared responsibility.
Moreover, integrating cybersecurity considerations into everyday business operations ensures that protective measures are not seen as obstacles but as essential components of organizational resilience. Regularly updating policies and rewarding proactive behavior can motivate staff to stay alert.
Responding to a Suspected Scam
If a fake invoice is detected or a payment is suspected to have gone to a scammer’s account, immediate action is critical:
– Notify the bank or payment processor to attempt a recall or freeze the transaction.
– Inform internal stakeholders and initiate a cybersecurity incident response.
– Report the incident to relevant authorities such as the local cybercrime unit or the FBI’s IC3.
– Review and strengthen internal controls to prevent recurrence.
Time is of the essence in these situations. The sooner a fraudulent transaction is flagged, the higher the chances of recovery.
Conclusion
Fake invoice scams are a persistent and evolving threat that exploit the busy nature of bookkeeping and finance teams. By understanding the anatomy of these scams-from vendor impersonation to exploitation of internal processes-businesses can better defend themselves against financial losses. Incorporating cybersecurity expertise, such as that offered by , alongside robust IT support from, empowers organizations to implement comprehensive protections.
Investing in technology, training, and procedural safeguards not only protects company assets but also preserves vendor relationships and corporate reputation. In an era where cybercrime is increasingly sophisticated, vigilance and proactive measures are the best defense against falling victim to business email scams.
By adopting a proactive stance and fostering a security-minded culture, businesses can transform their finance teams from potential targets into strongholds against fraud. This holistic approach ensures that fake invoices no longer slip past busy bookkeepers unnoticed, safeguarding both financial health and operational continuity.

articles.title: Explicando el mayor 'hackeo' de criptomonedas de la historia: cómo se ha hecho posible lo que parecía imposible
articles.text:
Lo que ha sucedido hace apenas unas horas es inaudito. Un grupo de hackers ha logrado robar aproximadamente 6.360 millones de dólares en criptomonedas de los monederos de Binance. TRM Labs, un laboratorio que se dedica a la inteligencia blockchain, está analizando minuciosamente lo que ha sucedido, y ha identificado transferencias desde varios monederos asociados a Binance hacia direcciones controladas por los atacantes en diez redes blockchain.
Este suceso es asombroso por varios motivos. El más evidente es el valor de las criptodivisas que han sido sustraídas. Y es posible que durante las próximas horas la cifra que he mencionado en el párrafo anterior se incremente. Además, resulta impactante que alguien haya conseguido robar varios miles de millones de dólares de una de las plataformas de criptomonedas más sofisticadas del planeta. Y, para más inri, casi todo el dinero salió en aproximadamente 20 minutos.
Este incidente no ha afectado solo a Bitcoin; también a Ethereum, Tron, Solana y XRP Ledger, entre otras criptos. Y, según TRM Labs, ha sido perpetrado por TraderTraitor, un grupo de hackers de Corea del Norte. Parece que nos hemos sumergido de lleno en la trama de un thriller, pero no. Todo esto es muy real. Y ha sido posible gracias al ingenio. De hecho, los atacantes no han necesitado romper la criptografía que protege los monederos. Con la tecnología actual, romper estos algoritmos mediante fuerza bruta resulta computacionalmente inviable. Lo que han hecho es si cabe más inquietante.
El auténtico protagonista del mayor robo de la historia es un ordenador portátil
Los algoritmos criptográficos de Bitcoin, Ethereum y las demás redes afectadas no han sido vulnerados. Según TRM Labs y Elliptic, la explicación más sólida de este suceso es que los hackers norcoreanos a los que se les atribuye la autoría del robo consiguieron comprometer los sistemas de Binance que permiten autorizar y firmar transacciones. Esta tesis tiene sentido debido a que las transferencias que llevaron a cabo los atacantes eran válidas desde un punto de vista criptográfico, pero no fueron autorizadas por Binance.
Las transferencias que llevaron a cabo los atacantes eran válidas desde un punto de vista criptográfico, pero no fueron autorizadas por Binance
Esto significa que los hackers no han roto la seguridad de la tecnología blockchain; lo que han hecho ha sido transgredir la infraestructura que permite operar sobre ellas. Y para llevarlo a cabo han atacado los hot wallets de Binance, que son monederos conectados a internet que se emplean para administrar las operaciones y atender las retiradas de las criptomonedas. Lo que los diferencia de los cold wallets es que estos últimos mantienen sus claves desconectadas o especialmente protegidas.
La investigación todavía está en marcha, pero los técnicos de Binance sospechan que este robo ha sido posible debido a que los atacantes han conseguido comprometer el ordenador portátil de un ingeniero del área encargada de gestionar y automatizar la infraestructura que permite ejecutar aplicaciones y servicios, conocida como DevOps. Por el momento es solo una hipótesis, pero parece la más plausible en este escenario.
Esto no implica que los hackers se hayan visto obligados a robar físicamente el portátil. La investigación de Binance parece indicar que consiguieron acceder remotamente a este ordenador usando malware o robando credenciales. Después posiblemente lo usaron para acceder a los sistemas internos de Binance, lo que probablemente les permitió alcanzar un contenedor de servicio y enviar órdenes de retirada no autorizadas.
Además, parece que usaron un mecanismo de Ethereum conocido como EIP-7702 para lograr que uno de los monederos de Binance delegase su comportamiento a un contrato inteligente controlado por los atacantes. Todavía hay muchos flecos sueltos, por lo que posiblemente no conoceremos con detalle todo lo que ha sucedido hasta que Binance termine su análisis forense y todas las hipótesis estén respaldadas por evidencias sólidas.

articles.title: Javi Linares, asesor financiero: "Un móvil de 1.400 euros parece asumible por 39 al mes, pero ahí está la trampa de las cuotas"
articles.text:
A la hora de comprar un móvil, soltar 1.400 euros de golpe impone bastante más que pagar 39 euros al mes. Pero la facilidad para encajar un pago pequeño puede llevarnos a aceptar un gasto que comprometa el presupuesto durante años.
El asesor financiero Javi Linares aborda esa diferencia en una entrevista con La Vanguardia, donde habla de “la trampa de las cuotas”. Lo explica con un ejemplo: “Pagar 39 euros al mes durante 36 meses por un móvil puede parecer razonable”. Haciendo cuentas, ese coste durante tres años de pagos suman 1.404 euros, al que habría que añadir cualquier coste adicional que pudiera tener la financiación.
Pero esa facilidad aparente para pagar ciertos artículos puede hacernos caer en un error: el de financiar compras que se deprecian deprisa o pagar a plazos experiencias que terminan mucho antes que sus pagos. “No tiene sentido seguir pagando durante meses algo que ya hemos consumido”, señala el experto.
Al financiar varias compras, podemos acumular gastos para los meses siguientes sin percibirlos con la misma claridad que un crédito. Que cada operación sea pequeña no evita que la suma deje poco dinero disponible.
Por ejemplo, una compra de ropa repartida en tres pagos y un teléfono financiado durante tres años tienen calendarios muy distintos por lo que puede ser útil apuntar en una hoja o en las notas del móvil cada cargo, su fecha y cuántos quedan para no llevarnos ningún susto.
La otra comprobación es cuánto cuesta aplazar. El Banco de España explica que una financiación sin intereses puede incorporar comisiones o gastos. El tipo de interés nominal (TIN) puede ser cero y la tasa anual equivalente (TAE), que incorpora esos costes, resultar positiva. Si tampoco hay comisiones ni gastos, la TAE será del 0%, y eso es justo lo que tenemos que asegurar.
Si ya tenemos varias financiaciones abiertas, Linares recomienda “priorizar las deudas con intereses elevados” y revisar los gastos que más pesan en las cuentas, que suelen ser habitualmente la vivienda y el coche.
Con las cantidades ya anotadas, podemos comprobar qué queda para gastos necesarios en el mes más ajustado. Si la nueva compra solo encaja contando con un ingreso extra todavía incierto, se puede probar con un presupuesto menor o esperar a que termine otra financiación.

articles.title: Rare meteorite from Mars gives us a view into its ancient crust
articles.text:
Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one.
A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. “It’s very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth,” Liu says.
A filtered collection
“We don’t fully understand why old Martian rocks are so rare on Earth,” Liu said. Part of the answer may lie in how a piece of Mars gets here. It takes a large impact to launch a rock off the planet, and not every rock can survive that. “If the impact hits into loose powder, it may not get cemented to become a rock and fly off Mars’ gravity,” Liu said. “So the natural impact already acts as a filter. Weak rocks do not make it off Mars.”
That left scientists with a biased collection.
“Even to date, none of our collected Martian meteorites are similar to what we found on the surface,” Liu said. The partial exception is Black Beauty, which has a bulk chemistry that matches orbital measurements. But Black Beauty is a mix of soil and many small rock fragments. Teghaza 001 is a single, intact igneous rock.
Teghaza 001 was acquired through the desert meteorite trade, where hunters comb the Sahara for dark stones that stand out against the sand. Its eight stones, weighing just under 800 grams in total, were bought by a private collector, who sent a piece to the University of New Mexico for classification. There, planetary scientists Carl Agee and Karen Ziegler measured its oxygen isotopes. “Each planetary body has a very characteristic oxygen isotope value,” Liu says. Teghaza 001’s values matched those of other Martian meteorites.
At first, the rock was classified as a shergottite, the most common (and young) type of Martian meteorite. But Agee noticed some oddities and reached out to Liu. One of Teghaza’s minerals had been altered on the inside while its outer part stayed pristine, the reverse of how weathering on Earth works. The oxygen isotopes looked a bit strange, and there was some manganese-rich material similar to what Liu had studied in Black Beauty.
“When I got to the sample, I looked around, I said, ‘That’s boring,’” Liu said. “The high-manganese material is actually terrestrial, but I quickly realized the sample is very different, very special.”
Teghaza 001 is made mostly of feldspar, a pale mineral common in the crusts of rocky planets. It has darker pyroxene crystals mixed in; according to Liu, those resemble some rocks exposed in the lunar highlands. Its crystals are rather big, up to a millimeter across, which scientists interpret as an indication it cooled down slowly. “For slow-cooled rock, they tend to have time to grow bigger,” Liu said.
By comparing the crystals with lab experiments and terrestrial rocks, the team estimated Teghaza 001 cooled by roughly 0.01° Celsius per year, indicating it formed from magma that never erupted but instead solidified inside the crust.
Clocks reset by water
The team dated the rock in several independent ways. Zircon grains gave about 4.11 billion years. Phosphate minerals and rubidium-strontium dating gave similar ages. “Doesn’t matter what type of zircon we are analyzing or what mineral we are analyzing, we get this very consistent age. And we didn’t expect that,” Liu said.
It is notoriously hard to reset the age of zircons, and the impact that launched the rock, while strong enough to forge high-pressure minerals, wasn’t hot enough to do it. “To change it, you really require some kind of hydrothermal fluid,” Liu said.
Sodium-rich rims on feldspar grains and sodium trapped in the zircons support the idea that hot water percolated through the rock shortly after it formed. So 4.1 billion years marks its last soaking, the youngest of what were probably several alteration events. “The crystallization age would be older than 4.1 billion years,” Liu said.
Teghaza 001 is also unusually rich in oxygen-18, a heavier form of oxygen, with about two parts per thousand more than other Martian meteorites. Neither crystallization nor gas escaping from magma can produce a difference that big. Because water that reacts with rock at low temperatures near the planet’s surface forms minerals rich in heavy oxygen, the team thinks the magma either swallowed bits of crust that had already interacted with surface water or reacted directly with fluids that had picked up the same heavy signature.
This implies that “There was active circulation of water through Martian crust,” Liu said. “When this rock was forming, we do have a hydrosphere on Mars, and that hydrosphere is reacting with Martian crust intensely.” The water must have been circulating through the crust and reacting with magma before it had even finished cooling. “It’s actually more dynamic and more active than we thought,” Liu said. She argues that this finding fits the picture of a wet early Mars and points to potentially habitable environments in its crust.
Teghaza 001 also reveals details about Mars’ interior. The rock crystallized near the surface, but the magma it formed from came from much deeper. Ratios of trace elements that resist alteration, like the zirconium to titanium ratio, differ from those in every other Martian meteorite. The team’s melting models matched the rock’s chemistry best when its mantle source contained garnet, a mineral that is stable in the Martian mantle only at depths of more than 160 kilometers.
Studies of other Martian meteorites suggest that as an early ocean of magma solidified on Mars roughly 4.5 billion years ago, the mantle separated into three to five reservoirs. Teghaza 001’s source does not match any of them. “In the first few hundred million years, the Martian mantle was evolving in a way that’s more complicated than we thought,” Liu said.
The orbital view
Comparing the rock’s chemistry with orbital maps, the team suggests it most likely came from the southern highlands, northwest of the giant Hellas impact basin. “No matter how many meteorite samples we have, we will always have this question: Where are they coming from on Mars?” Liu said.
Orbital data can narrow a source down to a patch of roughly 100 by 100 meters at best, which often amounts to one pixel in our remote sensing data. When Teghaza 001 left Mars is also an open question. “We only did the minimum required to make the world know this sample is special,” Liu said, adding that two or three groups are already studying it to get further insights.
The real game-changer, Liu said, would be samples collected with careful geological context, like those Perseverance has gathered in and around Jezero Crater. Liu would like to see some from terrains as old as Teghaza 001 or older. “If these samples come back, there are so many discoveries that can be made,” Liu said. “This could revolutionize our understanding of Mars and the early solar system.”
Jacek Krywko is a freelance science and technology writer who covers space exploration, artificial intelligence research, computer science, and all sorts of engineering wizardry.

articles.title: AI, ML, and Data Engineering InfoQ Trends Report 2026
articles.text:
In this episode of the podcast, members of the InfoQ AI and ML editorial staff and friends of InfoQ discuss the current trends in the domain of AI, ML and Data Engineering.
One of the regular features of InfoQ are the trends reports, which each focus on a different aspect of software development. These reports provide the InfoQ readers and listeners with a high-level overview of the topics to pay attention to this year.
InfoQ AI, ML and Data Engineering editorial team met with an external guest to discuss the 2026 trends in AI and ML areas, and what to watch out for the next 12 months. In addition to the written report and trends graph, this podcast provides a recording of a discussion where expert panelists discuss how innovative AI technologies are disrupting the industry.
Key Takeaways
- Language models have shifted from large size models to the small language models. We are also seeing the rise of reasoning models that can think through math and logic problems before responding.
- AI agents are one of the biggest trends of 2026. Agents are moving from personal agents to the agents working with teams, to companies using agents across entire organizations.
- System One models like TypeSafe AI’s Jev will see more adoption because of their faster inference and lower costs compared to the LLMs.
- AI evaluations have been getting a lot of attention this year. Evaluations are a way to help us to make sure that the agents do the right thing for the right tasks.
- Physical AI has seen significant developments in 2026. We are starting to connect the software intelligence to machines that can perceive and act in a physical world.
- Our panelists’ AI predictions for next year include: More innovations in US based robotic companies, cheaper and faster models, limitations on AI in the areas of energy and AI infrastructure, every AI agent will incorporate some form of the Jev model into the AI agents, applications using smaller specialized agents for mixed models, AI will be even a bigger part of our daily lives and niche areas will be settled where AI will be really valuable and where human intelligence is still required.
