Hien Luu: This probably started maybe four or five years ago. And in terms of with the coding agent now is pretty powerful. But as you build a project, typically you want to have a plan in advance in terms of what you want, the capabilities and whatnot, and not jump to the coding agent immediately to build. So it is borrowing what we know as a good practice to do, but now codified it in a form for the coding agent that you work with. So if you build a brand new, like a greenfield project, for example, you build a spec up, what is it about? What are the capabilities that you want?
And then you have a brainstorming session with your coding agent to provide a context that it needs before you actually go and build it. I think there's a lot of good practices there that people have built around this. And I think most people recognize that's a good practice. I don't hear much more about it now because as people actually practicing it and the AI factory is another that's probably in the last few months of really how to infuse AI into the various steps of your software development life cycle.
The typical use case is, "Hey, somebody raised a bug. How do you get AI to take that from beginning to end of actually take the PR, do an analysis, trying to recreate the problem, come up with a fix, submit a PR, and then you go through the rest of the steps of review and testing and so on?" That is as we all have too many things to do, too many tasks. And I think if we can help automate that, that will accelerate another dimension to accelerating the software development life cycle.
Srini Penchikala: If the AI agents fix the bugs they created in the first place.
Chip Huyen: I want to ask this question about multi-agent system. When I say use multi-agent system, which pattern do usually go for? So for example, is this one orchestrator? Is it speeding up multiple workers? Or do you have different agents working in parallel? And if that's the case, then how do you do the communications across different agents working on the same complex task?
Arthur Casals: Basically, the formal definition goes back to agents working together in a social capacity in terms of their interaction with each other to solve a common problem. And in that sense, they can have a common goal, shared goals, distributed goals, and they can use orchestrators, they can use different architectural patterns. So for multi-agent systems per se, the definition is very broad in terms of how they can appear.
But in practice, what we see is mainly related to orchestration and communication. So since they have to work together and they have to do that in a social manner, which means communicating, so FIPA standards and things like that, everything revolves around orchestration and communication. So I have different protocols for communication, different architectures for orchestration. A lot of work on just these two.
Chip Huyen: Yes. So I'm very interested in agent-to-agent communications. So actually recently I use multi-agent a lot. So I have some complex tasks. I would get a bunch of agents to work together. So I actually build this protocol to let them like, "Okay, when you start working on a task, it's a part of big system. So as an agent working on the same task, so we can message them to make sure that you guys can coordinate and don't overlap". So what happened after that is that my task didn't get done at all. I keep getting a lot of messages and it turned out one agent started forwarding tasks to the other agent.
And then that agents forward that to another agent and then none of them did the work. And I'm spending half an hour just checking, "Okay, where does this go? We end up doing it?" And nobody did it. So I feel like communication is one thing, but for agent to realize, "Okay, this task is relevant in my name and I should do it", versus, "Okay just going to farm it out to a bunch of other agents". So you need to be aware of what other agents are doing and the scope of that. How do you manage that?
Arthur Casals: You try. You don't do it. You try to do that because thing is, depending on how you're tackling problem. For example, one of the simplest ways of doing that is using a blackboard messaging to see what everyone's doing, so they're just posting back and have the shared, let's say, context for that. But what if you have two multi-agent systems talking to each other? The problem starts that you have different IDs, you can have different ID schemas for agents, and you have different vocabulary, you have different definitions for the tasks. You don't have a shared states. You don't have shared states, period.
And then you have research, you have a lot of things. So for the past decades, when you see all the work that was produced, they're trying to tackle specific problems in specific setups. So for example, how do you tackle the problem of one multi-agent (system), so have shared environment, shared everything, trying to... You have to delegate a task that you can't do for some reason. So an agent starts doing something and for some reason wasn't able to keep doing that. You have to find another agent that's willing to do that.
Just for that, you need a setup. Are your agents benevolent? Do you have to put a premium on that or no? Let's take the happy path. All of them are benevolent, are trying to help. Okay, so here comes the big question. How do you define the equivalence of a task to achieving a goal? So I want you to get from point A to point B. Okay, so getting there by car or getting there by bus, it should be the same or not, they have time restriction. One thing that you'd find when you go deep and deep and deeper on that is that if you don't have a very specific shared setup or very specific shared conditions, the difficulty of the problem increases exponentially.
So one of the problems of the multi-agent systems area that we have and we know that we have is that we have a lack of standards. So we have standards for communicating, for example, have messaging standards. We do have some protocols in place, but you don't have a standard architecture or standard state description or standard environment description for that sense. That's part of the problem. You have two multi-agent systems with two different setups, two different structures, data structure, descriptions, whatever, and then you have to start tackling the particulars. So how do you do that? Then going back to your problem, how do you solve that?
You have to start by compartmentalizing your problem like, "Okay, this is my box. So I'm trying to solve this problem in this very specific box, these very specific conditions and set up and descriptions and good luck from here on". As long as you have an alien agent coming up or a different multi-agent system, so you have different boxes. So start over again. That's the usual path. Not sure it actually answers your question, but it is what it is.
Chip Huyen: No, it's a very hard problem. I'm wondering if any of you, also would love to hear from Hien and Daniel, have you used the box orchestrations ability of different models? First of all, in Claude or in Codex, you can ask an agent, "Okay, spin up my workers to do this task to make things faster". Have you ever used them and do you have any impressions on them?
Hien Luu: I haven't done that extensively. Maybe Daniel.
Daniel Dominguez: No. What I do is I work with them like an ecosystem of specialized agents. So for example, you could have one agent which is responsible for coding. We can have another which is responsible for testing. We can have another which is responsible for security, another for deployment. And perhaps you can have a supervisor agent coordinating all of them. So at that point, all of the challenge is to looking like a familiar to a distributed systems engineering.
So you have an identity, you have permissions, you have observability, you have orchestration, you have failure recovery and that communication between components between all those agents. So that's why I think agent engineering will increase becoming more like a system engineering discipline rather than just prompt engineering or orchestrate those agents individually.
Chip Huyen: Yes. So when you mentioned that made me think about the sandbox system, I did see from the trend from this year and last year is a lot of sandbox companies and I've been in sandbox for agents. So do you only using sandboxes for agents? For example, each agent had you work in an isolated work tree or something like that or it's dependent on the task?
Daniel Dominguez: Yes, for me it mainly dependent on the task.
Chip Huyen: So something I've been wondering about, so we have compute architecture, so AWS, we have GCP, we have Azure, and usually a company is a shop right now. "Hey, I'm a GCP shop. So one of my things is run on Google Cloud", or something like that. I wonder will the same thing happens to AI? Because a lot of companies have subscriptions or they have contract with multiple providers. Do you see a future where people will just stay with one provider, maybe OpenAI can have owners this model? Or do you think that people would have a multi-provider system?
Daniel Dominguez: Yes. In my opinion, I think it's going to happen the same that is happening with cloud computing. I mean, you are not tied to just one cloud provider, you work with multi-cloud providers. So with AI, it's going to happen the same. You are going to be tied to multi-AI providers working on different things of your workflow or different task. But I don't see just being attached to only one provider.
For example, I work with AWS, but I have multi-cloud providers working on different states of my workflow with GCP and Azure. So with AI, I think it's going to happen the same. You can say, "Okay, I prefer Anthropic, but in the end we'll end up working with OpenAI stuff, with Grok, with any other providers". So that's going to happen.
AI Evals and Guardrails [53:47]
Srini Penchikala: Thank you. Yes, I would like to touch a couple more topics and we can wrap up. It's been a great discussion, but I still have a couple more topics. I want to make sure that we share our thoughts with the audience. The first one is the evaluation frameworks. Definitely this has been a big topic this year. I even heard in one of the conference presentations that 2026 is the year of AI evaluations.
So I know there are a lot of different ways of doing this. There are harnesses and the LLMs being used as judges, LLM-as-Judge. So how do you measure AI effectiveness, AI agentic effectiveness in general? What kind of metrics do you see in your own experience? How do we make sure that the end-to-end process has enough checks and balances? Maybe Hien can start us off on that. What are you seeing in terms of agentic evaluation space?
Hien Luu: This is a very important topic for companies that are bringing their AI agents to production, particularly the one that for their customers, not so much about internal ones. If you look at example from DoorDash, they build an AI assistant for ordering food. You have other companies that are building for customer support agents for external users. And we all know that LLMs are not deterministics and building agents, they can take the wrong turn, they can make the wrong tool calls and stuff like that. So evaluations is a way to help us to make sure that the agents do the right thing for the right tasks at the highest level is that.
And without evaluation, how would you know that it's gone rogue or do something that's unexpected, not according to your company's policies and all that stuff like that. And there's methodology behind that. And by the way, we're going to have a sessions on that at QCon SF. One of the experts on evaluation is going to be there. And companies not only have to do this, but they have to incorporate this as one of their core steps in building AI agents. And a lot of company ending up building something called evaluation harness, which help drive the whole evaluation flow from getting the data, running the evaluation or tests, as we all know tests, right? And then assessing the quality at the end.
And that help drive the decision whether it's a go or no-go for release. So anytime that you're building serious customer-facing agent, you have to incorporate and spend time and effort of doing evaluation right. If you build an internal agent, you're probably not going to spend a whole lot of time on it, but if you are building a real serious agent for your company, then definitely a must. And you see many examples across companies from LinkedIn, DoorDash, Ubers and such, and many cases study on that.
Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Hien, definitely. I think this area is going to see more it all comes together. So any other panelists, any other thoughts from anybody else? How do you evaluate your own AI systems?
Daniel Dominguez: Yes, I think I completely agree with the idea that this year is becoming the year of evaluations for models and agents. So once an agent can perform an action, evaluating only the model is not enough. So you have to evaluate the whole system, you have to evaluate the model, the tool, the context, the agent loop, the environment. So here is where the metrics changed as well.
So it's not only whether the answer was correct, so it's whether the agent completed the task, how much cost, how long it took, how many interventions were necessary, and whether it did something unsafe along the way. So I think all these evaluations were just starting to see how are we going to evaluate all this workflow regarding agents and regarding LLMs and regarding the interactions that they do in our job.
Physical AI [57:49]
Srini Penchikala: Yes, good point. All those metrics are more relevant now with the overall. Yes. One more topic I definitely want to highlight in this discussion is Physical AI. Daniel, you've been looking at this for a while. We talked about this last year as well. How do we bring intelligence into the real world? So this AI agent is a software system, how do we bring that into the hardware, whether they're robots or whatnot? Now they're being called collaborative robots, cobots, and then even self-driving cars. Daniel, maybe you can start us off on this. What do you see here, what's happening and what we should be paying attention to?
Daniel Dominguez: Basically it's saying, "How do we bring AI into the physical world?" So over the last few years we have spent the time putting intelligence into software. Now we're starting to connect that intelligence to machines that can perceive and act in a physical world. So what you said, we are starting to see robotics, we're starting to see autonomous vehicles, drones, and industrial systems are now part of this transition. What I think makes physical AI fundamentally different from software agents is that mistakes have physical consequences on the physical AI.
So one thing is that in software, an agent can make a mistake generating their own file, but a robot can move their own equator. So it's going to be a whole different level of mistakes. So the reliability, simulations, safety, verification, evaluations are going to become more and more important in the physical world. So based on that, all the foundation models for robots that are happening right now, another important shift is that robotics are starting to benefit from more of the same foundational model approach that transformed the language and vision.
So instead of programming every individual behavior manually, we're increasingly seeing models that combine vision, language, perception, and actions. So is that the robot can potentially understand instructions like, I don't know, "Pick up that object and put that on the table", and translate that into a high level intent of a physical work. So as you mentioned, there are a lot of projects regarding the physical model like Nvidia, like Google robots, where all these multimodal models are taking language and visual information and producing action for robots.
So that connection between language, perception, actions is what makes the space of robotics and physical AI more interesting. So we're going to start seeing things like simulation for digital twins robots, all the things that are going to happen for open robotics, all the things that are going to happen from AI agents to physical agents. All of this is just going to start moving faster and faster over the next year because right now the AI is here. Now we have to put it in our physical world.
Robots and Vision Language Models [59:59]
Srini Penchikala: Yes, that's going to be definitely one of the applications that's going to see a lot more attention, a lot more developments, whether it's manufacturing or any other physical industrial use cases. Any other thoughts? Chip, robots and vision language models, how do you see them working?
Chip Huyen: Yes, I think it's very, very exciting. Definitely a lot will say that it's the next frontier to get the models into the real world and we see a lot of progress. And I think the only challenge is that there are several challenges. We keep saying that robotics is like cars, like LLM to say, "Okay, we know we have a lot of robots in the real world". We have Waymos everywhere. We have Zoox. I'm not sure Zoox is out. So I have never driven one, but I see the advertising for it. So we see a lot of robots in the real world.
So people keep telling me that, "Oh, we know how to train massive LLMs, multimodal stuff. We know how to train robots setup in cars, we should know how to train robots to work with real world". But I don't think it's quite the same. So one big difference between robotics, models and LLMs, it's that the challenge of backtracking. For LLMs, when you're training on a virtual, on the computer, if it makes a mistake, you can run back. You can reset the state and continue. So you can do a lot of explorations and pick the best state.
You can't really do exactly robotics. You can't get a robot, "Okay, there's a staircase that's there". The robot falls and it breaks. You can't just run it back and get the same robot as before. So it makes exploration extremely, extremely hard. And another challenge is data. And so I have been looking into a lot of robotic setups. So a lot of them had to raise a lot of money. So having five of these companies raised what, billion dollars? I don't remember off the top of my head. We have a bunch of companies and a Generalist, Physical Intelligence, Sunday, Skild AI, which I'm very excited about.
If you look into it, the main difference is the approach on achieved data. So I think that people are still betting on what kind of data would help robot models to scale. Something tricky with AI models is that sometimes when it's small, they don't quite work. A model only works really well when they're big enough. For a long time with other language models, they generate trash and they suddenly boom, you have GD3 and GD4 and it's suddenly everywhere. So a lot of the bet is like, "Okay, the models are not working well yet. Is this because the approach is wrong or is it because you do not have enough data yet?"
So people had to make a bet on, "Will this kind of architecture, will this kind of training algorithm, will this kind of data be the right approach to scale?" So we see a lot of these companies making a big bet. So there are some companies that say, "Okay, we need real robotics data". So in China, the Chinese government is investing a lot of money into having a robot training center. We have humans operating real robots and just collect a lot of this data and it's extremely expensive. So a lot of people were like, "Okay, we do need this type of data. Maybe you can just go with some kind of video".
If humans can learn from watching video, can robots do it? So it was collecting a lot of this in videos. We have people paying people in different countries, just wearing the camera on their head and collecting videos. So it's very interesting, but since a lot of companies go into middle ground, like Physical Intelligence, I think it's Generalist, only Sunday they have gloves. So they were like, "Okay, videos are not put in for haptic information". Because a lot of time you can't judge from a video how much force it should put into squeezing an egg or a strawberry.
So you need real haptic information so that you have some gloves, people have to wear them and charge money for the object and get data to train the robots. So it's the middle way because you don't have the full robots, it's a lot cheaper, but it's also not just videos. But anyway, I ramble on. I think it's a very exciting space.
Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Chip. Yes, we are running short on the time remaining in this meeting. I know there are a lot of topics. We have talked about the topics that we think are definitely important to be aware of, but there are other topics that we can probably... We won't have time today, but I just want to quickly mention you can follow up offline as separate podcasts or articles.
So there's AI governance platforms that are coming up and then there's AI security and regulations is an important topic. AI observability is an evolving topic as well. And definitely the AI SRE and AI ops are also getting a lot of attention. So do you see anything else happening at very high level before we wrap up? Arthur, do you have any comments?
Arthur Casals: Yes, I think we could relating multi-agent systems and AI engineering because not as hopeless that might have seen when it's reship, but there's a lot of things that we could bind together and bring together to correlate to how we solve problems that we have using work that has already been developed. So that would be a great topic.
Wrap Up and Predictions for Next Year
Srini Penchikala: We can start wrapping up. So this is my favorite part of the podcast to request each panelist to make a prediction for next year and we'll take a checkpoint next year and see how these predictions have been realized. So yes, we can start off with Chip, what do you see? What's your prediction? If there is one thing you'd like to see happen or you think is going to happen in the AI space, what would it be?
Chip Huyen: I really want to see US robot companies that have robots ready to be bought. I know it's just very painful. I feel like in China you can just buy a robot, in the US you just cannot get from an American company yet. So I really want to see that shipping. I feel like we've been waiting for OpenAI and Anthropic IPOs for a while. I think they delay. Very curious to see how that's going to impact the market because if the IPOs go well, is the market going to go well, but if IPOs don't go well, what implication would it have for the funding and the AI market? I would expect to see a lot of cheaper and faster models, the TypeSafe style of model would be very interesting.
Srini Penchikala: Thank you. How about you, Daniel? What's your prediction?
Daniel Dominguez: I think we're going to start seeing limitations on AI. So for example, the phrase is going to be the energy. So all the AI infrastructure is becoming extremely power hungry. So I think the access for electricity, the capacity, cooling data center locations, that is going to become a biggest constraint for the growth of AI. So we may start seeing energy crisis for AI. The second prediction that I would like to share is like a futuristic prediction, but I think it's going to happen that all this AI infrastructure is going to start moving beyond the traditional data center and it's going to move into space. So I think putting AI into space is going to be more efficient, probably it's going to take a little longer, but it's going to be more efficient than keeping the AI here on earth.
And finally, I think the AI competition between the United States and China is going to increasingly look like a technological Cold War. So it's not about who has the best model anymore or who has the best chips. So it has to be with who has the manufacturer, who has the energy, who has the data center, who has the open models, the supply chains, and the access to compute. So we are already seeing that semiconductor access and domestic chip productions are becoming strategic issues in that relationship. So I think that for 2027, some of the biggest AI stories may actually happen outside the models themselves. And it's going to be more about the energy, the chips, the infrastructure, and on the geopolitics.
Srini Penchikala: And Hien?
Hien Luu: Just two things. Every AI agent will incorporate some form of the Jev model into the AI agents. And more and more of the communications are going to be between agent and agents moving forward as we figure out how to build, operate and bring all these agents to production.
Srini Penchikala: And Arthur?
Arthur Casals: I'll circle back to what I said at the beginning. I think and I expect that the most successful AI deployments that we will see will be much narrower than what we see right now in terms that rather than one agent with access to everything, we'll see a lot of things using smaller specialized agents for mixed models, for well-defined tasks. And the big difference will be in the surrounding system.
So you have trusted data, leave the permissions tests, and does it not back your visibility, but a way to see what the agent did and whether it's actually helped. Teams can not only do that, but can actually measure the cost and quality of a completed task. You can have ROI for tasks, not just the number of tokens of agents that use it. I think that this will be a great leap.
It aligns well with what Hien said on Jev and what Daniel said on the shifting away from big models, but I think that's where I put my chips in.
Srini Penchikala: Thanks, Arthur. Yes, I think I'll take a quick one minute to wrap up my comments. AI is a significant technology shift. And as we all know by now, after almost four years, it is not a fad or some temporary blip on the technology radar. It is here to stay. It is one of the major technology waves in the last, I don't know, 20-plus years. So my advice and request to our audience is we should take advantage of this technology transformation, not be afraid of it. Find ways to use AI tools to automate any workflows in your day-to-day life, whether it is in the office or in your personal life.
I mean, this is a tool that we can use to find more time to do the important things in our lives, let the agents and the tools do the routine tasks. So my prediction for next year is definitely, I agree with all of you, AI will be even a bigger part of our daily lives. And I always say this as a prediction, and I would like to see whenever we don't talk about AI anymore, it has become part of the fabric of our lives. I think then we can say we have really arrived. And so I think maybe more evolution, more development, but I think the niche areas will be settled where AI will be really valuable and where human intelligence is still required.
So thank you all for your time. We took a little bit longer, but there are so many topics and we can go on forever, but I think we need to wrap this up and we will follow up with any other topics later. So thank you for joining today. Have a great one. Until next time, thank you.

articles.title: Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
articles.text:
Omio founder’s advice to entrepreneurs: Find a problem worth solving and stick with it
At TechSparks 2026, Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of Omio Group, advised entrepreneurs to think globally from day one, tackle difficult problems, and stay committed for the long term.
AI has made it easier to build products, but entrepreneurs still need to decide what to build and whether they can stay committed long enough to turn an idea into a sustainable business.
For Naren Shaam, Founder and CEO of Omio Group, the answer is to solve difficult problems, stay focused, and avoid chasing the next big thing.
Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Shaam spoke about building Omio, which operates across 56 countries, and why Indian entrepreneurs should think globally from the beginning.
“If I were to rebuild Omio today, I would start here because there is so much growth and opportunity in India today. But the principles remain the same. You need to go after really hard problems and focus on solving them for a very long time,” he told YourStory.
Shaam founded Omio after identifying a problem in global transportation: operators had separate systems for trains, buses, and ferries. After moving to Germany, he spent two and a half years working on the supply side before launching the company's first product.
“Building a billion-dollar business is really hard. The stories of companies going from zero to a billion dollars very quickly are rare. Don’t get inspired by the exceptions as for most, it is a daily grind,” he said.
Think global from day one
Shaam believes entrepreneurs need not wait until they have succeeded in India before expanding overseas. While some businesses cater to local needs, sectors such as education, healthcare, and deeptech offer opportunities across markets.
“If your problem statement is already global, you should start early. We entered 30 countries in our first three or four years, even though people told us to win Germany first. That bet, despite the capital required and the mistakes we had to correct, probably helped make us become the company we are today,” he said.
AI has also made international expansion easier. Shaam recalled that when Omio expanded in Germany, it employed around 30 people to handle translations. That work is now done by AI.
However, lower barriers to entry also make it easier for competitors to copy products. Shaam believes entrepreneurs must therefore be more careful about where they invest their time and resources.
“The onus moves from bias to action to judgement: what should I focus on? Which industry has a bigger moat? What will that moat look like 10 years from now? Starting is easy now but choosing what to pursue and committing to it is the hard part,” he said.
AI may change distribution, but trust remains important
Shaam said AI agents could change digital commerce, including how people book travel. However, widespread adoption will depend on bringing down costs and finding sustainable business models.
“Consumers need these agents to be very cheap before they penetrate the market. There is a cost barrier and a business-model problem to solve. I see this as a major transformation and not an overnight event,” he explained.
Even as more transactions move to AI agents, Shaam believes businesses will still need to deliver reliable services in the physical world.
“Real life happens outside the internet. If an agent buys something or orders food, people need to trust that it will arrive every single time. Businesses that can solve these operational problems at scale will have something valuable to build on,” he said.
For aspiring founders, his advice was to focus on solving a problem rather than on the appeal of becoming an entrepreneur.
“Find a great problem. Don’t become an entrepreneur simply because you want to be one. This is a journey with long periods of darkness, and you need to be passionate enough about what you’re solving to keep going,” Shaam concluded.

articles.title: Hiring Your First Employee: Accounts, Devices and Access to Sort Out Before Day One - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Preparing for Your First Hire: Why It Matters
Bringing on your first employee is a significant milestone for any business. It signals growth, opportunity, and the promise of new capabilities. However, alongside the excitement comes a need for careful preparation-especially regarding accounts, devices, and access management. Without a solid plan, the onboarding process can become chaotic, leading to delays, security risks, or unhappy employees.
According to a survey by BambooHR, 31% of new hires quit within the first six months due to poor onboarding experiences. This statistic underscores the importance of having your systems and processes ready before that first day. Ensuring that accounts are set up correctly, devices are provisioned, and access is granted appropriately can set the tone for a productive and secure working relationship from the outset.
Moreover, studies show that effective onboarding can improve new hire retention by 82% and productivity by over 70%. These numbers demonstrate that investing time and resources into preparing for your first employee pays off in the long run.
Setting Up Employee Accounts: The Foundation of Access
One of the first steps in onboarding a new employee involves setting up their digital accounts. These can include email, internal communication platforms, project management tools, and access to any cloud services your company uses. It’s critical these accounts are ready before the employee’s start date to avoid unnecessary downtime or frustration.
To streamline this process, many businesses turn to external service providers. For example, companies opting for tech managed by Norterra benefit from expert support in managing IT infrastructure and user accounts, ensuring a seamless setup. These services can automate account creation, enforce password policies, and integrate Single Sign-On (SSO) solutions, which enhance security while simplifying the user experience.
A Gartner report highlights that organizations with automated onboarding processes reduce setup time by up to 60%, enhancing employee satisfaction and productivity. Automating account management also minimizes human error, reducing the risk of granting inappropriate access.
In addition, automated account provisioning can help ensure compliance with industry regulations such as GDPR or HIPAA by enforcing standardized security protocols. This reduces the risk of costly violations and protects sensitive company and customer data.
Devices: Provisioning the Tools for Success
Alongside accounts, the physical or virtual devices your new hire will use need careful consideration. Whether this is a company laptop, desktop, or mobile device, it must be configured with the necessary software, security tools, and company policies. Delays in device provisioning can hamper an employee’s ability to contribute meaningfully from day one.
Investing in a standardized device provisioning process helps maintain consistency and security. IT teams or managed service providers can pre-install essential software, configure VPN access, and apply encryption or endpoint protection solutions. Businesses that lack internal IT resources often find value in partnering with firms like the OCCSI security team, specializing in cybersecurity and device management, to ensure compliance with security standards.
According to a report from Cisco, businesses experience 70% fewer security incidents when devices are managed and monitored continuously. This highlights the importance of proper device management from the start to protect company assets and data.
Furthermore, standardized devices simplify troubleshooting and maintenance, reducing downtime and IT support costs. Having a consistent hardware and software environment also facilitates smoother updates and patch management, which are essential for security.
Access Management: Balancing Security and Usability
Granting access to systems and data demands a delicate balance between security and usability. Over-permissioning users can lead to data breaches, while under-permissioning can stall productivity. Implementing the principle of least privilege-that is, providing employees only the access necessary to perform their job functions-is a best practice that should be embedded in your onboarding process.
Role-based access control (RBAC) simplifies this by assigning permissions based on job titles or functions. When setting up your first employee, clearly define their role and map out corresponding access rights. Additionally, leveraging identity and access management (IAM) tools can automate access provisioning and revocation, reducing the administrative burden and enhancing security.
Recent data shows that 81% of data breaches involve compromised credentials, emphasizing the need for robust access controls and regular monitoring. Ensuring your new hire’s access is correctly provisioned-and promptly revoked if necessary-is crucial for protecting your business.
Implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA) is another critical layer of security. MFA requires users to provide two or more verification factors to gain access, significantly reducing the chances of unauthorized entry. Many IAM solutions integrate MFA by default, making it easier to enforce strong security policies from day one.
Training and Documentation: Supporting Your New Team Member
Beyond technical setup, preparing documentation and training materials related to IT policies, security protocols, and device usage is vital. Clear communication helps new employees understand expectations and reduces the likelihood of accidental security lapses.
Consider providing onboarding guides that cover acceptable use policies, password management, and procedures for reporting security incidents. This proactive approach not only supports compliance but fosters a culture of security awareness from day one.
Regular training sessions, whether virtual or in-person, can reinforce these policies and provide a forum for new hires to ask questions. According to a report by the Ponemon Institute, organizations that provide cybersecurity training reduce the risk of a data breach by up to 50%. This demonstrates the tangible benefits of investing in employee education as part of your onboarding process.
Additionally, encourage feedback from new employees about the onboarding experience. This can help identify gaps in your processes and improve future hires’ experiences, creating a continuous improvement loop.
Legal and Compliance Considerations
When hiring your first employee, it’s also essential to address legal and compliance aspects related to accounts, devices, and access. Depending on your industry and location, you may be subject to labor laws, data protection regulations, and cybersecurity standards that dictate how employee information and access should be handled.
Ensure that contracts and employment agreements include clauses about acceptable use of company devices and data. Inform new hires about your privacy policies and any monitoring practices in place to protect company assets. Consulting with legal counsel or HR experts can help you craft appropriate documentation that shields your business and clarifies expectations.
Additionally, maintaining audit trails of account creation, access grants, and device assignments supports compliance and can be invaluable during security investigations or audits.
Building a Scalable Onboarding Framework
While your first hire may be a small step, it’s important to build processes that scale as your team grows. Establishing clear workflows for account creation, device provisioning, and access management now will save time and reduce errors in the future.
Consider creating checklists or automated workflows that guide managers and IT staff through each onboarding step. Using centralized identity management systems and device management platforms can streamline administration and improve oversight.
By investing in a robust onboarding framework early, you set your company up for smooth expansion, minimizing disruptions and maintaining security as you add more employees.
Conclusion: Building a Strong Foundation with Proper Preparation
Hiring your first employee is a pivotal moment that requires more than just finding the right person. It demands meticulous preparation behind the scenes-setting up accounts, provisioning devices, and managing access thoughtfully. Leveraging managed IT services and cybersecurity experts can ease this process, ensuring your new team member is productive and secure from their very first day.
By prioritizing these elements in your onboarding strategy, you not only improve the employee experience but also protect your business as it grows. Proper preparation today lays the groundwork for a scalable, secure, and efficient operation tomorrow.
Taking the time to plan and execute a comprehensive onboarding process reflects your commitment to your new hire’s success and your company’s future. Remember, the foundation you build before day one will influence how effectively your employee integrates and contributes. With the right accounts, devices, and access sorted out in advance, you pave the way for a thriving, secure workplace culture.

articles.title: Una eléctrica alemana lanza un plan de “electricidad gamer” para hogares de alto consumo: recomienda superar 2.500 kWh anuales para compensar su precio base más alto y afirma usar energía renovable
articles.text:
El suministrador municipal de Krefeld (SWK Energie) vende una tarifa de luz enfocada a gamers. Se llama meinGAMING. Y su web se dirige a los que “consumen más y esperan más”. Por ejemplo, el que tiene en casa 4 ordenadores PC con RTX 5090. O bien el que carga 4 coches eléctricos diariamente. Pero todos tienen la misma luz.
En las preguntas frecuentes de la empresa se establece en qué contexto es interesante esta tarifa. Está pensada para los usuarios que consumen más de 2.500 kWh/año. Sea por gaming, streaming o porque tienen muchos dispositivos en funcionamiento. Es un valor orientativo de rentabilidad. Porque los precios son más altos en la parte fija que en otras tarifas, aunque el precio por kWh es menor. De hecho, si el consumo es claramente inferior, en la web se advierte que la parte fija es más importante y que quizás debería buscarse otra tarifa.
Los precios varían según la zona y el consumo. Los precios en la página de Colonia (3.500 kWh/año; 24 meses de contrato) son 26,68 céntimos/kWh y 25,16 euros/mes de fijo (25 de octubre de 2026). El suministro básico en esta zona, según esa página, cuesta 31,48 céntimos/kWh y 262,67 euros/año de fijo. En Múnich (las mismas condiciones), el precio es 29,88 céntimos/kWh y 16,69 euros/mes. Así que poco sentido tiene hablar de media nacional. Además, los precios varían con las semanas.
Tampoco es la más barata. En Colonia, la empresa afirma que se ahorran 228,75 euros en el primer año respecto al suministro básico (con bonus de 100 euros). Sin bonus serían 128,75 euros. En la propia tabla de comparación de la empresa aparece en el puesto 18 de 103. La más barata queda unos 70 euros por debajo en este primer año.
El consumo que cuenta es el de toda la casa
Ahora viene lo interesante (por lo menos si tienes un PC potente). NVIDIA informa de que la RTX 5090 tiene una potencia total de la gráfica de 575 vatios. Supongamos que nuestro equipo completo (con monitor) tiene 700W. Si jugamos 30 h/semana, tenemos un consumo anual de 1.092 kWh. Esto es menos de la mitad del umbral. Además, en un hogar de dos personas (viviendo en un piso con agua caliente central), el consumo medio es de 1.900 kWh/año. Así que, sumando ambas cifras, tenemos unos 2.992 kWh. Aquí es donde pasa el umbral. No es el PC.
Con los datos de la tabla (4,80 céntimos/kWh menos que el suministro básico en Colonia) tendríamos una ventaja de unos 52 euros al año por estas 1.092 kWh de PC. Solo si el resto de nuestro consumo compensa la cuota fija.
Por otro lado, están las condiciones. Podemos elegir 12 o 24 meses de contrato (con diferente precio). Después no tiene fecha de finalización. También cabe destacar que la garantía de precio (de hasta 24 meses) es solo por el precio de la energía (es decir, no bloquean impuestos/recargos). Por otro lado, existe un bonus de nuevo cliente (en esta página de Colonia es de 100 euros). Este bonus se aplica al finalizar el primer periodo. No se resta de la cuota mensual.
Esta tarifa solo funciona con el contador habitual de la vivienda. No funciona en el caso de que tengamos un contador adicional de calefacción (dos tarifas). El tiempo de cambio es de 2 a 6 semanas. La empresa se encarga de dar de baja el antiguo contrato.
El origen de la electricidad renovable
También destacan que su luz es renovable. En la web de la tarifa dicen que proviene de centrales hidroeléctricas de Europa. Que están respaldadas por garantías de origen (la cantidad que suministran está respaldada). Y que están certificadas anualmente por TÜV NORD CERT. No dicen que físicamente provengan de estas centrales.
Para entender qué certifica esto, veamos el caso español. Los certificados los emite la CNMC. En su blog de la CNMC explican que las garantías de origen son una certificación electrónica de que una determinada cantidad de electricidad ha sido producida a partir de renovables. Se trata de un sistema paralelo al flujo de electricidad. “No es posible conocer la procedencia real de los electrones que llegan a los hogares”.
Aunque en España no se puede contratar, el método sí es exportable. Primero es necesario conocer cuánto consume cada cosa. En un test de Xataka Home se midió un equipo con RTX 2070 que consume 200,6 W en pleno rendimiento. La gráfica de la RTX 5090 llega a 575 W (solo la gráfica).
Es importante medir el consumo de nuestro equipo. El segundo paso es analizar nuestro consumo anual (el de la factura). Es el dato que realmente cuenta. Para ello podemos usar el comparador de la CNMC.

articles.title: Vous ne pourrez bientôt plus consulter Reddit sans y être connecté
articles.text:
Pourquoi et comment Reddit va devenir une “expérience principalement connectée”
Un "grand changement" arrive sur Reddit : dans les prochains mois, il ne sera plus possible de consulter du contenu sur le site communautaire sans y être connecté. Un bouleversement que son PDG explique de plusieurs manières.
Ce 29 octobre 2026, via un post suivant l'annonce des résultats de Reddit du troisième trimestre 2026, son PDG Steve "spez" Huffman a fait une annonce majeure. Dans peu de temps, l'ouverture caractéristique de la plateforme, qui permet notamment d'en consulter le contenu sans y être connecté, ce sera terminé.
C'est la fin d'une ère pour Reddit (et l'Internet ouvert)
Comme le souligne l'homme, depuis son lancement en 2005, la majorité du contenu de Reddit est accessible sans avoir besoin d'y être connecté. Qui n'a jamais trouvé une réponse à une question sur ce gigantesque forum en quelques secondes depuis une recherche Google grâce à ce système ouvert ? Eh bien, malgré des chiffres de visites et de revenus en hausse, c'est une page qui va se tourner.
	
Il s'agit d'une évolution majeure pour Reddit, que nous ne prenons pas à la légère. Mais je pense que c'est la bonne prochaine étape pour la plateforme et pour notre avenir.
Trois points viennent principalement expliquer ce changement, qui risque de drastiquement réduire le nombre de visiteurs de Reddit.
Tout d'abord, la plateforme veut proposer davantage de personnalisation aux utilisateurs. Huffman explique : "Notre objectif est de vous aider à trouver ce qui vous intéresse le plus et de favoriser l'esprit communautaire, les liens et le sentiment d'appartenance qui font de Reddit ce qu'il est. Ce changement va dans ce sens : il vous permettra de découvrir plus facilement ce qui vous intéresse le plus et de vous rendre rapidement là où vous le souhaitez."
Ensuite, il s'agit d'une mesure de protection contre les bots et les IA qui aspirent et utilisent le contenu de Reddit sans besoin d'être connecté. En octobre, Reddit aurait ainsi perdu une moyenne d'un million de visites hebdomadaires depuis les moteurs de recherche, dopés aux résumés IA.
	
Reddit est désormais tellement vaste que, sans une certaine personnalisation, il perd tout son intérêt. Pire encore, il ne fonctionne tout simplement plus.
Enfin, la question de la publicité est également centrale. Le PDG déclare que ce système de connexion obligatoire "permet de proposer des publicités plus pertinentes. C'est bénéfique pour les résultats commerciaux, mais aussi pour les utilisateurs. Une publicité non ciblée n'est qu'un gaspillage d'espace pour tout le monde."
Personnalisation, protection et publicités
Concernant la date d'arrivée, des tests vont être menés sur des marchés en dehors des États-Unis sans plus de précision dans les prochains mois. Le but sera d'évaluer l'impact de ce changement sur les utilisateurs et sur le business lui-même, afin de fixer les bonnes limites. Il n'est donc pas impossible que la plateforme finisse par faire machine arrière si ses visites et ses revenus ne suivent pas.
Pour tenter de rassurer, Huffman précise : "Et pour être clair, quand on parle de « se connecter », on parle littéralement de se connecter. On n'a pas besoin de votre nom. On n'a pas besoin de savoir qui vous êtes. On n'a pas besoin de connaître votre identité." De plus, il souligne que le mode incognito a été retravaillé dans l'application et que la personnalisation peut être désactivée.

articles.title: Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
articles.text:
Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain
- Date:
- October 26, 2026
- Source:
- Norwegian University of Science and Technology
- Summary:
- Scientists have filmed tiny magnetic vortices called skyrmions melting out of an organized lattice for the first time, revealing new ways to manipulate these unusual structures. The breakthrough could help make brain-like computers a reality, potentially enabling dramatically smaller and more energy-efficient technology.
- Share:
Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.
A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.
Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).
Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.
"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.
Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers
The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.
One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.
"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.
Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.
Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.
The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.
Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time
Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.
Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.
In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.
"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.
The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.
A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing
Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.
The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.
"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.
Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.
By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.
"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Raphael Gruber, Jan Rothörl, Simon M. Fröhlich, Maarten A. Brems, Fabian Kammerbauer, Maria-Andromachi Syskaki, Elizabeth M. Jefremovas, Sachin Krishnia, Asle Sudbø, Peter Virnau, Mathias Kläui. Real-time observation of topological defect dynamics mediating two-dimensional skyrmion lattice melting. Nature Nanotechnology, 2025; 20 (10): 1405 DOI: 10.1038/s41565-025-01977-2
