articles.title: Banks must become ‘invisible’ to compete in digital finance
articles.text:
Banks must anticipate customers’ needs and embed financial services into everyday transactions to compete with digital platforms, executives from Access Holdings and OPay told Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos.
Daniel Awe, head of Fintech Foundry at Access Holdings, said banking’s next phase would require institutions to offer services when customers needed them, rather than wait for people to visit a branch or open an application.
“The future of banks is going to be in everyday people, where banks become invisible,” he said during a panel titled “The Next Bank: Competing in the Age of Programmable Money”.
His argument extends the shift from branch banking to mobile services. Moving a transaction onto a phone changes how customers access a bank; integrating finance into activities such as paying school fees or replenishing stock changes when they encounter it.
“When the customer is engaging you, it’s not the future of banking. It’s the banks that now have to place themselves in the life of the customer,” Awe said.
Chukwudinma Okafor, chief compliance officer at OPay Nigeria, said the starting point should be customers’ practical needs, rather than the availability of new technology.
“For us at OPay, the major focus is just to address one thing, and that’s customers. You have to meet the customers where they need you,” he said.
OPay sent developers, technology professionals and sales teams to markets across Nigeria to observe how traders worked and gather feedback, Okafor said. Requests for different sounds to signal successful and failed point-of-sale transactions illustrated how small changes could make a service more useful.
The example highlighted a distinction in the discussion: anticipating customers’ needs can involve sophisticated infrastructure, but the improvement customers value may be straightforward.
Modernising the systems
Awe said traditional banks would also need to overhaul the infrastructure supporting their products. Conventional core banking systems alone were insufficient for competing with fintechs and technology companies offering financial services.
That transition would have to be gradual, preserving reliability and compliance while addressing the risks created by increasingly interconnected systems.
“Whatever you want to achieve, you have to put security in the middle,” he said.
Okafor said digital-first companies had benefited from starting with more modern infrastructure, including cloud-based systems, while established banks were increasingly adopting similar technologies.
Despite their competition for customers, both speakers argued that banks and fintechs remained dependent on one another.
Awe said partnerships combined banks’ financial capabilities with fintechs’ ability to serve particular customer groups. Some businesses required approaches that companies such as OPay could provide more readily, he added.
Okafor pointed to fintechs’ reliance on commercial banks for settlement and the handling of customer funds. Cooperation was also necessary to respond to fraud when money moved between institutions.
“Ultimately, we need each other for the ecosystem to work well,” he said.
The discussion also turned to Nigeria’s approach to cryptocurrency and stablecoins, with Awe describing differing priorities among regulators.
He said the Securities and Exchange Commission had shown greater appetite for cryptocurrency-related activities, while the Central Bank of Nigeria had been more cautious because of monetary policy and consumer protection concerns.
According to Awe, the central bank was examining stablecoin use cases through a regulatory sandbox, allowing approved participants to test services under supervision.
He characterised stablecoins as less volatile than other cryptocurrencies. That distinction was his assessment of their appeal to the regulator, rather than a guarantee of their stability.
For banks weighing new technologies, the broader challenge identified by the panel was to make services easier to access while maintaining the security and reliability customers expected. Becoming less visible in a transaction would require substantial work on the systems behind it.

articles.title: ¿Quieres invertir en criptomonedas? Conoce su valor y cómo ha fluctuado en las últimas horas
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 77.996,72 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de 0,285% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de -0,823% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.230,99 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de -0,07%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 707,58 dólares, con un cambio de -6,73%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 55.711 dólares, tras una variación de -5.8099546.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,08 dólares tras presentar un cambio de -4,69% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Su avance en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: Platform Calgary unveils 10 most promising startups ahead of Calgary Innovation Week |
articles.text:
Platform Calgary is in for a buzzy beginning to November as the innovation hub prepares for its annual Calgary Innovation Week celebration.
Kicking off on Nov. 2 and running until Nov. 5, Calgary Innovation Week is a city-wide event celebrating Calgary’s tech, innovation, and startup ecosystem. This year’s events include seminars, workshops, networking events, and the annual Launch Party celebrating Calgary’s 10 most promising startups for 2026.
“The startups at the heart of Calgary’s tech ecosystem are driving remarkable sector growth in 2026,” said Jen Lussier, Platform Calgary’s CEO, in an emailed release. “Under our theme ‘Built Here. Backed Here,’ we are proving world-class startups can launch, scale and thrive here.”
“The startups at the heart of Calgary’s tech ecosystem are driving remarkable sector growth in 2026.”
Jen Lussier, Platform Calgary
The week is scheduled to start with a keynote speech from Jay Kiew, an alumnus of Deloitte, TELUS, and ADP, who was recognized as a Thinkers360 thought leader on agentic AI and change management. Kiew’s keynote will touch on how companies can navigate uncertainty, build resilient teams, and scale effectively.
Other notable events include sessions on roadmapping for quantum for startup founders, an introduction to vibe coding, attracting financing via crowdfunding, and a seminar celebrating and discussing the recent multimillion-dollar acquisition of Calgary’s PurposeMed by dating platform Grindr, with PurposeMed COO and co-founder Pete MacLeod.
RELATED: Platform Calgary appoints Jennifer Lussier as CEO
Innovation Week closes out with the 16th iteration of Platform Calgary’s Launch Party, showcasing this year’s 10 most promising startups. The 2026 cohort includes:
- Agrivanna: an AgTech startup using AI to optimize livestock grazing operations.
- Black Owl Systems: an accounting software provider built for CFOs and corporate finance.
- Candidly AI: an AI tool for garnering stakeholder feedback at scale.
- Fledge: a digital wellness platform.
- Leeg: a workforce intelligence platform.
- Made It Legal: a contract review tool and AI platform.
- Paradigm Inputs: a commerce and ergonomic intelligence platform for crop-input brokers in Western Canada.
- Splice N Connect: a startup manufacturing non-invasive sensors to monitor power grid cables and prevent blackouts.
- Verano.ai: an agentic AI platform automating regulatory monitoring and compliance.
- Waypoint Budget: An AI-driven personal finance app that automates budgeting.
Last year’s Innovation Week brought 70 organizations together to host events, with hundreds of attendees. Platform Calgary reported that of those attendees, more than 35 percent were entrepreneurs or corporate professionals, and more than 24 percent were tech professionals.

articles.title: Benchmarking Nvidia’s Vera CPU for the data center — standalone Vera tested against Granite Rapids-AP and EPYC Turin
articles.text:
Benchmarking Nvidia’s Vera CPU for the data center — standalone Vera tested against Granite Rapids-AP and EPYC Turin
Vera debuts with strong Python performance and unmatched memory bandwidth.
Nvidia’s Vera CPU is an important next step in the company’s years-long spearheading of AI infrastructure buildout. It’s arriving just as the shift to agentic AI workflows has created unprecedented demand for data center CPUs, and it’s designed specifically for this moment, at least according to Nvidia’s marketing bullet points. Although the idea that anyone developed a CPU for a shift in demand that arose just six months ago is reaching, as our benchmarks below show, Nvidia’s claims about Vera aren’t full of hot air.
Based on the workloads we have now — there aren’t standardized end-to-end agentic benchmarks focused on the CPU right now — Vera has strong indicators about its usefulness in agentic workflows. It offers chart-topping performance in Python, for instance, which makes up much of the backbone of the AI software ecosystem.
It also shows commanding memory bandwidth, both at the socket level and system level, with the high-speed C2C interconnect between Vera chips. In contentious agentic environments where agents may be querying large databases, that bandwidth is critical.
Specialization is one thing, but Vera is arriving in a hotly contested server market with custom Arm chips penetrating the data center and the old guard of x86 chips from AMD and Intel, which not only have a foundation in the data center, but also an extensive list of clients that work with their systems. Regardless of how Vera performs, that’s no small undertaking.
What’s surprising about Vera isn’t that it performs well in these agentic-adjacent workloads, but that it offers competent performance in general-purpose server workloads as well, often managing to match or beat the comparable AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids-AP chips. The scales are more balanced when looking at frontend workloads, with the core density available on x86 CPUs often the winner, but Vera trades that density for strong performance in backend, data-rich operations.
| Nvidia Vera specifications |  | 
|---|---|
| Cores / Threads | 88 / 176 | 
| L2 cache | 2 MB per core | 
| L3 cache | 164 MB per CPU | 
| Memory | Up to 1.5 TB SOCAMM2 LPPDDR5X | 
| Memory speed | Up to 9600 MT/s | 
| Memory bandwidth | Up to 1.2 TB/s (aggregate), 14 GB/s (per core) | 
| PCIe | 88 PCIe 6.4 lanes (CPU only), 96 PCIe 6.4 lanes (Vera Rubin), bifurcation down to x2, CXL 3.1 | 
| Configurable TDP | 250W - 450W | 
It’s an impressive showing for Nvidia's first custom core, called Olympus, and a stark improvement in nearly all aspects over Grace, which used an off-the-shelf Arm core design. The 88-core CPU is built on the Armv9.2-A architecture, including two threads per core through Nvidia’s “spatial multithreading.”
The chip is characterized by a 10-wide decode, similar to Arm’s AGI, as well as Nvidia’s second-gen Scalable Coherency Fabric (SCF). You can read more about the SCF and the Olympus core in our Vera deep dive, but SCF is critical to Vera’s performance. It’s a mesh that distributes L3 across the die, offering up to 3.4 TB/s of bandwidth across the die.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Vera has high memory bandwidth as well, leveraging replaceable SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X at 9600 MT/s, offering up to 1.2 TB/s of total memory bandwidth or around 14 GB/s per core, more than double that of AMD’s dense Turin designs.
We’ve heard a lot about the speeds and feeds of Vera, however. It’s time to understand its role in the modern AI data center, as well as see how it performs in our benchmarks against the x86 competition before AMD’s Venice and Intel’s Diamond Rapids start rolling out.
| Test platforms |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Test Platform | Memory | Tested Processors | 
|---|---|---|
| 2P Nvidia MGX Vera reference platform | 16 x 96 GB (1.5 TB) Samsung LPDDR5-9600 ECC SOCAMM2 | Nvidia Vera | 
| 2P Supermicro SYS-222HA | 24 x 64GB (1.5 TB) Micron DDR5-8800 ECC MRDIMM | Intel Xeon 6980P | 
| 2P AMD Volcano reference platform | 24 x 64 GB (1.5 TB) SK hynix DDR5-6000 ECC RDIMM | AMD EPYC 9965, EPYC 9755 | 
Understanding the CPU's role in agentic AI
Depending on where you’re at in the fast-moving world of agentic AI, you probably have a different definition of what exactly an agentic CPU is. Given the rise in prominence of agentic CPUs, the understanding of what makes a CPU tick for this type of workload has been largely defined by two companies: AMD and Nvidia. Although the points they’ve driven about concurrency and the varied work of agents are correct, it’s useful to derive a definition from how we’re seeing agentic platforms deployed right now.
Let’s back up from there and look at real agentic workflows in action to better understand where CPUs fit into this chain. As we’ve seen with Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots, there’s a class of persistent agent that gives you a slice of compute in the cloud. These CPU-only racks communicate with inference servers to actually run the models, but their workload is defined by concurrency. It’s not about the performance of an individual sandbox but instead how each sandbox performs when the chip is fully loaded.
Concurrency provides important context to some of the workloads companies like Nvidia and AMD have described. Some tool calls are more demanding, like code compilation and large database queries, but reading/writing files, running code tests, and going online in a headless browser is not demanding CPU work in isolation. When the chip is handling potentially thousands of these tool calls, however, slight advantages start to pile up. And, the CPU topology plays a bigger role in how performance is sustained as agent sessions increase.
That’s one major tenet of an agentic CPU, one that can maintain performance with high concurrency. The other is variability, which touches on the CPU, but also the larger infrastructure available. Mark Lohmeyer, VP/GM of AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, described an example to Tom’s Hardware about planning a vacation with an agent. Using AI to plan a vacation is just about as trite as examples get, but Lohmeyer sheds some light on the unique challenge of agentic workloads from the hyperscaler perspective.
In the example, Lohmeyer described planning a vacation over the course of a month, where he would suddenly prompt the agent to do a bunch of work, but may not return to prompt again for another week. “The actual use of the underlying compute, it's happening in basically bursts, right? There's like a burst of use at the start, maybe for an hour, and then it goes away, and then a couple days later, [it] bursts again for some other purpose and goes away,” Lohmeyer said. “They're very long-running workloads, effectively long-running, but often idle, basically.”
Agentic calls for a lot of power on demand, as the right alignment of this bursty work on a server with hardware contention can bring everyone’s sessions to a crawl. This factors into the type of work the CPU is doing, as well, which can include heavy code compilation, graph traversal, and large database queries. Scale that up across several agents, all with their own independent loops that don’t neatly align with each other, and the CPU problem for agentic AI becomes clear.
In the August 2026 study, Architectural Implications of Agentic AI Workflows, from researchers at The University of Texas at Austin and Microsoft Azure, the paper describes three tasks of the CPU in an agentic flow. In addition to a scheduler for GPU inference, which is how CPUs function in one-shot-style LLM queries, CPUs also serve as orchestrators for maintaining agent states and communication, and as runners that call tools and execute agent logic (often in Python).
The paper also shows this contention that can happen when multiple agents are running at once, passing requests to the GPU, receiving responses, acting, and then passing requests back. We’re looking at a cross-section of four agents over less than half a minute, and you can already see how small CPU-based tasks can align, as well as create hangs between GPU time.
Nvidia has been clear that Vera is an agentic CPU, though defining the performance of an agentic loop is still a work in progress. “The industry built a pretty good way to benchmark traditional workloads,” Lohmeyer said. “I think this is happening now for GPUs and TPUs for inference, for example. I think we're going to need the same type of industry-level benchmarks for agentic workloads that are probably still emerging.”
Standardized benchmarks that look at the full agentic loop aren’t available yet. We have our own internal tests that we’re running and hope to have data for soon, and we’ve seen some vendor-level benchmarking from companies like Modal, but the broader industry hasn’t come forth with a set of benchmarks for the end-to-end agentic loop along the lines of a SPEC or TPC yet.
Although those tests aren’t available yet, we can still look at CPU performance through the lens of an agentic workflow, prioritizing aspects of performance that are important for agentic loops. We can also look at common workflows for agents, including code compilation for coding agents and database performance for retrieval agents. We can look at things like JSON parsing through the simdjson library, evaluating how these CPUs parse the large JSON files agents use to communicate. And we can look at the foundation of much of the AI ecosystem with Python performance.
That’s the focus of our benchmarking here, to establish where Vera stands among the x86 competition from AMD and Intel in well-known benchmarks. Hopefully we’ll have the opportunity for further testing in the near future to evaluate full agentic loops once that testing procedure is finalized.
Although we’re evaluating performance through an agentic lens here, Nvidia did not limit what tests we could run nor place any stipulations on our coverage. We’re thankful to Nvidia for providing us with remote access to a dual-socket Vera system for the purposes of testing, but beyond configuration checks to ensure the platform was operating as expected, we were left to run the tests we wanted to run. That includes several tests that are applicable to agentic workflows, but also tests from our general server CPU benchmarking suite, including Java, cryptography, compression, and rendering performance.
A gentle reminder for readers
Servers are not client PCs. You have much smarter operators with deeper access to the hardware, and often a software stack that’s unique to the specific workload at minimum, and highly tweaked and optimized for that workload at a maximum. With client CPUs, we can say that an AMD X3D chip is the best for gaming, or that Intel’s latest flagship offers the highest single-threaded performance. Servers depend much more on use cases.
In a typical review, we’d say that X is better than Y for Z purpose, and back that up with data. Here, that commentary is more muted. The reality is that hyperscalers maintain large fleets with a variety of hardware that can fit any purpose, and enterprises need to choose the hardware best suited not only for their operations, but also for TCO and a list of at least a dozen other variables that are specific to that business.
Nvidia Vera SPEC CPU 2026 estimates
So far, the primary benchmark we’ve had for Vera is SPEC CPU 2026 intrate, so we ran the full SPEC CPU 2026 suite to check Nvidia’s performance claims, as well as look at floating point performance. For anyone who hasn’t read SPEC CPU benchmarks before, there are a few disclaimers before heading into the results.
All of the runs here are estimates, and that’s due to how SPEC reporting works. There are strict reporting rules, and we’re not reporting these results to SPEC directly. The charts say “estimated,” but the numbers aren’t a guess. We ran SPEC CPU 2026 following the standard testing procedure, using the same compiler and flags for each CPU.
For the compiler, we used GCC 15.2 with a few common flags, including link-time optimization and march/mcpu to expose the correct instruction support to the compiler. We also used the general-purpose jemalloc memory allocator across all of the tests we ran.
Starting with the overall intrate, this is a series of applications primarily dealing with integer operations instead of floats, and the SOP is to run a copy of the application on each thread available. The test looks at what a CPU is capable of with many applications running at once, measuring throughput.
Nvidia’s numbers aren’t dissimilar from our own. In the company’s white paper, it showed Vera ahead of the EPYC 9755 by 3%, and with our tests, Vera is ahead by 1.5%. Keep in mind the considerably higher 512-thread count of the 9755 system here against the 352-thread Vera system. Vera absolutely runs away with performance when breaking down the score per-core.
Despite the core density of Intel’s 512-thread Xeon 6980P in a two-socket configuration, it’s not in the conversation here. Retesting with oneAPI represented an impressive 10% increase in performance with Intel-optimized binaries, but even against optimized code, Vera is 8.6% ahead with generic GCC.

No one is realistically running a single application on servers utilizing every thread available like this, but the numbers are there to browse if you’re interested.
Nvidia Vera Python and AI benchmarks
If there’s any direct benchmark for agentic AI right now, it’s Python performance. There isn’t one universal language for AI agents, but Python (and, to a lesser extent, TypeScript) make up the foundational agentic frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen. A strong agentic CPU right now is defined in part by strong Python performance, and Vera has exactly that.
Starting with a broad overview, you can see the total average test times for PyBench above, with Vera leading the pack. It’s 4% ahead of the EPYC 9755, which itself leads Intel’s Xeons and the larger 9965. Python is largely single-threaded, especially for these basic, built-in functions, so we see the 9755 pair leading the 9965 pair throughout all of our Python benchmarks.

PyPerformance provides a much more granular look at Python performance, evaluating start-up times for the Python interpreter, regular expressions, and even full Python applications. The story doesn’t change, however. Outside of a couple of misses in web server-focused tests, Vera tops the charts across the board.
The AI ecosystem right now is largely built on Python, so strong performance here is a good early indicator of strong AI performance in the data center. Of course, this space is rapidly evolving, and other languages are working their way into the ecosystem. For this moment, however, Python is critical, and it’s an aspect of performance Vera nails.

We also ran Llama.cpp with a CPU BLAS backend, checking text generation and prompt processing (at different token lengths) on the CPU using gpt-oss-20b-q8. For prompt processing, much of the process is handled on the GPU, so this pure-CPU benchmark isn’t totally representative of a real deployment. However, the CPU still plays a role here, particularly in tokenization.
Unsurprisingly, we can see the single 6980P topping the charts in prompt processing, with a 2P Xeon 6980P coming up in second place, likely on the back of Intel’s AI-specific ISA extensions. We expect AMD to further extend support for these instructions in Zen 6, which should level the playing field.

Nvidia has touted the memory bandwidth of Vera as one of the chip’s strongest points, and the industry-standard STREAM memory bandwidth benchmark backs up those claims. Vera comes with a memory bus width more than twice as large as Grace, plus a large jump up to LPDDR5X-9600. It’s capable of up to 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth through the LPDDR5X interface, and up to 1.8 TB/s of bandwidth between Vera sockets.
AMD’s support for DDR5-6000 is relatively slow, and although Intel offers more bandwidth with MRDIMMs reaching up to 8,800 MT/s, Vera is in a league of its own here. That’s true without optimization, as well. After my initial STREAM pass, Nvidia suggested passing the OpenMP “spread” policy, which distributes processes as far away from each other as possible to reduce cache/memory contention.
With AMD and Intel, we see a slight regression with this setting, but it offers Vera a massive jump in memory bandwidth. Undoubtedly, the scales will start to level off as AMD and Intel roll out their next-gen Venice and Diamond Rapids parts, both of which tout much higher memory bandwidth than their predecessors.

Database performance for Vera is strong across our ClickHouse and SQLite benchmarks. In max-thread SQLite, Vera is only beaten by a single-socket 6980P server, and it jumps into the lead in our like-for-like 64-thread and 128-thread tests. ClickHouse provides some interesting data that goes beyond a steady-state SQL database.
On the second and third runs of ClickHouse, Vera is competitive with a dual EPYC 9755 server, but from a cold cache, Vera is much faster, racking up an advantage of nearly 40% in the first run.
For bringing that data in, we measured JSON parsing speed with simdjson, which, as the name suggests, relies heavily on modern SIMD instructions. Turin has a natural lead here with its native AVX-512 execution.

In cryptography workloads, Vera falls behind the pack significantly in the John The Ripper password cracker, while trailing the massive core arrays of its competition in OpenSSL.

HPC is usually the domain of dense CPUs, but Vera performs well in a variety of HPC tasks that we tested. In Discrete Fourier Transforms (DFT) using FFTE, Vera tops the charts, as it does in Octave and CloverLeaf. Although not strictly HPC, Vera falls in the middle of the pack in intensive mathematical operations like m-queens, and it trails chips with massive core arrays in the heavily threaded Primesieve.

Code compilation is a more contentious workload, with Vera trading blows against AMD and Intel depending on the workload. Starting with the compilers themselves, Vera takes a strong lead in a timed GCC compilation, beating out a dual 9755 system by 12%. It falls into last place in our LLVM compilation tests, however, both using standard Makefiles and Ninja. These tests measure the time it takes to compile the compiler itself, not the time it takes to compile an application with it.
Elsewhere, Vera shows up strongly in ImageMagick and PHP compiles while losing out slightly to the dual 9755s in Godot. Compiler performance is important to agentic AI given the prominence of coding agents, which often need to build software from source as part of an agentic coding workflow.
Nvidia Vera encoding and rendering benchmarks
Encoding and rendering workloads aren’t the focus of Vera, but we ran our standard list of benchmarks, which includes some rendering and encoding tests. Vera has strong performance here in some applications, though it certainly takes a backseat to the headline Python and memory performance shared earlier in this article.

We normally run Blender, though there isn’t an official Arm Linux version available, so we skipped the test here. Instead, we have the cross-platform C-Ray and POV-Ray. Vera manages to outclass even the 768 threads available on a 2P EPYC 9965 server, both at 1080p and 4K. Vera also leads in POV-Ray, though on a technicality. Every server we tested was tightly coupled short of the 2P 6980P server.
For a more granular look, we have OSPRay, where Vera tops the charts in real-time path tracing, though falls short of the AMD and Intel flagships in real-time scientific visualization. The “dim_512” subset is worth drawing attention to. Strong AVX-512 performance allows AMD to offer three or even four times the performance of Vera in this workload.
Nvidia makes a delayed debut
Although Vera isn’t Nvidia’s first data center CPU, it’s the first one that the company is aggressively pursuing with the same fervor that it carries with its accelerators. It’s an impressive chip, often punching far above its weight class, especially in those workloads that can show off its unique capabilities and topology.
Still, it’s a single 88-core chip arriving in a market characterized by granular SKU lists to meet a wide range of specific workloads. Vera won’t be the right choice for all of them, which is something that Nvidia itself has already stated. “The world is not going to be served by one SKU of CPU. And that's not our intention,” said Nvidia’s Ian Buck when Vera was revealed in March.
That’s not the intention with Vera, but the performance against contemporary x86 CPUs shows that Nvidia’s new push into standalone data center CPUs has legs, more so than the various building-block-style Arm chips we’ve seen from hyperscalers, certainly. If nothing else, Vera demands some attention from AMD and Intel.
The x86 crew is responding shortly, with Zen 6 queued up to roll out through the end of the year and Intel’s Diamond Rapids targeting a 2027 release. As you can imagine, we'll be putting those chips through their paces as well.

articles.title: Spotify quiere que cambies tus canciones favoritas con IA, pero hay un problema
articles.text:
Spotify está pensando en llevar aún más lejos su apuesta por la inteligencia artificial. Un reporte afirma que la plataforma trabaja en una nueva función que permitirá crear remixes personalizados de canciones mediante IA. La nueva función podría debutar el próximo año, aunque primero necesitará conseguir la aprobación de los artistas y las discográficas.
Según Financial Times, Spotify lanzará un remixer como un complemento para sus suscriptores durante 2027. Esta característica ofrecería funciones para mezclar canciones y transformarlas; por ejemplo, un usuario podría convertir una canción folk en una versión dance o experimentar con distintos estilos. La función también podría generar interpretaciones que simulen la voz de otros artistas, aunque esto ya es un terreno más complejo que depende de otros factores.
A diferencia de plataformas como Suno o Lyria, que permiten crear canciones desde cero usando IA, el enfoque de Spotify está en pistas ya publicadas y autorizadas en su plataforma. Esto buscaría reducir los conflictos relacionados con la propiedad intelectual y evitar una demanda. Para ello, la compañía ofrecería una forma de monetizar las nuevas experiencias creadas por los usuarios.
Todo esto podría sonar interesante, excepto porque el remix de Spotify no será gratis. El reporte menciona que la compañía podría cobrar entre cuatro y cinco dólares adicionales al mes por el acceso a las herramientas basadas en IA. Si bien la cifra no es definitiva, al menos nos da una idea de que la empresa pretende obtener ingresos con esta iniciativa.
Los remixes con IA de Spotify necesitan el apoyo de las disqueras
Uno de los principales obstáculos para llevar a cabo esta clase de iniciativas son los dueños de los derechos, que en este caso son las disqueras. Spotify ya cerró acuerdos con sellos como Universal Music Group, Merlin, Kobalt y Believe, pero todavía falta convencer a Sony y Warner Music. De no contar con la autorización, la función de remix con IA solo estaría disponible para un número limitado de canciones.
Además del visto bueno de los grandes sellos, Spotify también necesita que los artistas accedan, por lo que contempla que cada uno pueda decidir si quiere participar en el programa. Esto último podría impulsar o hundir la función de remix, ya que la industria musical no ve con buenos ojos a la IA, sobre todo cuando se trata de replicar estilos o voces humanas. Algunos artistas han mostrado apertura a explorar nuevas tecnologías, mientras que otros rechazan por completo cualquier uso de la IA en sus obras.
Es difícil saber si los remixes se implementarán en 2027 o quedarán como un experimento interno. Spotify cree que un sistema que permita compartir los beneficios económicos de la nueva función ayudaría a convencer a los artistas. Las reproducciones de las mezclas con IA contarían como reproducciones de la canción original, generando más regalías a los dueños de los derechos de autor.
Si Spotify consigue la aprobación de todos los involucrados y lo convierte en un negocio rentable, la plataforma podría inaugurar uno de los primeros modelos comerciales de música generativa con respaldo de artistas y disqueras. Actualmente, Spotify ya usa un asistente de IA que encuentra y recomienda música.

articles.title: How Ghana’s TrustCheck helps shoppers vet online sellers before they pay - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ghanaian startup TrustCheck has built a review and trust platform that allows consumers to check out businesses, especially social media sellers, before they part with their money.
Launched in January of this year by Elliot Brenya, Tema-based TrustCheck lets users look up a business, read verified customer reviews, and see a trust score out of 100. The score combines a business’s rating, review volume, how responsive it is to customers, verification status and any open disputes.
“A lot of buying in Ghana now happens on Instagram, TikTok, X and WhatsApp. You see a product, message the seller, send money by Mobile Money and hope it arrives,” Brenya told Disrupt Africa. “Most of the time it does, but when it doesn’t, there is usually no way to get your money back and no record that warns the next person. TrustCheck is meant to be that record.”
Brenya was inspired to build the platform after being scammed while buying a mobile device, having relied on fake ratings for the vendor.
All reviews on TrustCheck are moderated before going live, and reviewers can attach proof of purchase, such as MoMo receipts or order chats, which only moderators can see. Businesses cannot pay to have reviews removed, but can claim their pages for free, respond to reviews and apply for verification. This month the startup also launched a scam check for phone numbers, MoMo numbers, social media handles and websites, as well as a public API that returns a business’s trust score.
“There are global review sites, but they were built around formal businesses with websites and card payments. The sellers people in Ghana worry about most are an Instagram page, a TikTok shop or a WhatsApp number,” Brenya said. “Nothing gives you one searchable place, built for how people here actually buy and pay, that you can check in a minute before sending money.”
The platform is free for shoppers, and makes money by charging businesses for verification and premium tools. It also runs display advertising. Bootstrapped so far, TrustCheck has around 300 registered reviewers and over 50 businesses listed, 20 of which have signed up to manage their pages. It has secured its first paying business customers, though Brenya said revenue remains small.
“Encouraging on the consumer side and slower on the business side, which is what we expected,” he said. “A page they don’t control, with reviews they can’t delete, feels like a risk at first. The ones who have engaged see it the other way round: a page with real reviews and replies is the best proof a small online seller can show a new customer.”
TrustCheck is focused on Ghana for now, but sees West Africa as the obvious next step.
“The problem is the same in Nigeria, Ivory Coast, Kenya and anywhere else where social commerce and mobile money have grown faster than ways to check who you are paying,” Brenya said.

articles.title: Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
articles.text:
Too much code, too little shipped: Why AI needs a software factory
Can AI run the entire software show? At TechSparks 2026, ForgeCode CEO Tushar Mathur explained how AI agents can automate software development while engineers focus on quality and results.
AI can generate code faster than ever, but getting it tested and reviewed and into production is a different challenge.
Engineering teams are increasingly using AI agents to write code, fix bugs, and build features. But faster coding does not necessarily mean faster software delivery.
As code generation accelerates, reviews pile up, testing slows down, and teams struggle to coordinate the growing volume of changes.
At TechSparks 2026, Tushar Mathur, CEO of Forge Code, explored this problem in his session, Anatomy of a software factory. He explained how AI-native engineering organisations can move beyond automating individual coding tasks to building systems that manage the entire software development lifecycle.
“Just because code is becoming easy and faster to generate doesn't mean your overall SDLC becomes faster,” Mathur said.
From coding assistants to software factories
The traditional software development process focused heavily on writing code efficiently. Teams spent time defining requirements, preparing specifications and designing architecture to reduce the effort needed during implementation, he said.
With AI taking over more coding work, the bottlenecks are moving elsewhere.
Mathur described how organisations can end up with large volumes of pull requests awaiting review, longer testing cycles and more bugs than existing regression suites can catch.
Hiring more engineers or running more AI agents is not necessarily the answer. More people can increase coordination costs, while adding agents without effective feedback loops can generate code that overwhelms the systems responsible for reviewing and testing it.
“The reason why this happens is because there's no signal,” Mathur said, explaining why simply connecting automated steps does not create an effective software factory.
An assembly line that learns
Mathur presented Forge Code as a software factory that coordinates AI agents across the development lifecycle. The process begins with triaging requests, creating specifications and implementing features.
Agents then verify changes before they move towards deployment, with human engineers stepping in when decisions or feedback are needed.
The system also monitors production, using the resulting insights to inform future tasks. This creates a feedback loop in which the factory can identify problems, improve its workflows and generate new work from what it learns.
Mathur said Forge Code was running around 100 agents in the background during his presentation, working on features, compatibility and bug detection.
He outlined six principles for an effective software factory: autonomous operation, scalability, cost efficiency, measurability, self-improvement and alignment with business goals.
The last principle is particularly important.
Instead of treating every request as a coding task, the factory should work towards outcomes such as improving customer retention or meeting compliance requirements. Teams can then prioritise features based on the value they deliver.
Engineers become supervisors
In this model, engineers spend less time directing every task and more time monitoring outcomes, reviewing signals and improving the system. Business leaders can also contribute requests and priorities directly, allowing the factory to translate organisational goals into a development backlog.
Writing code faster is great. Shipping better software is the real win.
For engineering teams, the trick is turning AI-powered speed into reliable products, measurable gains and business results.

articles.title: Does Tech Support Need to Be Local? Remote Fixes, Site Visits and Where Distance Matters - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The Changing Landscape of Tech Support
In today’s fast-evolving digital world, businesses rely heavily on technology to operate efficiently and maintain a competitive edge. As a result, the demand for reliable tech support has never been higher. However, one major question continues to spark debate among business leaders and IT professionals alike: does tech support need to be local? Advances in remote support technology have transformed the way IT services are delivered, but there are still scenarios where proximity plays a crucial role. Understanding when and why distance matters can help organisations make informed decisions about their tech support strategies.
The question of whether tech support must be local touches on broader themes of efficiency, cost, security, and customer satisfaction. With the proliferation of cloud computing, sophisticated remote access tools, and global connectivity, many routine IT problems can be solved without a technician physically present. Yet, as technology infrastructures become more complex, and businesses face unique challenges, the importance of local presence in tech support cannot be dismissed outright.
The Rise of Remote Tech Support
Remote tech support has become increasingly popular due to its convenience, cost-effectiveness, and rapid response capabilities. IT professionals can troubleshoot software issues, configure systems, and even manage networks without physically being on site. According to a recent survey, 70% of IT support tasks can be resolved remotely, highlighting the effectiveness of virtual assistance in day-to-day operations.
This shift has also been fueled by advancements in remote access tools, cloud computing, and secure VPN connections, enabling technicians to work efficiently regardless of their physical location. Businesses in the Lanham MSP industry have embraced these innovations, finding that remote support can reduce downtime and eliminate the need for costly on-site visits.
Remote support platforms often include features such as screen sharing, remote desktop control, and automated diagnostics, allowing technicians to pinpoint and resolve issues swiftly. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the adoption of remote support practices as businesses adapted to distributed workforces and limited physical access to office spaces.
However, while remote tech support excels in addressing software-related issues, configuration errors, and network troubleshooting, it is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Certain categories of problems inherently require physical intervention, underscoring the ongoing relevance of local tech support.
When Local Presence Still Matters
Despite the benefits of remote tech support, certain situations necessitate a local presence. Hardware malfunctions, physical network issues, and complex installations often require hands-on intervention. For example, a server failure or a malfunctioning printer cannot always be fixed through remote commands alone. In these cases, having tech support personnel nearby can significantly reduce resolution time and minimise the impact on business operations.
Moreover, some organisations prefer local tech support providers due to the personalised service and stronger relationships that develop from face-to-face interactions. This can be particularly important for businesses with sensitive data or custom IT environments that benefit from a deeper understanding of their infrastructure.
Local support is crucial when rapid physical response is needed to prevent costly downtime. For instance, manufacturing facilities or data centres experiencing hardware failures require technicians on site immediately to avoid production losses or data corruption. Additionally, local technicians are often better positioned to navigate the physical layout of an organisation’s infrastructure, facilitating quicker repairs and maintenance.
When evaluating tech support options, companies may also consider providers like tech support from Orbis, who offer a blend of remote and on-site services tailored to client needs. This hybrid approach can combine the speed and efficiency of remote fixes with the reliability of local expertise.
Hybrid Models: The Best of Both Worlds
Many IT service providers now offer hybrid support models that leverage the strengths of both remote and local assistance. These solutions typically start with remote diagnostics and troubleshooting, escalating to on-site visits only when necessary. This approach optimises resource allocation, reducing costs and improving response times.
Data shows that organisations utilising hybrid IT support models report a 30% decrease in downtime compared to those relying solely on traditional on-site support. Additionally, hybrid models offer scalability and flexibility, allowing businesses to adapt their support needs as they grow or face new challenges.
The hybrid model’s flexibility can also accommodate different service level agreements (SLAs), enabling businesses to prioritise critical systems for immediate on-site support while handling less urgent issues remotely. This tailored approach not only improves operational efficiency but also enhances customer satisfaction by aligning support services with actual business needs.
Industry-Specific Considerations
Different industries have varying requirements when it comes to tech support. For example, manufacturing plants with complex machinery often require immediate on-site assistance to avoid costly production halts. In contrast, software companies may operate predominantly in the cloud, making remote support more practical and efficient.
Businesses in regulated sectors such as healthcare and finance might also prioritise local support for compliance and security reasons, ensuring that sensitive information is handled under strict protocols. For example, healthcare providers managing patient data under HIPAA regulations may require on-site support staff trained in data privacy to comply with legal standards.
Similarly, industries with critical infrastructure, such as utilities and transportation, often mandate local tech support to ensure rapid response in emergencies. These sectors cannot afford prolonged downtime or security breaches, making proximity a key factor in their IT support strategies.
Understanding these nuances can guide companies in selecting the right balance between remote and local services, tailoring support models to meet their operational and regulatory demands.
The Impact of Remote Work Trends
The global shift towards remote and hybrid working models has transformed tech support dynamics. With employees accessing corporate networks from diverse locations, the ability to provide remote assistance quickly and securely has become vital. A recent study found that 85% of IT departments increased their remote support capabilities in response to the rise of distributed workforces.
However, this trend also underscores the importance of robust network infrastructure and cybersecurity measures to support remote interventions without compromising data integrity. Local tech support teams often play a critical role in maintaining these systems and responding to physical security incidents.
While remote technicians can address software and connectivity issues, local personnel are needed to handle hardware replacement, network cabling repairs, or physical access control system maintenance. This dual approach ensures seamless support for a workforce no longer confined to a single location.
Moreover, as organisations adopt bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies and cloud-based collaboration tools, the complexity of managing IT environments increases. Tech support must now navigate hybrid ecosystems that combine on-premises hardware with cloud services, further highlighting the need for both remote expertise and local presence.
Evaluating Cost and Efficiency
Cost considerations are central to decisions about tech support models. Remote support generally offers lower operational expenses by minimising travel and on-site labour costs. However, for complex issues requiring physical repairs or installations, local support is indispensable.
Efficiency gains from remote fixes can translate into faster problem resolution and less downtime, directly impacting productivity and revenue. On the other hand, delayed on-site response times can lead to extended outages and higher indirect costs. Striking the right balance involves assessing typical support needs, incident frequency, and business priorities.
A recent industry report noted that companies using remote support services saved up to 40% on IT support costs annually compared to those relying exclusively on on-site visits. However, it also emphasised that local support remains essential for maintaining critical infrastructure and handling emergencies.
When budgeting for tech support, organisations should factor in not only direct costs but also potential losses from downtime and productivity disruptions. Investing in a hybrid model can provide cost savings without compromising service quality, ensuring resources are allocated efficiently.
Future Outlook: Integrating Emerging Technologies
Emerging technologies like augmented reality (AR) and artificial intelligence (AI) are poised to reshape tech support further. AR can enable remote technicians to guide on-site staff through repairs visually, reducing the need for specialist visits. AI-driven diagnostics and automated issue resolution will expand the scope of remote fixes even more.
For example, AR headsets can overlay instructions in real-time, allowing less experienced local personnel to perform complex repairs under remote expert supervision. AI algorithms can proactively detect anomalies, predict failures, and even initiate self-healing processes, minimising human intervention.
Despite these advancements, the human element remains essential. Complex problem-solving, strategic IT planning, and relationship building continue to require direct interaction, often best achieved through local presence.
Furthermore, as technology evolves, so too will the definitions of “local” and “remote.” Virtual presence tools and robotics may blur these lines, enabling support that transcends physical distance while retaining the benefits of proximity.
Conclusion: Distance Matters, But Context is Key
The necessity of local tech support depends largely on the nature of the IT issues, industry requirements, and organisational preferences. While remote fixes have proven highly effective and cost-efficient for many routine tasks, site visits remain critical for hardware repairs, installations, and personalised service.
Businesses would do well to consider hybrid models that combine remote and on-site support to maximise efficiency and minimise downtime. Understanding the specific needs of your organisation and leveraging providers who offer flexible solutions can ensure your tech support strategy is both resilient and responsive in an increasingly digital world.
Ultimately, the question is not whether tech support must be local or remote, but how best to integrate both approaches to serve your business effectively. By recognising where distance matters and where it doesn’t, organisations can craft support strategies that deliver optimal performance, security, and customer satisfaction.

articles.title: Adieu la Renault 5 à 139 € par mois : le leasing social se vide de ses Renault et Peugeot
articles.text:
Leasing social 2026 : Renault et Peugeot ferment les commandes, une seule marque française résiste
Elle avait été la star de l'édition 2025, la citadine que tout le monde s'arrachait. Trois mois après la relance du leasing social, la Renault 5 électrique a disparu de la vitrine, puis le reste de la marque au losange a suivi. Peugeot avait déjà baissé le rideau à la fin de l'été. Il reste pourtant des milliers de places à prendre et une seule marque française tient encore la boutique.
Relancée le 16 juillet pour une troisième saison, la location sociale de voitures électriques devait permettre à 50 000 ménages modestes de rouler en électrique pour moins de 200 € par mois. 16 semaines plus tard, le compteur affiche 39 000 commandes, selon franceinfo. Les modèles les plus demandés, eux, se sont évaporés : à la fin octobre, plus aucune Renault ni Peugeot n'est proposée dans le cadre du dispositif.
Leasing social 2026 : la Renault 5 électrique quitte le dispositif en premier
Au lancement, l'affiche avait de quoi séduire. La Renault 5 E-Tech Evolution s'affichait à 139 €/mois, la Twingo E-Tech à 130 €, la Renault 4 à 170 € et la Mégane à 190 €. La citadine rétro a cédé la première : dès le 7 septembre, Renault ne proposait plus aucune de ses deux versions.
Fin octobre, la Twingo et la Renault 4 ont à leur tour quitté le dispositif. Selon L’Automobiliste, Renault invoque des capacités de production saturées et réserve ses volumes aux clients qui paient le tarif catalogue.
Chez Peugeot, la page s'est tournée encore plus tôt. La marque s'est arrêtée à 5000 contrats pour préserver sa rentabilité, rapporte Automobile Propre, alors que ses e-208, e-2008 et e-308 étaient épuisées dès la fin août. Fiat, Jeep, Alfa Romeo, Lancia et Kia ont eux aussi fermé les commandes.
Rentabilité et stocks : pourquoi les constructeurs ferment le robinet
L'équation tient en deux chiffres. L'aide de l'État couvre 29 % du coût d'acquisition dans la limite de 6500 €, ou 9000 € si la voiture et sa batterie sont produites dans l'Espace économique européen. Le loyer, lui, plafonne à 200 €/mois sur au moins trois ans. Quand les chaînes tournent à plein, chaque Renault 5 cédée dans ces conditions ampute la marge.
Stellantis a fait le pari inverse, le groupe revendiquant 25 000 des 39 000 commandes, soit 64 % du total.
Modèles électriques encore disponibles : Citroën reste en lice
Les retardataires se tournent désormais vers la Citroën ë-C3, à partir de 94 €/mois, et sa déclinaison ë-C3 Aircross, à 181 €. Fin septembre, Mondial.paris recensait aussi l'Opel Frontera et le Hyundai Inster.
Doté de 401 millions d'euros financés par les certificats d'économies d'énergie, le dispositif n'a aucune date de clôture puisqu’il s'arrête à épuisement de l'enveloppe. Il reste réservé aux foyers dont le revenu fiscal de référence ne dépasse pas 16 880 € par part, qui dépendent de leur voiture pour travailler et n'en ont pas profité en 2024 ou 2025. Plus de 100 000 ménages en ont déjà bénéficié depuis sa création.
Avec 11 000 places encore libres et une vitrine réduite à une poignée de modèles, l'objectif des 50 000 bénéficiaires n'a plus rien d'acquis.

articles.title: Starlink lleva al límite la ley de la oferta y la demanda: ahora sus precios pueden subir o bajar cada mes
articles.text:
Mientras los operadores europeos tratan de unirse para hacer frente al dominio de Starlink en el mercado de la conectividad vía satélite, la compañía de Elon Musk continúa ganando peso y cada vez tiene un mayor número de usuarios en España.
Eso le ha llevado a introducir varias novedades en su oferta comercial que le van acercando a los operadores tradicionales, como un programa de recompensas, tarifas con router incluido y sin permanencia, e incluso alguna que otra subida de precios.
Ahora, sin embargo, ha llevado a cabo dos movimientos que nos han sorprendido a muchos. Por un lado, ha bajado ligeramente los precios de esas tarifas, y por otro, ha añadido una cláusula en la que advierte que esos precios podrán bajar cada mes.
Precios dinámicos en vez de fijos
Todos estamos más que acostumbrados ya a las tradicionales subidas de precio que los operadores (especialmente, las marcas premium) llevan a cabo, como mínimo, una vez año. También hemos compañías como O2 o Digi ofreciendo diferentes precios en función de la zona del país en la que resides.
Lo que no habíamos visto hasta ahora era que la cuota mensual de la factura de internet pueda subir de un mes para otro por culpa de la demanda. Y esa es precisamente la cláusula que acaba de añadir Starlink en sus tarifas.
Si te metes en su web oficial, verás un apartado donde tienes que introducir tu dirección para comprobar los planes y precios disponibles en tu zona. En nuestro caso, las cuotas serían las siguientes:
- Residencial 100 Mbps: 31,50 euros al mes (en lugar de los 35 euros que costaba antes).
- Residencial 200 Mbps: 40 euros al mes (en lugar de los 45 euros que costaba antes).
- Residencial Max: 58,50 euros al mes (en lugar de los 65 euros que costaba antes).
Esos precios, que en mayo sufrieron un incremento, ahora se han reducido, pero a cambio Starlink se reserva el derecho de modificarlos al alza o a la baja avisándote con un mes de antelación:
Cada lanzamiento de satélite amplía nuestra red y, a medida que crece la capacidad en tu zona, los precios pueden bajar. Cualquier aumento de precio estará impulsado por la demanda y ayudará a mantener el servicio disponible y rápido para todos. Te avisaremos con un mes de antelación antes de que entre en vigor cualquier cambio.
Eso significa que, a medida que SpaceX lance más satélites al espacio para aumentar y mejorar la cobertura de Starlink, los precios pueden ir abaratándose. El problema es que la compañía advierte que, si la demanda aumenta (cosa que está sucediendo), esos mismos precios pueden encarecerse. Y como cliente, sólo serás avisado de los cambios de un mes para otro.

articles.title: Un sous-marin volé de 4 tonnes a été mis en vente sur Leboncoin pour 100 €
articles.text:
Aussi surprenant que cela puisse paraître, deux hommes ont eu l’idée de voler un sous-marin de quatre tonnes et de le mettre ensuite en vente sur Leboncoin. Heureusement, le véhicule a été rapidement retrouvé, comme le rapporte l’Est Républicain. Celui-ci était entreposé sur un terrain à découvert en l’attente d’un acheteur.
Un sous-marin de 4 tonnes volé
Entre le 1ᵉʳ et le 21 octobre, un sous-marin de quatre tonnes a été volé dans l’Ain (Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes). Bien entendu, les malfrats n’ont pas subtilisé l’engin dans les abysses, ce dernier servait de décoration dans un magasin de plongée. Ils ont tout simplement remorqué le sous-marin et sont repartis avec. Le gérant du magasin a immédiatement alerté la police lorsqu’il s’est rendu compte du vol, tout en débutant sa propre enquête qui l’a amené sur…. Leboncoin.
L’engin mis en vente sur Leboncoin pour 100 euros
Heureusement, le véhicule sous-marin a été retrouvé très rapidement par le gérant du magasin de plongée. Il faut dire que le véhicule avait été mis en vente sur le site Leboncoin pour la modique somme de 100 euros. Cette somme de 100 euros est en réalité un faux prix pour attirer ceux intéressés par ce sous-marin dont la valeur estimée avoisine plusieurs milliers d’euros. Les malfrats auraient ensuite effectué des négociations avec les potentiels acheteurs.
Les enquêteurs ont regroupé les différentes informations disséminées dans l’annonce et ont identifié le profil du vendeur. Ils ont ensuite placé le vendeur sous surveillance et sont ainsi parvenus à localiser le sous-marin volé. Le véhicule a finalement été retrouvé le 26 octobre à environ 120 kilomètres du magasin de plongée, dans le secteur de Planoise.
Deux hommes, âgés de 27 ans et 47 ans, ont été arrêtés. Le sous-marin était entreposé chez l’homme de 27 ans, sur un terrain à découvert. La police précise que leurs justifications concernant ce vol sont à l’heure actuelle « parcellaires ». Il faut dire que le vol d’un sous-marin de quatre tonnes doit être difficile à justifier. Quoi qu’il en soit, le gérant du magasin de plongée pourra bientôt récupérer son élément de décoration.

articles.title: Microsoft finally fixes VPN issues caused by September updates
articles.text:
Microsoft has resolved Always On VPN connection failures triggered after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 security updates.
The Always On VPN remote access solution runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network when their devices connect to the Internet. It has replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server.
Microsoft has previously mistakenly flagged this known issue as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates.
The company first acknowledged it in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying the Always On VPN failures were triggered on Windows 11 systems by the September 2026 security updates when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP.
On Wednesday, Microsoft confirmed that this issue has finally been fixed for users who installed this month's KB5127936 preview update.
"This update fixes an issue that affects Always On VPN connections after installing September security update," it said. "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed. In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'"
Workaround also available
Microsoft also provides a temporary fix for users who don't want to install the preview update and would rather wait for next month's Patch Tuesday cumulative updates.
This requires admins to choose one of two tunneling protocols to prevent Always On VPN failures on affected devices.
"IT administrators can mitigate this issue by changing the Always On VPN profile from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, either SSTP only or IKEv2 only, depending on their environment and configuration," Microsoft said.
"Organizations should select the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements."
The October 2026 preview update also fixes a known issue preventing non-admin users from connecting to devices via Remote Desktop when the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 non-security preview update (or Windows updates released since then).
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Josep Albors, experto en ciberseguridad, sobre apagar el móvil como aconseja Sánchez: “Para la mayoría de los usuarios sirve de poco”
articles.text:
Pedro Sánchez ha hablado de apagar el móvil 5 minutos cada día. Fue en La Revuelta donde lo comentaba en el momento en que hablaba sobre el tema del espionaje con Pegasus. Josep Albors, responsable de Investigación y Concienciación de ESET España, comenta: “Para la mayoría de los usuarios, que nos enfrentamos a amenazas más mundanas, este consejo, en materia de ciberseguridad, sirve de poco”. Además, dependiendo de cómo se instale y active, el programa malicioso tendrá efecto o no.
“Solo se aplica para casos concretos en los que el malware está presente en la memoria RAM, que se borra cuando reinicias el dispositivo”, explica Albors. El problema de esta memoria es que es temporal y se vacía al apagar el teléfono. En el caso de que la infección solo se active en memoria (sin persistencia), puede ser interrumpida por el apagado.
El problema es que, si el software malicioso está instalado en el terminal, al apagar y encender el móvil no va a desinstalar la app maligna. Así pues, puede volver a activarse al encenderlo. Además, no podemos estar seguros de que la infección haya desaparecido por el hecho de que el móvil vuelva a funcionar correctamente. Es necesario conocer la naturaleza de la amenaza y trabajar sobre su causa.
Los límites del reinicio frente al malware
Por otro lado, en la Agencia de Seguridad Nacional de EE. UU. (NSA) se recomienda apagar/encender el dispositivo semanalmente. Esto puede ayudar a cortar ciertas infecciones. Sin embargo, esto no quiere decir que sea una forma generalizada de protegerse de malware. Además, no soluciona el problema de seguridad que se ha usado para acceder al móvil (como indica el informe de la agencia francesa de ciberseguridad).
El programa espía de NSO Group (Pegasus) permite acceder a la información del móvil. También puede usar la cámara o el micrófono. Existen algunas versiones que pueden activarse en memoria (sin persistencia). Esto complica su detección. De esta manera, apagar el dispositivo puede eliminar el programa activo. Aun así, el atacante puede conservar un medio de acceso para volver a entrar.
Hay que tener en cuenta que, aunque eliminemos el spyware con un reinicio, si no corregimos la vulnerabilidad que se ha explotado, simplemente con conocer el número de teléfono de la víctima, puede volver a infectarse este dispositivo. Además, existen ataques que no requieren que el dueño del móvil pulse ningún enlace o descargue ningún archivo.
También hay que destacar que no todas las versiones son iguales. Se han documentado versiones que son resistentes al reinicio. Además de esto, al hacer persistente el malware, puede dejarse más rastro en el sistema. Así pues, no podemos asegurar que, al apagar y encender el móvil, quedará eliminada esta clase de infección.
Este tipo de espionaje (con herramientas que emplean las agencias estatales en sus objetivos seleccionados) es muy diferente a lo que suele preocupar a la mayoría de los usuarios. Según Albors, frente a las amenazas habituales, poco ayuda el reinicio. Los usuarios deben preocuparse de amenazas como apps maliciosas o enlaces fraudulentos.
Qué hacer para proteger el móvil
Por otro lado, también puede ser útil apagar/reiniciar el móvil de vez en cuando. Por ejemplo, para cerrar apps en segundo plano o resolver problemas de memoria. Es útil en ciertas circunstancias para que el móvil funcione más fluido. Sin embargo, esto no quiere decir que esté limpio de malware.
Para ello es importante mantener actualizado el dispositivo (con las correcciones de seguridad). También es relevante no fiarse de enlaces que no hemos pedido. Además de esto, es muy recomendable no instalar apps que no provengan de los canales oficiales. También es interesante disponer de una solución de seguridad que analice el dispositivo y las conexiones. El alcance de estas herramientas depende del SO y de los permisos que tengan.

articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.text:
Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- RIKEN
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
- Share:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.
Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors
Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.
Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.
This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.
To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.
"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%
The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.
When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.
The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors
The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.
This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.
"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."
The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.
"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.
Story Source:
Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yi-Hsien Wu, Leon C. Camenzind, Patrick Bütler, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Hsi-Sheng Goan, Seigo Tarucha. Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03466-2
