articles.title: Elon Musk's SpaceXSI offers to buy hundreds of homes near its data centers, as long as owners don't sue
articles.text:
Winners & losers: It appears that Elon Musk's recently renamed SpaceXSI has found a way to stop local residents joining a noise-pollution class-action suit against its data centers: buy up their homes on the condition they don't sue.
Real estate agents have been going door to door in the Colonial Hills neighborhood of Southaven, Mississippi, on behalf of the tech giant, offering to buy residents' homes if they don't join the ongoing lawsuit, writes The Guardian.
One realtor told a resident that the plan is to buy 418 homes, and that 18 homeowners have already agreed to sell. The realtor and local mayor say the homes will house SpaceXSI staff.
In January, the EPA closed a loophole that xAI had relied on by treating off-grid turbines like temporary "non-road engines." Federal regulators clarified that such turbines must meet the same Clean Air Act requirements as stationary power plants. But the Colossus 1 and 2 sites continue to use gas turbines without the required air-pollution permits. The EPA has said the permit requirements are a matter for the state to enforce.
SpaceXSI has since promised that it will remove all its unpermitted turbines in a year, but noise pollution is still angering residents.
"It sounds like an airplane engine but it's continuous, it's incredibly loud," Elizabeth Rose, a piano teacher who lives about two miles from the site, told The Guardian. "I've been woken up at 2am by it, I've been woken up at 3am by it. I sometimes have to just get away from it because it makes me so angry."
 – SemiAnalysis (@SemiAnalysis_) September 17, 2025
"There's a high-pitched hum and then another sound like an airplane over your house. It's been so torturous I can't sleep; I just leave the house or turn on some music until I fall asleep completely exhausted," said Jason Haley, one of the suit's three plaintiffs. "It drives you insane. You also lose hope because you're being ignored or dismissed. There's no escape."
The homes are being offered for purchase at market value – the average house price in the area is $180,000. Musk himself spends up to four nights a week in an Airstream trailer in the Memphis area as he personally oversees the construction.
A class-action lawsuit was filed against the company in June over claims of near-constant noise, vibrations and other nuisance-level harms from the facilities.
SpaceXSI denies the claims, arguing that has adjusted its power output and installed sound-dampening walls to reduce the impact on the neighborhood.
Southaven mayor Darren Musselwhite said city monitors have recorded no noise levels above the local limit of 70 decibels, though some experts warn that sustained noise at even 50 decibels can harm health.
Musselwhite added that the buyouts won't turn Colonial Hills into a company town. "The buyout has multiple purposes which are to provide homes for some employees and a goodwill gesture from a good corporate citizen for those who perceive the industrial development near them as a negative," he said.
This isn't the first time SpaceXSI has tried to appeal to residents. It tried offering 50% discounts on its Starlink satellite internet service to locals earlier this year, but only around 2,000 people out of 250,000 signed up.

articles.title: Microsoft Retires Azure Deployment Environments with No Replacement Product
articles.text:
Microsoft is retiring both halves of its Azure developer-environment offering. Azure Deployment Environments goes on February 22, 2027, with no successor product. Microsoft Dev Box follows on September 18, 2028, pointed at Windows 365, which Microsoft states plainly is not an equivalent.
The Deployment Environments retirement guide lists alternatives, and none of them is a product. Microsoft suggests "direct infrastructure-as-code deployment with Azure Resource Manager templates or Bicep," reusable Azure verified modules "when teams need standardized, governed building blocks," and CI/CD workflows "when environment provisioning can be integrated into repositories and pipelines." On the partner ecosystem it is blunter: "None of the third-party solutions we identified directly support a Bicep or ARM lifecycle. Use Bicep or ARM directly in Azure for deployment."
That is a hyperscaler leaving the environment-as-a-service category and telling customers to hand-roll what the product did. Microsoft says nothing about why it is withdrawing.
InfoQ covered the general availability in May 2023, when Microsoft launched the service at Build as the answer to exactly that problem. Senior program manager Sagar Chandra Reddy Lankala wrote then that "by enabling self-service deployment for developers, Azure Deployment Environments also benefits platform engineers," who could publish a catalog of standardized, pre-approved templates instead of provisioning environments one by one.
The service itself was free, with customers paying only for the Azure resources their environments created.
Self-service from a governed catalog is the capability going away, and it is the one the retirement guide does not replace. Bicep, verified modules, and pipelines rebuild the provisioning. They do not rebuild the catalog, the role rules, or the developer-facing portal. That territory belongs to Backstage, Port and Humanitec now.
Engineer Ikiru Yoshizaki, posting in Japanese as guitarrapc_tech, made the same objection from the user side when the retirement guide appeared. The advantage, he wrote, lay in the areas that could not be done easily with Bicep, Terraform or Pulumi. He did not spare the product either, adding that right to the end the API was unstable and the documentation sparse, and calling it sad that the value was never recognized.
Teams have sixteen months. Microsoft’s instruction is to inventory "ADE environments, definitions, catalogs, environment types, projects, dev centers, deployment subscriptions, identities, and role assignments," using the Azure Advisor Service Retirement workbook to find them, then validate a replacement for each scenario and move users and automation across. What happens on the date is only partly specified: "ADE create, deploy, redeploy, and other write operations are expected to be blocked. Inventory, read, log, and delete operations are planned to remain available for a time-bound cleanup period." How long that period runs is not stated.
Dev Box has a longer runway, though its clock started earlier than the headline date suggests. The service "starts its closing-down period at 16:00 UTC on 14 September 2026," more than a month ago, before full retirement at 17:00 UTC on 18 September 2028.
Microsoft’s own FAQ is unusually direct about what the move involves. Asked whether Windows 365 is a one-to-one replacement, the guide answers: "No. Windows 365 is the recommended path forward, but architecture, licensing, management, networking, image delivery, and developer self-service can differ. Validate each workload and don’t assume complete feature parity." Developer self-service is on that list, and it is the capability that made Dev Box a developer-platform product rather than managed desktops.
InfoQ covered the Dev Box general availability in July 2023, when that model ran on three roles: infrastructure admins handled security and networking, dev team leads built pools per project, and developers took boxes from enabled pools themselves. Amanda Silver, then corporate vice president in the Developer Division, said more than 10,000 Microsoft developers were using it internally.
There is no migration tool either. Teams should "provision the target Cloud PCs, recreate required policies and configurations, deploy applications, and transfer user data through approved processes." And the consequence of missing the date is stated without hedging: "Microsoft Dev Box won’t be available after retirement. Expect deletion of remaining customer workloads."
Windows 365 is a Microsoft 365 product rather than an Azure service, managed through Intune and licensed separately. Teams that adopted Dev Box as Azure infrastructure, billed and governed alongside the rest of their estate, are being moved to a different commercial surface. Azure Virtual Desktop, Microsoft’s Azure-native virtual desktop service, is not named anywhere in the retirement guide, though it remains under active development and reached a general availability milestone as recently as September.
The retirements are also entangled, since both products share dev center and project resources. The Deployment Environments guide warns against deleting shared dev centers "until you confirm that they have no remaining Microsoft Dev Box dependency."
Neither guide explains the withdrawal. The Dev Box notice says investment is going to Windows 365. For Deployment Environments there is no equivalent statement, only a list of things to build yourself.

articles.title: PHP2Shell : en combinant les failles PHP à une faille root Linux, des pirates infiltrent un réseau lié au gouvernement américain
articles.text:
Les attaques PHP2Shell prennent une nouvelle ampleur. En associant les deux failles critiques de PHP à une vulnérabilité du noyau Linux, des pirates auraient compromis 25 systèmes Palo Alto Networks, dont trois dans un environnement lié au gouvernement américain.
Les premières exploitations réussies de PHP2Shell avaient déjà prouvé que des attaquants pouvaient exécuter des commandes à distance sur des serveurs vulnérables, mais la campagne découverte par Dream Research révèle une offensive autrement plus élaborée. Cette fois, les pirates ont combiné les deux failles PHP à Fragnesia, une vulnérabilité du noyau Linux divulguée au printemps dernier, pour prendre le contrôle de pare-feu Palo Alto Networks dont les interfaces d'administration étaient accessibles depuis Internet. Une opération qui leur aurait permis de s'introduire jusque dans le réseau interne d'une organisation liée au gouvernement américain.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
De PHP2Shell aux privilèges root, trois failles pour prendre le contrôle des serveurs
Pour rappel, les deux vulnérabilités PHP2Shell, référencées CVE-2026-109618 et CVE-2026-109619, permettent à un attaquant non authentifié d'exécuter du code à distance sur un serveur PHP vulnérable. Ces commandes s'exécutent toutefois avec les droits limités du serveur web, qui ne peut normalement pas modifier les fichiers système les plus sensibles. Pour contourner cette restriction, les pirates à l'origine de la campagne retracée par Dream Research ont exploité une troisième vulnérabilité, CVE-2026-46300, surnommée Fragnesia.
Évaluée à 7,8 sur l'échelle CVSS, Fragnesia appartient à la même famille que Dirty Frag. Elle touche le sous-système XFRM ESP-in-TCP du noyau Linux, qui permet de transporter des paquets IPsec chiffrés à travers des connexions TCP. Pour déchiffrer ces paquets, Linux manipule des fragments de données en mémoire, parfois partagés avec le cache de fichiers du système. Le noyau doit alors en créer une copie avant de les modifier afin de préserver les données d'origine, étape que Fragnesia permet de faire sauter pour altérer directement, en mémoire, le contenu de fichiers normalement protégés contre l'écriture.
Les chercheurs ont retrouvé les outils et les journaux d'une attaque conçue sur mesure pour compromettre des pare-feu Palo Alto Networks exécutant des versions vulnérables de PAN-OS 12.1 et 12.2. Sans avoir à fournir d'identifiants de connexion, les pirates ont pu prendre pied sur ces équipements grâce à PHP2Shell, puis exploiter Fragnesia pour modifier les règles d'authentification de Linux et accéder au compte root sans mot de passe. Ils ont ensuite installé un webshell PHP, se réservant ainsi la possibilité de revenir ultérieurement. Le tout en moins de quinze minutes, d'après les éléments recueillis.
Des milliers de pare-feu ciblés, vingt-cinq systèmes compromis
Pour trouver des équipements à attaquer, les pirates ont utilisé FOFA, un moteur de recherche permettant de repérer les appareils accessibles depuis Internet. Ils ont ainsi recensé quelque 19 000 pare-feu du fournisseur ciblé, puis identifié les versions logicielles d'environ 5 000 d'entre eux. Après avoir écarté les équipements incompatibles avec leurs exploits et limité leurs recherches aux États-Unis, au Japon, à Taïwan et à la Corée du Sud, ils ont constitué une liste de 240 cibles.
Les attaques automatisées, menées les 23 et 24 octobre, auraient permis de compromettre 24 pare-feu. Sur 22 d'entre eux, les pirates se seraient contentés d'installer une backdoor. Sur les deux autres, appartenant à une même organisation liée au gouvernement américain, ils ont cherché à pénétrer plus loin dans l'infrastructure. Le premier a cessé de répondre peu après sa compromission, mais les pirates ont utilisé le second pour établir un tunnel SSH vers le réseau interne, puis prendre le contrôle du serveur central de gestion des pare-feu.
Cette nouvelle intrusion aurait porté à 25 le nombre total de machines compromises, dont trois dans cet environnement américain. Depuis le serveur d'administration, les attaquants ont récupéré les configurations des pare-feu, dont ils ont extrait plusieurs clés privées, notamment celles associées aux certificats TLS et à l'authentification des équipements, et déchiffré le mot de passe d'un compte de service LDAP utilisé pour communiquer avec Active Directory. Grâce à ce compte, ils ont pu recenser les utilisateurs et les groupes du domaine, avant de tenter de découvrir d'autres mots de passe et de créer des comptes clandestins.
Dream Research soupçonne une opération liée à la Chine, sans pouvoir l'attribuer à un groupe identifié. Palo Alto Networks a depuis vérifié les outils utilisés par les pirates et confirmé les résultats de l'enquête. Son équipe Unit 42 suit cette activité sous la référence provisoire CL-UNK-1280 et évoque un attaquant sinophone dont les horaires d'activité correspondent au fuseau UTC+8. Le 28 octobre, la CISA a confirmé l'exploitation active de Fragnesia en l'ajoutant à son catalogue des vulnérabilités exploitées.
Les correctifs du noyau Linux existent depuis mai, et ceux de PHP2Shell depuis le 21 octobre. Palo Alto Networks déploie également des mises à jour pour les versions vulnérables de PAN-OS et recommande de supprimer tout accès public aux interfaces d'administration, en réservant leur utilisation aux adresses IP internes autorisées. Sur les équipements déjà compromis, les administrateurs devront aussi rechercher les accès laissés par les pirates.

articles.title: Macbook Pro mit Touchscreen? Diese Apple-Gadgets hätte es unter Steve Jobs nicht gegeben
articles.text:
Nicht nur das Macbook Pro mit Touchscreen: Diese Apple-Gadgets hätte es unter Steve Jobs nicht gegeben
Nach der Vorstellung des ersten Macbook Pro mit Touchscreen war Meme-Time in den sozialen Netzwerken. Viele Tech-Accounts posteten einen kurzen Ausschnitt von der Vorschau auf das Betriebssystem OS X Lion von 2010. Denn schon damals hatte der Apple-Mitgründer eine klare Meinung von Touch-Displays an Laptops.
Touchscreens wollen vertikal sein
    „Nach einem längeren Zeitraum wird Ihnen der Arm abfallen.“
Jobs war der Meinung, dass Touch-Oberflächen nicht vertikal sein wollen. Das funktioniere eben nicht, weil es ergonomisch furchtbar wäre. “Nach einer kurzen Zeit werden Sie ermüden und nach einem längeren Zeitraum wird Ihnen der Arm abfallen”, so Jobs. Stattdessen verwies er auf das damals schon existierende Multitouch-Trackpad, das ebenfalls Gesten wie „Pinch to Zoom“ unterstützt, mit dem Nutzer:innen Bilder vergrößern können. Das sei „der beste Weg, den wir gefunden haben, um ein Notebook um Multitouch zu erweitern“. Seine Aussagen untermauerte Jobs zudem mit Hinweis auf die Befragungen von Nutzer:innen.
Niemand will einen Stylus
Auch bei anderen Produkten würde der Apple-Gründer vermutlich nicht mitgehen. Da wäre der Apple Pencil. “Wer will schon einen Stylus?” fragte Steve Jobs schon 2007 bei der Vorstellung des ersten iPhones. Den müsse man erst herausholen, wieder wegstecken. Man verliere ihn. „JACH“, muss der ausgeschriebene Wortlaut des Geräusches sein, mit dem Jobs seinen Meinungsvortrag zu Eingabestiften abschloss.
Zugegeben, damit bezog er sich eben auf jenes vorgestellte iPhone und nicht auf das iPad, für das der Apple Pencil ursprünglich gedacht war. Allerdings unterstützt das neue iPhone Duo den Apple Pencil mit USB-C-Anschluss. Nutzer:innen könnten damit skizzieren oder Notizen festhalten. Wahrscheinlich ist es sinnvoll, dass der große innere Bildschirm mit dem Stift funktioniert. Steve Jobs hätte es aber vielleicht gefallen.
Das iPad als Zwischending
Und dann wäre da noch das iPad, das Jobs als Zwischenkategorie zwischen iPhone und PCs und Laptops betrachtete. Man sollte daran arbeiten können, klassische Computer sollte es aber nicht verbannen. Zwar brachte Apple auch seine iWork-Suite mit Pages, Numbers und Keynote auf das iPad. Allerdings waren die Apps so gestaltet, dass sie sich (wie heute natürlich auch) mit dem Mac synchronisieren ließen. Steve Jobs selbst zeigte gegen Ende der Vorstellung des ersten iPads zudem weitere Vorteile der Zusammenarbeit mit dem Mac. Man konnte Fotos, Kontakte, Apps und mehr synchronisieren. Eine iCloud gab es damals schließlich noch nicht.
Mittlerweile ist das iPad diesem Zwischenstatus längst entwachsen. Es ist problemlos möglich, seinen kompletten Arbeitstag auch am Apple-Tablet zu gestalten. Es unterstützt Eingaben via Maus und Tastatur, bietet seit iPadOS 26 eine komplett dynamische Fensterverwaltung und arbeitet mit externen Bildschirmen zusammen. Der einfache Computer, den man im Lesesessel zur Hand nimmt, um im Netz zu surfen, Mails zu beantworten oder E-Books zu lesen, ist es längst nicht mehr.

articles.title: Madrid's Talky raises €1.5 million to teach AI the unwritten rules of accounting | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Talky Labs, a Spanish startup developing AI-powered technology to automate accounting and financial operations, has raised €1.5 million in a pre-Seed funding round to support team expansion, further product development and improvements to the company’s technical infrastructure.
The investment, closed in September 2026, saw participation from venture capital firms HelloWorld, Silence VC, Motive Force, and Aera Capital. Alongside angel investors Sebastián Gunningham; CEO of Remitly, Paul Golbaum; CEO of Lightbase and former CTO of Seedtag, and Javier Morenés, among others.
“Two years ago, I met my co-founder Jorge Beamonte at a networking event. That night, I called my mom and told her: ‘Mom, today is the most important day of my life. Everything is about to change,‘” said Maximilian Letón in a public statement.
Talky’s funding comes amid a series of European investments in AI-powered accounting and financial operations during 2026.
In Belgium, Dytto raised €1.5 million to develop its AI assistant for accountants, while Denmark’s Plinto secured €2.9 million for automated financial controls. Germany’s mika raised €6 million for AI-powered accounting and tax services, and UK-based Zalos obtained €3.1 million for enterprise finance automation.
In Spain, Barcelona-based Dolfin secured €2.1 million for adjacent financial workflows.
Together these rounds amount to approximately €66.8 million, including Talky’s investment.
“Every company has its own way of doing accounting, and it’s almost never written down. Talky learns those criteria, applies them to the hard cases and turns them into information for better decisions,” adds Jorge Beamonte, co-founder and CEO of Talky.
Founded in 2025 by Jorge Beamonte; CEO, and Maximilian Letón (23); COO, Talky aims to help businesses automate financial processes that traditionally depend on accountants’ experience and knowledge of internal company practices. Despite operating with a team of just nine employees, the startup reports having processed more than 1.8 million documents and over €2 billion in client expenditure through its platform.
The company addresses a common challenge in corporate finance departments: accounting decisions often rely on information scattered across enterprise systems, spreadsheets, emails, contracts and individual employees’ knowledge. While conventional automation tools can process standard transactions, unusual invoices or exceptions frequently require manual intervention, creating delays and increasing the risk of errors.
Talky’s platform uses AI to learn from a company’s historical accounting records and the expertise of its financial teams. Rather than relying exclusively on predefined rules, its technology identifies how previous transactions were handled, extracts relevant accounting criteria and applies that knowledge to new financial operations.
When the system encounters an unfamiliar situation or lacks sufficient information to make a decision, it identifies the appropriate employee to consult.
According to the startup, its technology processes between 86% and 93% of accounting documents without human intervention. The platform can read invoices, suggest accounting entries, review tax information and reconcile bank transactions before recording the results in the client’s enterprise resource planning (ERP) system.
The funding comes as Talky looks to expand its presence among large enterprises and financial services providers managing high volumes of transactions. Its founders have identified recruitment as a central priority, with plans to grow the team while continuing to develop the platform alongside existing customers.

articles.title: Thousands of “ghost students” use AI to steal millions in student loans, DOJ says
articles.text:
The US has charged five individuals as part of the first broad federal crackdown on “ghost students”—fraudsters who steal the identities of hundreds of Americans to pose as fake college students and steal student loans.
In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from “a network associated with Kenyan nationals” after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that “this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya,” while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun.
“If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build a future—we will find you,” McDonald said. “Whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you.”
At a press conference, McDonald was joined by FBI and Department of Education officials to explain how the scheme works.
It starts with bad actors purchasing personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans—most frequently targeting high school graduates who never attended college and went straight into the workforce.
Once they have that sensitive data, they fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) while seeking to enroll in universities and community colleges. If accepted, student aid is distributed first to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Dozens of Americans have opened bank accounts to act as money mules for fraudsters, the DOJ said.
To keep money flowing, bad actors use AI to fill out applications, complete coursework, and even make it appear that a student is attending virtual sessions.
“It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class,” McDonald said at the press conference. “Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester.”
Oblivious Americans stuck with bills
So far, the DOE has “identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens,” officials said at the press conference. If all those accounts are ghost students, total losses come close to $130 million, the DOJ said.
For Americans whose data is stolen, there’s little opportunity to discover the scheme until the government comes collecting on loans years later. In the meantime, victims’ credit can be damaged. Once they detect the scheme, they’re stuck defending against demands to repay inflated student loans, which McDonald admitted is messy.
“The Department of Education does a great job to help unravel that mess, but it is a mess that no one should have to endure,” he said.
In connection with the arrests, officials said they “identified more than $32 million in actual loss tied to these specific subjects” and “we believe that actual total is substantially higher,” with “millions more suspected.”
The DOE’s Office of Inspector General first detected the fraud patterns that brought the alleged scheme to light. The FBI then helped identify how many accounts were impacted, tracing money to US and foreign bank accounts and crypto wallets. In one case, a defendant “used multiple bank accounts across several financial institutions to receive over 700 fraudulently obtained federal student aid refund deposits, totaling approximately $1,439,548,” the DOJ said. In another, “one person received more than $1 million in deposits that were linked to more than 300 fraudulent student accounts,” Inside Higher Ed reported.
At the press conference, First Assistant US Attorney Theophani K. Stamos for the Eastern District of Virginia said that data analysis “identified unusual, suspicious patterns of behavior” that the FBI said indicated “coordinated fraud was happening involving FAFSA.” Those patterns gave investigators “a solid basis and a solid lead to open further inquiries that have led to indictments,” Stamos said.
To keep the crackdown going, his office has sent “approximately 50 referrals to 26 FBI field offices across the country” to hunt down stolen taxpayer funds.
“We are just getting started. Working with partners around the world, we are sending a clear message: student aid belongs to real students, the data always leaves a trail, and we will follow it wherever it leads,” Stamos said.
Automated fraud detection isn’t perfect
The DOJ suspects this scam has been running since at least 2021, growing increasingly sophisticated as AI opens new avenues for loan theft.
“These fraudsters are exploiting Americans who have never been to college before, preventing the Department of Education from cross-checking applicants,” the DOJ said. “Many known victims have reported attaining only high school diplomas—and are shocked by their faked attendance at an institution hundreds of miles away.”
At the press conference, Undersecretary of Education Nicholas Kent accused the Biden administration of leaving Americans unprotected.
“When we walked in the door last January, we were extremely troubled to find that the Biden administration had turned off nearly every fraud detection measure,” Kent said.
Trump’s DOE said it introduced online identity verification requirements that Kent claimed would stop ghost students from ever receiving funds. Relying on automated systems to flag behaviors and reject fraudulent FAFSA applications, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, vice chair of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, insisted that fraud could be easily stopped without allocating staff and resources or overly burdening the US government.
“The computers help us find it, and we keep the money in the agency,” Ferguson said.
The automated system isn’t perfect, however, and advocates have warned that false flags burden schools, meaning students’ access to aid could be delayed as administrators work through the added identity-verification processes.
Glitches have already affected fraud detection and student applications. In August, the DOE confirmed a technical issue from June 29 to July 6 prevented fraud evaluation results from being shared with certain FAFSA forms. After detecting the glitch, the DOE reprocessed those applications.
Real students may be flagged as fakes
Colleges and universities are also considering adding fees to stop the ghost student fraud.
Some advocates have acknowledged that the fraud deprives real students of funds. But they’re concerned that both the fees and online identity verification could become barriers to access to higher education for low-income students.
To verify their identities through the online FAFSA portal, students are expected to have government-issued IDs on hand in “real time.” They hold the IDs up to their cameras, and automated systems review them. A senior DOE official told Insider Higher Ed that the systems are “similar to the ones used by financial services companies like banks” and that he believed they are the same ones used by rental car companies.
Automated systems then assign a risk rating to the student, and anyone flagged as “high risk” is rejected. Once a student is rejected for aid, it’s up to the university to conduct any follow-up to verify if the application was real.
MorraLee Keller, a senior consultant for the National College Attainment Network, told Inside Higher Ed that “a lot of low-economic kids may not have secured, for example, a driver’s license” and may be set back in the application process while trying to obtain alternative IDs. That could also add fees during the application process.
Students may also be subject to automated fraud detection when seeking to make corrections to their FAFSA, which could delay fund distribution if a false rejection is issued.
“We want to make sure that timing doesn’t interrupt the aid getting credited to their account to pay their bills on time so that they could start classes, get refunds to go get their books, and all those kinds of things,” Keller said.
The Trump administration has said that it expects the number of real students flagged as fraudulent to be low. But the president of the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, Melanie Storey, pushed back “a little bit” on that claim during a podcast from the association recently, asking “the department to quantify the volume of in-person verification that will remain,” Inside Higher Ed reported in April. At the time, Aaron Lemon-Strauss, executive director of the FAFSA program, replied, “I’m not going to be able to give you a number yet.”
Storey noted that many people complete the FAFSA form at in-person events, further narrowing potential false positives as the government expands its ghost student crackdown. For any students who “accidentally get caught in the net,” Lemon-Strauss recommended that universities remain vigilant and take action to ensure support goes to Americans who need it most.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: How Grey plans to turn FX paychecks into credit
articles.text:
Grey, the Y Combinator-backed cross-border payments company, is looking to use foreign currency salary records to help remote workers access credit, addressing a gap in how traditional lenders assess professionals earning internationally.
Speaking on the Moonshot Podcast at Moonshot by TechCabal 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, Idorenyin Obong, Grey’s co-founder and chief executive officer, said many remote workers struggle to establish creditworthiness because conventional credit bureaus have limited visibility into income earned from foreign employers.
He said Grey plans to use income and transaction data accumulated over the past six years to develop credit services for these customers.
“This is built on our own data and income intelligence from the last five to six years,” Obong said.
The planned offering forms part of Grey’s expansion into salary management following the launch of Paycheck on Wednesday.
The product allows professionals earning in US dollars, British pounds, and euros to automatically divide their salaries between spending, savings, and emergency funds.
With Paycheck, Obong said that a customer receiving $1,000 monthly could choose to allocate 20% to savings, another 10% to other financial needs, and retain 70% for immediate expenses. Users can adjust these allocations rather than follow a fixed spending formula.
Eligible Paycheck customers can also earn up to 3% annual interest on their US dollar Pouch, Grey’s savings feature. The product includes an emergency fund designed to help users work towards saving three months’ salary over a year, alongside salary tracking and other account benefits.
“We need to build a bit more around the lifestyle of salary customers; if a customer wants to save, we can help them with that, and then offer them interest. If a customer wants to travel, we can help them with that,” Obong said, adding that Grey is looking to support flight bookings and provide eSIMs for customers travelling internationally.
“That was where the thinking came from. We still saw a gap here because I think there’s a lot of innovation we could still build for our customers; we saw that gap and decided to start with it.”
Grey’s move underscores the changing needs of remote workers who initially used cross-border fintech platforms primarily to receive foreign payments.
As international employment becomes more established, these customers increasingly need tools to manage their earnings, build savings, and potentially access loans.
However, Grey has not announced when the credit feature will become available or disclosed its proposed lending rates and borrowing limits.
For now, Paycheck is starting with customers earning at least $300 in foreign-currency salaries.
While salary management and savings benefits are already available, Grey’s planned credit offering could extend those services to remote workers whose international earnings are often overlooked by traditional lenders.

articles.title: Zest's new AI agent finds restaurants and books reservations over text | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Zest, the restaurant discovery app that launched earlier this year, is already thinking about a future where mobile apps are no longer the primary interface. On Thursday, the startup introduced a new feature: a personal AI-powered “restaurant concierge” that lives in your text messages, similar to other popular AI agents like Instinct or Poke.
The launch reflects a broader shift in how startups are thinking about AI, as conversational AI agents take on tasks that had previously required users to launch stand-alone mobile apps. For Zest, that means bringing its restaurant recommendations into texts, then allowing users to immediately take the next step of booking a table.
“The agent is the product now,” explains Zest founder and CEO Mario Gomez-Hall. “You text it, and it answers from your own history and your friends’. It doesn’t need weeks of conversation to learn you because it starts from where you’ve actually been,” he said.
Originally founded in November 2024, with $1.8 million in pre-seed backing from Alexis Ohanian at 776 and Steve Jang at Kindred Ventures, the app’s unique feature is that it links up with users’ credit cards to track where they’re actually eating out to get a sense of their tastes and interests. With this data on hand, Zest can make tailored suggestions of what places you might like to try next, whether that’s in your own city or suggestions of places to try when you’re traveling.
The credit card data used by Zest’s app is imported via the financial services company Plaid, which is used by banks and other fintech and budgeting apps. Zest says it focuses only on those transactions in the food and drink categories when making its personalized map and lists.
The startup’s latest idea is to tackle the same problem — where should I go to eat? — from a new angle. It will now make its suggestions from inside a text message thread and can turn to AI to do things like check availability and make the reservation for you through connected services like OpenTable, Resy, and SevenRooms.
To work, users will text the Zest concierge at (212) 470-6067. What’s even better is that Zest can be dropped into a group chat, where it can blend everyone’s tastes to find places the whole group will love. Here, it can also settle indecision with an in-thread voting feature and then can book a table for the group without leaving the conversation.
Users can ask Zest for recommendations based on a number of factors, like cuisine, craving, occasion, dietary restrictions, or neighborhood, and can ask questions about the restaurants, like how busy the place may be, or whether it offers Wi-Fi, and more. Plus, you can ask Zest to send you the menu to help you make a decision.
In TechCrunch’s tests, the AI worked fairly well, offering a list of suggestions for new places matched to our tastes that also fit particular conditions, like time of day, party size, location, and other factors. While finding an open table is something other apps have offered for years, there’s a convenience factor in being able to just text back and forth about the various options and have it tell you the available booking times.
The company began testing the concierge last month, but decided to hold the launch until it could add the booking capabilities; over time, the startup is considering moving Zest beyond restaurants to offer recommendations for businesses, shopping, and more.
By shifting to texts, Zest hopes the company can scale beyond its initial thousands of users and generate revenue.
“Booking and ordering are the first revenue lines. Zest books your table through OpenTable or Resy today, with food ordering coming, and there are transactions there to participate in,” said Gomez-Hall. “The reason that gets interesting is that Zest learns your taste faster than a general assistant does, because it starts from where you’ve actually been instead of asking you questions. That’s worth something well beyond dinner,” he added.

articles.title: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak
articles.text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.
Here are this week’s highlights:
Iran suspected in US military freezer hacks
US officials suspect Iran-linked hackers caused freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at around six military base commissaries starting in late August, Nextgov reports, citing people familiar with the matter. At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, a freezer entered defrost mode and heated its contents, and Cyber Command and Defense Department law enforcement units are investigating with French authorities, after hackers overrode refrigeration controls at some 350 French establishments earlier this month.
Most servers rely on UEFI code hit by critical boot flaw
A critical 16-year-old buffer overflow (CVE-2026-97631) in TianoCore EDK II, open source code that most of the world’s server vendors and data centers use through firmware suppliers such as AMI, Insyde and Phoenix, means the flaw affects most servers worldwide, Ars Technica reports. An attacker with local network access can send an oversized ICMP error message to a machine while it boots over the network (PXE) to hang the process or, if the target’s firmware build is known, run code at the highest privilege level before defenses such as Secure Boot take effect. Only machines that use network boot are exposed, and the flaw, found by Anthropic and Google researchers, became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure after AMI published a code fix, leaving organizations to seek firmware updates from their vendors.
Anthropic disputes scope of ex-DOGE startup’s AI-led intrusion
Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers, says its AI agents found ways into Anthropic’s internal systems in less than 12 hours by abusing weaknesses in third-party business software, reaching meeting transcripts, salary and job offer data, and Slack discussions about the company’s most advanced models, according to a draft report reviewed by the Washington Post (paywalled). Anthropic, which received the findings through its bug bounty program, says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached, that it cut off the startup’s access the same day, and that Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected. It also accuses Cathedral of breaking the bounty program’s rules by not disclosing all of its activity.
Midterm spending disclosures stall after FEC intrusion attempt
The US Federal Election Commission took its electronic filing system offline after someone attempted to breach its systems, according to an internal FEC email seen by Reuters, leaving political groups unable to submit campaign finance reports a week before the November 3 midterm elections. The outage blocked the 24-hour and 48-hour reports that track last-minute spending on specific races, although past filings remained searchable. The system was restored on October 28.
Hackers obtain national ID numbers, card PINs in University of Copenhagen breach
The University of Copenhagen says hackers who gained access to one of its test environments obtained personal data on about 525,000 current and former members of the university community, including names, phone numbers and personal email addresses, along with national identity (CPR) numbers for many of them. The attack was detected on October 20 and contained, but the PIN codes for the ID cards of roughly 20,000 staff and students were also compromised and have since been reissued. The university says it does not yet know who is behind the attack or what the motive was.
ENGIE data breach traced to tool used by sales partners
French energy giant ENGIE says attackers stole customer data after gaining access to a tool its partners use for customer prospecting and marketing energy offers, but that its own internal IT systems were not compromised. The incident is limited to customers in France, and notification letters say the stolen data includes names, contact details, customer IDs, contract numbers and energy supply point identifiers, but no banking information. ENGIE has not said how many customers are affected, and no group has claimed the attack.
Fake ChatGPT and Claude bots probe sites for leaked secrets
Cequence has tracked a single threat actor that rotates through about 32 AI bot identities (including crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Perplexity) while scanning websites for files that commonly hold secrets, such as .env files, cloud credentials and private SSH keys. Running from a major cloud provider since at least late September, the scanner used more than 300 IP addresses in a single day and, on one day in October, reached 48% of the Cequence-protected organizations that saw any AI bot traffic. Cequence warns that a bot’s self-declared identity can’t be trusted, noting that the impersonator accounted for more than 80% of traffic labeled as AI bot traffic at some organizations.
Cloudflare and SGLang fix cross-tenant data leak in AI inference
Cloudflare says that between August 27 and September 9, 155 responses from the GLM 5.3 model on its Workers AI platform contained data from other customers’ recent requests to the same model, all involving prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. The leak resulted from a configuration mismatch that left the model’s KV cache smaller than its advertised context window, combined with a bug in the SGLang inference engine that allowed over-length requests to read cache data left behind by earlier sessions. Cloudflare fixed the issue after Knostic researcher Gadi Evron reported it via HackerOne, found no evidence of deliberate exploitation, and recommends that SGLang operators update to version 0.5.22 or later.
Defense worker, Russian money movers targeted over North Korean IT scheme
John Allen Kurrle Jr., 62, a defense contractor employee with a Top Secret clearance, has pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy for aiding a North Korean remote IT worker scheme by letting foreign individuals use his identity (and that of a third person) to apply for remote jobs and hosting victim companies’ laptops at his home. The applications led to nine job offers from US companies, and Kurrle faces up to 20 years in prison. Separately, OFAC sanctioned 10 individuals and one entity supporting North Korea’s IT worker schemes, including two Russians who allegedly converted the workers’ crypto earnings into cash, two North Koreans who managed Russia-based IT worker groups, and the Russia-based First Financial and Technical Development Center (FFTDC), which deploys North Korean IT workers abroad.
Rockwell aims SecureOT at OEMs facing CRA and machinery rules
Rockwell Automation has added OEM-focused capabilities to its SecureOT offering to help machine builders prepare for cybersecurity requirements under the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and Machinery Regulation. Built on the SecureOT Platform, the additions include machine-level inventories of hardware, software and firmware, vulnerability identification, continuous monitoring for newly disclosed flaws after deployment, and exportable compliance reports for customers and auditors. Rockwell is also offering assessments and advisory services to help OEMs find gaps, set up governance processes, and align with standards such as IEC 62443.
AI moves deeper into ransomware, C2 malware and grey-market tooling
Sophos says the Gold Ogre group behind Aur0ra ransomware has used AI extensively, with agents orchestrated through Cursor handling network discovery, credential attacks and lateral movement with limited human involvement, after the operators bypassed guardrails by framing the intrusions as authorized red team work. Cisco Talos has detailed NIK C2, a new AI-integrated command-and-control framework whose Windows implant can steal credentials, stream keystrokes and deploy screen-locking ransomware. Symantec and Carbon Black, meanwhile, warn of a grey-market relay service, seen at a dozen organizations mostly in mainland China, that installs the genuine Codex and Claude Code CLIs but reconfigures them to route all requests through third-party servers with sandboxing disabled.
Related: In Other News: ICS-Sniper Attack, Hacking XWorm Malware Operators, $250k Chrome Exploit

articles.title: Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
articles.text:
Akai teased its new MPC Sample Key on Instagram earlier this week, and said it plans to open-source its software so the modding community can hack it to their hearts’ delight. While there’s no word yet on when the device will launch or how much it will cost, The Verge has received exclusive images of the upcoming instrument that offer some details about its feature set.
Exclusive details about Akai’s MPC Sample Key
The open-source MPC Sample Key won’t be focused on chopping up drum breaks.
While the Sample Key shares many of the same controls as the MPC Sample — including the three context-sensitive encoders, a large main encoder — it seems designed for pitched sample playback, rather than chopping up drums. In fact, the “chop” button from the MPC Sample is missing entirely from the Sample Key.
The dedicated pitch and mod wheels are another clue there. But there are also buttons for changing the octave range of the 25-key keyboard, as well as ones labeled “chord” and “arp.” Presumably, those enable a chord playback mode and an arpeggiator. While using an arpeggiator to play back drum samples can be a fun way to create rhythms, it’s more commonly used for melodic and bass parts. And a chord mode would be basically useless for drums. Those options also appear to replace the chop function from the standard MPC Sample.
There also appears to be a dedicated looper that could be useful for live performance and layering sounds. And, instead of the Flex Beat effects from the original MPC Sample, there’s something called “Swarm.” Though what that is isn’t exactly clear at the moment.
Like the first entry in the Sample series, the Key has a built-in mic and speaker for all-in-one music production. While we haven’t gotten a glimpse at the back panel yet, the config options on the front suggest that, in addition to MIDI, the Sample Key will have CV outs for integrating with modular synths.
Correction October 30th: The MPC Sample Key is 25 keys, not 37.

articles.title: 7 new movies and TV shows to watch on Netflix, Prime Video, and more this weekend (October 30) — The One About Matthew Perry, Minions and Monsters, and more
articles.text:
7 new movies and TV shows to watch on Netflix, Prime Video, HBO Max, and more this weekend (October 30)
Netflix's Matthew Perry documentary and the latest Minions film lead this week's round-up
Happy Halloween to all who celebrate the spookiest time of the year. And, whether or not you'll be trick and treating this weekend, the world's best streaming services have released some must-see new movies, shows, and documentaries that you can enjoy with our without candy.
There's something for everyone, too. From the latest Minions-starring movie to a Netflix documentary about the late Matthew Perry, I'm confident one of the below recommendations will appeal to you. Enjoy — and don't eat all of your Halloween sweets in one sitting! — Tom Power, senior entertainment reporter
The One About Matthew Perry (Netflix)
It's rare for a documentary to headline one of our streaming round-ups. Given the subject matter, though, I suspect few would argue with The One About Matthew Perry doing so.
A docufilm about the much-loved actor best known for playing Chandler Bing on Friends, it explores the man behind the Hollywood icon. With intimate testimonies from Perry's family and closest friends, The One About... offers a raw, unedited look at a star whose light shone brightly —despite his well-documented battles with drugs and alcohol — before his sudden death in late 2023.
Hopefully, The One About Matthew Perry will be a celebration of his life and legacy, and an inspirational testimony to his candidness and tireless advocacy against substance abuse. — TP
Minions and Monsters (Peacock)
Everyone's favorite, babbling yellow bean-like creatures are back. That's right, the Minions have returned for another standalone feature, this time in Minions & Monsters, which is out now on Peacock.
Set in 1927, it follows James, Ed, Henry, and company as they attempt to make a monster movie of their own amid the Golden Age of Hollywood. Unsurprisingly, things go awry pretty quickly, forcing the titular beings to save the day once more.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Praised by critics for its love letter-style approach to Old Hollywood, Minions & Monsters didn't perform as well as its predecessors did at the global box office. Is that down to Minions burnout? Who's to say, but you can see if it lives up to the hype by tuning in at home. — TP
The Gilded Age season 4 (HBO Max)
The Gilded Age season 4, which premieres on HBO Max this Sunday, skips ahead six months from last season's finale and sees Bertha Russell's relentless social climbing come under scrutiny.
Previously, Bertha forced her daughter Gladys into a marriage with the Duke of Buckingham to secure her social standing, causing her husband George to leave her, as he was furious with the decision. By season 4, George has completely moved out and now everyone's gossiping about their failed marriage.
Outside of Bertha's dramatic life, season 4 features real historical moments like the dedication of the Statue of Liberty in 1886, so there's a lot for period drama lovers to enjoy. — Lucy Buglass, senior entertainment writer
Apocalypse Z: New World (Prime Video)
Zombie movies are a Halloween staple and Prime Video's got you covered with a new Spanish-language release.
Apocalypse Z: New World is the follow up to Amazon's Apocalypse Z: The Beginning of the End. You could even have a double bill, if you like.
This time, we follow a new protagonist as he sets out from the refuge of the zombie-free Canary Islands to the mainland (anyone else getting 28 Years Later vibes?) in search of essential supplies. It's a risky decision, and there's danger at every turn. There'll no doubt be thrills in abundance here, and I can't wait to watch it all unfold. — LB
Dexter: Resurrection season 2 (Paramount+)
Dexter Morgan's going through a midlife crisis in Dexter: Resurrection season 2. It's been four years since the show revival's debut outing, and there's a lot for us to catch up on even beyond what Dexter is going through on a personal level.
Indeed, the titular character is caught between two major serial killers, while his son Harrison launches a career as an NYPD homicide rookie. On top of this, expect to see some ghosts from Dexter's past, too.
Will he ever catch a break? It certainly doesn't seem that way, but it's entertaining for all of us Paramount+ viewers, at least. — LB
Nocturne (Apple TV)
Apple has become many people's go-to streamer for top-tier television — and Nocturne is the latest offering to try to add its name to the tech giant's growing list of unmissable shows.
Billed as a gripping crime drama, the Apple TV Original stars Liev Schreiber as Jonah, a soldier-turned-homicide detective who relocates to a small Pennsylvania town alongside his family, including surrogate daughter and FBI agent Saga (Zazie Beetz). However, when they suddenly garner the attention of an imprisoned yet cunning serial killer Jurek (Stephen Graham), a twisty-turny game of cat and mouse ensues.
Episodes 1 and 2 are out now, with the final four releasing weekly up to November 27. — TP
Last One Laughing: Halloween (Prime Video)
Last One Laughing is back with a Halloween special, featuring some of the biggest names in comedy.
Returning contestants Daisy May Cooper and Lou Sanders are joined by Jack Dee, Phil Wang, Reece Shearsmith, Harriet Dyer, and Tom Allen. They're all hoping to be — you guessed it — the last one laughing and win the series. But, it's not easy, and there'll be guest stars and surprises intended to make them lose their composure.
Thankfully, we're allowed to laugh as much as we want. And host Jimmy Carr is likely to be right there with us, given his reactions from the past two seasons. — LB

articles.title: Saffron Box dreams of one day turning Canada into the next saffron superpower | BetaKit
articles.text:
Vikash Sangwan spent too much time sitting behind a computer. Like so many young Indian expatriates, Sangwan came to Canada in the 2010s looking to advance his career. An engineer by trade, he entered through Canada’s Federal Express Entry program and later landed a nine-to-five at one of the Big Four consulting agencies. But after years of working a desk job, Sangwan was desperate for change.
Today, Sangwan’s working environment is split between the glassy towers of Calgary, where he continues to work as a consultant with KWA Analytics, and a rustic, retrofitted barn in the neighbouring foothills. It’s there that Sangwan tends to more than 40,000 saffron bulbs that make up the inventory for his startup, Saffron Box.
“We want early investors and ecosystem partners to see that our [technology is] thoroughly proven before deploying at commercial scale.”
Vikash Sangwan,
Saffron Box
Pound for pound, Saffron is the most expensive spice in the world. It routinely sells for as much as $18,000 USD ($25,000 CAD) per kilogram on the wholesale market. To contextualize that, cocaine retails wholesale in Canada for around $18,000 per kilogram.
While saffron’s not an illegal substance, its supply chain is similarly fraught. Global supply is heavily concentrated, with around 90 percent of saffron originating from Iran. Secondary markets—the largest among them India and Afghanistan—have in recent years declined amid climate-change-induced droughts, driving up prices even further.
Sangwan’s Saffron Box is hoping to capitalize on that market scarcity, while also changing it.
Canadian-grown saffron
Founded in February 2026, Saffron Box is using vertical farming techniques and climate controls to attempt to replicate the precision horticulture required to grow the infamously fickle plant. In doing so, Sangwan hopes to create a whole new market stream for saffron right here in Canada.
Saffron Box is still very much an early-stage company. A husband-and-wife team, the company has no commercial customers. Instead, Sangwan is focused on research and development.
“Three years ago I tried growing corms [the garlic-like bulbs from which the saffron flower grows] in a basement grow tent and completely failed. Last year, I upgraded to a custom walk-in cooler in my residential garage. Now, we’ve scaled up to the barn level specifically to prove out the commercial ROI and unit economics,” Sangwan told BetaKit.
Cultivated from the saffron crocus flower, saffron grows in an inverted lifecycle, blooming in the autumn, producing foliage throughout the winter, and going dormant in the summer. In order to harvest the stigmas—the waxy portion of a saffron flower’s female reproductive system—that constitute the spice, precise conditions need to be met. In nature, those conditions are only found along a narrow stretch of geography with Mediterranean-like weather.
“In nature, Saffron breaks its summer dormancy only when prompted by a specific sequence of autumnal climate shifts,” Sangwan told BetaKit in an email.
That actually makes growing the spice outside of its natural harvest season more difficult in hot places like Iran, where growers need to invest in expensive cooling systems to produce multiple harvests throughout the year.
Images courtesy Saffron Box
Inside his barn, Sangwan is leveraging the brisk Alberta weather to avoid those costs.
“By mid-October, Canadian ambient outdoor temperature naturally matches the thermal profile required for floral induction,” Sangwan said.
Sangwan has set up an industrial air-handling unit to circulate that October air into the barn, keeping the temperature at the eight to 10 degrees Celsius needed to trigger saffron flowering. He pairs that with a hydronic boiler system (a heating device using heated, closed-loop water) that can supply targeted heat to counteract cooler winter temperatures that would otherwise destabilize the microclimate.
Sangwan cultivates his saffron corms without soil, meaning they can be stacked by the tens of thousands along vertical farming shelves, where they’re helped along the growth cycle with specialized light arrays and moisture monitoring.
“Throughout the transition, sensor arrays continuously monitor ambient temperature and moisture to maintain relative humidity,” Sangwan said. “When the flowers emerge, we deploy spectrum-tuned LED [lights] with targeted ratios of blue-to-red light.”
Big dreams start small
Ultimately, Sangwan hopes to commercialize his saffron farm. The founder envisions a future where Saffron Box’s product is grown in insulated, trailer-pod vertical farms capable of producing multiple yields per year regardless of the season.
“By controlling the climate … and staggering dormant batches, we [could] achieve up to four harvests per year rather than a single seasonal bloom,” he said.
Sangwan sees a future where these farm pods could be franchised out to independent growers nationwide, serving as a foundation for Canada to transition from saffron importer to exporter.
RELATED: After 15 years, GoodLeaf proves there’s profit in vertical farming
“Deploying this modular fleet would not only satisfy North American [saffron] consumption, but it would position Canada as a premier exporter,” he said.
That dream is, admittedly, quite a way off. While Sangwan claims to have secured at least one of the 53-foot trailers he hopes to convert to a vertical farming facility, he has not yet physically retrofitted it nor validated its ability to match the precision climatics present in his barn model, nor the economic viability of franchising said pods. 
To do that, the 36-year-old entrepreneur would need some serious capital. He’s not there yet, but said the company is actively seeking pre-seed investment. “Physical fabrication is our immediate milestone, which our open pre-seed capital raise is structured to fund,” Sangwan said. 
A/B testing
Just because Saffron Box isn’t ready to begin franchising out vertical farms doesn’t mean the company isn’t making efforts to expand beyond its current footprint. Sangwan has secured an outdoor plot of land in British Columbia’s Fraser Valley—which he says is about as close to the ideal climate for saffron as one can find outdoors in Canada—where he’s propagating another 20,000 saffron plants using traditional methods. The plan, he says, is to execute a comparative study between the indoor and outdoor yields.
“Running both parts simultaneously allows us to gather … the data and compare indoor, climate-controlled corm reproduction rates, sizing, and mortality, against traditional cultivation,” Sangwan said.
Sangwan is also in the midst of validating his multi-harvest thesis, staggering crop cycles through the year until June of 2027 in an effort to de-risk his business model. He hopes that by proving his methods, he might better attract the investors who could take his lofty dreams closer to reality.
“We want early investors and ecosystem partners to see that our biological triggers and CapEx models are thoroughly proven before deploying at commercial scale,” he said.
Some might say Saffron Box’s vision of Canada as a global saffron supplier is unrealistic. But so is the idea of growing saffron on the Canadian prairie in the first place. And so far, Sangwan’s been able to do just that.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy of Saffron Box. Photo by Vikash Sangwan.

articles.title: Alerte sur le vortex polaire : pourquoi la France est encore très loin du grand gel
articles.text:
Faut-il craindre une perturbation du « vortex polaire » ? Ces derniers jours, de nombreuses publications sur les réseaux sociaux évoquent un « réchauffement stratosphérique soudain », qui pourrait amener des températures glaciales jusqu’en France.
Le phénomène existe bien, mais ses effets sur la météo en France dans les prochaines semaines restent très incertains, y compris pour les prévisionnistes.
Selon La Chaîne Météo, dans un tweet diffusé ce mardi 27 octobre 2026, « le vortex polaire pourrait se faire bousculer par un réchauffement stratosphérique (SSW) très précoce début novembre », plus exactement aux alentours du 6 novembre. La chaîne d’information météorologique estime que « ce SSW serait un record de précocité », mais juge ses conséquences en France encore très incertaines.
Qu’est-ce que le vortex polaire ?
Comme l’explique Météo-France, le vortex polaire correspond à une « zone de basses pressions en altitude centrée sur les pôles géographiques ». Cette zone est toujours présente près des pôles, indique le National Weather Service, qui précise bien qu’il ne s’agit pas d’un phénomène nouveau. « Le terme ‘vortex polaire’ n’a été popularisé que récemment, attirant ainsi l’attention sur un phénomène météorologique qui a toujours existé », souligne le service météorologique des États-Unis.
Ce vortex peut influencer la météo, y compris en France, en fonction de sa position ou de son réchauffement, en engendrant potentiellement une vague de froid.
Il existe deux vortex polaires.
- Le premier, dans la troposphère, se situe vers 6 à 8 km d’altitude et existe toute l’année.
- Le second, dans la stratosphère, au-dessus de 10 km d’altitude, n’existe qu’en hiver : c’est de lui qu’il est question ici.
Vu depuis le pôle Nord, ce vortex tourne dans le sens inverse des aiguilles d’une montre, porté par des vents qui soufflent d’ouest en est. Cette ronde maintient l’air froid près du pôle.
Le réchauffement stratosphérique soudain : quel impact en France ?
Ce vortex ne pèse pas sur la météo française tous les ans. La majeure partie du temps, il reste centré sur le pôle en hiver, et l’Hexagone connaît une circulation d’ouest classique, avec une succession de perturbations venues de l’Atlantique. Mais, « certaines années, suite à un réchauffement stratosphérique soudain, le vortex peut se déplacer vers les latitudes moyennes en Europe, ce qui peut dans ce cas avoir des conséquences sur la météo en France, avec un coup de froid ou une vague de froid », résume Météo-France.
Mais pourquoi parler de « réchauffement » quand on redoute le froid ? En hiver, le cœur du vortex stratosphérique descend vers -70 à -80 °C. Lors d’un réchauffement stratosphérique soudain, sa température peut grimper de 50 à 60 °C en quelques jours, précise Météo-France. Les vents d’ouest faiblissent alors, s’inversent parfois, et une partie du vortex peut glisser vers les zones tempérées avec son air polaire.
« Il n’y a pas lieu de s’alarmer lorsqu’on entend parler du vortex polaire, mais il convient de se préparer à des températures plus basses », indique le National Weather Service.
Le vortex polaire va subir une « perturbation majeure », selon les modèles
Revenons maintenant à l’épisode en cours. Dans un long fil publié sur X, Guillaume Jauseau, étudiant en physique-chimie à l’université de Toulon et créateur de la plateforme météo RecordPy, développe une analyse du phénomène.
« D’après plusieurs modèles, ce vortex va subir une perturbation majeure. Ses vents d’ouest devraient s’affaiblir énormément, voire s’inverser selon certains scénarios. C’est cette inversion qu’on appelle ‘réchauffement stratosphérique soudain’ (SSW) », explique-t-il. Selon Guillaume Jauseau, ce SSW se forme avec des ondes de Rossby, qui sont « des courants d’air qui font le tour de la Terre puis ondulent en butant sur les montagnes. Ces ondulations montent jusqu’au vortex et s’y brisent comme des vagues. L’air polaire descend alors, se comprime et se réchauffe. »
Et El Niño, dans tout ça ?
Selon le compte spécialisé Météovillages sur X, le phénomène climatique El Niño tiendrait un rôle dans l’apparition de ce réchauffement stratosphérique soudain, en générant des ondes d’air géantes qui montent en altitude et déstabilisent le vortex polaire.
Un épisode El Niño est bien en cours dans le Pacifique. La Nasa le qualifie déjà d’ « historique ». Selon l’Organisation météorologique mondiale, il devrait se maintenir jusqu’en février 2027.
Une perturbation précoce, avec 3 semaines d’avance
Début novembre, les projections montrent un potentiel affaiblissement très marqué du vortex polaire, relève Guillaume Jauseau. « Les courbes chutent jusqu’à 0 et certains membres passent même en négatif, symptôme d’une inversion des vents. Le plus marquant reste la précocité : tous les ensembles tombent sous les extrêmes de saison. »
Cette perturbation du vortex polaire se distingue donc surtout par sa date, très précoce si elle se confirme. Le compte Météovillages indique que ce SSW serait alors le « plus précoce jamais envisagé avec 3 semaines d’avance sur l’ancien record. »
Du froid glacial en France ? Pas forcément
Quant aux impacts de cette perturbation, Guillaume Jauseau reste très prudent, expliquant que « même confirmé, un SSW n’apporte pas forcément du froid. Encore faut-il que la perturbation redescende de la stratosphère jusqu’à nous. » Un scénario qui n’est pas garanti, abonde Météovillages.
Les prévisions saisonnières penchent d’ailleurs vers la douceur. Dans son bulletin de tendances publié ce jeudi 29 octobre pour novembre, décembre et janvier, Météo-France juge le scénario d’un trimestre plus chaud que la normale le plus probable sur l’Hexagone et la Corse, avec une probabilité de 70 %. Elle précise toutefois que « des épisodes ponctuellement plus frais que la normale peuvent survenir ». Un coup de froid de quelques jours resterait donc compatible avec un début d’hiver globalement doux.

articles.title: Wikipedia pidió a un tribunal que la IA deje de reproducir sus artículos
articles.text:
La Fundación Wikimedia, la organización que opera Wikipedia, presentó un escrito ante el tribunal de Nueva York que juzga a OpenAI y Microsoft por el uso de artículos de prensa para entrenar IA. No toma partido: pide que entrenar modelos sea uso legítimo, pero que los chatbots no reproduzcan textos sin licencia.
El documento es un amicus curiae, que presenta quien no es parte del juicio para aportar argumentos al juez. Según The Verge, Wikimedia advierte que las posturas de ambas partes impulsan una aplicación “excesiva y simplificada” de la doctrina del uso legítimo, la excepción que permite emplear obras protegidas sin permiso en ciertos casos.
El litigio reúne las demandas a ambas empresas que presentaron The New York Times, el Daily News, The Intercept, el Center for Investigative Reporting, Ziff Davis y un grupo de autores de libros. El Times sostiene, por ejemplo, que OpenAI copió su sitio web para armar los datos de entrenamiento.
OpenAI y Microsoft responden que entrenar modelos de lenguaje es uso legítimo. La empresa dueña de ChatGPT dijo que la reproducción de textos es “un error poco frecuente”. Microsoft afirmó en un escrito de septiembre que, según un análisis de expertos, su asistente Copilot rara vez repite oraciones completas de las noticias.
Wikimedia plantea que los chatbots no pueden reproducir artículos
Wikimedia propone una salida intermedia. Según The Verge, que cita una publicación de la fundación, extraer datos de sitios web no debería considerarse infracción, y entrenar un modelo con obras protegidas y sin licencia debería ser uso legítimo cuando aporta “algo nuevo y diferente” respecto de las fuentes originales.
La excepción, de acuerdo con esa posición, son los sistemas que recuperan copias de un texto para responder a una consulta y lo entregan desplazando la lectura de la obra original. En ese caso, la fundación sostiene que corresponde pedir licencia, porque el resultado sustituye al original y no lo transforma lo suficiente.
Para Wikipedia, eso significaría citar la fuente original bajo su licencia Creative Commons, que también exige que cualquier adaptación se publique con la misma licencia. La fundación sostiene que servicios como ChatGPT reproducen texto de licencia libre sin respetar esas condiciones.
Cada extremo tiene un riesgo, según el escrito. Un triunfo total de los editores permitiría que los titulares de derechos bloqueen incluso usos innovadores. Un triunfo total de las empresas de IA sería “una luz verde para ignorar los términos de licencia y fragmentar el flujo de conocimiento” entre autores humanos y lectores.
Wikipedia, fuente de datos y también afectada
La fundación afirma en el escrito que sus sitios son una de las fuentes de datos más críticas para entrenar sistemas de IA. Esos mismos sistemas, agrega, desvían visitantes y debilitan a las comunidades de voluntarios que mantienen la enciclopedia.
El 5 de octubre, Wikimedia informó que agentes que cree operados por OpenAI hicieron millones de solicitudes automáticas a sus interfaces públicas y rastrearon millones de páginas, sobre todo de Wikidata y Wikimedia Commons. Según la fundación, ese tráfico pudo contribuir a una interrupción parcial del servicio de consultas en mayo.
Wikimedia también reconoce el valor de estos modelos: pueden ayudar a los editores a combatir el vandalismo, detectar violaciones de derechos de autor y publicación de datos personales, y encontrar artículos que necesitan mejoras.
“Un fallo que no aplique con cuidado los principios del uso legítimo podría amenazar la sostenibilidad del conocimiento libre”, dijo el asesor jurídico general de la fundación, Stephen LaPorte. La directora ejecutiva, Bernadette Meehan, afirmó que ampliar el acceso al conocimiento con IA es “un objetivo poderoso”, pero que debe respetar a quienes lo producen.
Wikimedia no es la única que intervino. El Gobierno de Estados Unidos presentó en septiembre un escrito a favor de OpenAI, según Reuters. Esta semana se sumaron escritos de la Asociación de Editores Estadounidenses, que respalda a los demandantes, y del profesor Matthew Sag, que no apoya a ninguna parte.
El juez Sidney Stein evalúa los pedidos cruzados de sentencia sumaria. Según Sag, su fallo será el primero del Segundo Circuito sobre si entrenar modelos con libros y artículos es uso legítimo, y el primero en el mundo que trate los reclamos de editoriales de noticias.

articles.title: What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
articles.text:
What worries Entire co-founder Thomas Dohmke about the future of tech?
Former GitHub CEO Thomas Dohmke is taking on his old company. His startup, Entire, launched a GitHub alternative this week, replacing traditional pull requests with Trails, a review system that uses AI agents to evaluate code changes while developers oversee the work.
A month before that launch, The New Stack asked Dohmke what excites him most about technology’s future and what worries him. He welcomed the ability to turn more of his ideas into working software. His concern was about learning.
“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding,” Entire’s co-founder and CEO told TNS at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose in September. “I think it’s fundamental for every kid out there to not only learn math and biology and geography, but also understand the basics of computer science.”
“What worries me is that people think they no longer need to learn coding.”
Dohmke was one of several people we posed those questions to at the conference. Their answers reveal enthusiasm for what more people can now build, along with some concerns about understanding, safety, and access to these new tools.
For Josh Bentley, SAP’s senior director of community advocacy, broader access to technology means people can build things in hours or days that once took weeks or months. His concern: Whether that speed comes with enough understanding.
“People are getting recognized as a builder when they really don’t understand the context of what they’re building,” Bentley said.
Darko Mesaroš, distinguished developer advocate at AWS, was similarly excited about more people being able to build software. He also worried about bad code and “AI slop.”
“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally.”
“I want people to be able to build more stuff, but I want people to build stuff more intentionally,” Mesaroš said.
For Mark Cavage, Docker’s president and chief operating officer, the concern was whether the industry could quickly establish the safeguards and efficiencies needed around AI agents.
“The thing that worries me about it, of course, is that actually we as an industry don’t figure out quickly enough how to bring ourselves new efficiencies and trust and safety around it,” Cavage said.
Cassidy Williams, GitHub’s senior director of developer advocacy, was excited that people can ask a machine to help turn an idea into something real. She also raised concerns about safety guardrails and the cost of participating.
Williams wants people to have accessible tools and “not be priced out from being able to be a part of the future.”
The pace of change itself was a source of excitement for Matt Hobbs, head of Cloud, Engineering, Data, and AI at PwC.
“Everything that I just built, I could rebuild again and do it better, do it faster, do it safer, do it more ready for enterprise scale,” Hobbs said.
Frederic Branczyk, vice president of data engineering at Dash0, described his outlook as cautiously optimistic. He was excited about what AI enables his company to offer customers and how it uses the technology internally, while acknowledging the uncertainty ahead.
“None of us really have the answers to all the problems that we’re facing together,” Branczyk said.
The conversation is part of The New Stack’s six-video Inside WeAreDevelopers series. The other five videos explore what developers should learn next, what teams are building, and what brings people together:
- What should every developer get hands-on with right now? — Speakers make the case for experimenting with GPU programming, local AI models, agent frameworks, and sandboxes.
- What people missed at WeAreDevelopers — From technical debates to unexpected career connections, attendees explain what happens beyond the stage.
- What tech industry experts enjoy most about developer events — Hallway conversations, old friends, and extended debates offer something a recorded session can’t.
- Exciting releases for developers — Speakers share updates on agent tools, Git infrastructure, observability, and cloud sandboxes.
- What tech leaders are focused on right now — Teams discuss agent development, engineering guardrails, infrastructure, and data privacy.
