articles.title: Microsoft débranche Copilot sur les TV LG et Samsung, un an après son arrivée
articles.text:
Présenté comme une nouvelle façon d'interagir avec son téléviseur, Copilot n'aura finalement pas fait long feu. Microsoft confirme l'abandon de son assistant IA sur les Smart TV LG et Samsung dès le 1er décembre 2026. Un retrait qui s'inscrit dans un repositionnement plus large de Copilot.
L'intelligence artificielle devait aussi révolutionner notre façon d'utiliser un téléviseur. Annoncée au CES 2025, l'arrivée de Microsoft Copilot sur les Smart TV LG et Samsung promettait notamment de faciliter la recherche de contenus et de permettre aux utilisateurs de dialoguer avec leur écran.
Mais l'expérience tourne court. Le 28 octobre, Windows Central révélait l'apparition d'une notification sur un téléviseur LG annonçant la fin prochaine du service. Nous avons vérifié, Microsoft a bien précisé son calendrier depuis, sur son site d'assistance : Copilot ne sera plus accessible sur les téléviseurs LG et Samsung à partir du 1er décembre 2026.
Une intégration qui avait déjà fait polémique chez LG
Sur le papier, Copilot devait enrichir l'expérience des téléviseurs connectés en apportant les capacités conversationnelles de l'IA de Microsoft. Chez Samsung, l'assistant faisait partie de Vision AI Companion, une plateforme réunissant plusieurs agents IA sur les téléviseurs récents et certains moniteurs connectés, dont les Smart Monitor M7, M8 et M9.
Chez LG, l'intégration était restée beaucoup plus rudimentaire. En décembre 2025, des propriétaires de téléviseurs avaient découvert un raccourci Copilot ajouté automatiquement à leur interface webOS, sans possibilité de le supprimer. Le constructeur avait ensuite précisé qu'il ne s'agissait pas d'une application native, mais d'un simple lien ouvrant le site de Microsoft dans le navigateur du téléviseur. Face aux critiques, LG avait finalement annoncé la possibilité de retirer ce raccourci.
Cette polémique a-t-elle contribué à précipiter l'abandon ? Rien ne permet de l'affirmer. Microsoft n'a donné aucune explication officielle sur les raisons de cette décision, mais le retrait intervient dans un contexte de changement de stratégie pour Copilot.
Microsoft recentre Copilot, mais l'IA reste dans les téléviseurs
L'arrêt sur les Smart TV n'est pas un cas isolé. En mai, Microsoft avait déjà annoncé l'abandon du développement de Copilot sur les consoles Xbox. Puis, en août, plusieurs fonctions grand public, notamment les podcasts générés par IA, la recherche approfondie et les conversations de groupe, ont disparu de Copilot.
Microsoft a également engagé la fusion de ses applications Copilot grand public et Microsoft 365. Une réorganisation qui suggère une volonté de simplifier son offre et de privilégier davantage les usages liés à la productivité, plutôt que de multiplier les déclinaisons de son assistant.
Ce changement de cap ne signifie toutefois pas que LG et Samsung renoncent à l'intelligence artificielle. Sur ses modèles 2026, LG propose notamment Multi AI Search au sein de son AI Hub, avec Google Gemini parmi les modèles disponibles. Chez Samsung, Vision AI Companion perdra l'un de ses agents, mais conservera notamment Bixby, Gemini et Perplexity, selon les modèles et les marchés.
Le retrait de Copilot pose néanmoins la question de l'utilité de ces assistants conversationnels dans le salon. Sur un ordinateur, l'IA peut accompagner de nombreuses tâches. Sur un téléviseur, où l'essentiel des interactions consiste encore à chercher un programme et à lancer sa lecture, les fabricants doivent davantage démontrer ce qu'elle apporte réellement… Un défi auquel Microsoft a visiblement choisi de ne plus participer.

articles.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
articles.text:
MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.
- Share:
A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.
The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.
By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.
In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.
"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "
A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle
The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.
Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.
"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."
The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.
From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot
The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.
For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.
When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.
The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.
"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."
For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.
They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.
The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.
To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.
"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."
Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot
Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.
The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.
This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.
The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.
By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.
Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.
The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.
The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.
How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim
With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.
The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.
Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.
"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."
To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.
As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.
Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.
The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.
"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."
The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Jennifer Chu. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Maheera Bawa, Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, Seanbiron Johnson, Ritu Raman. 2D Skeletal Muscle Thin Film Actuators Enhance Efficiency of Biohybrid Robots. Advanced Functional Materials, 2026; DOI: 10.1002/adfm.78065
Cite This Page:

articles.title: Apple Mac Studio: 512 GB RAM kosten so viel wie ein Neuwagen
articles.text:
Apple Mac Studio: 512 GB RAM kosten so viel wie ein Neuwagen
Mitte Oktober hatte Meta sein neues lokales KI-Modell Muse Spark Open vorgestellt. Das sei für Apple-Silicon-Prozessoren optimiert. Damit waren jedoch weder ein Macbook Air mit M3-Chip, noch ein Pro-Modell mit M4-Max-Prozessor gemeint. Wer das Modell nutzen will, braucht gleich zwei Mac Studio in einer Konfiguration, die Apple jetzt anbietet. Und die hat es in sich. Technisch, aber auch preislich.
Allein der Arbeitsspeicher kostet 17.000 Euro
Die Rede ist von der Variante mit 512 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher, die Apple für Ende Oktober versprochen hatte und nun tatsächlich im Online-Store verkauft. Wer seinen Mac mit derart viel RAM ausstatten will, hat dabei allerdings wenig Auswahlmöglichkeiten. Denn in der „günstigen“ Konfiguration mit M5-Max-Chip ab 2.999 Euro lässt sich der Arbeitsspeicher gar nicht aufrüsten. Er bleibt auf 36 Gigabyte beschränkt.
Klickt ihr im Konfigurator auf die 512 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher, zeigt euch das Formularfeld an, dass ihr schon zum voll ausgestatteten M5‑Ultra-Prozessor mit 36 Rechen- und 80 Grafik-Kernen greifen müsst. Nur diese Variante unterstützt derart viel RAM. Allein das Upgrade auf diesen Chip kostet euch 5.030 Euro zusätzlich. Hinzu käme dann noch der Sprung von 96 auf 512 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher. Allein dafür zahlt ihr noch einmal 17.050 Euro extra.
Wollt ihr dann noch den SSD-Speicher maximal ausreizen, zahlt ihr für das Upgrade von ein auf 16 Terabyte noch einmal 8.250 Euro extra. Insgesamt landet man so bei 33.329 Euro. Zum Vergleich: Ein kompaktes E-Auto wie der Citroën ëC3 kostet in der Basisvariante neu direkt beim Hersteller 20.140 Euro.
Für KI und Kreative
Natürlich ist ein Mac Studio in dieser Konfiguration kein Gerät für den Alltag im Homeoffice. Apple richtet sich an Kreative wie Filmemacher:innen, die mit einem solchen Computer hochauflösendes 8K-Material bearbeiten. Als weitere Zielgruppen nennt Apple selbst Datenwissenschaftler:innen, die auf solchen Maschinen KI-Modelle trainieren.
Außerdem eigne sich der Mac eben zum Ausführen lokaler KI-Agenten wie jenem von Meta. Dafür braucht man, wie gesagt, allerdings gleich zwei dieser voll ausgestatteten Mac Studios.

articles.title: Breet makes the case for simpler crypto payments at Moonshot
articles.text:
Making cryptocurrency payments easier to use is as much a challenge as building the infrastructure behind them, Breet chief operating officer Vivian Mbene told Moonshot by TechCabal in Lagos on Wednesday.
Mbene said the company’s biggest task was making a complicated product appear simple to customers, allowing businesses to accept digital assets without taking on the operational demands of managing them.
Breet, founded in 2019, converts cryptocurrency into cash for individuals in Nigeria and Ghana. It also offers an application programming interface that allows businesses to accept crypto payments and receive settlement in local currency.
The proposition separates the payment method from the currency a merchant ultimately wants to hold. Customers can pay with digital assets, while businesses receive local money without having to build a crypto operation of their own.
For Mbene, the objective is to reduce the work required to complete that transaction. “We’re just obsessed with simplicity,” she said.
That approach places much of the complexity behind the scenes. Functions such as monitoring transactions, routing deposits and converting currencies need to work together without requiring merchants to manage each step themselves.
But making the process look straightforward can create a different problem: convincing customers and business partners to trust it.
“Sometimes simplicity brings suspicion, and when it’s powered by crypto, the suspicion kind of doubles,” Mbene said.
Her remarks highlighted a tension for crypto payment providers. A simpler interface can reduce the effort involved in using a service, but it does not necessarily remove doubts about the technology underneath it.
Breet’s pitch is that businesses should be able to use crypto as a payment channel while continuing to manage their finances in familiar currencies. For providers pursuing that model, the commercial test is whether they can make accepting digital assets both straightforward and credible to merchants.

articles.title: The Elder Scrolls 6 is reportedly titled "Sentinel," and a reveal might come soon
articles.text:
In brief: Bethesda has provided virtually no substantial information about The Elder Scrolls VI since officially announcing it more than eight years ago. If recent reports are to be believed, that might be about to change. While the game's release window remains unclear, the upcoming anniversary of its immensely popular predecessor could give parent company Microsoft an opportunity to renew enthusiasm for its gaming business.
Sources familiar with Bethesda's inner workings have informed The Verge that The Elder Scrolls VI will be subtitled "Sentinel," and that Microsoft will reveal the title next month. The game may still be years away, and Microsoft is reportedly considering an Xbox-exclusive launch.
The upcoming open-world RPG will center on Hammerfell, a region of the Elder Scrolls universe featured in The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard and The Elder Scrolls Online but not in a mainline title since The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall, released in 1996. Sentinel is a major city in Hammerfell and the capital of the kingdom of Sentinel. The area is home to the Redgarruds, one of several races that appear throughout the series.
Any announcement from Microsoft would likely happen on November 11, the 15th anniversary of the previous entry, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. Skyrim is one of the best-selling RPGs of all time and maintains one of the industry's biggest modding communities.
It remains unclear whether Microsoft might try to use the follow-up to lift sagging Xbox sales or release it on PlayStation as well, as Bethesda did with prior titles before Microsoft acquired the studio. A reveal next month, likely without gameplay footage, might also be seen as an attempt to show proof of life amid ongoing layoffs affecting thousands of Microsoft employees.
New Xbox CEO Asha Sharma recently teased The Elder Scrolls VI by revealing that its subtitle has eight letters. Sentinel immediately became one of the most widely guessed titles, and fans have long speculated that the next game would feature Hammerfell.
Bethesda technically announced The Elder Scrolls VI at E3 2018 but showed only the title and a brief landscape shot. Since then, studio head Todd Howard has only provided scant details.
Earlier this year, he said the game will resemble its predecessor more than other recent games from the studio like Fallout 76 and Starfield. Starfield, which launched to a mixed reception, provided a learning experience, and Bethesda has since optimized its production pipeline on Creation Engine 3, which will power Elder Scrolls VI.

articles.title: Bloomsco raises $1 million pre-seed from BDC, Telegraph for military training platform | BetaKit
articles.text:
As defence spending grows in Canada, a Montréal AI startup is hoping to serve the education and training gap between contractors and the military.
The news: Bloomsco, which is developing a software platform that defence contractors can use to create training materials for the military, announced on Thursday a $1-million pre-seed equity round from BDC Capital’s Seed Venture Fund and Montréal-based Telegraph Ventures.
The company said it will use the funding to grow its engineering team and refine its tech for use in classified and air-gapped environments (meaning it’s isolated from the internet).
From the source: “The whole focus of a military is training people well to do the work they need to do,” Bloomsco co-founder and CEO Hugh McGuire said in an interview with BetaKit. “With more complex technologies that are changing fast, how do we build a training system that is able to adapt?”
The context: Bloomsco uses AI to turn technical manuals, data, and product specs into training plans, learning materials, and simulation scenarios that the end customer can adapt as they see fit. It has already secured a contract with the Department of National Defence (DND) to create a qualification standard and training plan for an officer role.
McGuire founded Bloomsco alongside CTO Hadrien David, who was a founding engineer at healthtech company Dialogue. Though neither has a background in defence, they found validation in their idea through retired Vice-Admiral Ron Lloyd, a former commander of the Royal Canadian Navy and a former chief data officer at the Department of National Defence (DND), who is now a Bloomsco adviser.
Final thought: With new military spending, the Canadian Armed Forces is set to buy a flood of new equipment and technology. For example, Canada started a new defence drone procurement initiative to fast-track buying uncrewed drone and counter-drone systems. Bloomsco is betting that there’s enough demand for learning how to use this technology that it will create more contracts.

articles.title: Analysts find looming launch crisis is "more severe" than anticipated
articles.text:
A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years.
The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.
“What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved,” said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. “What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s.”
The report tallies a number of familiar factors that have gone into this crisis: the war in Ukraine taking Russian rockets off the Western market; Amazon Leo demand; developmental delays in a new generation of rockets, from New Glenn and Vulcan to Neutron, Terran R, and Nova; and more recently, the retirement of the Falcon 9 as a rocket for commercial service.
At a time when the supply of commercial rockets is contracting, demand for satellite launch is soaring, from megaconstellation operators such as Amazon to a flurry of small satellite startups. The report estimates the crunch will become most acute in 2028 but should then slowly improve.
“How should people react and plan around this?” Henry asked. “To be honest, I don’t have a good answer. If you haven’t booked your launch already, and you need one, you’re late.”

articles.title: Passkeys Are Better Than Passwords. But They Are Not Enough.
articles.text:
For decades, passwords have been one of cybersecurity’s most persistent weaknesses. Users forget them, reuse them, share them, and surrender them to convincing phishing sites. Attackers steal credentials, automate credential stuffing, and increasingly use artificial intelligence to make social engineering more effective.
What are passkeys?
Passkeys promise to eliminate much of this problem.
Built on public-key cryptography, passkeys replace shared secrets with cryptographic credentials. There is no password for an attacker to steal, intercept through phishing, or reuse against another service. Properly implemented passkeys are also phishing-resistant because authentication is bound to the legitimate service.
That represents a significant improvement over passwords and many traditional forms of multi-factor authentication (MFA). But it does not answer a more fundamental question: Just because someone successfully authenticated, should we continue to trust that identity?
Passkeys strengthen authentication. They do not eliminate identity risk.
What Passkeys Get Right
Traditional authentication frequently relies on passwords combined with one-time passcodes, SMS messages, or push notifications. While stronger than passwords alone, these methods remain vulnerable to phishing, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, MFA fatigue, SIM swapping, and social engineering.
Passkeys fundamentally change that model. Instead of presenting a reusable secret, the user’s device holds a private cryptographic key while the service retains the corresponding public key. The private key is not transmitted during authentication.
This provides meaningful protection against phishing, credential stuffing, password database theft, and other attacks built around stealing reusable credentials. Passkeys can also improve usability because users no longer need to remember complex passwords or repeatedly retrieve authentication codes.
Organizations should welcome that transition. The mistake would be assuming that stronger authentication solves the broader identity security problem though.
Authentication Is Not Identity
When passkey authentication succeeds, the system has strong cryptographic evidence that a credential associated with an account completed the authentication process.
But was the account legitimately established? Has the underlying identity been compromised? Is the device trustworthy? Is an attacker operating through an authenticated session?
A perfectly functioning authentication mechanism cannot compensate for an identity that should never have been trusted.
If an attacker establishes or takes control of an account before a passkey is bound to it, the organization may subsequently perform highly secure authentication of the wrong person. The stronger the authenticator becomes, the more important the integrity of enrollment becomes.
What Happens When the Device Changes?
Legitimate users also do not always authenticate from the same device. Phones are lost, stolen, damaged, or replaced. Employees receive new laptops. Consumers switch technology ecosystems.
Passkey synchronization addresses many of these scenarios by making credentials available across supported devices. But organizations still need to accommodate legitimate users who arrive without access to the expected passkey.
At that point, the challenge shifts from authentication to recovery and re-establishing trust. How does the organization determine whether someone requesting access from an unfamiliar device is the legitimate account owner?
If the fallback relies on a password, SMS code, email link, knowledge-based question, or help desk process, attackers may target that weaker recovery path.
The passkey has not been compromised. The attacker has gone around it.
Organizations therefore need a secure way to re-establish identity trust before associating a new authenticator or device with an existing account.
Authentication Is Only One Moment
Another gap emerges after authentication. Many identity architectures effectively operate according to a simple sequence: Authenticate, grant access, and trust the resulting session.
Modern identity-based attacks do not necessarily stop at the login screen. Attackers can hijack authenticated sessions, compromise trusted devices, abuse privileges, manipulate account attributes, or conduct anomalous transactions. In these situations, the authentication mechanism may have worked exactly as designed.
The question cannot simply be, “Did this user authenticate successfully?” It must also be, “Do we still have sufficient evidence to trust this identity and its activity?”
Layer Identity Threat Detection on Top
This is where identity threat detection complements passkeys.
Instead of treating successful authentication as a permanent declaration of trust, organizations can continuously evaluate identity risk. Device characteristics, identity attributes, behavioral anomalies, network intelligence, account changes, transaction context, and threat indicators can help determine whether an identity remains trustworthy.
This does not require adding friction to every interaction. A risk-based model can allow legitimate users to proceed normally while escalating controls when risk changes.
A known user authenticating from an established device and behaving normally may require no additional intervention. The same account attempting recovery from an unfamiliar device, changing critical account attributes, or conducting anomalous activity could trigger additional identity verification.
The model changes from authenticate once and trust thereafter to establish trust, continuously evaluate risk, and respond when trust changes.
The Future of Identity Security Must Go Beyond Authentication
Passkeys and identity threat detection address distinct parts of the identity attack surface.
Passkeys reduce risks associated with passwords, credential theft, credential stuffing, and phishing. Identity threat detection addresses risks surrounding authentication, including enrollment, recovery, device changes, session compromise, and anomalous activity.
As organizations eliminate passwords, attackers will adapt. Instead of attacking the authenticator directly, they will look for opportunities around it.
That does not mean passkeys failed. It means they succeeded in making one part of the attack surface harder.
Passkeys answer an important question: Does this user possess a legitimate credential required to authenticate?
Identity threat detection addresses the question that matters throughout the identity lifecycle: Should we still trust this identity?
Organizations need to answer both.
Related: Phishing Toolkit Uses Passkeys to Maintain Access After Password Resets
Related: Google Now Syncing Passkeys Across Desktop, Android Devices

articles.title: PaperFoam secures €2 million loan to scale sustainable packaging made from starch and natural fibres | EU-Startups
articles.text:
PaperFoam, a Dutch company that manufactures sustainable, biodegradable, starch-based packaging, has secured a €2 million loan from Invest International to expand its production facility in the Czech Republic and strengthen working capital for its Malaysian and U.S. plants.
The Hague-based Invest International is a Dutch government-backed organisation that helps Dutch and Dutch-linked businesses overcome barriers by providing financial support, foreign market knowledge, and sector expertise.
Jeroen Plag, Chief Investment Officer at Invest International, said, “PaperFoam is a great example of a Dutch innovator that has travelled a difficult path from promising technology to an internationally scalable company. Our involvement dates back to 2020, when we supported the company during its first expansion into the Czech Republic.
“With this new investment, we’re helping to enable the next phase of growth at a time when traditional financiers still view it as too risky. For the Netherlands, it’s crucial that we help green leaders in the manufacturing industry scale up. This way, we retain innovation within our own country and demonstrate that sustainability and international competitiveness go hand in hand.”
Founded in 1998, Paperfoam was founded by Vertis Holding, a former Dutch IT company. The Barneveld-based company is a global provider of biodegradable starch-based packaging solutions, with production facilities in the Netherlands, the Czech Republic, the United States, and Malaysia.
PaperFoam b.v. is owned by PaperFoam Holding b.v. Since March 2023, Nissha Co. Ltd., a Japanese stock-listed company, has owned 30% of PaperFoam Holding b.v. The other 70% is owned by Sustainable Pioneers Holding b.v., a Dutch entity.
PaperFoam states that it develops packaging solutions based on starch and natural fibres as a fully fledged alternative to conventional plastic and paper. Using its patented foaming technology and natural raw materials, the company creates lightweight packaging with an “exceptionally low” carbon footprint. The material is also fully compostable, and the fibres can be easily recycled into paper.
PaperFoam Plus is thicker and stronger than PaperFoam and is designed as a sustainable alternative to EPS (Expanded Polystyrene). It offers protective qualities (drop-tested up to 5 kg), is up to 5 mm thick, and is compostable in both home and industrial composters.
The company serves customers in sectors such as consumer electronics, medical, dry food, and cosmetics. 
Willem Derkman, CEO of PaperFoam, said, “Developing an innovative and sustainable alternative to traditional packaging requires time, investment, and partners who are willing to look further ahead. Thanks to the ongoing support from Invest International, we have been able to take important steps in our international growth. This funding helps us further expand our production capacity and efficiently serve new markets and clients.”
According to the company, production machinery from Dutch suppliers Kuyer Metaal in Nijkerk and Shuffle-Mix in Barneveld makes the expansion possible in part.

articles.title: Google's first data center satellite is online and writing poetry | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.
After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨
Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.
A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.
The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.
Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.
If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.
Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.
Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.
In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles. 
Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.
Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

articles.title: Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Bloatware in Aftermarket Auto Parts
This story is interesting:
One Civic owner purchased a cheap aftermarket head unit off Amazon, and decided to have Claude work its magic on it, like it would a smart TV. What was reportedly discovered isn’t surprising, but is worth knowing about.
Among the pre-installed bloatware—or spyware, if you’re being less charitable—was a voice assistant equipped with WebView, an Android system component that lets apps display content off the web. This apparently always used about a third of processing power, even while idle, which isn’t great. There were also Baidu location services, a call recorder (!), a DAB radio client that is pretty much useless in the U.S., and Adobe Acrobat, presumably so your passenger can entertain themselves with PDFs on the go.
It’s interesting because it exposes all the insecurities in this piece of IoT software. But I think the real story is that a random person was able to do this reverse-engineering with the help of AI. Expect a lot more stories like this in the future.
Rontea • October 30, 2026 1:06 PM
Cheap aftermarket devices—especially ones running Android variants—are the definition of untrusted hardware. They’re loaded with services and apps you didn’t ask for, phone home to places you don’t control, and often keep running even when you think they’re idle.
Stick to reputable vendors, keep them segmented, and if you must tinker, know exactly what firmware you’re flashing and where it came from. Trust is earned, not assumed.

articles.title: Counting agents is the wrong scoreboard: Better questions for enterprise leaders
articles.text:
Counting agents is the wrong scoreboard: Better questions for enterprise leaders
Not how many agents, but which outcome. Not can it advise, but can it execute.
Ask a room of executives about agentic AI and within about ninety seconds someone will ask how many agents they ought to be running. It has become the default measure of progress: a number you can put on a slide, benchmark against a competitor, and report upwards.
It is also the wrong question.
Senior Vice President for Oracle UK & Ireland.
Across the 200-plus workshops my team and I have run with enterprises in Europe and the Middle East, the organizations getting real value from AI tools are not the ones with the longest agent inventory. They are the ones who never framed the problem that way to begin with. They started by identifying a business problem or point of friction and worked backwards. Everyone else started from the technology and went looking for somewhere to put it.
There are four questions I hear constantly that are quietly steering good companies into Pilot Purgatory. Here they are, and here is what I would ask instead.
Don't ask how many agents. Ask what outcome you are improving.
Much of the last two years of enterprise AI has been about helping people work faster. Copilots that answer questions, assistants that summarize the meeting you have just sat through, tools that get you past the blank page. These are genuinely useful and I would encourage everyone to switch them on.
But speed is not the same as value, and agent count is not the same as either. No enterprise ever created value by accumulating agents. Value shows up in real business outcomes such as fewer payroll errors, faster shift scheduling, lower supplier sourcing costs, better win rates, cash collected sooner.
That is the difference between an agent and an agentic application. An agent help with an individual task. An agentic application coordinates teams of specialized agents to deliver a business outcome. If you cannot name the KPI an agent is moving, you do not have a use case. You have a demo.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Don't ask whether AI can recommend. Ask whether it can finish the job.
The most persistent confusion I encounter is between advice and execution. Plenty of systems can now sense a situation, spot the pattern and tell you what should happen next. That is real progress. It also leaves almost all of the work exactly where it was.
Take sourcing. An assistant can flag that a category is overdue for renegotiation and suggest you run an event. Someone still has to create that event, chase the responses, score them against commercial criteria, route the approvals correctly, update the contract and shepherd the whole thing to a close.
An agentic application does that work, under policy, with human oversight and approval where required, and with a record of what it did and why.
The test is simple. At the end of the interaction, is the process further forward, or do you just have a better-informed human facing the same queue?
Don't ask which model tops the leaderboard. Ask whether it understands your business.
Benchmark scores dominate the AI conversation and matter far less in the enterprise than most leaders assume. Raw model intelligence is rarely the binding constraint.
A frontier model understands procurement as a discipline. It does not understand your supplier list, your delegation-of-authority matrix, your contractual obligations, your current inventory position, or the three exceptions your finance director signed off in March. Without that, sophistication amounts to a well-argued guess.
Enterprise context is the differentiator: trusted enterprise data and business context, including the policies, approvals, transaction history, organizational structure and live process state that already sit inside your core systems. The closer agentic capabilities are to the systems where business processes, data, security, and approvals already live, the more effectively agents can understand context and act within establish controls.
Don't ask for one system that does everything. Ask how the specialists coordinate.
There is a persistent hope that enterprise AI will eventually resolve into a single, omniscient digital assistant. Businesses do not work that way, so their AI will not either.
Organizations are ecosystems of specialists: finance, HR, supply chain, service, sales, each with its own expertise, obligations and objectives. The equivalent in AI is not one agent that knows everything, but coordinated teams of agents that know their own domain and work towards a shared goal.
Hiring is a good illustration. One agent surfaces and screens candidates. Another prepares onboarding. A third confirms the budget is genuinely available. A fourth keeps the hiring manager's approvals moving. Individually, each is modestly useful. Together they move a business process from vacancy to first day. The value sits in the coordination, not the components.
Systems of outcomes
What connects all four questions is a shift in what enterprise software is actually for. For decades our applications recorded what had happened. We are now entering the era of systems of outcomes: software that reads the state of the business, reasons over it, and acts to keep work moving towards a defined objective.
That shift demands different questions from leadership. Not how many agents, but which outcome. Not can it advise, but can it execute. Not how clever is the model, but how well does it know us. Not one brain, but one team.
Get the questions right and the technology decisions become considerably easier. Get them wrong and you will assemble an impressive collection of agents, tools, and models that nobody can tie to a number that matters.

articles.title: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
articles.text:
Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math, Altman said:
Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

articles.title: James Gunn quiere a Margot Robbie como Harley Quinn en el Universo DC
articles.text:
El Universo DC de James Gunn (o DCU) busca hacer borrón y cuenta nueva respecto de adaptaciones previas de sus personajes principales. Por supuesto que existen unas pocas excepciones, siendo la más notoria la del Peacemaker de John Cena. Y el propio cineasta ha reconocido que le encantaría que Margot Robbie se una a la saga como Harley Quinn.
Durante su participación en un pódcast, James Gunn confirmó que su idea es, eventualmente, introducir a Harley Quinn dentro del Universo DC que lidera. También reconoció que Margot Robbie es su opción número 1 para darle vida al personaje, considerando el trabajo que ya hizo con el personaje en tres películas previas.
Sin embargo, el jefe de DC Studios también reconoció que no está del todo convencido de cómo podría justificar un potencial regreso de la actriz australiana a este rol. Gunn mencionó que aún es difícil determinar si las películas de Escuadrón Suicida son canon o no en la actual franquicia que lidera.
A esto se suma otro detalle no menor: que James Gunn aún no introdujo al Joker en su Universo DC. La existencia del villano es fundamental para que Harley Quinn pueda tener su espacio, sea o no con Margot Robbie como intérprete.
"Creo que, en este contexto, Harley Quinn es uno de los elementos más difíciles de justificar como parte del canon del DCU. La relación de Harley con el Joker es muy particular, ¿verdad? Pues bien, todavía no hemos introducido al Joker en el DCU. A Batman sí lo hemos establecido; ya sabemos que existe. Lo hemos visto brevemente en Creature Commandos, pero no sabemos si el Joker existe ya. Y, obviamente, el Joker forma parte del pasado de Harley", explicó el cineasta.
¿Puede Margot Robbie sumarse al DCU como Harley Quinn?
Gunn ratificó que su plan es, tarde o temprano, incorporar a Harley Quinn a su Universo DC. También sostuvo que la primera opción para interpretarla estará en manos de Margot Robbie. El cineasta incluso mencionó que la decisión de considerar canon o no al Escuadrón Suicida va a depender de lo que haga la actriz.
"Margot Robbie es una de mis actrices favoritas con las que he trabajado. [...] Me encanta su interpretación de Harley. No sé si ella quiere volver a interpretar a Harley; puede que ya haya pasado página. Se ha convertido en una de las estrellas femeninas más grandes del mundo. Por eso, no sé qué piensa al respecto de todo esto", indicó el guionista y director, y agregó: "Harley es un personaje que, casi con total seguridad, voy a utilizar en el DCU. Si Margot quiere interpretarla, haré lo imposible por encajarla en ese universo. Pero si no es así, entonces podría optar por otra persona, sin necesidad de estar condicionado por lo que le ocurre a Harley en esta película. En resumen: es Margot quien debe decidir si Escuadrón Suicida forma parte del canon o no".
Será interesante ver si en el futuro Margot Robbie desea regresar al rol de Harley Quinn como parte del Universo DC de James Gunn y Peter Safran. Hasta aquí, la actriz dio vida al personaje en tres películas: Escuadrón Suicida (2016), de David Ayer, Aves de presa (2020) y El Escuadrón Suicida (2021), esta última de James Gunn.

articles.title: Google testa IA em satélite e avança em projeto de data centers espaciais
articles.text:
O Google conseguiu executar um modelo de inteligência artificial (IA) em um satélite e receber resposta gerada fora da Terra. O teste representa avanço experimental do Project Suncatcher, iniciativa da empresa que investiga a possibilidade de levar data centers de IA para a órbita terrestre.
Em publicação no blog da companhia, o Google informou que inicializou processadores Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) a bordo do equipamento. Durante os testes, o modelo Gemma 4 foi executado diretamente no satélite e recebeu comando para criar um haicai sobre estar no espaço.
A IA produziu versos sobre a Terra vista do espaço, o fluxo de dados e a luz das estrelas. A empresa também realizou outros experimentos, incluindo a criação de limeriques com temas espaciais e respostas a comandos relacionados à telemetria.
Projeto quer levar processamento de IA para o espaço
- O Project Suncatcher é uma iniciativa experimental do Google que explora a possibilidade de instalar infraestrutura de computação para IA em satélites;
- A proposta é investigar se equipamentos em órbita poderiam executar tarefas de IA fora dos tradicionais data centers terrestres;
- O satélite utilizado no experimento foi lançado no início de outubro;
- Agora, a próxima etapa envolve testar o funcionamento das TPUs sob condições mais exigentes, incluindo variações de temperatura e exposição à radiação no ambiente espacial.
Leia mais:
- Google leva anúncios do Modo IA a novos países; Brasil está na lista
- OpenAI quer comprar chips do Google em união inédita de rivais
- Dona do Google fica abaixo das expectativas e acende alerta sobre gastos com IA
Próximo passo envolve conectar dois satélites
O Google também trabalha para avançar na comunicação entre equipamentos em órbita. Depois dos testes iniciais, a empresa pretende alcançar outro marco em 2027: colocar dois satélites em operação interconectada.
A ideia é verificar se os sistemas conseguem executar tarefas de maneira confiável e trocar informações no espaço. Esse tipo de demonstração seria importante para avaliar a viabilidade de uma infraestrutura orbital de computação.
Por enquanto, o teste com o Gemma 4 comprova apenas que um modelo de IA conseguiu processar comandos a bordo de um satélite e gerar respostas. A construção de data centers espaciais ainda depende de etapas técnicas e experimentos adicionais.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: On a trouvé un excellent écran OLED gaming qui perd 130 € pour le lancement du Black Friday
articles.text:
Le Black Friday n’attend plus la fin novembre. Boulanger a lancé le sien dès la fin octobre, avec déjà des centaines d’offres tech. Si vous préparez votre configuration de jeu pour l’hiver, les écrans OLED font d’ailleurs partie des produits à surveiller. Ils restent plus chers que les écrans LCD classiques, d’où l’intérêt de guetter les remises.
L’enseigne vend l’ASUS ROG XG27AQWMG à 469 € au lieu de 599,99 €, soit 21 % de remise.
Que vaut l’écran ASUS ROG XG27AQWMG ?
Malgré son appellation « 27 pouces », la dalle WOLED de l’ASUS ROG XG27AQWMG mesure 26,5 pouces de diagonale réelle. Elle affiche une définition QHD de 2 560 x 1 440 pixels. L’image reste fine, et la carte graphique a moins de travail qu’en 4K. Sa fréquence grimpe à 280 Hz, avec un temps de réponse annoncé de 0,03 ms. De quoi profiter d’une excellente fluidité et limiter les traînées derrière les objets en mouvement, notamment dans les jeux compétitifs.
ASUS utilise une dalle Tandem WOLED, qui superpose plusieurs couches émissives. Le constructeur annonce 1 500 cd/m² en pointe (une valeur atteinte en HDR, sur une petite partie de l’écran seulement), une certification DisplayHDR True Black 500 et une couverture de 99,5 % de l’espace colorimétrique DCI-P3. Côté connectique, on retrouve deux ports HDMI 2.1, un DisplayPort 1.4, deux ports USB-A et une sortie casque. L’écran est également compatible FreeSync Premium Pro et certifié G-Sync Compatible par Nvidia pour synchroniser l’affichage avec la carte graphique et éviter les déchirures d’image.
Le pied se règle en hauteur, s’incline, pivote à gauche et à droite et bascule en mode portrait.
À ce prix, l’ASUS ROG XG27AQWMG est-il une bonne affaire ?
À 469 €, cet ASUS ROG XG27AQWMG affiche un tarif particulièrement intéressant pour un moniteur OLED de 27 pouces. Pour GTA VI, attendu le 19 novembre, vous pourrez y brancher une PS5 ou une Xbox Series via l’un des deux ports HDMI 2.1 : le jeu ne sort pas sur PC au lancement.
Comme toutes les dalles OLED, celle-ci risque le marquage (une image fantôme qui s’incruste) lorsque des éléments fixes restent affichés pendant de longues périodes. ASUS intègre sa suite OLED Care Pro pour limiter ce risque, avec notamment un capteur de présence qui affiche un écran noir quand vous quittez votre bureau. Le Black Friday officiel aura lieu le 27 novembre 2026, mais rien ne garantit que le prix descendra davantage d’ici là. À 469 €, il passe sous la barre des 500 € avec la dernière génération de dalle WOLED.
Black Friday 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Depuis une dizaine d’années, le Black Friday s’est infiltré dans le calendrier commercial des grandes marques et enseignes françaises. Avec l’expérience, on peut vous dire que cet événement fait partie des meilleurs moments pour faire de bonnes affaires.
Les dates du Black Friday
Bien qu’il porte encore le nom du vendredi noir, le Black Friday s’étend désormais sur un mois chez de nombreux revendeurs. Un format moins typique qui lui retire un peu son petit côté FOMO. On dirait presque les soldes, finalement. Mais c’est aussi moins le rush, ce qui est une bonne chose pour ceux qui veulent faire des achats plus raisonnés. Globalement, on peut résumer ce Black Friday en quatre temps forts :
- Début novembre : les avant-premières Black Friday.
- Autour du 20 novembre, selon les enseignes : la Black Week commence généralement plusieurs jours avant le jour J.
- 27 novembre : la date du Black Friday, même si les offres commencent généralement avant et se prolongent le week-end des 28 et 29 novembre.
- 30 novembre : le Cyber Monday.
Quels sites participent au Black Friday ?

articles.title: Palma de Mallorca está en la cuenta atrás para las protestas de Blocus. Y ya hay quien pide suspender clases en institutos
articles.text:
Si te das un paseo hoy por el centro de Palma, probablemente verás escaparates tapiados (incluidos los de alguna multinacional), vigilantes y sobre todo mucho nerviosismo entre los comerciantes, que ya hablan de adelantar su hora de cierre. El motivo: Blocus Mallorca ha llamado a manifestarse esta tarde en plaza de España, en el corazón mismo de la capital balear. Y a la vista de lo ocurrido el sábado en Barcelona, donde una convocatoria similar se saldó con saqueos y destrozos, nadie quiere arriesgarse.
Incluso hay quien reclama que se suspendan las clases en los institutos de las zonas que “puedan quedar afectadas”.
“Suspensión preventiva”. El Sindicat Independent, Autonom i Unitari (SIAU) no quiere jugársela y ha exigido formalmente a la Consejería de Educación balear que tome “medidas urgentes” ante la concentración de Blocus convocada para hoy en Palma. Para ser más precisos, plantea una “suspensión preventiva de la actividad presencial” en las escuelas que “puedan quedar afectadas” por las movilizaciones.
En un escrito dirigido a más organismos, incluida Inspección Educativa y los directores de dos institutos de Palma, SIAU insiste en la necesidad de “garantizar la seguridad” tanto de los alumnos como del profesorado y demás personal.
La clave: la atmósfera. “La preocupación ha aumentado después de que varios establecimientos comerciales del centro de Palma hayan empezado a proteger los escaparates y a anunciar cierres anticipados ante la posibilidad de que se produzcan incidentes durante las protestas”, insiste.
SIAU es un sindicato joven (se creó en 2022) y está lejos de ser el de mayor representatividad en la educación balear, pero aun así su petición ha despertado el interés de la prensa regional. Y es lógico. Como recuerda el propio SIAU, sintoniza con la preocupación que muestran otros sectores de Palma en las horas previas a la protesta de Blocus.
Escaparates tapiados. Los medios baleares cuentan desde ayer cómo hay negocios del centro de Palma que están adoptando medidas para ‘blindarse’ ante posibles saqueos. O al menos intentarlo. El caso más llamativo es el de FNAC. Los responsables de la tienda, situada a solo unos metros de la plaza de España, el punto de la convocatoria de Blocus, han cubierto sus cristaleras con paneles de corcho. No muy lejos, una residencia ha optado también por tapar su entrada.
Los comerciantes de ‘Els Geranis’, un importante eje comercial del centro de Palma, reconocían estos días su inquietud a Diario de Mallorca. “Estamos preocupados porque nadie nos ampara. Estamos muy cerca del lugar de la protesta”, advierte Mercedes Carvajal, su presidenta. Algunos negocios han optado por vaciar escaparates y guardar la mercancía y, en general, se habla de dos medidas: contratar seguridad privada y adelantar la hora de cierre. Hoy mismo la federación comercial AFEDECO distribuyó una circular con ese mismo consejo: anticipar los cierres.
“Solo queremos ser escuchados”. En el centro de todas las miradas está la movilización prevista para hoy a las 19.30 h en la plaza de España bajo la consigna de Blocus Mallorca. La convocatoria se movió en los últimos días a través de un grupo de Telegram que acabó eliminándose. En su último comunicado, los administradores insistían en que la concentración sería “totalmente pacífica y sin ningún tipo de violencia”. Aun así, las noticias que hablan de amenazas de “saqueos” mantienen en guardia a los comerciantes.
Aunque el grupo de Telegram ‘Gen Z’ se eliminó el martes, la convocatoria balear sigue promocionándose desde cuentas de Instagram y TikTok que usan la denominación Blocus. De hecho, hay dos perfiles en Instagram en los que se ha compartido un mismo cartel con el encabezamiento “Blocus Mallorca” y que habla de los integrantes de la ‘Acampada por la Vivienda’ con quienes probablemente los manifestantes coincidan hoy.
¿Y qué dice? “No tenemos ningún tipo de intención de hacer daño […], respetamos que cada uno exprese sus ideas. No somos enemigos de nadie, solo queremos ser escuchados”, arranca el comunicado de Blocus, que concluye sin embargo con una advertencia tan (o más) importante: “En el caso de que haya un ataque hacia uno de nuestros manifestantes, procederemos a la destrucción masiva de las tiendas de acampada”.
La Delegación del Gobierno ha explicado a Europa Press que de momento no se ha comunicado formalmente la convocatoria de ninguna protesta. Eso no quita que se esté coordinando ya con la Policía Nacional y se prevea un dispositivo.
🚩Detenido el creador de los canales de comunicación “Blocus Vlc” en los que instigaba a saquear comercios de la ciudad ➡️Dirigía y daba órdenes al resto del grupo, informándoles de la fecha y hora de los asaltos e incitando al resto a que publicitasen el grupo en #RRSS 👮♂️Los canales de comunicación se han cerrado, llegando a superar uno de ellos los 400 usuarios
— Policía Nacional (@policia) October 29, 2026
El recuerdo de Barcelona. De fondo hay un factor clave: la naturaleza difusa de Blocus, que podría definirse como una red de cuentas efímeras que organizan movilizaciones a través de Telegram, Instagram y TikTok. La de Palma no es la única. Hace unos días un estudio de la startup Golden Owl reveló que Blocus tenía activas convocatorias para el 31 de octubre y 2 y 30 de noviembre (tras las elecciones) en una docena de ciudades españolas. De hecho, en Madrid están también expectantes ante una posible movilización este sábado.
Aunque hay aún incógnitas sobre el origen, funcionamiento y objetivo de Blocus, un movimiento que en un inicio pareció inspirarse en las protestas estudiantiles de Francia (Blocus es “bloqueo” en francés), el fenómeno ha despertado una atención especial tras lo ocurrido el sábado en Barcelona.
Allí una convocatoria bajo la misma etiqueta desató disturbios con un saldo preocupante: 23 comercios dañados, 15 policías heridos y más de 130 detenidos. 89 eran menores y solo unos cuantos tenían antecedentes por desórdenes públicos. Un análisis de VerificarTVE detectó comentarios sobre saqueos y actos violentos en grupos de WhatsApp y Telegram relacionados y localizados en Madrid y Barcelona.
