articles.title: Flock can't seem to take no for an answer, as its cameras reappear in another city that rejected them
articles.text:
A hot potato: It's fair to say that Flock is one of the most hated companies in the US right now. So, what better way to improve its public image than to ignore a city's instructions and reinstall two cameras when explicitly told not to – and it's not the first time this has happened.
The surveillance giant's latest PR disaster took place in Dayton, Minnesota, reports The Drive. The city's local government posted on Facebook that the Police Department was made aware of a maintenance work order produced by Flock on September 17, 2026.
The city notified Flock a day later, informing it that the program was on hold and no work orders were to be completed. But the company appeared to just ignore this, reinstalling its cameras and putting them into service.
Local residents spotted the cameras and informed police, who were directed to remove the devices.
In August, Dayton voted to cancel its contract with Flock, joining hundreds of US communities that have removed or stopped using the company's cameras.
Dayton City Administrator Zach Doud later said Flock took five days to acknowledge the city's contract cancellation and informed officials that removing its surveillance equipment would take 60 days.
This isn't the first time Flock has seemingly ignored a city's orders to remove its cameras. In September, Grass Valley, California, which had also canceled Flock's contract and removed its cameras, was shocked to find that two of them had been reinstalled.
Flock essentially blamed the city. It said the company handles the removal of the cameras as part of the cancellation process, but because the city took them down before the process was complete, the system assumed there was an equipment failure. This caused it to generate replacement work orders, resulting in crews being dispatched.
There have been numerous negative stories about Flock and its privacy-invading cameras since reports emerged that police officers were using its technology to stalk former partners, prompting cities to drop the cameras at a rapid pace.
But while you may see fewer Flock cameras lining the streets, the company's surveillance technology might instead be flying through the air. The company said in August that its Drone as First Responder, or DFR, tech – which can also read license plates from the air – is its fastest-growing segment. The aircraft can fly at 400 feet and reach 60 mph, while a 40x optical zoom allows operators to see details from a distance.

articles.title: Kubernetes just formed a workload conformance group. Here’s why it matters for AI teams.
articles.text:
Kubernetes just formed a workload conformance group. Here’s why it matters for AI teams.
Welcome to the final edition of Road to KubeCon, where we track the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem each week on The New Stack as we head into KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, November 9-12 in Salt Lake City, Utah.
This week we explore how Kubernetes is getting new guidance for running AI workloads, including a new book from TNS, a dedicated Kubernetes working group, and advice on running LLMs across multiple GPUs.
Also in this day-before-Halloween-timed column, we’ve got OTel operators speaking a new language, security horrors from the latest AGNTCon + MCPCon, and untangling the dark webs of Kubernetes pod troubleshooting gone awry.
Join the conversation with HPE at KubeCon
HPE will have a big presence at KubeCon NA this year. The gold sponsor will be at Booths 151 and 145, where they’ll present live sessions throughout the day on topics spanning vSphere, HPE Kubernetes Service (HKS), distributed inference, setting up cloud storage for Kubernetes, and more.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments.
This year, the focus is on gaining visibility and control across Kubernetes environments across VMs, infrastructure, and clouds. If you’d like to schedule a meeting with an HPE representative, contact jennifer.osuna@hpe.com.
TNS publishes Kubernetes guidebook for 2027
In partnership with HPE, The New Stack has published a helpful book containing ten checks for teams running AI workloads on Kubernetes. The book, Kubernetes in 2027: Building Platforms for AI, Autonomy, and Scale, is available for download now.
Written by contributing writer Chris J. Preimesberger, the guide spans the full lifecycle, covering how to stress-test infrastructure before launch, how to meet the nuanced demands of agentic AI, what to watch for, and how to develop stronger permissioning models for agents.
Since agentic AI is prone to bursty, unpredictable behavior, arming your infrastructure with the right approach on Kubernetes is an important first step to production stability and success with AI at scale.
Kubernetes gets a Workload Conformance Working Group
Workload types have been expanding for years. And AI undoubtedly adds more variety. Against this backdrop, on Tuesday, October 27, the Kubernetes community announced a dedicated Workload Conformance Working Group.
According to Broadcom’s Nabarun Pal, writing on behalf of WG Workload Conformance on the Kubernetes blog, “The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes.” To do so, they’ll need community input, Pal adds.
The Kubernetes AI Conformance test already determines whether a cluster can run AI or machine learning (ML) workloads. Yet none currently exists for workloads, requiring workarounds, manual exploration, or monitoring for signs like node drain or permission issues. So the new WG aims to create a similar standard for workloads.
It’s a significant step forward as the Kubernetes community grapples with a growing variety of workloads, including AI. Interested parties can read the working group proposal for more information, join the Slack channel, or attend biweekly meetings to get involved.
OpenTelemetry Transformation Language reaches v1
Earlier this week, the OpenTelemetry (OTel) project reached a milestone: the OpenTelemetry Transformation Language (OTTL) has reached v1. It’s stable for traces, metrics, and logs, and is included within Collector Contrib v0.164.0 and onward.
As Grafana Labs’ Tyler Helmuth recounts on the OTel blog, OTTL was created in 2022 as the configuration language for the transform processor. The domain-specific language lets you modify, filter, and enrich telemetry data directly at the collector level.
Longevity-thinkers will like this: They’ve also made a big backward-compatibility promise for OTTL. “If you write OTTL statements, the syntax and the standard functions stay backward compatible,” says Helmuth.
As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation.
Solving LLMs on shared GPUs
Putting all AI workloads on a single GPU is expensive and inefficient. But how do we pack multiple LLMs on shared GPUs safely, without a bunch of guesswork or manual toil?
Ratnopam Chakrabarti, a senior solutions architect at AWS, took to X to share an early preview of his upcoming joint Nvidia–AWS session, which will seemingly answer this question for KubeCon attendees.
He says his KubeCon session will “demonstrate an agent pipeline that profiles workloads and handles model colocation on GPUs, all in real time.” It’s one of many KubeCon sessions this year tackling AI optimization on Kubernetes.
Troubleshooting GKE workloads with VPC Flow Logs
This week on the Google Cloud blog, Google Cloud product managers Nishant Kumar and Whitney Jenkins describe a common issue for cloud operators: Kubernetes pods are ephemeral, making them hard to troubleshoot.
As they describe, “In a standard cloud network, flow logs provide that view by recording connections between IP addresses, ports, and protocols.” In Kubernetes, however, pods are temporary; they add, and by the time you track them down, they’ve often already vanished — leaving little evidence or records to inform troubleshooting.
The workaround, at least for those using Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), is its built-in VPC Flow Logs. This feature uses Google’s virtualized network to log every sampled flow with metadata like pod, workload, namespace, and service.
It’s one example of how cloud-native platforms are continuing to advance the infrastructure around Kubernetes to increase its visibility and usability.
AGNTCon + MCPCon prioritizes agent security
Is your agent installing malware without your knowledge? It’s a real possibility.
The latest AGNTCon + MCPCon event this month in San Jose, California, featured plenty of interesting talks that might resonate with the cloud-native community looking at the agent trend with big, worried eyes.
For instance, Snyk’s Liran Tal gave a talk entitled Your AI Agent Installed Malware Because a SKILL.md Told It To. Tal covered how agents often get tricked into running malware and offered some guidance on how to prevent it.
Vstorm’s Antoni Kozelski and Bartosz Adam Gonczarek also presented how they built an e-commerce MCP server and let the agent experiment with purchases across four different hosts. It behaved drastically differently in each scenario.
The session opened a conversation about where authorization rules that allow or disallow agents from taking irreversible steps should live. For Vstorm, it meant placing them on the server, not locally. They’re also following up with a webinar on the subject soon.
These stories are just two examples of what we’re seeing a lot: the unintended consequences of giving AI agents the keys to the kingdom. Cloud-native operators should watch for stories like this as they build the foundational infrastructure to support agents.
See you at KubeCon
Road to KubeCon is an eight-part series presented by HPE. Before you go, explore how HPE Software helps IT teams do more with less complexity.
And that’s a wrap for this year’s Road to KubeCon series! It’s been a privilege and an adventure profiling the top movements in the cloud-native world over the past two months.
In this weekly column, we covered many areas across eight editions, spanning updates to Kubernetes itself, like the Kubernetes 1.37 update and the move to cgroup v2.
Much of the discussion centered around how cloud-native technology is evolving for AI. We looked at case studies around Kubernetes inference at scale, and how agent harnesses are evolving.
Another recurring theme was increasing operator visibility. We saw how OpenTelemetry and Prometheus are converging and how to spot idle GPUs and optimize.
Arguably, the biggest takeaway is that the Kubernetes ecosystem is facing major shifts to meet the challenges of running AI workloads at scale. Is it up for the task?
KubeCon NA is anticipated to tackle this question head-on, from discussion at the co-located events to the main keynotes, sessions, and the showcase floor.
View the Road to KubeCon archive for all editions in this series, along with other insights from the TNS and HPE teams. A big thank you to the column’s sponsor, HPE, for making this column possible, and to the community members who shared their insights.
Now, we’re excited to continue the conversation in person at KubeCon NA!
See you there.

articles.title: No tiene rival: la cámara del nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max es lo mejor que hay ahora mismo en el mercado
articles.text:
Hay algunas verdades absolutas: el sol sale por el este, una hora está compuesta de 60 minutos, que el agua hierve a 100ºC y desde ayer, que el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max tiene la mejor cámara que existe en el mercado. Posiblemente muchas personas piensen que estamos exagerando pero sólo tienes que echar un vistazo a la galería que figura más abajo para que veas de lo que es capaz.
La nueva serie vivo X500 fue presentada oficialmente ayer martes, pero nosotros llevamos probando el modelo Pro Max varias semanas. Nos hemos ido a China con él, hemos recorrido las calles de Madrid y Barcelona con él y el resultado, en todos los escenarios, siempre ha sido sobresaliente.
La realidad es que vivo lleva años sacando flagships con una cámara magnífica, siempre de la mano de ZEISS. Ya el modelo del año pasado, la serie vivo X300, era para muchos la mejor cámara, aunque es cierto que todavía podía existir alguna duda. Este año esas dudas quedan disipadas.
Además del modelo vivo X500 Pro Max hemos probado el kit de teleobjetivo y lo que ha conseguido vivo es sencillamente increíble. Hay otros teléfonos que posiblemente se acerquen mucho, como el Oppo XFind 10 Pro Max, pero en la foto finish, es vivo el que se lleva el título.
La importancia de una buena cámara
En general, como teléfono, el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max es muy bueno. El nivel que han adquirido los teléfonos Android hoy en día es magnífico, y más aún si le metes un procesador como el MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro. El resultado es un teléfono que funciona de manera muy fluida y que derrocha potencia en todo momento. A eso le añades baterías de cada vez más capacidad, en el caso del vivo X500 Pro Max una de 6.750 mAh con carga rápida de 90W y una capa de personalización propia a cargo de OriginOS 7, y tienes un teléfono sencillamente perfecto.
Por eso, en los últimos años, el foco especial está puesto en la cámara, donde los fabricantes pueden poner toda la carne en el asador. Sensores más grandes, estabilizadores ópticos, mayor resolución… Y es precisamente en la cámara donde más se nota la diferencia entre dos teléfonos de gama alta.
Durante este año hemos visto como grandes fabricantes, como Samsung o incluso el propio iPhone, han introducido pequeñas mejoras en su cámaras, pero siempre hay aspectos donde se notan las costuras. En escenarios de poca luz o interpretando una imagen tras usar el zoom.
vivo ha solucionado eso y el salto de calidad que ha dado entre el modelo del año pasado a este se nota bastante. Hemos puesto su cámara a prueba en multitud de escenarios y el resultado ha sido siempre sobresaliente.
Qué secretos esconde la mejor cámara del mercado
Si nos fijamos a nivel de hardware y especificaciones, el módulo de cámaras del nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max se compone de: una cámara principal TrueDynamic de 50 megapíxeles, un teleobjetivo de 200 megapíxeles, un ultra gran angular de 50 megapíxeles, todo ello co-desarrollado con ZEISS. A esto le añadimos un sensor de enfoque láser.
Sobre el papel muy bien pero, siendo honestos, muy pocas personas entienden la repercusión que tiene un sensor u otro en el resultado de una fotografía. O que más megapíxeles no es automáticamente sinónimo de mejores fotografías. Por eso, vamos a ver en detalle cómo funciona en conjunto el módulo de cámaras y lo que es capaz de hacer.
Por ejemplo, tiene un sistema de estabilización profesional que funciona a la perfección sin importar el mal pulso del fotógrafo. Esto no es sólo importante a la hora de grabar vídeo sino también en esos momentos donde se necesita dejar el teléfono quieto en tiempos prolongados de exposición, por ejemplo haciendo fotos de noche.
También tiene un sistema de seguimiento de objetos, llamado Lock-On Subject que lo que hace es mantener el enfoque en la persona, incluso si sale momentáneamente del plano. Esto cobra también especial importancia en la parte de vídeo, donde puede granar enfocando hasta en 60 fps. Esto se complementa con las funciones Pro AF Tracking Video en 4K a 120 fps y Auto Framing Video, que permiten realizar un seguimiento preciso de los sujetos y mantenerlos correctamente encuadrados.
Acercando lo que está lejos, muy lejos
Para cualquier persona que prueba la cámara la primera vez, uno de los aspectos que más sorprende es la capacidad del zoom de la mano de su teleobjetivo ZEISS APO, con una distancia focal equivalente a 85 mm. Pero llama mucho, muchísimo, más la atención el extensor de teleobjetivo ZEISS, que permite alcanzar una distancia focal equivalente a 400 mm. Coges el teléfono, le pones la carcasa especial y ya puedes acoplar el teleobjetivo e incluso un disparador que sirve también como agarre, para que sea mucho más cómoda la experiencia de fotografiar.
No importa lo lejos que se encuentre. Durante estos días, hemos intentado llegar a sitios muy lejanos y el nivel de detalle es increíble. Además, donde no llega (por razones obvias de distancia) las capacidades del teleobjetivo, lo completa el uso de la Inteligencia Artificial, que recompone la imagen cargándola de detalles pero de manera muy realista.
Además, gracias al buen detalle de las imágenes, puedes hacer recortes muy concretos que cuando se amplíen, apenas perderán detalle.
Qué maravilla de grabación de vídeo
En nuestro día a día tenemos que grabar cantidad de recursos para redes sociales. Hasta ahora, solíamos usar una cámara réflex profesional y decidimos probar a salir sólo con el vivo X500 Pro Max. Nos encomendamos a la cámara principal ZEISS TrueDynamic, que ofrece todo lo necesario tanto para creadores de contenido como para todas aquellas personas que quieren obtener un resultado perfecto en sus grabaciones de vídeo. La manera en la que ajusta el rango dinámico, las condiciones de luz, el tratamiento de color… es lo más cercano a la realidad que hemos podido ver hasta ahora.
Uno de los modos que más nos ha gustado es el Cinematic Pro Log Video, que permite capturar más detalles tanto en las zonas iluminadas como en las sombras, ofreciendo una mayor flexibilidad creativa en la edición, similar a la que proporcionan las cámaras de cine profesionales. Es una cámara muy polivalente, que se adapta a la perfección a la situación y a las condiciones.
También nos ha gustado mucho el modo 4K Cinematic Portrait Video, que combina calidad de imagen cinematográfica con mejoras inteligentes para los retratos en vídeo. Y para los que necesitan editar después, el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max puede grabar en resolución 4K a 240 fps.
Como curiosidad, nos llevamos también el nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max a un concierto para poner a prueba el modo Escenario 3.0.
Esto es sólo la teoría de una experiencia que nos ha dejado boquiabiertos, pero en los próximos días verás vídeos en nuestras redes sociales sobre aspectos relacionados con la cámara. No te pierdas nada de lo que publiquemos durante los próximos del ya considerado: mejor cámara en un teléfono.

articles.title: Google hit with criminal probe over unapproved AI data center deforestation — 816 acres of forest destroyed in Finland as wolves flee into local villages, facility threatens 40% power bill hikes
articles.text:
Google hit with criminal probe over unapproved AI data center deforestation — 816 acres of forest destroyed in Finland as wolves flee into local villages, facility threatens 40% power bill hikes
The local Fins have a reputation for their low propensity for data center protests, but they are being tested.
A criminal investigation into the environmental damage caused by Google’s Finnish subsidiary has been launched. Tuike Finland Oy is being investigated after five complaints were received regarding the Muhos data center project, according to an official police statement published today [machine translation].
The police say that the investigation is backed by Finland’s Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV). Google/Tuike Finland Oy is accused of suspected breaches of environmental law and environmental damage. Other lesser criminal offenses related to ambiguities and shortcomings in the drainage and water management are also being investigated.
Since Google representatives have previously publicly apologized for the unauthorized forest clearings near Muhos, which have turned 816 acres of forest into an expanse of mud, there seems little doubt it is guilty of some wrongdoing. Rather, it is the scale of the punishment and any proposed remedies that will probably be of most concern to execs from the tech giant now.
As well as the awful mess Google has made near Muhos, it seems to have also jumped the gun and plowed ahead with data center development by clearing 500 acres of forest near Otanmäki.
Though the horse has already bolted, Reuters reports that a Google rep said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites. Maintaining?
Last week we reported that wolves had descended on Finnish villages after their habitats had been destroyed to make way for the Google AI data centers. Data center developments were already a thorny issue with locals. Potential construction and operating noise, pollution, utility competition, and environmental damage concerns were overshadowed – for some – by the presence of wild animals that had moved out of the forest.
Google sees Finland as an attractive location for data center development with its cool climate, affordable power, and government endorsement of AI projects. It has also benefitted from being able to develop in low population density areas and from a populace with a low propensity for protest. However, Google is testing the Finnish public with its trampling of the environment. The wolves, pollution, potentially 40% higher electricity bills, and other impacts weren’t helping its case, even before this criminal investigation.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Finnish government representatives have yet to comment on the case.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

articles.title: MacBook Pro tactile : Apple veut vraiment que vous mettiez vos doigts sur l'écran
articles.text:
Apple semble ne pas savoir sur quel pied danser à propos de l’arrivée du tactile sur son MacBook Pro. Gadget pour certains ou fonctions utiles pour d’autres, difficile de vendre cet ajout auprès d’un public aussi varié. Une chose est sûre : Apple veut aller plus loin avec l’expérience tactile de macOS.
« Ça ne fait que commencer » : l’expérience tactile de macOS va s’améliorer
John Ternus l’a expliqué, « il y a des moments où le tactile est pratique et confortable » sur le nouveau MacBook Pro tactile. Une amélioration mise en avant dans la communication d’Apple : la marque a surtout invité des créateurs de contenu en ligne à sa présentation, qui sont les plus susceptibles de l’utiliser, et elle a axé ses vidéos d’annonce sur cette fonction. D’un autre côté, Apple a pour défi de ne pas déboussoler les clients actuels ou historiques de son MacBook Pro. Son dirigeant a précisé dans la presse que « la fonction tactile ne dévalorise en rien le produit. Il ne l’alourdit pas, il ne l’épaissit pas. » Difficile de voir ce qu’Apple pense vraiment, alors que le principal obstacle à l’achat de cet ordinateur reste son prix.
Néanmoins, comme l’a écrit le journaliste de Bloomberg Chris Welch, en employé d’Apple a répondu aux questions des journalistes ce mercredi. Il « a déclaré que l’entreprise ne faisait que commencer l’optimisation de macOS pour les écrans tactiles. » On peut ainsi s’attendre à des nouveautés sur cet usage dès l’année prochaine avec l’arrivée de macOS 28, qui devrait être présenté lors de la conférence WWDC 2027 qui devrait avoir lieu en juin prochain.
Que permet déjà l’écran tactile du nouveau MacBook Pro ?
Il faut dire que pour le moment, Apple a offert le service minimum sur les fonctions tactiles de son ordinateur avec son écran Proled XDR. Un simple toucher fait un clic, deux touchers rapides font deux clics, pincer l’écran à deux doigts permet de zoomer en avant ou en arrière, etc. Apple a essentiellement reproduit les clics et les gestes du trackpad sur l’écran pour ne pas perdre ses utilisateurs. Certains gestes sont mêmes configurables. Cela a l’avantage d’avoir beaucoup d’applications Mac existantes qui répondent au doigt sans avoir besoin d’être retouchées. Bonne nouvelle, on peut interagir au doigt avec la nouvelle Dynamic Island qui a été ajoutée sur ce MacBook Pro.
Dans les usages plus précis, par exemple les peuvent tester des applications iOS et iPadOS directement sur l’écran du MacBook Pro ; pratique pour éviter d’installer leurs applications à chaque test. Apple a pensé à optimiser certains de ses logiciels : Pixelmator Pro (pour dessiner ou peindre), Logic Pro (pour jouer sur un clavier virtuel), Final Cut Pro (pour déposer des clips à l’endroit voulu), Creator Studio, etc.
Pour aller plus loin, Apple n’aura pas seulement besoin d’ajouter de nouvelles fonctions tactiles. L’entreprise compte s’appuyer sur les développeurs d’applications tierces et elle a déjà prévu le coup. Ces derniers disposent de nouvelles API de gestes à l’échelle du système pour créer des interfaces réellement tactiles.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: Password Managers for Teams: Sharing Logins Safely Without a Sticky Note in Sight - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The Growing Need for Secure Team Password Management
In today’s fast-paced business environment, teams often need to share access to various digital tools and platforms. From project management software to customer relationship management (CRM) systems, multiple team members require login credentials to collaborate effectively. However, this convenience comes with a significant risk: insecure password sharing practices. Writing passwords on sticky notes, emailing them unencrypted, or sharing them verbally can expose critical business data to cyber threats, leading to costly breaches and operational disruptions.
According to a 2023 report by Verizon, 81% of hacking-related breaches involve stolen or weak passwords, highlighting the urgent need for more secure methods of managing login credentials. This widespread vulnerability emphasizes how traditional password-sharing methods are no longer sufficient in the face of sophisticated cyber attacks. Businesses, especially those operating with distributed or remote teams, must rethink how they manage and share access to sensitive accounts.
Furthermore, a recent survey by Cybersecurity Ventures found that the average cost of a data breach involving compromised credentials reached $4.35 million in 2023, up 15% from previous years. These alarming figures underscore the financial and reputational risks associated with poor password management and sharing practices.
What Makes Password Managers Essential for Teams?
Password managers are software solutions designed to store, generate, and manage complex passwords in an encrypted vault. For teams, these tools offer a centralized platform to securely share login credentials without exposing the actual passwords. This eliminates the need for risky practices, such as sharing passwords verbally or jotting them down on physical notes. The tech managed by iTi Communications can help businesses implement robust cybersecurity strategies, including setting up and managing password managers tailored for team use.
Beyond simple storage, password managers enable teams to generate strong, unique passwords for each account, reducing the risk that a breach of one service compromises others. They also allow administrators to set granular access controls, ensuring that only authorized team members can view or use certain credentials. This is particularly important for businesses that deal with sensitive client data or intellectual property.
Integrating a reliable password manager can significantly reduce the risk of unauthorized access and data breaches. Businesses that leverage password managers report a 50% reduction in security incidents related to credential theft. This statistic reflects how implementing proper password management solutions can transform an organization’s security posture and foster safer collaboration among team members.
Moreover, password managers streamline workflows by enabling auto-fill features and seamless cross-device synchronization, reducing the friction often associated with password entry. This convenience encourages team members to adopt stronger security habits without sacrificing productivity.
How Experts at The KR Group Facilitate Secure Team Access
The experts at The KR Group specialize in integrating password management tools within broader IT infrastructure. They assist organizations in selecting the right platform based on team size, business needs, and security requirements. By leveraging their insights, companies can establish role-based access controls, ensuring that only authorized personnel can view or share specific credentials.
This approach not only protects sensitive information but also simplifies auditing and compliance-key considerations for industries governed by stringent data protection regulations such as GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS. The KR Group’s expertise extends to tailoring password management workflows that align with regulatory mandates, helping organizations avoid costly fines and reputational damage.
Moreover, The KR Group supports seamless integration of password managers with Single Sign-On (SSO) solutions and identity management systems, creating a unified and user-friendly authentication experience for teams. This integration reduces password fatigue and improves overall security hygiene across the organization.
Key Features to Look for in Team Password Managers
While numerous password managers exist, selecting the right tool for your team involves evaluating several critical features:
– Shared Vaults and Access Controls: Enables teams to share credentials securely with defined permissions, limiting exposure to only those who need access.
– Password Generation and Auto-Fill: Helps create strong, unique passwords and reduces manual entry errors, which are common sources of security vulnerabilities.
– Audit Trails and Reporting: Tracks access history for accountability and compliance purposes, allowing administrators to monitor who accessed what and when.
– Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Adds an additional security layer beyond just passwords, significantly reducing the risk of unauthorized access.
– Cross-Platform Compatibility: Ensures seamless access across desktops, mobile devices, and browsers, supporting diverse work environments.
– Emergency Access and Password Recovery: Allows designated team members to regain access in case of emergencies without compromising security.
– Integration Capabilities: Ability to integrate with existing IT infrastructure such as SSO, identity providers, and security information and event management (SIEM) tools.
Implementing a password manager with these capabilities can lead to a 33% decrease in time spent on password-related support requests, freeing IT teams to focus on strategic initiatives. (https://www.lastpass.com/resources/password-security-report) This efficiency gain translates to cost savings and enhanced operational effectiveness, making password managers a valuable investment beyond just security.
Overcoming Common Challenges in Team Password Management
Despite the clear benefits, some organizations hesitate to adopt password managers due to concerns about complexity, cost, or user adoption. To address these challenges, companies should invest in user training and choose intuitive platforms that integrate well with existing workflows. This reduces resistance and accelerates adoption across all team members.
Developing a clear password-sharing policy aligned with the organization’s security framework reinforces responsible behavior. Policies should define who can access shared credentials, how passwords are updated, and the procedures for onboarding or offboarding team members. Combining technology with governance ensures that password sharing is both safe and efficient.
Another common challenge is ensuring that password managers remain up-to-date and patched against vulnerabilities. Partnering with managed IT services can alleviate this burden by providing regular maintenance and security assessments.
Furthermore, organizations should consider scalability when selecting a password manager. As teams grow or change, the solution should accommodate new users and evolving security requirements without disruption.
Future Trends in Password Management for Teams
Looking ahead, passwordless authentication methods such as biometrics and hardware tokens are gaining traction. Technologies like FIDO2 and WebAuthn standards are enabling secure, phishing-resistant login experiences that eliminate the need for traditional passwords in some contexts.
However, password managers remain indispensable as they bridge the gap during this transition, especially for legacy systems and third-party applications that do not yet support passwordless methods. They also continue to evolve by integrating AI-driven features that detect anomalous login behaviors, automate credential rotation, and provide real-time security alerts.
Moreover, advancements in AI are enabling smarter password management solutions that can detect anomalies and automate security tasks, further protecting teams from credential-related threats. For example, AI-powered systems can identify unusual access patterns that may indicate compromised accounts and prompt immediate action.
As remote and hybrid work models persist, the need for secure, flexible, and user-friendly password management will only increase. Organizations that proactively adopt advanced password management solutions position themselves to mitigate risks and maintain operational resilience.
Conclusion
Securely sharing passwords within teams is no longer a luxury but a necessity in safeguarding business assets. By adopting modern password management tools and partnering with trusted IT experts, organisations can eliminate risky practices like sticky notes and unprotected emails. Investing in the right password management solution today is a proactive step toward a safer, more efficient future for any team. With the right technology, policies, and expert support in place, businesses can foster a security-conscious culture that empowers teams to collaborate confidently without compromising sensitive information.

articles.title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget?
Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume.
The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence.
In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults.
The operating model in one view
Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing.
Stage 1: Attribute every dollar
You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0, and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys.
Setup is four steps:
- Turn on IAM principal data in your CUR 2.0 data export.
- Tag your IAM principals with business dimensions such as team, application, and cost center. For federated access, configure your identity provider to pass session names and tags through OIDC or SAML claims.
- Activate those tags as cost allocation tags in AWS Billing (console or the UpdateCostAllocationTagsStatus API).
- Analyze the tags: they surface in CUR 2.0 with an iamPrincipal/ prefix (for example, iamPrincipal/team) and appear in AWS Cost Explorer under the IAM category within 24–48 hours of activation, ready for filtering and grouping by team, application, or cost center.
This is invoice-grade, per-identity attribution with no custom infrastructure.
The shared-role problem
The pattern that deserves the most attention is the shared-role problem, because it is where most platforms silently lose attribution. A large language model (LLM) gateway that calls Amazon Bedrock through a single IAM role attributes every dollar to that one role, eliminating per-user visibility entirely. The fix is per-user session management. The gateway assumes the Amazon Bedrock invocation role once per user, passing the user’s identity as the role session name and their attributes as session tags, then caches those credentials for up to an hour (one AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) call per user per hour, not per request).
This needs two roles: a gateway execution role holding sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession permissions, and the Amazon Bedrock invocation role it assumes. The result is line_item_iam_principal entries like assumed-role/BedrockRuntimeRole/gw-alex, each carrying its user’s tags: per-user and per-tenant attribution restored behind a shared gateway.
A note on application inference profiles and Projects
Amazon Bedrock offers two more attribution mechanisms, each suited to a different pattern. Application inference profiles are pre-created, per-application resources on the bedrock-runtime endpoint that carry cost allocation tags. You create one profile per application per model per AWS Region, and callers reference the profile ARN, which fits teams with a small and stable set of applications and models. Projects and workspaces serve the bedrock-mantle endpoint (Responses API, Chat Completions API). A project isn’t tied to a specific model, so a single project ID spans many models, which fits teams whose model usage changes frequently. You pass the project ID at client initialization, and its tags flow to CUR 2.0 and Cost Explorer (see Manage AI costs with Amazon Bedrock Projects). Projects are the attribution path for OpenAI-compatible workloads on Amazon Bedrock.
For bedrock-runtime workloads, we recommend IAM principal attribution through session tags as the primary mechanism. It scales with your identity system, requires no pre-created resources, and covers every model and API operation. Application inference profiles work well when a small, stable set of business units needs invoice-grade billing separation without changes to identity design. Use projects for bedrock-mantle workloads that use the Responses API or Chat Completions API.
Stage 2: Make every request observable
CUR tells you who spent. Invocation logs tell you what happened. Amazon Bedrock supports model invocation logging of request data, response data, and metadata to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or both. Use Amazon CloudWatch for fast operational queries and S3 plus Amazon Athena for long-term business intelligence (BI) access. Treat logging as infrastructure, not a manual toggle: provision the log group or bucket through code, define retention and encryption policies, and validate delivery during environment setup. If logging exists only in development or only in one Region, your cost program becomes fragmentary the moment usage grows.
Logging also closes the latency gap: CUR attribution lags roughly 24 hours, but CloudWatch plus OpenTelemetry can power near-real-time dashboards showing per-developer spend within minutes (Analyzing Claude Code usage with CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry demonstrates this end to end).
Request metadata for workload-level attribution
Raw logs answer identity-level questions. To answer workload-level questions (which feature, workflow, or tenant generated the tokens), stamp request metadata on every call. Amazon Bedrock captures this metadata in the invocation logs for later analysis:
The following example uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock through the US cross-Region inference profile. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. For availability by Region, see Model support by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Bedrock doesn’t enforce request metadata, and teams drift into inconsistent schemas quickly when every application does its own thing. The platform team should inject mandatory metadata centrally in a shared SDK wrapper or gateway, normalize the key set, and treat metadata coverage as a platform health metric.
Diagnostic queries
With logs and metadata in place, CloudWatch Logs Insights answers the standing questions. Who consumes the most tokens:
The same query grouped by requestMetadata.application and requestMetadata.workflow instead of caller produces the workload-level leaderboard: the view product and engineering teams will ask FinOps for the moment chargeback conversations start.
Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.
Stage 3: Enforce budgets
With attribution and observability in place, enforcement becomes an architecture choice rather than a wish. There are three viable tiers. The right one depends on your spend velocity, your risk tolerance for overspend, and how your tools connect to Amazon Bedrock.
Tier 1: Monitor and alert (no blocking)
Amazon Bedrock writes principal identity into the billing pipeline automatically. You put AWS Budgets on top for threshold alerts, with the OpenTelemetry dashboards from Stage 2 closing the 24-hour CUR gap for day-to-day visibility. Nothing to deploy, native AWS billing, and no added latency on inference calls. It works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. Nothing can hard-stop spend, so you see the problem after it happens. Right for early adoption, where alerting plus human intervention is sufficient. Two builder guides walk through it: Limiting Bedrock usage and controlling costs, and Deep dive on managing Bedrock in Claude Code with AWS Budgets and Tags.
Tier 2: IAM tag enforcement (deny on breach)
An aggregator AWS Lambda function tallies per-user token and dollar counters in Amazon DynamoDB from invocation log data. When a user breaches their threshold, the function adds their identity to a shared IAM deny policy (denying bedrock:*) until a monthly reset or admin override. This enforcement runs entirely on IAM and Amazon Bedrock logging, with no third-party component in the inference path, and it works with tools that call Amazon Bedrock directly. The Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock in the AWS Solutions Library provides a deployable variant. It checks each user’s usage against per-user and per-team limits when it issues credentials, and withholds credentials once a user exceeds their limit. Because that check uses usage telemetry emitted by the client, its figures can differ from CUR. In either form, enforcement is asynchronous. A block takes effect seconds to minutes after the breaching call for an IAM policy update, or at the next credential refresh for the credential check. Your platform team owns the pipeline. This tier is right for teams that need real enforcement, can tolerate that lag, and want to keep third-party software out of the data path.
Tier 3: Gateway enforcement (synchronous block)
A gateway sits in the inference data path and enforces budgets synchronously, returning HTTP 429 the moment a user or team exceeds their limit. You get sub-second blocking, per-user model allowlists, token rate limits, and centrally enforced routing rules. The trade-off: a component in the data path that must be deployed, scaled, and security-reviewed. Clients must be configured to send their requests through the gateway.
For Claude Code and Claude Desktop fleets, the Claude apps gateway for AWS is the official recommendation. It ships inside the CLI binary and runs as a single stateless container backed by PostgreSQL. It provides OIDC identity, centrally managed policy, OpenTelemetry telemetry, multi-Region Amazon Bedrock routing, and per-user/group/org spend caps out of the box. For mixed-model workloads spanning multiple providers, general-purpose gateways remain the right choice: LiteLLM through the Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate reference architecture, or a serverless alternative described in Build a proactive AI cost management system for Amazon Bedrock, Part 2.
Choosing a tier
Two factors dominate.
Connectivity: If developers call Amazon Bedrock directly with no proxy, only Tiers 1 and 2 are viable.
Spend velocity: If spend is already in the millions per month, build enforcement now. If alerts can hold the line for another quarter, invest in Stages 1 and 2 first and add enforcement when the data demands it.
Most organizations should phase it: observe at Tier 1, then step up. Treat all three as bridges, not destinations: the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens already codifies agent cost governance as a first-class architectural concern, and the attribution foundation from Stage 1 is what any managed enforcement will sit on.
Stage 4: Optimize the defaults
Most Amazon Bedrock waste is not individual carelessness. It is platform defaults nobody set. The two highest-impact levers are both platform-controlled.
Model routing
Not every task needs a frontier model. Routine completions (boilerplate, linting suggestions, small refactors) can run on smaller, cheaper models with quality reserved for complex reasoning, through intelligent prompt routing within a model family or routing rules at the gateway (see Reduce costs and latency with Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing and prompt caching for the full walkthrough). Which workflows can downshift is an empirical question: pull the workload leaderboard from Stage 2, run a quality evaluation on the cheaper model for the top entries, and route what passes. For agentic coding fleets, where boilerplate dominates call volume, more than half of calls landing on cheaper models is an achievable target.
Prompt caching
Prompt caching rewards stable repeated prefixes. As of October 2026, the published Amazon Bedrock pricing for Anthropic Claude models in US East (N. Virginia) bills a cache write at 1.25x the base input rate with the 5-minute time-to-live (TTL) (2x with the 1-hour TTL). A cache read is billed at 0.1x the base input rate on Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and at 0.05x on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5. Check the pricing page for your model and Region, because these multipliers vary by model and can change. The break-even math is friendlier than teams assume. With the 5-minute TTL, a single reuse already pays for the write, and ten calls against a stable prefix cost roughly a fifth of the uncached price (about 22 percent at a 0.1x read rate, 17 percent at 0.05x). The only losing case is writes that are never re-read, which cost 25 percent extra with the 5-minute TTL and double with the 1-hour TTL. So the platform dashboard should track cache-read volume against cache-write volume per workflow. A low read ratio means the prefix is not actually stable (usually a timestamp or session ID embedded before the cache point).
Candidates surface directly from the invocation logs:
Note: Field paths shown in the preceding query are illustrative. Verify against your invocation log schema, which may vary by model, API operation, and logging configuration.
Application-level optimization
A third class of savings (just-in-time retrieval instead of stuffed context, compaction of long conversations, distilling stable high-volume workflows onto smaller models) belongs to application teams rather than the platform. The platform’s job is to make those savings visible: publish the per-workflow token leaderboard, set token limits per model and workflow, and let the teams that own expensive workflows see exactly where they stand.
Stage 5: Operate the loop
The first four stages produce data. This one turns it into decisions. The platform team runs a standing health dashboard with four signals:
- Model mix: Which models are called and how often, the direct measure of routing discipline.
- Failed request rates: Errors, throttles, and timeouts. Each retry adds latency, and a client-side timeout on a request that still completes on the service side can be billed twice, once for the abandoned call and once for the retry.
- Cache effectiveness: The read-versus-write ratio from Stage 4.
- Metadata coverage: The percentage of production calls with complete metadata. Every uncovered call is an attribution blind spot that quietly degrades every other number.
When a signal drifts, the remediation is a policy change (routing rules, token limits, metadata enforcement), not an email asking teams to be careful.
The money loop
FinOps runs the money loop on the same data. When attribution is clean, anomaly detection becomes an investigation stream rather than a panicked all-hands: a spike in a tagged team or application triggers a lookup in the Stage 2 leaderboard, not a war room. Chargeback runs from CUR groupings by team and application.
Scorecard
The following thresholds are starting points, not prescriptions. Calibrate them against your own fleet data and pricing tier before adopting them as policy.
| Dimension | Metric | Green | Yellow | Red | 
| Unit economics | Cost per successful outcome | ≤ budget | 1–1.5x budget | >1.5x budget | 
| Per-dev cost | Daily spend per developer | <$100 | $100–$300 | >$300 | 
| Model routing | % of calls to cost-efficient-models | >50% | 30–50% | <30% | 
| Cache efficiency | Cache-read hit ratio | >60% | 30–60% | <30% | 
Green means the workload operates inside its economic envelope. Yellow means routing or caching discipline is slipping. Red means spend is concentrating in premium models or uncached context, and the Stage 3 and 4 controls are the remediation path. Review this scorecard on a regular cadence (weekly for high-velocity fleets, biweekly otherwise) and treat it as the joint FinOps-plus-platform decision surface.
Conclusion
In this post, you learned how to build a five-stage operating model that takes Amazon Bedrock spend from uncontrolled to fully governed:
- Attribute every dollar to an owner using IAM principal tags, session tags, and CUR 2.0.
- Observe every request through model invocation logging and stamped request metadata.
- Enforce budgets at the tier that matches your risk: monitor-only, IAM deny on breach, or synchronous gateway blocking.
- Optimize platform defaults with intelligent prompt routing and prompt caching to remove waste centrally.
- Operate a scorecard and review cadence that turns telemetry into policy decisions.
Notice the first row of that scorecard: cost per successful outcome, not cost per call. That distinction is where this playbook hands off. Everything here makes Amazon Bedrock spend visible, attributable, capped, and efficient, but a workflow can be perfectly efficient and still not be worth running. Deciding that requires measuring the agent against the human process it replaced, which is a product and analytics discipline rather than a FinOps one. What the cost platform contributes is the foundation: clean attribution and per-workflow cost data are exactly the inputs that outcome measurement joins against.
Build the five stages and you can answer, end to end: who spent it, why, and whether it was controlled. That is what it means to manage Amazon Bedrock cost, and it is the difference between a monthly bill review and an operating model.
To get started, deploy the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock reference architecture for Stages 1–3, then use the cost attribution best practices documentation to configure your tagging strategy.

articles.title: Apple et Microsoft rejoignent le réseau de surveillance russe
articles.text:
Depuis le début du mois, Apple et Microsoft figurent dans le registre russe des « organisateurs de diffusion d'information ». Concrètement, les deux groupes doivent garder les échanges de leurs utilisateurs en Russie et les remettre aux services de sécurité sur demande.
Ce registre est géré par Roskomnadzor, le régulateur russe des télécoms, lequel y avait déjà ajouté Google Meet en janvier.
Messages, appels, métadonnées : ce que Moscou peut réclamer
Puisque les deux géants sont désormais dans le registre, ils doivent non seulement stocker les messages, les appels audio et les vidéos des utilisateurs russes, mais aussi les fournir aux agences de sécurité dès qu’elles le demandent. Notons que le processus est effectué sans procédure judiciaire. D’après Bloomberg, elles doivent aussi garder pendant trois ans les informations sur les utilisateurs et sur la transmission de leurs échanges. Cela correspond aux métadonnées, c’est-à-dire aux interlocuteurs et à l’horaire plutôt qu’au contenu. Le tout doit rester sur des serveurs situés en Russie, donc soumis au droit russe.
Apple et Microsoft rejoignent Google Meet, WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat, Cloudflare ou encore Blizzard Entertainment. Les entreprises qui refusent s’exposent à des amendes, puis à une restriction d’accès à leur service dans le pays. Ni Apple ni Microsoft n’ont commenté, ni indiqué si elles comptaient se conformer à ces règles.
Cette décision s’ajoute aux blocages et restrictions qui visent déjà WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal et FaceTime. En février, nous rapportions que WhatsApp et YouTube devenaient inaccessibles en Russie, quelques jours après les restrictions sur Telegram. Moscou voulait alors orienter sa population vers MAX, une messagerie nationale sans aucun chiffrement des communications.
Pourtant Microsoft se retire de plus en plus du marché russe. L’éditeur a suspendu ses nouvelles ventes dès mars 2022, puis réduit fortement ses activités sur place en juin, avec plus de 400 salariés concernés d’après Bloomberg. En août 2023, il a prévenu ses clients professionnels qu’il ne renouvellerait plus leurs licences après le 30 septembre, même si les analystes estiment que jusqu’à 90 % des entreprises russes utilisaient encore ses produits. Début 2024, Microsoft prévoyait aussi de couper l’accès à ses services cloud (Teams, OneDrive, Azure ou Office 365) aux sociétés enregistrées en Russie, en application des sanctions européennes, mais pas aux particuliers. Reste à savoir quels services de Microsoft sont concernés par le registre : les informations disponibles ne le précisent pas.
De son côté, Apple a été sanctionnée en 2022 pour ne pas avoir stocké de données iCloud sur des serveurs locaux. Depuis l’invasion de l’Ukraine, le groupe a aussi suspendu ses ventes de produits et limité Apple Pay, mais il a gardé l’App Store, source de plusieurs litiges. Roskomnadzor lui a fait retirer des applications de VPN, et l’autorité de la concurrence a ouvert en août une procédure, car Apple ne préinstalle ni MAX ni la boutique d’applications RuStore sur ses appareils. Apple respecte en général les lois locales, mais il lui arrive de retirer une fonction plutôt que de s’y plier. En 2025, après une demande d’accès aux données des utilisateurs britanniques, elle a désactivé Advanced Data Protection au Royaume-Uni uniquement.
Source : Bloomberg via 9to5Mac et AppleInsider.

articles.title: Größter Kunde von SpaceX ist nicht mehr die US-Regierung, sondern eine KI-Firma
articles.text:
Größter Kunde von SpaceX ist nicht mehr die US-Regierung, sondern eine KI-Firma
Anthropic ist jetzt der größte Einzelkunde von SpaceX. Das berichtet die Finanznachrichtenagentur Bloomberg unter Berufung auf eine anonyme Quelle. Die soll bestätigt haben, dass sich hinter „Kunde B“ im jüngsten Geschäftsbericht von SpaceX, das sich inzwischen auch „SpaceXSI“ (für „SpaceX Super Intelligence“) nennt, die KI-Firma verbirgt. Auf sie entfällt demnach rund ein Drittel des Umsatzes. Grundlage sei eine milliardenschwere Partnerschaft, die Anthropic im Frühjahr mit SpaceX geschlossen hat. Dabei sicherte sich das Unternehmen einen Großteil der KI-Rechenkapazitäten von xAI – Musks KI-Firma, die inzwischen in SpaceX aufgegangen ist. Auch deshalb konnte das Unternehmen nach dem Rekordbörsengang erstmals einen Milliardengewinn verbuchen.
Braucht SpaceX die Nasa nicht mehr?
Die Zahlen untermauern eine Entwicklung, die das US-Technikmagazin Ars Technica kürzlich in einer ausführlichen Reportage beschrieben hat: Mehr als ein Jahrzehnt lang hing Musks Raumfahrtfirma am Geld der US‑Regierung. Inzwischen ist es andersherum: Die Nasa ist beim Transport von Menschen ins All komplett auf SpaceX angewiesen, während sich das Unternehmen immer weiter von ihr abwendet.
So soll die Raumkapsel Crew Dragon nur noch bis 2030 Astronautinnen und Astronauten ins All bringen. Die Trägerrakete Falcon 9 könnte laut dem Bericht schon 2028 ausgemustert werden. Um lukrative Regierungsaufträge bewirbt sich SpaceX demnach nicht mehr in jedem Fall.
Geld soll künftig aus der KI kommen
Bloomberg und Ars Technica kommen übereinstimmend zu dem Schluss, dass SpaceX sein Geld künftig vor allem mit KI verdienen will. Das riesige Rechenzentrum in Memphis, das an Anthropic vermietet ist, ist dabei nur der Anfang. Musk will KI-Rechenzentren in großem Stil ins Weltall verlagern, weil dort „kostenlose“ Energie durch die Sonne zur Verfügung steht. Ob das technisch funktioniert, ist allerdings umstritten.
In der Raumfahrt setzt SpaceX nun alles auf das Starship. Die Riesenrakete soll deutlich mehr Nutzlast transportieren als bisherige Systeme. Ars Technica weist jedoch darauf hin, dass es kaum Hinweise darauf gibt, dass SpaceX noch an einem Aussetzmechanismus für große Nutzlasten arbeitet – also an der Technik, die Satelliten im All freisetzt. Der bisherige Mechanismus eignet sich für Starlink- und Rechenzentrumssatelliten, nicht aber für große Weltraumteleskope, wie die Nasa sie braucht.

articles.title: Del cobre a la luz: cómo la fotónica podría reducir el consumo energético de la inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
La expansión de la inteligencia artificial aumenta la capacidad de cálculo requerida por los centros de datos y, con ella, la demanda de electricidad, agua y cobre. Ante ese panorama, empresas tecnológicas y laboratorios desarrollan sistemas que usan luz para transmitir información y reducir el calor de los equipos, una alternativa que podría disminuir la energía destinada a enfriarlos.
La tecnología se llama fotónica. En lugar de mover la información mediante señales eléctricas a través de cables de cobre, la transporta con luz por fibra óptica. La fibra ya se utiliza en las comunicaciones de larga distancia, pero ahora la industria busca incorporarla a las conexiones internas de estas instalaciones, entre servidores, procesadores y equipos de red.
“Creo que estamos llegando al final de la era del cobre”, afirmó Chris Sharp, director de Tecnología de Digital Realty, en declaraciones recogidas por la BBC. Con esa frase no sugirió que el metal dejará de utilizarse, sino que su peso en las conexiones internas podría disminuir.
Una instalación de 100 megavatios puede requerir unas 400 toneladas de cobre, según el medio británico. La mayor parte se destina a la red eléctrica y a los equipos de refrigeración; del total, unas 70 toneladas se usan en los servidores y cerca de 20, en el cableado que los conecta.
La transmisión de datos con luz genera menos calor
El cobre conduce las señales eléctricas con eficacia, aunque ese proceso produce calor. El efecto cobra importancia en edificios que reúnen miles de procesadores, incluidos los que se utilizan para entrenar y operar herramientas de inteligencia artificial. A mayor temperatura, mayor es la energía que debe destinarse a mantener los equipos dentro de un rango seguro.
La fotónica busca reducir esa carga térmica. Para aplicarla, los fabricantes deben unir componentes ópticos, que trabajan con luz, y circuitos electrónicos, que funcionan con electricidad. En algunos casos, esa integración se realiza en los propios procesadores.
“Se puede ahorrar muchísima energía”, dijo Callum Littlejohns, subdirector de Cornerstone Labs, una fábrica de componentes de fotónica de silicio, según la BBC. La diferencia reside en que la luz no genera el mismo calentamiento que la corriente eléctrica cuando transmite datos.
Menos calor puede traducirse en una menor necesidad de electricidad para refrigerar los servidores. Cuando las instalaciones emplean agua para ese fin, esa reducción también podría aliviar su demanda hídrica. El impacto, de todos modos, depende del sistema de enfriamiento y del diseño particular de cada centro de datos.
La fibra óptica ofrece otra ventaja: permite enviar varios flujos de información por un mismo canal. De ese modo, se puede ampliar la cantidad de datos que circula por la red sin multiplicar el cableado al mismo ritmo, una posibilidad relevante para instalaciones que conectan cada vez más servidores.
La producción a gran escala todavía presenta obstáculos
El uso de luz para transmitir datos existe desde hace décadas, pero fabricar componentes fotónicos integrados en grandes volúmenes resultó complejo. Por su parte, Peter O’Brien, responsable de investigación sobre integración de sistemas fotónicos en el Instituto de Investigación Tyndall de Irlanda, explicó que investigadores y empresas llevan años trabajando en este campo, aunque las dificultades de fabricación demoraron su adopción.
“Lo que está ocurriendo ahora con la óptica y la fotónica es que se está produciendo una especie de reinicio”, señaló O’Brien ante la BBC. El respaldo de compañías de procesadores, entre ellas Nvidia, impulsó el interés por una tecnología que busca salir de aplicaciones limitadas y alcanzar un uso más extendido.
El reemplazo de conexiones de cobre por fibra no será inmediato. Andrew Wheeler, vicepresidente sénior de Hewlett Packard Labs, recordó que la industria eléctrica lleva años perfeccionando el diseño, la producción, las pruebas y la instalación de sus componentes. La fotónica aún necesita reducir costos y consolidar procesos de fabricación confiables.
La temperatura y el tendido de fibra exigen nuevos cuidados
Los dispositivos ópticos generan menos calor que sus equivalentes eléctricos, pero no eliminan el problema térmico. Otros equipos del centro de datos continúan elevando la temperatura ambiente y los componentes que trabajan con luz son sensibles a esas variaciones.
Wheeler advirtió que la fiabilidad de estos sistemas depende de que fabricantes y operadores mantengan controles estrictos sobre la temperatura. Por eso, la adopción de la fotónica requerirá cambios en el diseño de las instalaciones y nuevas rutinas de mantenimiento.
El tendido de fibra también demanda capacitación específica. Sharp explicó que estos cables no toleran curvas muy cerradas, una diferencia frente al cableado de cobre. Los responsables del diseño de redes, los técnicos de soporte y los instaladores deberán considerar esas condiciones para evitar pérdidas de señal y fallas de conexión.
Para Ofer Shapiro, director ejecutivo de Resolight.ai, el ahorro podría ser mayor si la luz se utilizara tanto para transportar datos como para procesarlos. La empresa propone reemplazar los equipos electrónicos que dirigen el tráfico entre servidores por otros que funcionen de forma íntegramente óptica, con el fin de evitar conversiones constantes entre señales de luz y eléctricas.
Esa posibilidad todavía se encuentra en una fase posterior. Por ahora, el desafío principal consiste en aumentar la fabricación de estos componentes y abaratarla. Littlejohns indicó que algunas de estas piezas son más grandes que las de los procesadores convencionales, por lo que pueden producirse con equipos de generaciones anteriores de la industria electrónica.

articles.title: Fin a 28 años de historia: Telefónica dejará de encargarse de prestar el Servicio Universal de Telecomunicaciones
articles.text:
A partir del 1 de enero de 2027, Telefónica dejará de ser la operadora obligada a prestar el servicio universal de telecomunicaciones, ese mínimo de teléfono fijo e internet que puede pedir cualquiera, viva donde viva. Así lo prevé el proyecto de orden del Ministerio para la Transformación Digital y de la Función Pública. El texto salió a audiencia pública el 7 de octubre de 2026, y con esta orden se cierran 28 años de historia.
Casi tres décadas de Telefónica. El servicio universal arrancó en España en diciembre de 1998, con la liberalización de las telecomunicaciones, y desde entonces ha sido Telefónica la que ha cargado con él, tal y como recoge un documento de la antigua Comisión del Mercado de las Telecomunicaciones. Al principio giraba alrededor de la línea de teléfono fijo, pero desde el 1 de enero de 2012 incluye también una conexión a internet de 1 Mbps, según el mismo documento.
Una banda ancha con poco tirón. Pero esa banda ancha universal nunca ha sido demasiado popular, entre otras cosas debido a sus límites de descarga y a una velocidad que siguió anclada en 1 Mbps hasta 2022. Ese año, con la Ley General de Telecomunicaciones, el mínimo pasó a 10 Mbps, la cifra que sigue vigente según el proyecto de reglamento del servicio universal.
Por qué el Ministerio da el paso. El proyecto de orden sostiene que la fibra, el cable, el acceso fijo radio y el satélite forman “un extenso abanico de tecnologías” que permite constatar “la universalización de las redes de muy alta capacidad para todo el territorio nacional”. De hecho, el texto destaca un “excelente nivel de cobertura” de fibra óptica y 5G, además de la evolución de las redes por satélite. Y con ese panorama, apoyándose en el artículo 35.6 de la Ley General de Telecomunicaciones, el Ministerio concluye que el teléfono y la banda ancha fijos quedan “garantizados por las circunstancias normales de explotación comercial”, así que no renovará a Telefónica cuando su designación termine el 31 de diciembre de 2026.
Qué podrás pedir desde 2027. A partir de esa fecha dejará de haber un único operador designado, y cada compañía tendrá que ofrecer el servicio universal dentro de la zona en la que dé cobertura, según el proyecto de orden. Las condiciones las concreta el proyecto de reglamento, que el Ministerio sometió a audiencia pública el 22 de abril de 2026 y que todavía está en tramitación. Si sale adelante tal cual, tanto particulares como microempresas, pymes y organizaciones sin ánimo de lucro podrán exigir 100 Mbps de bajada, 5 Mbps de subida y una latencia media máxima de 690 milisegundos, además de la función de Texto en Tiempo Real (RTT) en las llamadas.
Además, el proyecto de reglamento obligaría a todos los operadores a aplicar a quienes cobren el Ingreso Mínimo Vital un descuento de al menos el 25% sobre su precio comercial, tanto en el alta como en la cuota mensual.

articles.title: Pixxel deepens US push with dedicated federal subsidiary
articles.text:
Pixxel deepens US push with dedicated federal subsidiary
Pixxel Federal will build on its existing enagements with NASA and the National Reconnaissance Office, as the Bengaluru-based company seeks to expands its satellite intelligence, advanced sensing and software business with American government agencies.
Bengaluru-based spacetech startup Pixxel has established Pixxel Federal, a US subsidiary aimed at expanding its business with American civilian, defence and intelligence agencies.
The move reflects the growing role of privately operated satellites in government operations, from national security and resource mapping to environmental monitoring. It also signals Pixxel’s ambition to move beyond supplying specialised satellite imagery towards offering a broader combination of sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems.
The subsidiary will build on the company’s existing engagements with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO).
“The US government market represents a significant opportunity for Pixxel as we expand our capabilities beyond hyperspectral imaging into advanced sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems,” said Pixxel's founder and CEO Awais Ahmed, adding that the new unit will enable it to work more closely with federal agencies, understand their mission requirements, and deliver solutions tailored to their needs.
A key part of the company’s offering is hyperspectral imaging, a technology that captures reflected light across hundreds of narrow wavelength bands, including those beyond the visible spectrum. Different materials absorb and reflect light differently, producing identifiable patterns known as spectral signatures. These can help distinguish minerals, vegetation, and other materials in ways that conventional satellite imagery may not.
The US Geological Survey uses hyperspectral surveys to identify minerals, soils and vegetation, illustrating the technology’s potential in resource exploration and environmental research.
Pixxels sees applications in defence and intelligence, including camouflage detection, terrain assessment, and identification of activities of interest. Other potential uses include locating critical minerals and rare earth elements, monitoring crops, and tracking environmental changes.
Allyson Jenkins, who previously led Pixxel’s public-sector business, has been appointed the CEO of Pixxel Federal. The subsidiary’s board includes retired US Army Lieutenant General Ray Palumbo, former Northrop Grumman executive Patrick M. Antkowiak, and former senior intelligence official Frank X. Avila.
Pixxel also plans to establish an office in the Washington, DC, metropolitan area.
The company’s government relationships have developed over the past two years. In September 2024, Pixxel was selected for NASA’s Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme, a multi-provider arrangement through which the agency purchases commercial Earth-observation data. In May 2026, the NRO named Pixxel, alongside EarthDaily and ICEYE under its Strategic Commercial Enhancements initiative to expand access to commercial sensing capabilities.
The wider industry is moving in the same direction. US policy has long encouraged government agencies to use commercial remote-sensing capabilities where practical, while retaining national-security safeguards. More recently, the Department of Defense and US Space Force have outlined strategies to integrate commercial space services into national security operations.

articles.title: Binance links $6.3 billion crypto theft to compromised DevOps laptop
articles.text:
Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has linked the theft of about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency to a DevOps engineer's compromised laptop.
The crypto exchange said the access let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions after they accessed a service container, and it hasn't yet found evidence of a leaked wallet private key.
"To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual," Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said.
Binance also said it "uncovered additional points of breach" but was "still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."
The company confirmed the breach in a statement shared with BleepingComputer on Thursday and reassured customers that their funds were safe.
"Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company's funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete," it said.
Since the attack, Binance has suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks, revoked authorizations for the affected address, and is working with blockchain intelligence partners and law enforcement to trace and recover the stolen funds.
Crypto theft linked to North Korean hackers
Although the company didn't link the incident to a hacking group or threat actor, blockchain analysis firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38.
"On October 29, 2026, an attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC. That makes this the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the USD 1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025," TRM said.
Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis confirmed TRM Labs' findings, stating with "a high degree of confidence" that TraderTraitor is responsible for the Binance $6.4 billion hack.
While stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle, Ripple, and others have frozen roughly $2.7 billion since the incident, the attackers still have control of about $2.4 billion that can't be frozen.
"Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about USD 2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly USD 2.7 billion," TRM added.
"The attacker raced the freezes by selling USDT to market makers and borrowing ETH against USDT on Aave. It now holds more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about USD 2.4 billion in assets beyond any issuer's reach."
The TraderTraitor hackers were previously linked to many other major crypto theft incidents, including the theft of $1.5 billion in the February 2025 Bybit hack. At $6.36 billion, the Binance attack is now the largest recorded crypto heist.
