articles.title: Grey targets dollar-free payments for African businesses
articles.text:
Grey, the Y Combinator-backed cross-border payments company, says it has built direct currency conversion routes to help African businesses pay suppliers across borders without first converting their money into US dollars, as it expands its services for businesses trading across the continent.
Speaking at a media briefing with journalists on the sidelines of Moonshot by TechCabal 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, on Thursday, Idorenyin Obong, Grey’s co-founder and chief executive officer, identified payment reliability and foreign exchange (FX) liquidity as two major challenges businesses face when making international transactions.
Payments between African countries can involve multiple currency conversions. For instance, a Nigerian business paying a supplier in Kenya may need to convert naira into US dollars before exchanging it for Kenyan shillings, adding another step to an already complicated transaction.
“Most times, if you’re trading within Africa, there’s always some form of intermediary currency,” Obong said. “We’ve built out these currency pairs, these exotic currency pairs, such that you never have to go in between to the USD.”
Obong said Grey has invested in payment infrastructure that allows customers in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana to collect and send money, supported by liquidity arrangements across multiple currencies.
The company said the infrastructure enables real-time settlement in several supported currencies, reducing the need for businesses to source FX through multiple intermediaries.
The problem extends beyond Grey’s customers. In October, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the global bank for central banks, said that many payments between African countries still pass through correspondent banking networks outside the continent, increasing costs and exposing businesses to operational risks.
Other payment providers are also trying to address the problem. The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), developed by Afreximbank in partnership with African institutions, has been expanding local currency payment infrastructure.
In February, it partnered with Kenya’s Pesalink network to connect regional payments with Kenyan banks and mobile money providers.
Reducing currency conversion steps is only one part of the problem for Grey. Businesses also need assurance that payments will reach suppliers within an expected timeframe, particularly when delays can disrupt procurement and trading relationships.
Obong said customers moving amounts as little as $50, and larger amounts reaching $1 million, can experience uncertainty over whether funds will reach their destination when needed. To address this, Grey provides estimated payment delivery times and says it has invested in infrastructure to improve the reliability of its international payouts.
“We spent the last six years building the infrastructure to ensure that we’re delivering at the last mile at 99.99% to our customers,” Obong said.
In February, Grey expanded into payments and settlement for businesses, as its consumer transaction volumes grew. During the briefing, Obong disclosed that the company had processed more than 40 million transactions and nearly $5 billion in payments since inception.
Grey Business, its multi-currency platform for startups and small businesses, has processed nearly $100 million since launching in February, according to the company. By June, the company said that the platform had processed $61.4 million in its first four months, partly driven by demand for stablecoin-based payments.
The company has also expanded payouts to China, allowing businesses to pay overseas suppliers in Chinese yuan.
Beyond business payments, Grey is trying to solve another problem: what happens after individuals receive money from abroad.
Obong said the company initially launched in 2020 as a currency exchange service but expanded into foreign currency accounts after discovering that customers struggled to receive international payments in the first place.
Remote work accelerated demand for those services, especially among professionals earning foreign currencies while living in African markets.
“Most of our customers were using Grey to receive their foreign salary. And so we decided to build what I would call simply a salary account for these customers,” he said.
That insight led the company to build Paycheck, the salary product Grey launched on Wednesday. The service allows professionals earning in dollars, pounds, and euros to receive and manage their salaries, with features designed to separate money intended for spending and saving.
Obong said Paycheck also integrates with Pouch, Grey’s savings feature, which allows customers to set aside money for goals such as education, travel, or major purchases. The company is exploring additional benefits, including credit and lifestyle rewards.
The push reflects Grey’s ambition to build services around customers’ financial activities rather than simply helping them receive or transfer money.
Grey also faced questions at the briefing about difficulties some customers encounter when accessing foreign currency accounts and obtaining support.
The company said it offers round-the-clock digital assistance and has a physical office, although it considers online support more effective for routing customer issues to its distributed teams.
Grey’s next challenge is proving that its expanding range of services can solve these problems consistently.

articles.title: Vous avez aimé Obsession ? Son réalisateur sort un nouveau court-métrage terrifiant sur YouTube
articles.text:
YouTube : le créateur d'Obsession sort le court-métrage parfait pour Halloween
Après le triomphe planétaire d’Obsession, le réalisateur Curry Barker dévoile un nouveau court-métrage disponible gratuitement sur YouTube, juste à temps pour Halloween.
Curry Barker, réalisateur venu de YouTube et habitué des vidéos virales, est de retour sur la plateforme qui a fait son succès. Après avoir enflammé le box-office au printemps dernier avec le film d'horreur Obsession, il vient de mettre en ligne un nouveau court-métrage sur le service de streaming vidéo.
Mama Bear : un retour aux sources horrifiques sur YouTube
Si Obsession a généré plus de 525 millions de dollars au box-office à travers le monde depuis sa sortie en mai dernier, cela ne veut pas dire que son réalisateur, Curry Barker, délaisse la plateforme qui l'a rendu célèbre. Le jeune réalisateur a dévoilé le court-métrage horrifique Mama Bear sur YouTube, pile à temps pour Halloween.
Sponsorisé par Windows, ce nouveau film de 5 min a été écrit, réalisé et monté par Barker. Il raconte l'histoire de Floyd (Jon Lee Richardson) alors qu'il reçoit un coup de téléphone qui va complètement bouleverser sa journée.
Regardez le court-métrage Mama Bear :
L'atmosphère inquiétante de ce court-métrage fait écho à Obsession, en particulier l'image d'une figure dissimulée dans l'ombre d'un coin de la pièce.
En plus de Richardson, le film met en scène Katie Sarife sous les traits de Lacey, Ericka Kreuz dans le rôle de Ms. Wilson et Joshua Snyder dans la peau du double de Floyd.
Une équipe rodée avant de nouveaux projets au cinéma
Le film rassemble plusieurs membres de l'équipe d’Obsession derrière la caméra, dont la costumière Blair James qui a révélé au micro du Hollywood Reporter que ce court-métrage a été tourné il y a un peu plus de trois semaines.
Le prochain long-métrage de Barker au cinéma sera Anything But Ghosts, un film programmé pour une sortie en salles en mai 2027. Le cinéaste est aussi attaché à un nouveau projet de remake de Massacre à la tronçonneuse.

articles.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
articles.text:
Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.
- Share:
A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.
Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.
The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.
A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision
Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.
To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.
"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."
The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.
Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.
A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare
To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.
When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.
The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.
The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.
"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."
The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.
Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough
The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.
Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.
The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.
"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."
Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.
Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices
The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.
In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.
Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.
"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."
As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort
articles.text:
GPT-6.1 Terra vs. GPT-6 Astra: One sacrifices accuracy for lower cost and higher speed at high effort
OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, marketing it as a cheap, fast model for high-volume everyday work, priced at a tenth of its GPT-6 Astra flagship.
As the mid-priced model in its GPT-6 family, OpenAI lists Terra at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, a mere tenth of Astra’s $10 and $50. The AI giant also reports that Terra completes tasks more than three times faster than Astra in its Agents’ Last Exam benchmark. Those computer-use results are not directly comparable to the three tests below.
Early benchmarks showed some limitations, alongside gains. Plotly reported that Terra caught three of five planted patterns in its analytics test and passed 40 of 43 questions overall. Artificial Analysis found that it guessed on 38% of questions it couldn’t answer instead of saying so, down from 88% for GPT-5.6 Terra in the same benchmark. DualEntry’s accounting benchmark put its accuracy at 78.2%.
In this AI arms race, each launch needs to be marketed as the best; otherwise, it risks being ignored. This can create a confusing experience for users, especially when reality doesn’t quite match the promise. I compared Terra with Astra on three synthetic tasks to see how their speed, estimated token costs, and accuracy differed. This is a separate test of those trade-offs, not a replication of OpenAI’s computer-use benchmark.
The tests
I ran the final version of each test once per model through OpenAI’s API with reasoning effort set to high. I didn’t set an output-token cap, though the models still have built-in output limits. I graded each test against keys I built and verified, after developing three versions of each test. These are single-run results on synthetic tasks, not estimates of repeatability or performance across all workloads. Matching the effort setting does not impose the same reasoning-token budget on both models.
Both models returned the same score on easy and medium-difficulty tests. To test the real soft spots, after the same results returned a third time, I ran hard tests against a weaker model, GPT-5 Mini, until Mini’s score was very low.
Here is the final iteration of the tests. These are the tests detailed in the remainder of this article. In the usage figures below, “out” includes reasoning tokens; the parenthetical reasoning count is a subset, not an additional charge. Costs are estimates calculated from the reported tokens at standard uncached input and output rates, excluding any tool charges or billing adjustments. They are not verified invoice totals.
- SQL reasoning – I built a fake database of 500 software builds and asked each model 25 questions about it. Some builds were deleted, some were retries, costs are in three currencies, and a few questions depend on time zones. Two of the questions can’t be answered from the data.
- Data validation – I gave each model a spreadsheet of 4,950 fake customer records and 19 rules they’re supposed to follow. Some rules only make sense across the whole file, like no more than three customers at one postal code and no referral loops; forty records break a rule, and 10 look wrong but are actually fine.
- Incident log triage – I wrote about 7,000 lines of logs from a fake outage across more than 20 services. I planted errors like drifting clocks, error messages blaming the wrong service, and unrelated changes sending alerts before the one that actually caused the outage.
SQL reasoning
This test showed the widest split between the two models. Astra scored 48/50 and Terra 26/50. Each of the 25 questions was worth two points, for a total of 50. An answer had to be exactly right to earn the two points, so a close answer earned zero. Unanswered questions also earned zero points. For the questions that can’t be answered from the data, the correct answer was to identify that. On every other question, a model that didn’t give an answer earned zero.
Terra processed all 500 rows and handled soft deletes, retries, and three currencies. Its one miss was the total run time for 151 builds in a single region. Astra’s answer came in 406 seconds short of the correct 31,428. Its answer was 31,022 seconds, about 1.3% below the stated correct total. The final answer alone doesn’t show whether the error came from addition, a skipped row, or a misread value.
Astra was more accurate in this run, but its incorrect total still needed checking. It generated 27,970 reasoning tokens, and the response took 319.7 seconds—more than five minutes.
On the six questions that required adding up costs or durations across all 500 rows, Terra didn’t attempt an answer. It wrote a SQL query for me to run instead and marked each one as not calculated. Terra didn’t make up numbers, which is good. But it left the hardest part of the job, running the query and getting the totals, for you to do yourself. This is the first time I’ve seen AI hand work back.
The bigger problem is that Terra answered six questions wrong. Four of them were counts that were off by just one or two. Terra gave those answers with the same confidence as its correct ones, so nothing signaled that they were wrong. If you used those numbers in a report, you wouldn’t know which ones to double-check.
I’m including the numbers for both Terra and Astra here, but since the results were so different, the lower price and faster time aren’t wins.
- Terra 133.1 s, 21,060 in, 11,554 out (10,707 reasoning), $0.079
- Astra 319.7 s, 21,060 in, 28,806 out (27,970 reasoning), $1.65
Data validation
Astra scored a perfect 50, and Terra scored 45. 40 of the 50 points came from the 40 records that broke a rule. A model earned one point for each record it flagged, as long as it named the rule the record broke. The last 10 points came from records that looked wrong but followed every rule. A model lost a point for every correct record it accidentally flagged as incorrect.
Before giving its answer, Terra warned that it couldn’t reliably check all 4,950 records against the rules and might miss some (as it did in the SQL test). The reported input fit within the model’s context window, and I did not set an output cap. Terra generated 1,841 reasoning tokens compared with Astra’s 12,831. The responses took 31.4 and 145.0 seconds, respectively; these elapsed times don’t isolate reasoning time.
Terra correctly flagged 35 of the 40 invalid records and flagged none of the valid records: 87.5% recall and 100% precision in this run. Its 45/50 score is a test score, not an accuracy percentage across all 4,950 records. Three of the five it missed only break a rule when you compare them with other records in the file, such as a customer who reused another customer’s phone number. Terra flagged everything correctly, but it missed five invalid records. The results don’t explain why it missed them.
Astra caught all 40, but it took more than four times as long and cost about 12 times as much. Terra used fewer reasoning tokens and missed records in this run; that association does not establish the cause of the misses.
The numbers:
- Terra 31.4 s, 234,045 in, 2,336 out (1,841 reasoning), $0.25
- Astra 145.0 s, 234,045 in, 13,369 out (12,831 reasoning), $3.01
Incident log triage
This one was a tie, with both models scoring 50. I graded this test using a 50-point list of what a correct answer needs to include. To earn the full 50 points, a model had to trace the outage to the settings change in the ledger service, find the three servers with wrong clocks, and avoid blaming the planted false leads. False leads included a fraud service update that was rolled back, a payments setting that changed seconds before the real cause, a database switchover, and an unrelated memory problem in the search service.
Error messages blamed the fraud service, but both models traced the outage to a settings change in the ledger service and spotted the three servers with wrong clocks. Neither model took the error messages at face value. Both checked the evidence underneath, which is what you’d want from an engineer during a real outage.
Astra cost about 11 times as much as Terra and took 2.6 times as long to complete the work. Most of Astra’s additional output tokens were reasoning tokens: 4,628 of the 6,650-token difference. Both models earned the same score here despite that difference. These runs don’t show whether additional reasoning led to better scores on the other tests.
The numbers:
- Terra 94.3 s, 251,651 in, 7,508 out (5,114 reasoning), $0.29
- Astra 244.5 s, 251,651 in, 14,158 out (9,742 reasoning), $3.22
Results
| Test | Terra (out of 50) | Astra (out of 50) | GPT-5 Mini (out of 50) | 
| SQL reasoning | 26 | 48 | 6 | 
| Data validation | 45 | 50 | 10 | 
| Incident log triage | 50 | 50 | 12 | 
| Total (of 150) | 121 | 148 | 28 | 
| Estimated token cost | $0.61 | $7.88 | — | 
| Total time | 258.8 s | 709.2 s | — | 
I included GPT-5 Mini’s baseline results for reference. I rebuilt these tests several times and kept making them harder because both models kept returning identical scores. Because I selected these harder versions after seeing earlier results, they shouldn’t be treated as a representative sample of everyday work. A low Mini score is a comparison point, not an independent measure of test difficulty.
What do I think?
In these three final high-effort runs, Terra generated fewer reasoning tokens and finished sooner than Astra. It scored lower on SQL reasoning and data validation, and tied Astra on incident log triage. That is a trade-off in the results, but it doesn’t tell us whether Terra was overwhelmed or why it made specific errors.
The measured totals were 258.8 seconds for Terra and 709.2 seconds for Astra, so Astra took about 2.74 times as long overall. At the stated standard uncached rates, the estimated token costs were $0.61 and $7.88; Terra’s cost was about 7.8% of Astra’s. Terra scored 121/150 and Astra 148/150 under these test rubrics. The runs show a cost, time, and score trade-off; they don’t show that OpenAI deliberately cut reasoning to achieve it.
Terra matched Astra’s scores on my earlier easy and medium versions, but that does not establish its accuracy on every task at those difficulty levels. On the final tests, I would be cautious about using it for unchecked numerical aggregation or exhaustive data validation. It may be an acceptable lower-cost alternative for some workloads, including tasks like the incident triage tested here, as long as you verify the results. Astra’s incorrect SQL total also reminds you to check its work.
Learning Path

articles.title: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
articles.text:
General Motors marketed its Smart Driver system as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their driving behavior. But in 2024, it emerged that GM had been sharing that data with brokers. Those brokers then sold the data to insurance companies, and some drivers found that their insurance became more expensive as a result. To make matters worse, many of those drivers claimed they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for such purposes.
Last year, GM and its OnStar subsidiary entered into a settlement with the FTC, prohibiting them from sharing some kinds of driver data with third parties. The settlement was finalized this January. That agreement banned the two companies from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data for five years. At the time, GM also discontinued Smart Driver across its entire range.
Now the automaker has reached terms with the District of Columbia and 35 states after their attorneys general joined together to sue GM as well.
GM said in a statement that “[s]afer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”
According to TechCrunch, the settlement with the states is notable in a third party is required to assess GM’s compliance with the new privacy program.

articles.title: Why Trust Is Becoming Essential for Agentic Commerce | BetaKit
articles.text:
When tickets for your favourite artist go on sale in the middle of a critical meeting, the idea of dispatching an AI agent to buy them for you sounds pretty appealing. But how do you know it will buy the right tickets, stick to your budget, and keep your payment information safe?
“Trust is foundational to agentic commerce being able to truly scale.”
Answers to those questions are becoming more important as agentic commerce scales in Canada and AI agents move from recommending purchases to making them. A Mastercard report predicts that by 2030, more than one in 10 online shoppers will routinely use agents to shop and pay.
Making those purchases secure takes a lot of work behind the scenes, and trust built into every side of the transaction. As the buyer, you need to trust the agent to follow your instructions. The seller has to know it’s legitimately acting on your behalf, while the financial institution needs to verify that the purchase matches what you authorized before approving the payment. All of this must happen in real time, with safeguards against fraud and attempts to manipulate the agent.
Canada is already putting the technology to the test. This fall, Mastercard worked with AI company Flybits and credit card issuer Rogers Bank to complete its first Canadian transaction through Agent Pay, its agentic commerce service. The transaction went beyond showing that an agent could make a purchase. The participants were able to verify that the agent was legitimate, had permission to act, and that the transaction amount matched the consumer’s authorized intent, said Amisha Parikh, vice-president, security solutions at Mastercard, Canada, in an interview with Betakit. “I think the real learning here was that it works,” she said.
“Human-led, agent-executed” transactions
For Canadian startups building AI tools, selling online or developing payment technology, that first purchase by an AI agent offers an early look at what it takes to make these transactions secure.
Parikh described the arrangement as “human-led, but agent-executed,” with the customer deciding what to buy and how much to spend.
In her concert-ticket example, you could specify two seats for a Toronto show, the dates you are available, your preferred sections, and a $500 budget. The agent has room to find tickets that fit. It should not decide that a more expensive show in another city is close enough.
“The agent is executing, but the human has set those guardrails,” she said.
Businesses already use tools such as multifactor authentication and biometrics to check that you, as the buyer, are who you say you are. When an agent shops on your behalf, they also need to confirm that it genuinely represents you and has permission to make the purchase.
Parikh said by using Agent Pay, the agent used is legitimate and has the customer’s permission to make a purchase on their behalf. “Verifiable intent becomes very important,” she said.
What if someone interferes?
Even an authorized agent can still become a target for attack. Just as someone could take over a customer’s account, they could potentially try to redirect an agent by giving it different instructions—an attack known as a “prompt injection.”
The risks also extend to where it shops. A fraudulent merchant could appear to offer exactly what the agent has been asked to find and draw it into a scam.
As merchants introduce agents of their own, software could interact on both sides of a purchase. Parikh says it becomes important to establish which person or business each agent represents and whether it is following their instructions.
Existing fraud controls also need to evolve to distinguish legitimate AI agents from malicious bots and recognize when an agent is acting with a customer’s authorization, she said.
This is where Mastercard’s Agent Pay Trust Framework helps address the need to recognize legitimate agents and assess the risks around their purchases. That means understanding who an agent represents, what it has permission to do, and whether the merchant can be trusted.
Mastercard brings together insights about identity, customer intent, behavioural patterns, and fraud risk to help banks and merchants better understand agent-led purchases. Parikh said the challenge is turning those signals into timely, actionable intelligence: helping to distinguish legitimate activity from potential threats, identify when additional checks are needed, and reduce unnecessary friction for customers.
Canada and the future of commerce
Parikh said advancing agentic commerce in Canada will require cooperation among financial institutions, retailers, government, academia, and payment networks.
She pointed to Mastercard’s Global Intelligence and Cyber Centre of Excellence in Vancouver as an example of how talent, research and partnerships contribute to advancing work on digital trust and intelligence.
“As AI capabilities evolve, she said, the safeguards around them must evolve, too. For agentic commerce, that means maintaining confidence that agents are acting with permission, within agreed limits, and with clear accountability.”
“Trust is foundational to agentic commerce being able to truly scale,” she said.
PRESENTED BY
Learn more about Mastercard’s approach to cybersecurity, digital trust and the future of commerce.

articles.title: European SpaceTech recieves a €560 million injection to promote European sovereignty | EU-Startups
articles.text:
A new partnership between Deutsche Bank and the European Investment Bank (EIB) is set to mobilise a €560 million investment towards European SpaceTech, helping businesses scale, bring new tech to market, and strengthen Europe’s independent space capabilities.
This will directly support companies across the space supply chain, from component manufacturers and launch technology developers to satellite applications and in-orbit services.
“This new partnership between the EIB and Deutsche Bank will help unlock investment in Germany and across Europe – backing the companies, supply chains and technologies that will make Europe’s space sector stronger, more competitive and ready to scale,” said Nicola Beer, European Investment Bank Vice-President.
The agreement follows a series of SpaceTech financing announcements across Europe in 2026.
In Germany, Munich-based The Exploration Company secured €387 million, HyImpulse Technologies raised more than €50 million, ATMOS Space Cargo attracted €25.7 million and deltaVision received €10.2 million.
Elsewhere, Finland’s ICEYE raised €450 million in primary funding, Spain’s PLD Space extended its Series C to €288 million and France’s UNIVITY secured €27 million.
Alongside further announcements involving AIRMO, Hydrosat and Arkadia Space, these financings exceeded €1.3 billion, independently of the proposed Deutsche Bank–EIB investment mobilisation.
EU-Startups previously reported on the EIB’s separate €30 million venture-debt loan to PLD Space in April 2026.
“Europe has the engineering talent to lead in space. Our job is to help finance its next stage of growth,” added Marc Mueller, Global Head Trade Finance & Lending at Deutsche Bank. “Working with the EIB, we can offer space businesses the long-term financing they need to invest, expand production and compete internationally.”
Agreed ahead of the European Space Agency (ESA) Space Investor Forum in Munich, this operation also builds on cooperation between the EIB and European Space Agency to address the financing needs of Europe’s space sector. ESA provides market intelligence and sector expertise to support the development of financing solutions that reflect the needs of space SMEs and Mid-Caps and enable the space sector to access finance.
It also helps connect these financing opportunities with the European space ecosystem, raising awareness among eligible companies and facilitating outreach to potential beneficiaries.
The initiative will support investment in technologies including reusable launchers and spacecraft, advanced propulsion systems, satellite manufacturing and Earth observation. These technologies underpin services ranging from communications and navigation to wildfire detection, pollution monitoring and security.
The financing will have a pan-European reach, with around half of investment expected in Germany and the remainder elsewhere in the EU.
“This partnership with Deutsche Bank will help companies across Europe’s space sector invest in the technologies, production capacity and supply chains needed to scale up and compete globally. In doing so, we are strengthening Europe’s capacity to deliver essential space services more autonomously,” said Robert de Groot, European Investment Bank Vice-President.”
Space businesses often face long development cycles, complex technologies and uncertain commercial returns, making conventional bank lending harder to secure. The partnership aims to give Deutsche Bank long-term funding and flexible financing structures to support commercially viable companies investing in their next stage of growth.
The partnership forms part of Space TechEU, the EIB’s dedicated space financing programme launched in November 2025, designed to mobilise an estimated €1.4 billion in investment with commercial banking partners.
The idea is that this will compliment broader EIB Group support through direct investment loans, venture debt, equity investment and advisory services. By combining these instruments with commercial bank lending, the Group aims to help European space companies secure financing at successive stages of development – from innovation to industrial expansion.
“Europe has a growing number of space companies with outstanding technologies that are ready to scale,” said ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher. “The next step is ensuring they have access to the capital they need to grow. This initiative can help open that path, enabling European space companies to scale up, compete and succeed.”

articles.title: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is 'a great opportunity to go deceive people' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary capturing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes’ final weeks before prison, is sparking national conversation as it becomes one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time. The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, intentionally refuses to characterize Holmes as a master manipulator or victim, instead highlighting her uncanny, almost hypnotic knack for making people pity her, even when they’re well aware of her crimes.
Tyler Shultz didn’t need to see “You Can See Everything” to make up his mind about Holmes. Shultz, whose first job out of college was at Theranos, was a key whistleblower who exposed the company’s dangerously inaccurate blood testing devices, which made their way into Walgreens stores and delivered faulty results to real patients. (Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion despite its technology never actually working — the company only used its own machines for a fraction of tests, instead outsourcing others to third-party equipment.)
There is little reason to keep talking about Holmes — her case is closed, and she’s in federal prison — but her con-artistry has fascinated the media (myself included) for the last decade.
In fact, as Shultz says in an interview with The San Francisco Standard, “the only reason we’re talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants us to be talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now.”
But the cautionary tale of Theranos takes on a new significance as we enter the peak of the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.
“I think the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. Elizabeth took that model and scaled it to $100 million,” Shultz told SF Standard.
His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable investor and board member himself.
“I believe that what [Holmes] did was raise the biggest angel round of funding of all time, but even at the smaller levels, I think investors need to recognize that when they put that type of money in someone’s hands, they are giving them tremendous power,” he added.
Theranos’ funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families, rather than venture firms. Theranos did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley.
At the time Theranos’ fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a shrill wake-up call for investors that they need to prioritize due diligence. But in the AI era, Shultz worries that investors may forget these lessons.
“A huge danger with AI is that I think it is really hard to do due diligence on it,” he said. “It’s really hard to tell the difference between what is something truly unique and new versus like, a ChatGPT wrapper… If you want to deceive people, I think this is a great opportunity to go deceive people.”
The first question posed by “You Can See Everything” lies in the premise of the movie itself. Why would a mother of two young children choose to invite a film crew to follow her final days with her family before surrendering to serve a prison sentence of over 11 years? The film poses questions that seem inscrutable, but this one seems pretty clear. She wants people to pity her, because this pity could be more useful for her future endeavors than hate or mockery.
In the film, we see Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, working on Haemanthus, a diagnostics company that they call “Theranos 2.0,” which has reportedly raised about $20 million in funding.
“You Can See Everything” doesn’t make Holmes look good, but it also glosses over the more heinous crimes of Theranos, like giving dangerously faulty medical information to real patients, or even its targeted harassment of Shultz himself when he was attempting to sound the alarm about his former employer. In the cultural zeitgeist, Holmes remains more of a joke than a persona non grata.
“I have this feeling of unease about what might come next,” Shultz said. “She’s certainly preparing and beginning her second act, and I don’t know exactly where it’s going to go.”

articles.title: Launching a business? GoDaddy’s Airo AI Builder can have your idea live in minutes
articles.text:
Your website says just as much about you as what your existing customers do, and that’s why you’ll want to make a good first impression. And, while it used to take months to put together a compelling website through code and toolkits, it’s now easier than it has ever been thanks to GoDaddy’s Airo AI Builder.
Airo AI Builder is a comprehensive website design tool that gives you the tools to construct a professional site, with a full commerce-ready backend, in minutes, not months, with code yours to keep so you can download it anytime.
Say It, Build It
If you remember the early internet, where sites were blocky, unintuitive messes built by code, you may fear that’s how your first effort will look. After all, how can you build something sleek and modern without knowing the first thing about website design?
Thankfully, GoDaddy’s Airo AI Builder removes all the friction of website construction without asking you to compromise on your ideas.

articles.title: Bulletproof Host Virtualine Loses Its Domain to FBI Seizure
articles.text:
The FBI has seized virtualine.net, the domain of a Russian-speaking bulletproof hosting services provider associated with various cybercriminal operations.
According to court documents, Virtualine, also known as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, has been hosting customers’ illicit services and helped them evade law enforcement takedown attempts.
In posts on cybercrime forums, Virtualine promoted support for various types of cybercriminal activity, including phishing, spam, carding, and more; advertised its ability to move customer services to unaffiliated infrastructure; and claimed it intentionally ignored abuse.
It also allowed users to post and sell explicit images and videos of minors and adults, and supported at least one customer that offered a hack-for-hire service aimed at stealing sexually explicit content from online accounts.
Despite receiving numerous takedown requests from law enforcement agencies in several countries, Virtualine continued to aid the customer and even helped them create a new website for uploading the illicit content. The provider continues to host the new website.
According to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, Virtualine has been used, among others, by ransomware groups and an infostealer operator.
“Virtualine received more illicit-attributed cryptocurrency than any other TRM-labeled bulletproof hosting provider, despite receiving less total value than several peers,” the company says.
The bulletproof hosting provider first emerged on the cybercrime forum Exploit in 2024, but claims to have been operating since 2019. It claimed to have had the largest collection of autonomous system numbers for malware and botnet hosting in 2025.
Most of the payments Virtualine’s labeled Bitcoin addresses have received came from a Russian drug marketplace (44%) and a large sextortion scheme (17%). A cryptocurrency mixer accounted for 13% of them and ransomware for 5%. In 2026, Virtualine also received payments from the StealC infostealer operators.
“A domain seizure disrupts how customers find and access a service. It does not, by itself, establish that the operator has stopped working, or that customers have lost access to all underlying infrastructure,” TRM notes.

articles.title: Razer Blade 18 RTX 5090 Laptop Review
articles.text:
Razer is often called the Apple of the gaming laptop industry. Like the MacBook Pro, the Razer Blade series is famed for being slim, stylish, powerful, and overly expensive. But does the Blade 18 with its RTX 5090 live up to that reputation, both the good and the bad, and can it compete with my favorite desktop replacement, the very similar Lenovo Legion 9i Gen 10?
The Blade configuration we received for review is an absolute beast of a gaming machine. In addition to packing Nvidia's flagship 24GB mobile GPU (175W TGP), there's a 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus, 32GB of DDR5-6400, a 2TB PCIe 4.0 SSD, and a 99Wh battery. There's also a dual-mode 240Hz/440Hz IPS display, which we'll get to later.
Thanks to the memory crunch, gaming laptops are priced like second-hand cars right now, but few are more expensive than this $5,400 machine.
The slim and sleek descriptors are definitely warranted here. It's amazing how Razer fits all this hardware into a chassis measuring just 15.74 × 10.84 × 1.10 inches. It's the same thickness as the Legion, in fairness, but more compact in its other dimensions.
It's also noticeably lighter at just over 7 pounds, making it easier to carry around than many other 18-inch laptops.
The Blade is stylish. The CNC-milled chassis, with its black anodized finish and illuminated green Razer logo, makes this look like the laptop Darth Vader would use. In a good way.
This chassis oozes quality and expense. There's not a hint of flex in it, and the lid stays firmly in place even when you're bashing away at the keys. It feels cool and smooth to the touch. I also like the clean look of having the power button integrated into the keyboard itself, rather than the usual massive button slapped between the keys and screen.
My only nitpick is that the lack of a lip makes it a little harder to open than the Legion, but Razer would likely argue that omitting it improves the aesthetics.
This is also one of those rare gaming laptops without LEDs (beyond the logo) on the outside of the chassis, so there are no rear light bars, underglow strips, illuminated vents, or edge lighting like you'd find on many rivals. Some people will likely see that as even more incentive to buy a Blade.
Connectivity, Ports, and Keyboard
The Razer Blade 18 offers a generous selection of ports, including three USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 connections, one Thunderbolt 5/USB-C port, and one Thunderbolt 4/USB-C port.
Both USB-C ports support DisplayPort 2.1 and up to 100W USB Power Delivery, although the Thunderbolt 5 port provides display output directly from the RTX 5090, while the Thunderbolt 4 port routes display output through Intel's integrated graphics. Razer doesn't indicate which Thunderbolt port is which, either.
There's also an HDMI 2.1 port, a full-size 2.5Gb Ethernet port, a UHS-II SD card reader, a 3.5mm combo jack, a proprietary power connector, and a Kensington security lock slot.
The Legion 9i Gen 10, in comparison, has one extra USB-C port, two Thunderbolt 5 connections instead of one, and supports up to 140W USB-C power delivery compared with the Blade 18's 100W maximum.
Wireless connectivity, meanwhile, consists of tri-band 2×2 Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) and Bluetooth 5.4.
An 18-inch laptop means you get a full-size keyboard with a 10-key numpad. There's 1.5mm of key travel, and Razer's Chroma RGB lighting offers a slew of customization options.
Below the keyboard sits a large glass touchpad that's responsive and pleasant to use, easily on par with the Legion's.
The Blade 18 offers a very impressive typing experience, but I definitely prefer the Legion in this department for its slightly stiffer keys and larger gaps between them. Also, despite the palm-rejection technology, there were a couple of occasions when the touchpad registered an accidental click while I was typing, but these were rare.
Display
The Blade's screen shares almost exactly the same specs as the Legion's: 3840x2400 at 240Hz, with the option to switch to 1920x1200 at 440Hz. Razer's machine is slightly brighter at 600 nits (vs. 520 nits), while both have a 3ms response time, 100% DCI-P3 coverage, and Nvidia G-Sync.
The part that puts many people off, though, is that both use IPS panels rather than OLED or mini-LED. They're the best IPS screens I've ever seen, but it's still easy to imagine that most consumers would prefer another panel type over the ability to play at up to 440Hz.
The Calman-verified, color-calibrated display looks superb on the Blade. Not OLED or mini-LED superb, but it's still super sharp, bright, crisp, and accurate.
If you want to try the 440Hz mode, you'll need to use Razer's app and restart the machine, just as you do with the Legion and its app.
It's difficult to choose a favorite between the two laptops, as their screens are so similar. The Legion's does pop more because of its glossy coating. However, that also causes its biggest problem: reflections in bright rooms and outdoors, something the Blade 18 handles much better. Razer's machine is actually great to use outdoors and in bright indoor environments, with almost no reflections on the screen.
Ultimately, being able to switch to 1920x1200 at 440Hz is a cool feature to have, especially with a machine packing an RTX 5090, but how many people beyond competitive or dedicated FPS players will actually use it regularly?
Gaming Performance
Razer's Synapse software offers five performance profiles when plugged in: Balanced, Silent, Performance, Turbo, and Custom. We'll be using Turbo for these benchmarks.
A 24GB RTX 5090 paired with a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus is always going to be a powerhouse. It's a shame I wasn't able to get the same GPU in the Lenovo laptop, which has an RTX 5080 and 64GB of RAM instead of 32GB. All titles were tested at 2560x1600 with no upscaling or ray tracing enabled.
2560 x 1600 in Turbo Mode
| Game / Scene | Settings | Avg. FPS | Min | Max | 1 % Lows | 0.1 % Lows | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Space Marine 2 / Mission 4: Servant of the Machine | High | 113.3 | 19.8 | 160.8 | 81.6 | 54.1 | 
| Black Myth: Wukong / Yellow Wind Sage boss | Very High | 73.7 | 42.3 | 141 | 49.2 | 42.8 | 
| 007: First Light / Market | Ultra/High Lighting | 68.2 | 32.4 | 104.1 | 50 | 28.6 | 
| Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced / Havana | Very High | 80.1 | 56.8 | 115.6 | 65.3 | 59.8 | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 / Japantown driving | High settings | 115.6 | 14.6 | 184.7 | 84.3 | 72.7 | 
| Baldur's Gate 3 / Baldur's Gate | Ultra preset | 133.2 | 73.5 | 247.6 | 87.3 | 80 | 
| Assassin's Creed Shadows / Yamashiro | High preset | 75.7 | 21.2 | 139.1 | 61.3 | 54.1 | 
| The Blood of Dawnwalker / Outdoors | High preset | 69.2 | 10.6 | 159.7 | 55 | 45.3 | 
| Onimusha way of the sword demo / Daidara fight | Ultra preset | 99.9 | 75.9 | 121.8 | 85.3 | 80.2 | 
Interestingly, the more expensive and powerful RTX 5090 Blade delivers only around 10 FPS more than the RTX 5080 Legion in most games, with an average performance advantage of ~9%, illustrating the relatively small gaming performance gap between the two mobile GPUs.
We also tested gaming at the Blade's native 3840x2400 resolution to see how the RTX 5090 handled them. Without upscaling, titles like Black Myth and First Light struggle, though several other titles were still very playable.
3840 x 2400 in Turbo Mode
| Game / Scene | Settings | Avg. FPS | Min | Max | 1 % Lows | 0.1 % Lows | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Space Marine 2 / Mission 4: Servant of the Machine | High | 60 | 36.1 | 82.7 | 46.5 | 42.7 | 
| Black Myth: Wukong / Yellow Wind Sage boss | Very High | 38.2 | 14.4 | 182.6 | 27.2 | 20.4 | 
| 007: First Light / Market | Ultra/High Lighting | 42.6 | 17.3 | 90 | 35.6 | 24.8 | 
| Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced / Havana | Very High | 48.5 | 32.9 | 98.6 | 40.7 | 38.4 | 
| Cyberpunk 2077 / Japantown driving | High settings | 69.5 | 34.5 | 142.7 | 55 | 48.7 | 
| Baldur's Gate 3 / Baldur's Gate | Ultra preset | 110.5 | 45.8 | 146.3 | 83.3 | 62.7 | 
| Assassin's Creed Shadows / Yamashiro | High preset | 54.4 | 40.1 | 110.5 | 45.7 | 41.4 | 
| The Blood of Dawnwalker / Outdoors | High preset | 42.2 | 20.7 | 132.7 | 33.2 | 10.4 | 
| Onimusha way of the sword demo / Daidara fight | Ultra preset | 57.7 | 48.5 | 66.6 | 49.6 | 48.5 | 
Synthetic Benchmarks
The RTX 5090 puts the Blade ahead of the Legion in 3DMark, leading by 14% in Steel Nomad and 10% in Time Spy. But that's another modest increase given the step up in GPU tier.
| Program | Test | Result | 
|---|---|---|
| 3DMark | Steel Nomad | 6,411 | 
| 3DMark | Time Spy | 23,948 | 
| Cinebench 2026 | Single Thread | 565 | 
| Cinebench 2026 | Multi Thread | 8,555 | 
Despite sharing the same Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, the Blade trailed the Legion by around 5% in Cinebench's multi-thread test and just 1.2% in the single-thread test.
Differences in power limits and cooling could explain the gap, as the RAM difference (64GB in the Legion versus 32GB in the Blade) is unlikely to have had much impact on the Cinebench results.
Thermals and Cooling
Packing 280W of total power into an aluminum chassis this comparatively thin and light really is impressive, but it also means things can get very hot. Despite the large vapor chamber and other cooling technologies, you start to feel the heat when pushing this Blade hard.
The area around the keyboard can hit 116-117°F, while the keys themselves can reach 109°F and the touchpad 100°F in extreme cases. The hottest areas of the Legion, in comparison, reached 109-111°F, while the touchpad and palm rests remained at around 89-91°F.
Personally, I noticed the heat in demanding games but never found the Blade too uncomfortable to use. It's something to consider, though.
During a 10-minute Cinebench 2026 multi-core run in Performance mode, the Blade 18's Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus peaked at 102°C on its DTS package sensor, with CPU power draw reaching 137W.
Package temperature averaged 79°C, but HWiNFO recorded thermal throttling, and the processor frequently hit its configured power limit. Under the same test conditions, the Legion 9i peaked at just 88°C without thermal throttling, despite reaching a higher peak power draw of 174W.
Storage Performance
Opting for a PCIe 4.0 SSD instead of a PCIe 5.0 drive like the Legion's is a bit of a disappointment in a $5,400 laptop. It's a decision that applies across the 2026 Blade 18 range, although one of its two M.2 slots supports PCIe 5.0, allowing owners to upgrade to a faster drive themselves.
The CrystalDiskMark results show excellent read and very good write performance, reaching 7,032 MB/s and 5,851 MB/s, respectively.
That's around 42% lower for reads and 55% lower for writes than the SK hynix Platinum P51 PCIe 5.0 SSD in the Legion, which reached 12,217 MB/s and 12,932 MB/s. However, most people are unlikely to notice much difference between the two in everyday use.
Battery Life and Noise
It goes without saying that gaming laptops, especially 18-inch ones, aren't really designed to spend long periods away from a wall socket. The Blade 18 performs well in this department compared to its competitors, though. It beat the Legion in our YouTube playback test, lasting around seven and a half hours compared to six hours.
Another area where the Blade beats the Legion is the noise it produces under load. I recorded an average of 48 decibels in Turbo mode, much quieter than the Legion's 57.5 decibels and considerably quieter than the Medion Erazer Beast 16 X1's 61 decibels. This is one of the quietest high-end gaming laptops I've tested.
Wrap Up
For an 18-inch laptop, the Blade 18 is ridiculously slim, sleek, and quiet, with enough power to tear through games at high and maximum settings.
It also looks beautiful, is built to survive a war, has plenty of ports, hugely impressive audio, much better battery life than you'd expect, and is lighter than many rivals, making it one of the most portable 18-inch gaming laptops.
The display is sharp, colorful, and accurate, but it's still an IPS panel. For some, this could be a dealbreaker in a $5,400 laptop. And to reiterate, not everyone will care about a 440Hz refresh rate.
The Blade is also one of the hotter laptops out there, and the lack of a PCIe 5.0 SSD is disappointing at this price, as is the 32GB of RAM. Moreover, the RTX 5080 model could be the better buy, potentially offering better value for $400 less.
Ultimately, though, there's no arguing that this Blade 18 is an absolutely stunning machine, and it's hard to imagine anyone with the money to buy one would be disappointed.
Pros
- An impressive combination of power, thinness, weight, and low noise for an 18-inch laptop
- Dual-mode IPS screen is beautiful, bright, and reaches 440Hz
- Stunning looks and premium build quality
- Impressive speakers
Cons
- A price that's hard to justify
- OLED and mini-LED options would have been welcome
- Can get quite hot
- 64GB of RAM and a PCIe 5.0 SSD would be expected for over $5,000

articles.title: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
articles.text:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will adopt a new standard that publishers can use to opt out of being scraped by AI, as reported earlier by Search Engine Roundtable. With this control, publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple AI companies, instead of setting them individually.
The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping
The new control will allow publishers to apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers.
The shared “policy token” signal is proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It will live within a website’s robots.txt file, which has long signaled which web crawlers can and can’t scrape a site — whether for search indexing, archiving, or AI training. Currently, sites have to signal their AI training preferences separately to each AI company.
The announcement comes as publishers grapple with the continuing influx of AI crawlers scraping their sites and feeding their content into AI models. Some companies and organizations have attempted to combat unauthorized scraping, with the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard giving publishers the ability to charge crawlers that visit their sites, and Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default.
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing a site if they encounter the shared token. Meta communications head Andy Stone also signaled support for the new setting, but doesn’t say whether the company will honor it. “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” Stone says. “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.”
Microsoft says it will offer granular controls that will give publishers the ability to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, the process of pointing an AI model to a verified source of information to reduce hallucinations. Microsoft notes that websites will still appear in Bing’s search results regardless of their preferences. Google previously implemented similar controls that allow sites to control whether their content appears in AI search features or is used for AI training, without impacting visibility in search.
While Anthropic has already adopted the signal, Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year. OpenAI says it will implement it in the “coming months.”
Update, October 30th: Added a comment from Meta.

articles.title: Suspected North Korean hackers steal $5.6 billion in crypto in record-breaking cryptocurrency heist, Binance withdrawals frozen — firm says it will cover losses as stablecoin networks move to freeze $2.4b in stolen assets
articles.text:
Suspected North Korean hackers steal $5.6 billion in crypto in record-breaking cryptocurrency heist, Binance withdrawals frozen — firm says it will cover losses as stablecoin networks move to freeze $2.4b in stolen assets
SpookITober refuses to end.
Update, Friday 30 Oct, 6:30 am ET: This developing story has been updated with information from Binance regarding how its system was compromised, and reports from security outlets claiming North Korea may be responsible. These details have been added to the story below.
From hereon, this month shall be called SpookITober. In yet another high-profile cybersecurity incident this month, Binance.com, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has been hacked, to the tune of $5.6 billion taken in various cryptocurrencies. As of this writing, withdrawals at the exchange are suspended until the company sorts out the situation, though it has stated repeatedly that "user funds remain safe," adding that it "will cover all losses." The U.S.-specific Binance.us website is so far reportedly unaffected. At least two security agencies, including TRM, have pinned the attack on an elite North Korean hacking unit.
"Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," the company said in an update on Friday. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it. We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them."
"TRM attributes this attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s premier hacking unit," the security firm said. "We base this assessment on robust on and off-chain intelligence sources," continuing to note that the group has been named responsible for a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. Per TRM, this latest instance bears many of the same hallmarks as earlier North Korean heists. According to CNN, an unnamed analyst at Pangolin Intelligence corroborated this story by "Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]."
Preliminary info breaks down the stolen amounts like so: $1.57b in Tether dollars (USDT), $1.45b in Bitcoin (BTC), $875m in Ethereum (ETH), $823m in Circle dollars (USDC), $234m in Tron (TRX), $88.5m in Ripple dollars (RLUSD), $75M in Wrapped-Beacon Ethereum (WBETH), $50m in Tether Gold (XAUT), and $447.5 million in other cryptocurrencies. The "dollar" currencies are all stablecoins, meaning they're pegged to $1 to represent dollars in the virtual space. Meanwhile, Tether Gold is pegged to the value of one troy ounce.
The stablecoin issuers all moved to blacklist the thief's main wallet (you can see it here on the Ethereum blockchain) in their smart contracts, a move that means the amounts in USDT, USDC, and RLUSD are frozen in place, totaling around $2.4 billion. It's possible, but not guaranteed, that the gold-pegged XAUT will also be frozen.
Note that this does not mean those funds have been recovered — the thief simply cannot do anything with those tokens, be it moving or exchanging. Normally in these situations, restitution from the frozen funds happens only after complainants provide proof of ownership, something that usually means copious time spent in courts.
The situation is a lot more grim for the amounts in pure cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum, among others. Since there is no governing entity for their blockchains, the most likely prospect is that the remaining $3.2 billion or so is forever lost in the ether — though some networks incorporate clawback mechanisms. Exchanges may block the thief when he eventually tries to cash out his virtual dough, but historically this hasn't been a reliable means of recovery.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Note that this is a developing story, so the tallies are subject to change. Should that amount be final, this heist would exceed the $1.5b stolen from Bybit in February 2025, of which only a paltry portion has so far been recovered. There's little info so far on the miscreant's means of larceny. Apparently, the Binance 14 , Binance 16, and Hot Wallet 34 hot wallets, which hold pooled customer funds, were drained. It's currently not known if this happened via stolen private keys, a compromised signing process, or another type of intrusion.
Binance has assured users that their funds are safe, and most importantly, that it will cover all losses. For what it's worth, the company has a means of insurance and a reasonable track record in these situations, though the amount of bullion pilfered today is exorbitant.
The company created its SAFU reserve fund in 2018, where it deposits 10% of its trading fees to cover any losses incurred from security issues. That fund currently sits at 15,000 BTC in it (verifiable here), or about $1.17b at the current BTC-USD price of $77,858. SAFU is a cold wallet, meaning its private keys are stored offline.
Back in May 2019, thieves made out with 7,000 BTC from Binance, amounting to around $40 million at the time. The company covered the entirety of the losses with SAFU funds.
However, while $1.17b is certainly a tidy sum, 'tis but a morsel of what currently looks like a multi-billion loss. Binance co-founder, shareholder, and former CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ) stated in a tweet that he too expects that users will be made whole.
As a final note, Binance is alerting everyone to be on the lookout for contact attempts impersonating the company and/or referencing the current situation. Expect a flood of emails, SMS, and phone scams in the coming months. Be especially wary of any "compensation" or "withdrawal restoration" offers, and never click any e-mail links or otherwise offer any account information — always use the official website or applications yourself directly.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: 70 000 dollars perdus par moto électrique vendue : LiveWire se donne un an de survie
articles.text:
Bientôt la fin des motos électriques LiveWire ? Dans ses résultats financiers du troisième trimestre publiés ce jeudi 29 octobre, la filiale électrique de Harley-Davidson dit douter de pouvoir poursuivre son activité au cours des douze prochains mois. Cette mention comptable, appelée « going concern » aux États-Unis, signifie que la direction n’est pas sûre de pouvoir financer l’entreprise d’ici un an. Dans la matinée, l’action du constructeur a perdu plus de 40 %, a relevé Electrek.
Pourtant, les ventes progressent : 241 motos électriques entre juillet et septembre 2026, contre 184 un an plus tôt. Sauf que la branche moto a perdu 17 millions de dollars d’exploitation sur la même période, soit environ 70 000 dollars (équivalent à 62 500 €) par moto vendue. Sa trésorerie est tombée de 82,8 millions de dollars fin 2025 à 39,9 millions au 30 septembre, et une dette arrive à échéance en décembre 2027.
Pour mémoire, Harley-Davidson avait sorti sa première moto électrique en 2019, avant de faire de LiveWire une marque à part entière en 2021. Depuis, la gamme s’est étoffée avec les modèles S2 Alpinista, Del Mar Mulholland et dernièrement avec les petites motos S4 Honcho. Aux États-Unis, LiveWire revendique 80 % des parts de marché sur les motos électriques de plus de 50 kW (67 ch) depuis janvier.
Un spécialiste des entreprises en crise aux commandes
Le 22 octobre, le conseil d’administration de LiveWire a créé un comité spécial de restructuration, chargé d’examiner toutes les pistes : levée de fonds, partenariat, vente ou restructuration. Ce comité a nommé Roy Gallagher directeur de la restructuration, ce qui fait de lui le principal dirigeant de l’entreprise.
Selon Auto Infos, il vient du cabinet Ankura Consulting Group, spécialisé dans la gestion de crise, et arrive après la démission du directeur général de LiveWire, Karim Donnez. LiveWire a aussi retiré sa prévision de perte d’exploitation pour 2026, qui tablait sur 70 à 80 millions de dollars. Elle prévient elle-même que rien ne garantit le succès de ces démarches.
Quel avenir pour LiveWire ?
Harley-Davidson, actionnaire majoritaire, doit maintenant trancher. Le groupe de Milwaukee mène déjà sa propre transformation sous la direction de son président, Artie Starrs, et Auto Infos juge que s’il garde un pied dans l’électrique, ce ne sera pas à n’importe quel prix.
Le taïwanais Kymco, qui fabrique les nouvelles S4 Honcho de LiveWire, ferait un partenaire logique. Pourtant, sa nouvelle direction a redonné la priorité aux moteurs thermiques, ce qui rend une entrée au capital peu probable. Si aucun investisseur ne se présente, Harley-Davidson a deux solutions : remettre encore de l’argent dans la machine pour tenter de la relancer ou abandonner l’électrique avec LiveWire.
En attendant, la marque peut espérer compter sur les S4 Honcho, vendues entre 5 500 € et 6 000 € en France, loin des modèles haut de gamme vendus jusqu’ici. LiveWire a aussi racheté Dust Motorcycles, spécialiste de la moto tout-terrain électrique. Un créneau en plein essor où la marque Stark Future arrive à faire son trou et dans lequel LiveWire pourrait bien tirer son épingle du jeu.
