articles.title: Deadly Intel Fab 28 explosion causes two-week shutdown, to cost $600 million and severely disrupt server chip manufacturing for six months — 10nm Xeon shipments stall during largest shortage in memory
articles.text:
Deadly Intel Fab 28 explosion causes two-week shutdown, to cost $600 million and severely disrupt server chip manufacturing for six months — 10nm Xeon shipments stall during largest shortage in memory
The most devastating semiconductor fab disruption in recent history.
The explosion at Intel's Fab 28 near Kiryat Gat, Israel, that happened earlier this month forced Intel to shut down the whole facility for two weeks, and now the company expects that it will cost it approximately $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters. The disruption is expected to affect server processors manufactured using Intel's 10nm-class process technologies and will reduce the company's shipments in both the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027.
"In Israel, we have been shut down for about two weeks," said Dave Zinsner, chief financial officer of Intel, during the company's earnings call. "We feel like we are going to be starting up production here by the end of this week."
The explosion occurred in mid-October, killed two, seriously injured one, and caused an extended shutdown of Fab 28, one of Intel's key manufacturing facilities for chips produced using its 10nm-class and Intel 7 process technologies (Intel 7 was formerly called 10nm Enhanced SuperFin). Intel expects the incident to reduce its Q4 2026 revenue by approximately $300 million, and a similar impact is anticipated in Q1 2027. The company also expects the accident to reduce its fourth-quarter non-GAAP gross margin by approximately 2%.
Intel has not identified the affected Xeon processor families, disclosed the number of wafers damaged, or specified when Fab 28 will return to full production capacity after it restarts this Friday.
Although Intel's latest Xeon 6 processors use compute dies produced on Intel 3 fabrication technology, they still use I/O dies fabricated on Intel 7 (aka 10nm ESF) fabrication process. Furthermore, Intel continues to sell previous-generation Xeon 5 Emerald Rapids (and even Xeon 4 'Sapphire Rapids', though it stopped accepting orders on these CPUs in late September) that are made on Intel 7 manufacturing technology.
While Intel has plenty of 10nm-capable fabs — including Fab 12, Fab 22, Fab 32, Fab 42 in Arizona as well as Fab 28 in Israel — the disruption comes as Intel struggles to satisfy strong demand for server processors, so Intel cannot completely offset the lack of output at one facility by adjusting manufacturing at the others (i.e., it has done everything it could by now). For sure, Intel will not repurpose product lines it uses to make I/O dies for Xeon 6 to make previous-generation CPUs. In addition, other fabs may lack product-specific manufacturing qualifications, or the time and costs required to transfer production between facilities are too high, keeping in mind that Fab 28 is about to restart.
In addition to lost production time, Intel faces potential losses from wafers that were undergoing fabrication when the accident occurred. The company is assessing work-in-progress inventory to determine which wafers can be recovered and which must be discarded and written off. Zinsner expects most wafer write-offs to occur in Q4 2026, which explains why the gross-margin impact will be concentrated in that quarter despite the disruption to shipments extending into early 2027.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
"Please note almost all of the $300 impact from Fab 28 is related to 10nm server products," Zinsner said.
Although Intel stresses that the shutdown primarily affects its 10nm-class server processors, the company has not disclosed whether the incident will also disrupt shipments of client processors manufactured using its Intel 7 (10nm ESF) process technology. Intel uses this node to manufacture a wide range of client CPUs, including its 12th, 13th, and 14th Generation Core processors, such as Raptor Lake. However, it is unclear whether Fab 28 manufactures any of these products and, if so, whether Intel can compensate for the loss of production by increasing output at its other Intel 7-capable facilities. Consequently, the shutdown could potentially affect the availability of some consumer processors as well.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Una pareja con cuatro hijos construye una casa de 232 m² en el desierto: usaron más de 360 toneladas de tierra
articles.text:
Después de pasar cinco años recorriendo Estados Unidos en caravana, Jonathan y Ashley Longnecker decidieron instalarse en el desierto de Arizona con sus cuatro hijos y levantar allí su propia casa utilizando sobre todo tierra. La vivienda tendrá 232 metros cuadrados y, en una de las fases de la obra, ya se habían empleado en ella más de 360 toneladas de tierra. Además, también tienen la ambiciosa la idea de que funcione sin las conexiones tradicionales de agua y electricidad.
De la caravana al desierto. Según explica la propia familia en la web de su proyecto, llamado Tiny Shiny Home, fueron esos años de viajes a tiempo completo los que los llevaron a buscar algo diferente, y acabaron comprando un terreno sin urbanizar de unas 4,45 hectáreas. Ese terreno está en el condado de Cochise, en el sureste de Arizona. Allí están construyendo la Hyperadobe Roundhouse, una casa formada por círculos cuyo avance van están documentando paso a paso con fotos y muchos vídeos.
Tierra metida en mallas. La técnica que da nombre a la casa es el hyperadobe, que consiste en rellenar largos tubos de malla con tierra húmeda y apisonarla capa a capa hasta formar muros resistentes, según detalla la guía que han publicado los Longnecker. Vamos, que el ladrillo se sustituye por tierra apisonada, a ser posible la del propio terreno.
Con este método los muros alcanzan unos 40 centímetros de grosor, según recoge El Imparcial en su reportaje sobre la casa. Y cuando completaron la vigésima hilada de sacos, la familia contabilizaba 400 toneladas estadounidenses de tierra, que equivalen a unas 363 toneladas métricas.
Cuatro círculos unidos. La vivienda está formada por cuatro círculos de diferentes tamaños conectados mediante muros rectos, siempre según el mismo diario mexicano. ¿Y por qué tanta curva? Pues porque, como explican los Longnecker en esa misma guía, los muros circulares son de por sí más resistentes que los rectos, ya que la propia forma estabiliza la pared frente a la gravedad.
Y antes de meterse con la casa practicaron con construcciones más pequeñas, como una oficina y un gallinero, para ir haciéndose con el método, algo que cuentan tanto en su guía como en el reportaje de faircompanies.
Agua de lluvia y sol. El proyecto contempla recoger el agua de lluvia a través del tejado y llevarla hasta un depósito con capacidad para unos 114.000 litros, desde donde una bomba la filtrará y la distribuirá por la casa, de nuevo según El Imparcial. Y la electricidad tampoco llegará de la red, porque está prevista la instalación de paneles solares y baterías para generarla y almacenarla.
A principios de octubre de 2026 la obra seguía avanzando, como muestra el diario de construcción del tejado que publica la familia, y su objetivo es demostrar que se puede levantar una vivienda con materiales del entorno y sin depender de los servicios convencionales.

articles.title: Una operación de espionaje de China tiene como objetivos a Jensen Huang y Nvidia, según The New York Times
articles.text:
La disputa por la supremacía mundial que están librando EEUU y China se sostiene ante todo sobre la inteligencia artificial (IA). En la base de este conflicto residen los chips que se utilizan para entrenar los modelos de lenguaje y ejecutar la inferencia, así como los recursos necesarios para producir estos semiconductores, como algunos minerales críticos. Y sobre la IA sobrevuelan las capacidades estratégicas de estos países que ya se están viendo beneficiadas por esta tecnología, como su desarrollo científico, técnico, económico o militar.
Las decisiones que han tomado los Gobiernos de Washington y Pekín durante los últimos cuatro años ponen encima de la mesa una realidad inapelable: ninguno de ellos está dispuesto a dar un solo paso atrás. A ceder lo más mínimo si ello implica una merma de su capacidad de ejercer presión. Ambos están usando las sanciones para protegerse y debilitar al rival, pero hay otro recurso que con frecuencia pasa inadvertido, y que, sin embargo, puede tener un papel decisivo en la evolución de este conflicto: el espionaje.
The New York Times ha destapado una presunta operación de espionaje diseñada por el Gobierno chino y articulada alrededor de Jensen Huang, el director general de Nvidia. Los servicios de inteligencia estadounidenses llevan al menos dos años siguiendo de cerca a Alice Huang, una ejecutiva de la empresa singapurense Megaspeed, y han llegado a una conclusión: trabaja para los servicios de inteligencia chinos. Huang Le, como también se la conoce, habría pasado inadvertida de no estar vinculada a uno de los pesos pesados de la industria de la IA: Jensen Huang, el director general de Nvidia.
Nvidia lo niega todo
La trama que describe The New York Times podría haber sido extraída del guion de una película de Hollywood, pero es muy real. El 26 de agosto de 2022 el Gobierno de EEUU comunicó a Nvidia que necesitaba una licencia especial para exportar a China dos de sus aceleradores para IA más avanzados: los chips A100 y H100. En la práctica esta medida intentaba evitar sobre todo que las organizaciones chinas que tienen algún vínculo con el ejército chino se hiciesen con estas GPU, y transformó a Nvidia en un arma arrojadiza que ha colocado a Jensen Huang en el punto de mira tanto de la Administración de EEUU como de la de China.
Las autoridades de EEUU sospechan que Megaspeed ha ayudado a las organizaciones chinas a conseguir los chips de Nvidia más avanzados
El líder de Nvidia se ha pronunciado públicamente en muchas ocasiones en contra de las restricciones a la exportación aprobadas por el Gobierno de EEUU. Ha advertido a los Gobiernos de Joe Biden primero, y Donald Trump después, de que esta estrategia impulsaría el desarrollo de la industria china de los semiconductores. No obstante, su disconformidad ha tenido otro efecto: ha alimentado las sospechas del Departamento de Comercio de EEUU, que es el responsable de velar por el cumplimiento de las restricciones de exportación. Y, de propina, lo ha colocado en el punto de mira de los servicios de inteligencia.
Entonces, ¿qué pinta Alice Huang en esta trama? La historia es rocambolesca. Su empresa, Megaspeed, opera centros de datos en el sudeste asiático y alquila capacidad de computación a varias empresas chinas, entre las que se encuentra Alibaba. Y las autoridades de EEUU sospechan que ha ayudado a las organizaciones chinas que no pueden conseguir los chips para IA de Nvidia más avanzados a obtenerlos. Pero hay algo más. También creen que Alice Huang y Jensen Huang mantienen desde hace al menos dos años una relación profesional y social muy estrecha.
The New York Times confirma que fueron fotografiados juntos en un bar de Taipéi (Taiwán), en junio de 2024, durante una reunión en la que también participaron otros ejecutivos del sector tecnológico. Todos ellos estaban bebiendo alcohol. En mayo de 2025, de nuevo en Taipéi, volvieron a coincidir en una cena de negocios con más proveedores de la industria, y fueron fotografiados saliendo juntos del restaurante. El relato del Times no afirma que Jensen Huang y Alice Huang tengan, o hayan tenido en el pasado, una relación sentimental, pero lo insinúa de una forma velada.
Nvidia ya se ha pronunciado oficialmente. Y lo niega todo. Asegura que la relación que tienen los dos Huang es estrictamente comercial. También sostiene que sus clientes reciben información ordinaria acerca de su negocio, pero en ningún caso secretos comerciales sensibles ni otros datos relevantes para la seguridad nacional de EEUU. La otra protagonista, Megaspeed, ha abierto una investigación interna y se ha mostrado dispuesta a colaborar con el Gobierno de EEUU.

articles.title: « Mentalité de loser » : le patron de Proton, Andy Yen, se défend sur Reddit, sans rien démentir — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le CEO et cofondateur de Proton, Andy Yen, a choisi Reddit pour répondre au média américain 404 Media. Dans un commentaire publié sur le forum r/ProtonMail, sous un fil consacré à l’enquête parue ce jeudi 29 octobre, il assure que sa citation a été « sortie de son contexte ».
Pourtant, il ne nie pas avoir écrit « conneries » et « mentalité de loser » à un salarié qui demandait quelques jours de test d’intrusion avant une mise en production, comme nous l’expliquions lorsque nous avons relayé l’enquête américaine. Sur le fond, il assume : chez Proton, qui revendique plus de 100 millions de comptes, quelques jours de relecture humaine en plus avant une mise en ligne ne sont plus jugés utiles. Il assure pourtant que l’entreprise garde « toujours » une relecture humaine.
Andy Yen affirme que Proton fait aujourd’hui « bien plus de revue de sécurité » qu’à n’importe quel moment de son histoire. Il ajoute que toute l’industrie voit sortir des bugs critiques « presque tous les jours », et cite « le récent bug PHP ». C’est une référence à PHP2Shell, deux failles corrigées le 21 octobre qui permettaient de prendre la main sur un serveur web à distance.
Pour Andy Yen, « plusieurs jours supplémentaires de relecture humaine » ne sont donc pas la bonne réponse. Selon lui, la relecture humaine, désormais « augmentée par l’IA », est devenue « exceptionnellement bonne » pour repérer des failles.
Des IA « non alignées », sans plus de détails
Andy Yen révèle aussi que Proton utilise « depuis un certain temps » des « modèles non alignés avec des compétences personnalisées » pour passer son code au crible. Dans le jargon de l’IA, l’alignement désigne l’entraînement qui pousse un modèle à respecter des règles, par exemple refuser d’écrire un programme d’attaque. Un modèle non aligné n’a plus ces freins, ce qui lui permet de s’attaquer à un code comme le ferait un pirate. Les « compétences personnalisées » font sans doute référence aux skills, ces instructions qu’on ajoute à un agent IA pour lui confier une tâche précise.
Andy Yen ne précise pourtant pas de quels modèles il s’agit, ni où ils tournent : sur les serveurs de Proton ou chez un prestataire. Pour une entreprise qui vend de la confidentialité, la question compte, d’autant que le code de Proton est déjà écrit en bonne partie avec Claude, l’IA américaine d’Anthropic. Il juge aussi l’approche « meilleure, et aussi plus rapide ». Or l’enquête de 404 Media rapporte qu’un ingénieur avait prévenu, dans la même conversation Slack, que l’IA ne réglerait rien « parce que la sécurité est basse dans nos priorités actuellement ».
Rien sur les embauches ni sur les finances
Andy Yen ne revient pas, en revanche, sur son message Slack qui faisait de 2026 la dernière année où Proton embauche des ingénieurs. Il ne dit rien non plus du document interne selon lequel Proton va rater son objectif de revenu annuel récurrent, faute de « vélocité suffisante », et reste « une entreprise qui sous-performe ». Pour 404 Media, c’est justement cet objectif de revenus qui pousse Proton à foncer sur l’IA.
Proton avait déjà réagi sur Reddit en début de semaine, après un premier article de 404 Media sur les entretiens de ses salariés sur l’usage de l’IA.
L’entreprise y affirmait ne pas faire « de licenciements en prenant l’IA comme excuse » et disait recruter dans toutes ses équipes. Ces entretiens sur l’usage de l’IA, que les salariés interrogés par 404 Media voient comme une menace sur leur poste, auront lieu du 4 au 11 novembre.

articles.title: Intel perd près d’un quart de sa valeur en Bourse, plombé par le ralentissement des PC
articles.text:
Des ordinateurs plus chers, des ventes qui ralentissent et une pénurie de mémoire qui s’installe : le marché du PC traverse une mauvaise passe. Intel prévient que les difficultés pourraient se prolonger en 2027.
Le processeur ne fait pas tout. Pour vendre un ordinateur, il faut aussi pouvoir l’équiper en mémoire à un prix acceptable. C’est précisément là que le marché se grippe : les composants deviennent plus chers, les machines aussi, et les acheteurs se montrent moins pressés de renouveler leur équipement. Cette situation frappe directement Intel. Après la publication de ses résultats, jeudi 29 octobre, son action a plongé de plus de 20 % dans les échanges suivant la clôture de la Bourse américaine. Les investisseurs s’inquiètent surtout des prochains mois, alors que le fabricant prévoit un ralentissement durable du marché du PC.
Des PC plus chers qui se vendent moins bien
Selon Lip-Bu Tan, le patron d’Intel, le ralentissement s’est accentué au cours des deux derniers mois. Face à des ventes moins dynamiques, les constructeurs cherchent à écouler les ordinateurs qu’ils ont déjà en stock et réduisent leurs commandes. Pour Intel, la conséquence est immédiate : moins de machines à assembler signifie aussi moins de processeurs à vendre. Le groupe anticipe un recul du marché du PC d’environ 12 % en 2026, puis de 10 % supplémentaires en 2027.
Le contraste est d’autant plus marqué que ses derniers résultats sont en progression. Intel a réalisé 16,5 milliards de dollars de chiffre d’affaires au troisième trimestre, soit 21 % de plus qu’un an auparavant. Mais cette croissance masque deux situations très différentes : son activité liée aux PC recule, tandis que celle des centres de données et de l’IA progresse fortement.
La pénurie de mémoire dépasse le seul cas d’Intel
Le problème ne vient donc pas uniquement des processeurs. La mémoire est indispensable au fonctionnement d’un ordinateur, et son prix entre directement dans le coût de fabrication d’une machine. Lorsqu’elle devient plus rare et plus chère, toute la chaîne en ressent les effets.
Pour l’acheteur, cela se traduit par des tarifs moins attractifs. Pour les fabricants de PC, il devient plus difficile de proposer des machines abordables tout en préservant leurs marges. Et pour Intel, la baisse des commandes finit par se répercuter sur les ventes de puces. Le fabricant ne prévoit pas de retour rapide à la normale : il s’attend à ce que le ralentissement du PC dure au moins jusqu’au premier semestre 2027.
Intel mise davantage sur les serveurs, avec une autre difficulté à résoudre
À l’inverse, les processeurs destinés aux serveurs suscitent une forte demande. Ces machines font fonctionner les services en ligne et une partie des applications d’intelligence artificielle. Leur rôle prend notamment de l’importance avec les assistants capables d’enchaîner plusieurs tâches, qui mobilisent différentes ressources informatiques. Intel réoriente donc une partie de sa production de puces pour PC vers les centres de données. Mais le groupe rencontre ici le problème opposé : il ne parvient pas à fabriquer suffisamment de processeurs pour satisfaire tous ses clients.
La situation est délicate pour le fabricant : les commandes ralentissent sur son marché historique, tandis que ses capacités de production limitent sa progression sur celui qui accélère. Pour les acheteurs de PC, le point à surveiller reste surtout l’évolution du prix de la mémoire. Tant que cette tension persiste, elle continue de peser sur le prix des machines et sur leur renouvellement.

articles.title: Cartes Pokémon 30 ans : Amazon ouvre les invitations pour les grands coffrets Ultra-Premium Mentali et Noctali
Run AI Models for Edge Application Development with Just a Few Commands | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
AI is expanding beyond the data center as developers build a new generation of agents to act at the edge: monitoring driver attention and cabin conditions, helping robots understand their surroundings and plan tasks, and coordinating fleets of machines on production lines. These physical AI applications rely on models that perceive, reason, and act within tight memory, power, and latency budgets. But getting a model ready to run can involve substantial setup.
NVIDIA DGX Spark, now available in a 64GB configuration, gives embedded developers a platform to prototype, fine-tune, and test models and agents. NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM provides a lightweight C++ inference runtime designed for embedded workloads, bringing the same inference framework to development on Spark and deployment on platforms such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor, NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor, and NVIDIA IGX Thor.
You can get started in just a few commands with the trtedge command-line interface (CLI). It downloads your selected model and builds TensorRT engines optimized for inference on Spark.
In this tutorial, you’ll run NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning, a text-only model, on Spark using TensorRT Edge-LLM. You’ll test prompts in your terminal and serve the model through an API for application prototyping. You’ll also enable DSpark speculative decoding to accelerate generation.
Prerequisites: Set up your development environment
To get started, you’ll need a DGX Spark with a supported NVIDIA software stack, NVIDIA CUDA 13, TensorRT 10.16.1.11 or newer within the 10.x series, and Python 3.10 to 3.12. The examples below were tested with TensorRT Edge-LLM 0.11.1 and TensorRT 10.16.1.11.
Open a terminal on your DGX Spark, create and activate a virtual environment, and install TensorRT Edge-LLM:
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv-edgellm
source .venv-edgellm/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install "tensorrt-edgellm[server]==0.11.1"
Note: The virtual environment keeps newly installed packages separate while allowing access to all system Python packages, including TensorRT.
Check the TensorRT version and confirm that the TensorRT Edge-LLM runtime loads:
python -c "import tensorrt as trt; v = tuple(map(int, trt.__version__.split('.'))); assert (10, 16, 1, 11) <= v < (11,), f'TensorRT >=10.16.1.11 and <11 required; found {trt.__version__}'; from tensorrt_edgellm import runtime; runtime.load()"
Note: If compatible system TensorRT bindings are unavailable, follow the NVIDIA TensorRT pip installation instructions to install a compatible TensorRT 10.x version in the activated environment, then rerun the verification command.
With the virtual environment still active, start a chat with Nemotron-3.5 Lightning:
trtedge chat nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4
On your first launch, wait for the model download (approximately 21GB) and engine build to finish. Files are stored in ~/.cache/tensorrt-edgellm by default, so allow space for both the model and engines. Later launches reuse matching cached engines.
Once the chat prompt appears, enter:
Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence.
Example response:
25°C is equal to 77°F.
Continue the conversation with follow-up questions, or type /exit to end the session.
Serve your model
Serve your model through a local OpenAI-compatible API on Spark for application development and testing.
With your virtual environment active, start the server:
trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000
The server builds or reuses an engine for this configuration. Once startup completes, open a second terminal on your DGX Spark and check that it is ready:
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8000/health/ready 
A response containing "status":"ready" confirms that the server is ready. Send your first prompt to the chat completions endpoint:
curl -fsS -N http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
  "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Convert 25°C to Fahrenheit. Answer in one sentence."
    }
  ],
  "stream": true,
  "temperature": 0,
  "max_tokens": 128
}'
The response streams as JSON events. Keep the server running for more requests, or press Ctrl+C in the server terminal to stop it.
Optional: Enable speculative decoding
You can speed up generation with DSpark speculative decoding, which uses a draft model to propose several tokens for the main model to verify in a single pass. To enable it with three draft tokens, press Ctrl+C in the server terminal, then restart the server with DSpark enabled:
trtedge serve nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000 \
  --speculative-config '{
    "method": "dspark",   
    "model": "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-NVFP4-DSpark",
    "num_speculative_tokens": 3
  }'
Once the server is ready, send another prompt to the chat completions endpoint to try DSpark-enabled generation.
You can experiment with num_speculative_tokens and other settings to tune generation speed for your workload. See the speculative decoding documentation to learn more.
Performance on DGX Spark 64GB
TensorRT Edge-LLM delivers low response latency and fast token generation with NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5 Lightning on DGX Spark 64GB.
The table below reports time to first token (TTFT) and generation speed with and without DSpark speculative decoding.
| Decoding | Workload | Median TTFT (ms) | Mean generation speed (tokens/s) | 
| DSpark OFF | SpeedBench 1K | 201.0 | 73.3 | 
| DSpark OFF | SpeedBench 2K | 329.5 | 72.8 | 
| DSpark OFF | HumanEval prompts | 98.1 | 73.4 | 
| DSpark ON | SpeedBench 1K | 203.0 | 108.5 | 
| DSpark ON | SpeedBench 2K | 331.6 | 105.3 | 
| DSpark ON | HumanEval prompts | 98.7 | 126.9 | 
Generation speed is the average token generation rate per request, excluding time to first token. DSpark uses three draft tokens. Peak total system memory use during inference with DSpark was 27.9GB, including the OS.
Measured on DGX Spark 64GB running DGX OS 7.6.0 (Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS), using NVFP4 with thinking enabled, batch size one, one concurrent streaming request, and a 128-token output limit. Average input lengths were 1,153 tokens for SpeedBench 1K, 2,247 for SpeedBench 2K, and 139 for HumanEval.
Next steps
Try another model from the supported models list and continue developing your application on Spark. Options include vision-language models that interpret images and video, as well as speech recognition and text-to-speech models.
Explore the TensorRT Edge-LLM documentation for model-specific workflows and requirements on your target embedded platform.
And visit the Nemotron developer page for resources to get started. Explore open Nemotron models and datasets on Hugging Face and Blueprints on build.nvidia.com.

articles.title: Binance estimates $6.3B impact from security breach, freezes $3B in crypto assets
articles.text:
Binance estimates $6.3B impact from security breach, freezes $3B in crypto assets
Binance said a preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop as the possible entry point for the breach. The exchange has suspended deposits and withdrawals and pledged to cover customer losses.
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has estimated the total impact of a major security incident at around $6.3 billion, with approximately $3 billion worth of affected digital assets frozen on-chain in coordination with blockchain partners.
In an update issued on October 30, 2026, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume said its preliminary investigation suggested that the incident may have originated from a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer. The attacker allegedly used the access to enter a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.
However, a subsequent investigation uncovered additional points of breach, indicating that the attack was more complex than initially suspected.
"This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it. We are still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them," the company said in a statement.
Binance CEO Richard Teng, in a separate communication to users, clarified that the attacker had not simply exploited an engineer's permissions and that the incident was not a single "one-click" action. He added that the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual.
The exchange said it had found no evidence of any compromise involving wallet private keys. Binance has estimated the total impact at approximately $6.3 billion, of which around $3 billion worth of assets have been frozen on-chain so far in coordination with blockchain partners.
Binance has temporarily suspended withdrawals while undertaking a security revamp of its withdrawal service and related addresses. It has also revoked authorisation for the affected address and engaged law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover the funds.
The exchange said deposits remain unaffected and continue to operate normally. It added that outflows had ceased after it paused withdrawals. Binance expects to resume withdrawal services within 45 hours as it completes the security checks and remediation process.
Assuring customers that their assets remain safe, Binance said it would cover all losses arising from the incident through its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company's own funds.
"We'll share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified," Teng said, adding that the exchange would also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation process was complete.
Binance said its teams were working closely with law enforcement agencies and blockchain intelligence partners to identify those responsible and recover the affected assets. The company has urged users to rely exclusively on its official communication channels for further updates as the investigation progresses.

articles.text:
Good morning, and cheers to an unforgettable Moonshot! ☀️
Moonshot 2026 is over, and what an eventful, blockbuster two days it has been. Thousands of founders, investors, operators, policymakers, and builders packed the National Theatre in Lagos, Nigeria, for conversations that stretched from AI and fintech to capital markets, commerce, cybersecurity, and the future of African technology. Packed stages, hurried hallway conversations, familiar faces, new connections, and ideas kept us talking long after the lights went out. If you were there, thank you for being part of it. If you missed it, we’ve got plenty of stories, interviews, and takeaways coming your way.
Thank you, Lagos!
—Emmanuel

Moonshot
Acecore wins $10,000 at Moonshot 2026’s TC Battlefield
If you thought African startups were running out of problems to solve, you only needed to spend some time at Moonshot 2026’s Startup stage in Lagos to reconsider.
Fertitude, a healthtech startup, pitched its digital platform that combines reproductive health tracking, AI-powered guidance, and access to healthcare specialists. Lena, an edtech startup, showed how it uses AI-powered games to help children learn subjects such as mathematics and science. Qiqi Farms pitched its technology-driven food distribution business, which connects farmers to markets and uses cold-chain infrastructure to deliver fresh produce.
These startups, alongside seven others, made the final ten of TC Battlefield 2026, TechCabal’s annual startup pitching competition, sponsored this year by Yango Group, the Dubai-based technology company. The competition allowed founders to pitch their businesses to investors and compete for $17,500 in equity-free funding.
After the pitches, Acecore won, taking home the $10,000 grand prize. The Nigerian climate-tech startup is building locally manufactured, AI-powered solar battery systems through its Powercell product. Paired with its Powercore app, the system allows users to monitor energy performance and manage their power supply, offering an alternative to unreliable electricity.
Supplya, a Nigerian startup that helps small retailers source inventory from manufacturers and access interest-free buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) financing, was first runner-up, winning $5,000. Navidyn Limited finished third, taking home $2,500.
TC Battlefield is an annual startup pitching competition, held as part of the Moonshot conference. It gives early-stage African startups a platform to showcase their products and compete for equity-free funding and other growth opportunities. The competition has become a recurring feature of Moonshot, with Ulé Homes, a Nigerian proptech startup that helps people finance rent payments, winning last year’s edition.
Founders who missed out this year have an opportunity for redemption. TC Battlefield will return at next year’s Moonshot.

Moonshot
Moonshot Day 2 recap from Muktar’s POV
It’s a wrap. Moonshot 2026, the biggest gathering in African tech, ended after two packed days at the National Theatre. You got it all. Uber drivers asked passengers if they were heading to “that event.” People were getting confused about the venue on Day 1. Over 7,500 people came through the doors, two large exhibition halls ran out of space, and the tweets did not stop coming.
If you weren’t there, you probably felt like you were missing out. I was there, and I can confirm you were.
This was our fourth Moonshot, and each one has been bigger and louder than the last—and this year raised the bar again.
I ran into my friend Kwadwo, who flew in from Ghana, only twice all day. Both times, he told me he had never expected anything like this from us. That means something coming from him: Kwadwo works at the Bank of Ghana, which runs its own big tech event next door.
Some of the biggest crowds came for Fu’ad Lawal and Sir Demola Aladekomo; Salem King and Chude Jideonwo; and Jessica Hope, Nana Aisha and Victor Fatanmi. Their sessions filled the conference rooms, with many people standing.
Away from the stage, in the National Theatre’s corridors, Moonshot did what it does best. Old friends found each other again, founders and investors swapped numbers and closed deals, and startups walked away with $20,000 at TC Battlefield.
Next year, Moonshot returns for three days, and you can safely guess it will be bigger. If, like me, you couldn’t be in two places at once and missed a few sessions, catch up on the best of them on our website.
More value with Mycoverai
You already have a great product. With MyCover.ai, create tailored insurance for your customers across fintech, e-commerce, logistics and more, built around your product, and their needs. Get started here.
Telecoms
Herotel must open its fibre network to rivals
Herotel built its fibre business like a private road. If you wanted to use the road, you also had to buy Internet from Herotel. South Africa’s competition regulator is now making it open the gates to rivals.
What happened? Herotel, South Africa’s third-largest fibre network operator, will begin selling wholesale access to its network to other Internet service providers (ISPs). The change was imposed as a condition of Vumatel’s takeover, completed in June. Vumatel now indirectly owns 99.9% of Herotel.
Third-party ISPs must also receive the same pricing, service quality, and delivery terms offered to companies inside Vumatel’s parent group.
Explain like I’m new here: Herotel started by connecting smaller towns and underserved communities using fixed wireless Internet, before expanding aggressively into fibre in 2019. Unlike most large South African fibre operators, it kept the entire customer relationship to itself. Herotel built and owned the fibre, then sold Internet directly over it.
Vumatel works differently. It builds fibre networks and lets dozens of ISPs compete to sell internet over those lines.
Between the lines: Open access changes Herotel’s economics. It no longer gets every retail customer connected to its infrastructure, because another ISP can now win that customer. But every rival that sells a package over Herotel fibre also becomes a wholesale customer.
That trade-off becomes more important as Herotel expands. It wants to reach another 800,000 homes, taking its footprint beyond 1.4 million, largely in places bigger fibre operators have historically overlooked.
Why it matters: Fibre is expensive to build and cheap to leave idle. Opening Herotel’s network gives more ISPs an incentive to sell connections over existing infrastructure, potentially increasing how many homes actually take up fibre.
Herotel is losing exclusivity over its roads. The bet is that more traffic can make up for it.
Capital markets
Banque du Caire’s IPO is 27x oversubscribed
For weeks, we’ve been talking about Banque du Caire’s imminent initial public offering (IPO), and the listing is now gaining momentum. Apparently, Egypt’s sixth-largest bank is popular with retail investors. The lender hasn’t gone public yet, but investors are asking for more shares than it has to give—a lot more.
What happened? Retail investors ordered about 9.29 billion shares in the Egyptian state-owned bank, even though only 343.1 million shares were available to them. That made the retail portion of the IPO about 27 times oversubscribed.
At the final price of EGP 5.30 ($0.10) per share, roughly EGP 49.2 billion ($921 million) was chasing just EGP 1.8 billion ($34 million) worth of stock. Investors will receive about 3.7% of the shares they requested.
Explain like I’m new here: The IPO was due to “execute” on October 29, while normal trading begins on November 2. Those are two different things.
Execution does not mean investors are already trading Banque du Caire shares with one another. It is the step where the IPO orders are finalised, shares are allocated to successful investors, and Banque Misr, Banque du Caire’s owner, completes the sale. Once those shares sit in investors’ accounts, regular trading can begin on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX).
Think of it as buying a concert ticket before the doors open. You already own your ticket, but the event has not started.
Between the lines: Retail demand looks huge, but oversubscription only tells us investors wanted the shares at EGP 5.30 ($0.095). The bigger test begins when trading opens, and buyers and sellers can set the market price.
Retail investors also have some protection. During the first 30 days of trading, they can submit shares for sale at the IPO price under a stabilisation arrangement.
If Banque du Caire trades comfortably above EGP 5.30 ($0.095), Egypt will have something more useful than a heavily oversubscribed IPO: evidence that demand survived the jump from the order book to the open market.

articles.title: Piratage de Binance : plus de 6 milliards de dollars de cryptos ont été volés, que s’est-il passé ?
articles.text:
Dans la soirée du jeudi 29 octobre, des pirates ont siphonné les portefeuilles de Binance, la plus grande plateforme d’échange de cryptomonnaies au monde, sur la blockchain. Binance estime le préjudice à 6,3 milliards de dollars, soit près de 5,5 milliards d’euros. C’est quatre fois plus que le précédent hack record, à savoir le vol de 1,5 milliard de dollars chez Bybit en février 2025.
« Un potentiel problème de sécurité »
D’après les investigations de la société d’analyse TRM Labs, les pirates sont passés à l’action vers 21 heures, heure de Paris. Les cybercriminels ont vidé les portefeuilles de Binance connectés à Internet. En une vingtaine de minutes, tous les fonds ont été transférés vers des adresses crypto contrôlées par les pirates. Dans un premier temps, Binance s’est montré prudent en indiquant avoir « connaissance de signalements concernant un potentiel problème de sécurité ». L’exchange s’engageait alors à mener une enquête. Changpeng Zhao, le fondateur de la plateforme, parle rapidement de la possibilité d’une « cyberattaque contre Binance ».
 Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak. We will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and the facts are fully verified.
The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B. We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far.
Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company’s funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete.
As an immediate precaution, Binance has:
– temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed;
– revoked the affected address authorisation;
– engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.
Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.
Please rely only on official Binance channels for updates. Please feel free to contact Binance Customer Support if you have any further questions.
https://t.co/ywB2mKFy0p
— Binance (@binance) October 30, 2026
À lire aussi : 351 millions de dollars de cryptos dérobées – la plateforme Bitget a été piratée par des hackers nord-coréens
Trois milliards de dollars gelés
Face à la cyberattaque qui frappe Binance, tout l’écosystème crypto s’est rapidement mobilisé. Tether, l’émetteur du stablecoin USDT, parvient à bloquer environ 1,56 milliard de dollars volés par les truands. Circle, l’émetteur de l’USDC, gèle quant à lui plus de 800 millions. L’objectif est d’empêcher les pirates d’exfiltrer les fonds sur des mixeurs, des outils qui vont mélanger les cryptos de façon à ce que Binance en perde la trace.
De son côté, Binance assure d’abord que les fonds de ses clients sont « totalement à l’abri », avant de promettre qu’il couvrira « toutes les pertes ». Dos au mur, l’exchange finit par suspendre tous les dépôts et les retraits, avant de confirmer une perte de 6,3 milliards de dollars. Trois milliards d’entre eux ont pu être gelés avant qu’il ne soit trop tard.
Binance découvre rapidement que l’attaque repose sur un ordinateur portable compromis, appartenant à un ingénieur chargé de l’infrastructure informatique. Les pirates se sont servis de la machine vulnérable pour accéder à un service interne de Binance. De fil en aiguille, ils ont pu lancer des retraits non autorisés sur les portefeuilles.
« Cela met en évidence à quel point la sécurité d’une plateforme financière dépend des appareils du quotidien et des personnes y ayant accès, ainsi que de la technologie protégeant ses portefeuilles », souligne Marijus Briedis, responsable chez NordVPN, dans une réaction adressée à 01net.
Bonne nouvelle, Binance n’a trouvé « aucune preuve de fuite de clés privées depuis les portefeuilles ». En clair, les pirates n’ont pas volé les clés des coffres, ce qui limite les dégâts.
À lire aussi : Crypto-crime – pourquoi 2025 a pulvérisé tous les records
La Corée du Nord à l’origine de la cyberattaque
Les chercheurs de TRM Labs attribuent le vol « avec une confiance élevée » à TraderTraitor, un gang lié à la Corée du Nord. Rattaché au groupe Lazarus, le gang est déjà accusé d’être à l’origine du casse de Bybit l’année dernière. Il est aussi soupçonné d’avoir piraté la plateforme Bitget en septembre. C’est également l’avis de l’enquêteur ZachXBT, qui a découvert qu’une même adresse est exploitée par les hackers de Bitget et ceux de Binance.
Binance promet de rembourser l’intégralité des pertes des utilisateurs. Les investisseurs sont couverts par SAFU, le fonds d’urgence de la plateforme, mis en place dans le sillage de la chute de FTX en 2022. Désormais, « les fonds des utilisateurs sont en sécurité », insiste la plateforme. Les dépôts sont d’ailleurs de nouveau ouverts. Toutefois, les retraits sont toujours bloqués, mais ils devraient reprendre dans les 48 heures.

Source : TechCrunch

articles.title: Abonnement Withings+ obligatoire pour l'export des données : voici la parade pour les balances Body et Wireless Scale
articles.text:
Fini l’abonnement obligatoire sur les balances Withings, un développeur crée une parade gratuite et open source pour récupérer les données
Pour contourner l’abonnement Withings+ imposé aux nouveaux clients souhaitant exporter leurs données de santé, un développeur a créé YourOwnWeigh, un outil gratuit qui libère les balances connectées des serveurs payants de la marque.
En imposant un abonnement payant à ses nouveaux utilisateurs pour synchroniser leurs données de santé avec des applications tierces comme Apple Santé, Withings s’expose à un premier retour de bâton.
Le développeur Tom Anthony a ainsi conçu YourOwnWeigh pour affranchir les balances connectées de l’infrastructure de la marque. Un premier pas qui devrait ouvrir une émancipation plus large dans les mois à venir, la communauté ayant très mal pris cette gabelle forcée.
YourOwnWeigh : libérer les balances Withings de leur abonnement
Le principe de YourOwnWeigh repose sur le remplacement de l’infrastructure de Withings par un serveur personnel. Compte tenu du faible volume de données généré par une pesée, l’ensemble peut être hébergé gratuitement sur un compte Cloudflare, explique le développeur. Pour opérer cette bascule, Tom Anthony a conçu une passerelle écrite en Python, fonctionnelle sous macOS 27 et Linux, la prise en charge de Windows étant en attente.
Une fois la balance placée en mode configuration via son bouton et reliée en Bluetooth à l’ordinateur, cet utilitaire récupère d’abord sur les serveurs de Withings les réglages existants, ainsi que les profils des utilisateurs enregistrés. L’outil télécharge ensuite le firmware officiel du fabricant et lui applique un patch pour rediriger la balance vers ce nouveau serveur. Il est ensuite installé sur l’appareil, toujours en Bluetooth.
Après cela, l’appareil se rallume et affiche un smiley au lieu du traditionnel message “Hello” de Withings, puis transmet ses mesures en wifi directement au serveur configuré par son propriétaire.
Pour exploiter ces relevés au sein de l’écosystème Apple, Tom Anthony fournit une automatisation via l’app Raccourcis qui importe régulièrement les mesures dans Apple Santé. Le développeur espère que d’autres contributeurs créeront des passerelles similaires vers d’autres services, tels que Google Health.
Pour l’heure, cette manipulation technique demeure réservée aux utilisateurs avertis et ne prend en charge que deux anciens modèles : la Body (WBS06) et la Wireless Scale (WS-30/WBS03). Les risques de blocage définitif restent toutefois limités, ces balances disposant en plus de deux emplacements mémoire qui permettent de conserver une copie de secours du logiciel d’origine en cas d’erreur lors de la mise à jour.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

articles.title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money.
Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion.
In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results.
The challenge
In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories:
- Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record.
- Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price.
- Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote.
Each exception triggered a five-step manual process:
- Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing.
- Research the root cause in vendor records.
- Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details.
- Wait for a response.
- Execute the resolution in the TMS.
With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth.
Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework.
From assessment to production
In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months.
How it works
The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable.
Agents
When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute:
- Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up.
- Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid.
- Accessorial Validation Agent checks whether unexpected fees (such as residential delivery or liftgate charges) are supported by the actual delivery events.
Each agent pulls specific carrier billing rules and policies before making a recommendation. After the exception is resolved, the system generates a plain-language note explaining what was found and what action was taken.
Each custom agent has an instruction prompt (defining its role, decision boundaries, and output format), a set of actions (integrations into SpeedShip), and access to carrier-specific knowledge bases. By using Amazon Bedrock, each agent accesses a suitable foundation model through a single API while inheriting existing AWS governance. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
Actions
The agents connect to SpeedShip through the same APIs that analysts use. That means the AI sees exactly what a human reviewer would see (contract rates, shipment details, delivery proof) and writes its resolution into the same workflow. SpeedShip has APIs on AWS, so the agents wire into the same endpoints as other existing systems.
Carrier knowledge base
Every carrier has different billing rules, fee definitions, and dispute procedures. Worldwide Express stores each carrier’s documentation: tariff rules, surcharge definitions, dispute steps, and variance thresholds. When an agent processes an exception, it retrieves that specific carrier’s policies and standard operating procedure (SOP) documents before deciding, so each decision is grounded in the carrier’s own rules. The same three agents handle all carriers without any carrier-specific code.
Human-in-the-loop
The approval step was necessary for FinOps adoption during the initial rollout. Initially, a human reviewer would use the existing SpeedShip UI to approve recommendations before they’re finalized. Eventually when accuracy exceeded 99 percent, bulk approval became the default.
Observability
Worldwide Express’s team built dashboards tracking automation rate by carrier, error rate by exception type, resolution time, and human override frequency. When a reviewer rejects a recommendation, the system logs the feedback. The team refines instruction prompts and knowledge bases based on rejection history, steadily increasing automation coverage.
End-to-end flow
The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from exception detection through the three specialized agents to human approval. In the diagram, exceptions from the data sources (the SpeedShip TMS, a shipping system, an electronic data interchange (EDI) server, and carrier and vendor portals) are detected and routed to one of three agents. Each agent runs on Amazon EC2 with Auto Scaling, uses an agent framework with its own prompt, tools, and carrier knowledge base, and calls Amazon Bedrock for model inference. The agents produce a resolution report. Cost finalization and an AI-written note then go to a human reviewer for approval in the SpeedShip analyst UI.
Results
Six months in, Worldwide Express has deployed the solution across over 40 LTL carriers. The agents currently close 10,000 (approximately 50 percent) exceptions weekly with a less than 1 percent error rate. This shifted the FinOps team’s time from routine resolution to complex, high-value disputes.
The impact shows up most clearly in the backlog of active exceptions, which fell from $15M in June 2025 to $4M six months later, a 75 percent reduction. Worldwide Express unlocked $10M in freed-up cash flow, over $1M in annual cost savings, and 60x first-year ROI. The company reports time-to-cash improving by four weeks.
        “With AWS, we’ve automated more than 40 percent of weekly billing exceptions, significantly reducing costs and accelerating billing cycles from days to minutes. Today, we release approximately $10 million more in customer billings each week at a speed that simply wasn’t possible before.”
— Nathanael Pearson, VP of FinOps, Worldwide Express
Looking forward
Worldwide Express is already expanding this approach to other parts of the Order-to-Cash cycle. For logistics companies managing high carrier volumes, the path forward is to start small. Automate the most repetitive exception type first, prove accuracy, then scale across the rest of the portfolio.
Conclusion
Worldwide Express’s exception automation shows what’s possible when agentic AI meets a well-scoped business problem. The combination of Amazon Bedrock, carrier-specific knowledge bases, and a human-in-the-loop approval design let Worldwide Express move from assessment to production in less than 6 months while maintaining financial controls. The company is now expanding automation to other Order-to-Cash processes.
To explore whether a similar approach might work for your organization, request a conversation with your account team or learn more about Amazon Bedrock. Partners like LTM can run a Proof of Value sprint with your own data.

articles.title: Nueva actualización de iPhone: iOS 27.3 llegaría en diciembre y con funciones nuevas de Salud
articles.text:
Apple prepara el próximo gran salto de software para el iPhone. Mientras iOS 27.2 llegó recientemente con mejoras para Mensajes, Siri AI y Fotos, además de un cambio de nombre para Apple Music, el desarrollo de iOS 27.3 ya se encontraría en una etapa avanzada.
Se espera que la versión beta esté disponible en los próximos días y que el lanzamiento público se concrete a mediados de diciembre, en línea con el calendario que la compañía mantiene desde hace varios años.
El dato llama la atención porque el ciclo de actualizaciones de este año presenta un desfase en la numeración. Esto se debe a que Apple reservó iOS 27.1 de forma exclusiva para el iPhone Duo, lo que corrió un número a todas las versiones posteriores del sistema operativo, aunque el cronograma de fondo siga siendo el mismo de siempre.
Cuándo se lanzará iOS 27.3 según el historial de Apple
Para estimar la fecha exacta de iOS 27.3, resulta útil mirar atrás. Las actualizaciones equivalentes a una “x.2” en ciclos anteriores se lanzaron siempre en la segunda semana de diciembre: iOS 26.2 llegó un viernes 12 de diciembre, iOS 18.2 un miércoles 11 de diciembre e iOS 17.2 un lunes 11 de diciembre.
Ese patrón sostenido durante tres años consecutivos permite proyectar con bastante certeza que iOS 27.3 seguirá el mismo esquema y se lanzará a mediados de diciembre, pese al corrimiento en la numeración que introdujo el iPhone Duo.
La lógica detrás de esta fecha no es casual. Apple busca publicar su última actualización relevante del año con margen suficiente antes de las vacaciones. De este modo, si aparece algún error grave tras el lanzamiento, el equipo técnico todavía tiene tiempo de desarrollar una corrección y distribuirla antes de que buena parte del personal se tome un descanso por las fiestas.
Antes de eso, se espera que la primera versión beta de iOS 27.3 esté disponible para desarrolladores en los próximos días, posiblemente el lunes 2 de noviembre, dando inicio al período de pruebas habitual previo a cada lanzamiento público.
Cabe recordar que, tras completar el ciclo de iOS 18, que se extendió hasta versiones como iOS 18.7 dedicadas a parches de seguridad y estabilidad, Apple modificó a fines de 2025 su esquema de nomenclatura de software, lo que explica la numeración actual bajo la serie iOS 27.
Las funciones de Salud que podrían regresar en la próxima actualización
Una de las novedades más esperadas de iOS 27.3 es el regreso de la aplicación Salud rediseñada. Esta versión renovada había aparecido brevemente en las primeras versiones beta de iOS 27.2, con una nueva pestaña de Longevidad y una sección denominada “Edad de salud”.
Sin embargo, Apple decidió retirar estas funciones antes del lanzamiento final de iOS 27.2. Se prevé que el rediseño regrese en iOS 27.3, esta vez con funciones adicionales que no llegaron a integrarse en el intento anterior.
Siri AI sumará más idiomas y avanza su llegada a China
Otro de los frentes activos en el desarrollo de iOS 27.3 tiene que ver con la expansión de Siri AI, el asistente rediseñado que Apple lanzó en inglés junto con iOS 27. Con la llegada de iOS 27.2, el asistente ya incorporó francés, japonés, coreano, portugués y español.
Apple adelantó que el chino tradicional, el noruego, el turco y el vietnamita se sumarán “antes de fin de año”, una referencia que apunta directamente a iOS 27.3 como la actualización encargada de completar esa expansión de idiomas.
En paralelo, Bloomberg informó que Apple planea introducir algunas de las primeras funciones de Apple Intelligence en China con el lanzamiento de iOS 27.3. No obstante, según esa misma información, Siri AI continuará sin estar disponible en ese mercado, al menos en esta etapa del despliegue.

articles.title: $2 Million+ Drained From Polymarket Traders in New Supply Chain Attack
articles.text:
Polymarket halted trading on its international platform on October 29 after users reported unauthorized withdrawals.
According to the prediction market’s status page, the exchange was first switched to cancel-only mode, with relayer actions suspended.
“We’ve identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole,” the company said.
Trading resumed about an hour later, and Polymarket pledged to reimburse all affected traders. It has not named the vendor or disclosed losses.
Researchers have linked the theft to malicious code served from DebugBear, a UK-based website performance monitoring firm. Polymarket’s US platform was reportedly unaffected.
DebugBear confirmed being “impacted by an ongoing security incident” and urged users of its real user monitoring (RUM) product to pull its snippet from their websites. It also said it brought in specialist incident responders.
Hudson Rock obtained a copy of the malicious JavaScript from a DebugBear address used by Polymarket. The code hunted for a logged-in user’s trading tools and portfolio. Depending on the account type, it then tried either to sell positions and move the proceeds, or to send position tokens straight to an attacker-set address.
“The sample reads credential-related material, but our review did not identify a routine that sends the credential map, a password, a seed phrase, or a private key to its reporting endpoint. Its central approach is to reuse authority already available in the authenticated application,” Hudson Rock said.
The firm also spotted a Polymarket production build, timestamped 17:59 UTC, with a change note about removing the DebugBear script.
Loss figures vary. A screenshot reviewed by Hudson Rock showed about $2.19 million at the script’s hard-coded fallback address, though the firm said this is not a verified tally.
Blockchain security firm GoPlus, which also attributed the attack to a supply chain compromise of DebugBear’s RUM script, puts losses at roughly $2.71 million. According to its on-chain analysis, the main attack path ran through 710 deposit wallets and 731 addresses, though the address count does not equal the number of victims.
Arkham data showed a suspected attacker wallet holding approximately $2.65 million. That is the same address hardcoded in the script as its fallback recipient.
Hudson Rock has not determined how the script was tampered with or how many users were hit. Its findings do not indicate that other DebugBear customers were targeted.
The attack came the same day Binance was hit by a roughly $6 billion hack that blockchain intelligence firms have attributed to North Korea. In June, Polymarket disclosed another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, with losses reported at around $3 million.

articles.title: Float’s Rob Khazzam on how Canadian companies should rethink AI spending | BetaKit
articles.text:
Rob Khazzam has a funny story about keeping business AI costs under control. A few months ago, he discovered his own usage was costing $2,364 a day. He’d selected an expensive model without realizing it would remain the default for new conversations, so even routine prompts were running up the bill.
For the co-founder and CEO of Float, the Toronto-based startup building Canada’s intelligent financial operating system, it was a lesson in a challenge facing many of its nearly 10,000 customers.
“We’re seeing an explosion of spending, an explosion of adoption.”
Rob Khazzam
Float CEO
When looking at the data across Canadian businesses using Float, “We’re seeing an explosion of spending, an explosion of adoption,” Khazzam told BetaKit in a recent interview.
AI spending on Float grew twelve-fold over two years and more than four-fold in the past year alone, he said. In the past year, seventy percent of customers had experienced a month when their AI bill jumped 50 percent.
But bringing those bills down isn’t always the right response. Khazzam says that leaders need to understand how AI spending helps their teams accomplish more, while being able to catch costly habits like his own.
Drawing on Float’s experiments and expensive lessons, Khazzam shared what’s changing his thinking about spending, hiring, and helping employees get more out of AI. Here are five of his hottest takes.
1. Treat AI spending as an investment in your team
A rising AI bill doesn’t necessarily mean the company is becoming more expensive to run. If the tools help employees accomplish more without adding as many new hires, that spending could support a more productive business.
It’s why Khazzam has moved away from treating AI as a software expense to cut whenever it climbs too high. Instead, he said, “The right frame to me is to look at your payroll and your token spend together, and look at that combined number as your human capital investment.”
At Float, token spend rose from the equivalent of 0.1 percent of payroll a year earlier to about five to six percent in October. Khazzam now looks at the two costs together as a percentage of revenue, with the understanding that the business will grow alongside the combined expense.
The test extends beyond efficiency: “Do you solve customer problems faster? Do you build better product experiences faster? Does your organization learn faster?”
2. As part of the hiring process, consider what role AI can play
Before adding someone new to a team, Khazzam asks managers to consider how AI could help existing employees handle the work.
“Anytime someone wants to post a role, send us an email and explain why you need to fill this role and how AI can support the work,” he said, describing Float’s approach.
Hiring may still go ahead; Float is hiring now more than ever, but the exercise is designed to create a pause to help managers reconsider the responsibilities and resources required and how their team builds with AI first.
AI can also change what a company needs from a role. Float’s designers now build working prototypes using an internal tool called Surf. Khazzam said that’s changed what he looks for in a design team compared with a year earlier.
3. Match the model to the work
More powerful AI models can cost more to use, but their additional capabilities are not necessary for every job. Editing an email, for example, doesn’t need the same resources as solving a difficult data science problem.
“In most use cases, the marginal benefit of a frontier model is not needed,” he said.
Managing that difference requires more than instructions telling employees which model to select. Khazzam favours permissions that give people tackling complex technical problems, such as data scientists and principal engineers, more discretion over access.
Companies also need to catch spending increases as they happen. He recommended setting thresholds and assigning someone responsibility for flagging when usage crosses them, investigating the causes, and recommending adjustments.
4. Let employees explore, then choose shared tools
Letting employees try different AI tools has helped Float discover useful applications. But as adoption grew, people were sometimes solving the same problem with different products, making collaboration harder.
“We had, for example, 20 people trying to solve the same problem using five different tools,” said Khazzam.
Monthly adoption reports showed who was using which products and consuming the most tokens. Float eventually consolidated its tools. Khazzam noted that standardizing made it easier for Float to manage permissions, protect sensitive information, and give employees access to shared business context.
“Because the power of AI is not just editing an email. It’s being able to have it understand your business, the problem you’re trying to solve, and perpetually get smarter.”
5. Give learning time to pay off
A higher AI bill may arrive before the benefits show up in financial results. Khazzam cautioned against concluding an investment has failed simply because revenue per employee has not immediately risen in proportion to spending.
“It takes time,” he said.
At Float, company-wide hackathons have provided a useful way to assess progress. Watching employees build and ship something useful in a day or two gave leadership the confidence to keep supporting experimentation.
The events extend beyond engineering and product to include marketing, sales, and other non-technical teams who take part to ship new workflows and customer solutions both in and out of the product. Employees then show colleagues what they’ve built, helping practical knowledge spread across the business.
Khazzam sees that kind of learning as an investment that can compound: employees using AI now have more time to develop their capabilities than those who wait.
“I’m completely fine overspending for the next six to nine months, and culling it back if it means that the sum total of hours our team has spent learning is as high as humanly possible.”
