articles.title: London’s Easol secures €26.78 million Series A extension as it launches AI agents for experience businesses | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Easol, a London-based experience commerce platform, has closed a €26.78 million ($30 million) Series A extension round, bringing its total raised to date to €53.57 million ($60 million).
The round comprises €17.85 million ($20 million) in equity and an €8.92 million ($10 million) debt facility. The equity portion was led by Y Combinator, with participation from Tiger Global, Foundation Capital, FMZ Ventures, Notion Capital, and Eight Roads. The debt facility was provided by Viola Credit.
“We built Easol to give experience businesses control over their entire business and bring their technology in-house. AI is now allowing us to do so much more, with rising costs and tighter margins we can now support experience creators in scaling their business growing revenue in ways we couldn’t have imagined when we first launched the platform in 2021,” said Ben Simpson, co-founder and CEO of Easol.
Founded in 2021 by husband and wife duo Ben and Lisa Simpson, co-founders of Rise Festival, who previously managed live experiences drawing two million guests annually across locations from the French Alps to the Sahara Desert. While running Rise Festival, the Simpsons grew frustrated with managing experience businesses across too many disconnected tools that offered no real data ownership.
“The technology and software solutions that experience businesses must stitch together to be able to offer a variety of different booking, payment and activity options develops a working environment for creators that is complex, inflexible, and expensive,” they told EU-Startups.com in 2022.
To overcome this disconnected tools bottleneck, they set out to build a platform that gave experience creators genuine control of their operations. As an all-in-one platform, Easol brings bookings, payments, marketing, customer support and guest data under a single connected system, all hosted on the client’s own domain and kept entirely within the business’s ownership. The company says it has never sold its customers’ data to third parties.
Easol now has offices in London, New York, and Los Angeles, and has powered experiences booked by 2.8 million guests across more than 135 countries so far in 2026. Its client roster includes Coachella, Stagecoach, Defected, Afronation, Rapha, Swingers – The Home of Revelry, Boots in the Park, State of Play Hospitality, Bingo Loco, Snowboxx, The Cube, and Hijingo, among others.
The funding enabled Easol to develop and launch Teammates, its new agentic AI tools built natively inside the platform. Teammates helps experience businesses to create their own AI agents covering sales, support and operations. These agents rely on live business data to identify missed revenue, resolve guest queries, update bookings and surface actionable insights automatically.
Easol says many experience businesses run on lean central teams, leaving significant revenue on the table. In early deployments, one Teammates agent reportedly identified approximately $50,000 in upsell opportunities from guests with no add-ons attached to their bookings, and generated the outreach to pursue them while another client recovered $28,000 in outstanding payments in seconds.
Eve Szlendak, Head of Sales, State of Play Hospitality UK, said, ”I used to spend up to three days building reports to capture every possible scenario. Now, the dashboards give me the information I need instantly.”
Since its earliest days, Easol has argued that digitising the experience economy is not merely a convenience but a commercial necessity. With surging demand for live and in-person experiences, the company sees AI as a competitive advantage to operate, analyse, and take action across whole businesses.

articles.title: Review: You Can See Everything blurs the view of Elizabeth Holmes' deceit
articles.text:
In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley’s golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company’s signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison.
Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything, which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals, went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it’s a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there’s no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling.
Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there’s nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else.
I get that manufacturing ambiguity is the much-ballyhooed point. I get that much of the film’s appeal lies in how much fun people have afterward vigorously debating their interpretations of key scenes. But there’s no real mystery here. Holmes is still spouting all the same talking points and self-justifications, still playing the victim, dodging accountability, and affixing blame on anyone except herself, just as she did all the way through her trial. The only mystery is why a convicted fraudster is still deemed worthy of our attention.
tl;dr: Elizabeth Holmes is back on her bulls—t, and some people are falling for the act all over again.
(Spoilers below the first gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)
There is already an excellent HBO documentary about Holmes and Theranos by Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney: The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, a companion piece to journalist John Carreyrou’s 2018 book, Bad Blood. (I reviewed Gibney’s latest, Musk, earlier this month.) Holmes was also the focus of the 2022 Hulu fictionalized miniseries (and associated podcast) The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried as Holmes. None showed Holmes how she clearly wished to be perceived, so she reached out to A24 about making a documentary to tell her side of the story.
You will be shocked to hear that Holmes believes she is innocent and thought all she needed to do was “speak her truth” in order to convince everyone else, too. It didn’t work on a jury of her peers—who deemed her the least credible witness of the entire trial—but apparently it worked on Fielder. At least he’s in good company: Holmes fooled a lot of smart, savvy people for years before a pair of whistleblowers (Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung) exposed her lies.
Fielder, for those unfamiliar with his work, is a comedian, best known for his Comedy Central series (currently streaming on HBO) Nathan for You. Fielder played a fictionalized version of himself as a recent business graduate who “consulted” for struggling local businesses in LA. The gimmick: Fielder’s advice, offered in his trademark deadpan style, was deliberately weird, such as suggesting an ice cream store offer a poop flavor to generate headlines and draw customers. In another episode, he faked a video, which actually went viral, of a pig rescuing a goat at the local petting zoo.
Fielder was also an executive producer on the (excellent) HBO series How To With John Wilson before creating the docu-comedy, The Rehearsal, in which another heightened reality version of Fielder helps people prepare for difficult conversations by re-creating the conditions and environments in which those conversations will take place, frequently building extravagant sets to do so. If cringe humor is your thing (think Sasha Baron Cohen, with whom Fielder has also worked), then you’ll likely find Fielder’s schtick appealing—and you’ll be far more likely to love You Can See Everything.
Still, at first glance, he was a puzzling choice to co-direct this film, as was Oppenheim, who calls himself a “docu-fantasist.” The two men met at some point, became friends, and wanted to work on a project together; Holmes and current partner Billy Evans were Fielder fans. Thus, You Can See Everythingwas born.
Who’s playing who?
WARNING: Spoilers begin here.
Fielder and Holmes engage in a stare-down contest
A24
Fielder and Holmes engage in a stare-down contest
A24
Holmes reacts to watching the fictionalized version of her rise and fall: the Hulu series The Dropout.
A24
Holmes reacts to watching the fictionalized version of her rise and fall: the Hulu series The Dropout.
A24
Fielder and Holmes engage in a stare-down contest
A24
Holmes reacts to watching the fictionalized version of her rise and fall: the Hulu series The Dropout.
A24
Fielder and Oppenheim don’t spend much time rehashing the Theranos debacle and Holmes’ subsequent trial and conviction, which is fine; that has been covered exhaustively elsewhere, including the Gibney documentary, and it’s not what they were interested in capturing. They’re more keen on the vibes than the facts. Holmes and Evans invited Fielder and the film crew to stay with them for the 34 days before her imprisonment, and given the strangeness of their initial interactions, Fielder became a major on-camera presence in the film.
The first half of the film is on the dull side, featuring lots of footage of Fielder and Holmes staring at each other, unblinking, in an attempt to convince each other of their sincerity. (Jimmy Fallon and Jamie Lee Curtis hilariously spoofed this dynamic in a cold open for The Tonight Show.) There is a tiresome segment quibbling over the relative meanings of the words “can” and “could.” Another segment dissects whether or not Holmes is capable of understanding the humor behind the classic “Who’s on First” sketch.
Fielder’s deadpan comedic style is used to good effect. Any laughs in that first half come from his reaction shots, such as his expression when Holmes insists, blue eyes extra wide, that she has never once lied in her entire life. And it’s just innately funny seeing him pop up again and again at the edges of the frame, like an awkwardly diffident stalker.
Much has been made of the scene where Evans insists Fielder film him working out at the gym—including a post-workout shower scene with Evans faux-nonchalantly displaying side-frontal nudity. It’s nothing we haven’t seen before; HBO flashes its viewers all the time. Still, I can never unsee Evans’ flaccid junk, so thanks for that image being burned into my retinas, guys. But it fits the sleight-of-hand theme Fielder and Oppenheimer develop throughout the film. On the one hand, we are literally seeing everything. On the other, it is only the illusion of transparency, because Evans is so relentlessly squirrely and evasive—when not outright combative—about answering Fielder’s questions.
Frankly, Holmes and Evans just aren’t sufficiently interesting to carry a three-hour film, which is why Amanda Seyfried is such a breath of fresh air when she turns up for the second half to help Fielder and Oppenheim work around the physical absence of their primary subject. Seyfried plays Holmes in several carefully staged re-enactments—a fascinating window into the actor’s process—but she also becomes Fielder’s sounding board and (at times) co-conspirator. The film comes to life when she appears, akin to tossing a firecracker into a lackluster dinner party.
Seyfried, for instance, goads Evans into revealing that he has power of attorney and manages most activity on Holmes’ X account. She challenges Fielder about being reluctant to include footage that might show Holmes in a negative light because he’s come to care about her. And the film doesn’t let Seyfried off the hook either, forcing her to confront how her portrayal in The Dropout might have been painful for Holmes, despite clearly being fictionalized to allow for taking a few liberties with the facts.
An “absurdist reality show”?
Holmes mid-body scan so an AI avatar can be used while she’s incarcerated

Ars Technica senior editor Sam Axon, who loved the film, describes it as “an absurdist reality show” or a “post-postmodern comedy rather than an interesting documentary” that is “more for fans of Nathan Fielder than for people interested in Theranos.” Fair enough. But it has been marketed as a documentary. That label carries certain expectations. Yes, Fielder and Oppenheim are deliberately (and skillfully) thwarting those expectations, but to what end? Savvy consumers already know that documentaries frame their subjects in specific ways. Gibney, for one, unapologetically makes documentaries that espouse his personal point of view, rejecting the so-called “view from nowhere”—i.e., the illusion of objectivity. And reality TV has been around for decades. We know it’s innately performative, and that cameras subtly alter human behavior, blurring the boundary between truth and fiction. This is not a novel insight.
Fielder makes a show of approaching his subject with an open mind in order to be more “objective,” but there are plenty of details that Fielder omits to better shape his preferred narrative. For instance, Evans claimed they took a private jet to the Texas federal prison, whereas the film shows them driving there. More significantly, it’s clear Fielder deeply dislikes Evans (by the end of filming, the feeling was mutual), which is why he deliberately features moments that portray Evans as a controlling, manipulative, and almost comically vain Silicon Valley bro.
Evans may be all of that and more, but Holmes is treated with kid gloves by comparison. This is not the smart, savvy, high-powered businesswoman who graced magazine covers and wowed tech reporters with her rosy vision of a diagnostic future free of anxiety-inducing blood draws. Even whistleblower Tyler Shultz has said this version of Holmes seems “broken.” But she’s still a very good liar.
Shultz points out in an article for STAT News that Holmes and Evans were living in the $125 million Green Gables estate just prior to filming. They moved to a smaller, average-looking rented condo on the beach for the duration of the shoot (which still rents for around $28,000 a month)—a strategy Holmes employed before when being profiled by journalists. And the disassembled Theranos blood testing device Holmes displays for the cameras—in the scene that triggered the “can” vs. “could” discussion—is not the correct device, per Shultz:
That was not the device I worked with 12 hours a day, not the device we hid from regulators, not the device that constantly failed quality controls, not the device we used to knowingly give patients inaccurate medical results. The device she showed Fielder on the kitchen table was not the reason she went to prison. Elizabeth showed him a future version of the Theranos product that was never completed and never used in order to lead Fielder down this BS semantic rabbit hole and to trick him into litigating the entirely wrong thing.
Did Fielder catch the misdirection? Was he taken in by the subterfuge, like so many before him? Or is he willfully ignoring those aspects because they don’t suit his purposes? I’ll take Gibney’s transparent subjectivity any day over Fielder’s ambiguous gamesmanship.
You Can See Everything is obsessed with whether Holmes is lying, believes her own lies, or even understands what lying entails. Perhaps it’s not that black and white. I’m willing to grant that Holmes’ tears at having to leave her newborn child to serve her sentence are genuine; any mother would be heartbroken. But it also serves her broader purpose of crafting a more sympathetic narrative. The portrait that emerges is one of Holmes as the victim of yet another controlling, abusive man. It’s her entire legal defense during her trial, re-created here for Fielder’s (and our) benefit, with Evans taking on the scapegoat role of Holmes’ former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, currently serving a 12-year sentence for his part in the Theranos debacle.
Fielder has built his entire brand around the unreliable narrator trope, while Oppenheim has been accused of misleading his subjects while making a 2017 short for The New York Times, so it’s fair to say both men might have a complicated relationship with the truth. Perhaps Holmes got the “documentarians” she deserved, and this is a match made in heaven. One can’t rule out the possibility that she and Evans were in on the game from the start. The entire film is an elaborate performance piece, manufactured for our post-truth consumption: ‘Haha, look at these people trying to out-manipulate each other for the cameras, like contestants on the latest reality show.’ Are you not entertained?
The cynical nihilism of it all is exhausting, and ultimately the joke is on us. Facts matter. Accountability matters. Even in a world awash in deep fakes and misinformation, there are still some truths that can be known, no matter how doggedly Fielder and Oppenheim try to muddy the waters. They want us to believe that Elizabeth Holmes is “unknowable and everything is ambiguous,” as Carreyrou—who, unlike me, loved the film and thinks it should win the Oscar for best picture—recently wrote on X. “She went after Tyler Shultz and Erika Cheung with everything she had. I was threatened with litigation on a daily basis for months on end. It was a ruthless cover-up of a breathtaking fraud, and she was at the controls. Just a little context for those who have forgotten or didn’t follow the original story.”
In the grand scheme of things, nobody cares what the science-and-culture writer at Ars Technica thinks about this film. I am firmly in the minority with my assessment, and I’m good with that. Oppenheim and Fielder will rake in box-office millions and collect a bunch of prestigious awards, including a possible Oscar. Holmes will serve her time—in fact, she’ll be eligible for a halfway house next year—and Evans is already hard at work raising capital for a new biomedical startup. Holmes will once again try to rehabilitate her image by spinning some new variation on how she did nothing wrong, the device really does work, and she is the victim here. It’s the only story she knows how to tell.
But we don’t have to keep falling for it.
You Can See Everything is now playing in theaters.
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban.

articles.title: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
articles.text:
Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday, Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union.
Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
The coffee chain aims to ‘recognize’ customers as they arrive.
It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with, which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also recently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.”
Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future.
Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT, and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards.
It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.”

articles.title: Ataque hacker à Binance: o que se sabe sobre o maior roubo de criptomoedas da história
articles.text:
Um ataque hacker conseguiu desviar US$ 6,3 bilhões em criptomoedas da corretora Binance. A ação é considerada o maior roubo já registrado na história do setor. Segundo as empresas norte-americanas TRM Labs e Chainalysis, os responsáveis seriam hackers ligados à Coreia do Norte. A Binance, entretanto, informou que sua investigação ainda não identificou os responsáveis pelo ataque.
No Olhar Digital News desta sexta-feira (30), conversamos com Jean Michel Guillot, diretor de negócios e soluções da DINAMO Cyber Security Company, empresa brasileira de cibersegurança. Ele explicou como os invasores entraram nos sistemas da Binance, que mecanismos de segurança poderiam prevenir ou limitar os danos, além de quais lições esse episódio deixa para empresas brasileiras que custodiam ou oferecem criptoativos a clientes.
Alessandro Di Lorenzo é editor do Olhar Digital e formado em jornalismo pela Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS).

articles.title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says he isn't worried about 'still not great' shopping agents and bots rendering the site useless
articles.text:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy says he isn't worried about 'still not great' shopping agents and bots rendering the site useless
'Not great' shopping agents still have a long way to go
- Amazon CEO says he isn't worried about AI shopping agents like Muse
- Amazon had blocked Meta's AI agent from its ecommerce site
- Jassy says the AI agent experience is still "not great"
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said he is not worried about the effect of AI-powered shopping agents such as Meta Muse, saying the services are still "not great".
Speaking after the company revealed yet another set of record financial results, Jassy told analysts barely any customers are using shopping agents as the experience is “still not great, nor more convenient than coming to a retailer directly.”
Jassy’s comments followed Amazon's decision to block Meta's new AI assistant, Muse, from accessing its online store in September 2026, claiming this would violate the conditions of use its customers have agreed to.
Muse is not doing the business...yet
Since its launch in September 2026, Muse has proven popular with customers, despite several examples of the service accessing information it was not supposed to.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently claimed that more than 10 million people across the US and Canada had already set up Muse, and that it had toppled ChatGPT as the top free app on the Apple App Store.
Experts have warned it may still not be up to scratch, after a security researcher found a worrying zero-day vulnerability which allowed attackers to gain access to people’s apps, such as WhatsApp or email.
Data from Surfshark also identified Muse as the most data-hungry chatbot around, outperforming all its competitors when it comes to data harvesting.

Meta has already signed up a range of top retailers, including Walmart, Best Buy and Shopify, to integrate with Muse, but Amazon has yet to join the group. The company is largely reliant on human shoppers visiting the Amazon website, where they can be exposed to advertisements and suggested products which nets the business its biggest returns.
Jassy did claim that more than 400 million customers have used Alexa for shopping in the last year, and that “customer interactions” had grown 570% year over year.
US customers using its Alexa also spent 50% more per order than those who do not use it, Jassy revealed, perhaps signaling that the service will be expanded in the coming months.
Via Fortune

articles.title: DoorDash said it's only received 'several hundred' orders from AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.
“I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said.
Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.
DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September, a CLI agent introduced in July, and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos. The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering.
The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors.

articles.title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence - Microsoft Research
articles.text:
At a glance
- Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances.
- To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings.
- The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss.
- Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material.
Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly.
Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence.
They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in.
We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform, which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars:
- Synthetic enterprise environments: simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data
- Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets
- Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation
Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data?
In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot.
Synthetic enterprise environments
Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve.
Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments: simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful.
Grounding in real world signals
To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources.
- O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates.
- Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions.
- SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization.
Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure.
Industry specific simulation
We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage:
- A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings
- A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews
- An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination
This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes.
Automated query generation
While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in.
The six-stage pipeline
We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios.
Validating synthetic quality
Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions:
- Structural fidelity: Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships?
- Contextual relevance: Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns?
- Behavioral realism: Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics?
- Content safety: Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals?
End-to-end automation
While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including:
- Reproducibility: Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases.
- Scale: The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand.
- Iteration speed: Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles.
- Cross-team consistency: Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels.
This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results.
PODCAST SERIES
Privacy and safety by design
Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline. Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk.
Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline.
This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible.
Results and impact
Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions.
On synthetic data quality, our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments.
On scale and efficiency, each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs.
On organizational adoption, our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure.
Conclusion
As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety.
Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next.
At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale.
Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets!

articles.title: Cette compacte électrique premium voit son prix baisser de 6 000 euros quelques semaines après son lancement
articles.text:
Le groupe Volkswagen est en pleine offensive sur le marché des véhicules électriques en Europe. Si on a souvent abordé les nouveautés de Skoda, Volkswagen et Cupra avec des modèles citadins, Audi n’est pas en reste puisque la marque a relancé l’A2 en version électrique. L’Audi A2 e-tron est désormais éligible à la prime Coup de pouce CEE, ce qui devrait bien aider ses ventes en France.
Une voiture premium éligible à l’aide
Généralement, les voitures premium dépassent les critères pour profiter du bonus écologique, désormais appelé Coup de pouce CEE. Elles doivent rester sous un tarif de 47 000 euros, mais l’Audi A2 e-tron s’y maintient pour plusieurs versions. Mais ce n’est pas tout, il faut aussi valider l’éco-score, qui favorise les voitures produites en Europe. Parfait, l’Audi A2 e-tron est produite à Ingolstadt, en Allemagne.
Tous les feux étaient au vert pour l’obtention du bonus écologique. Et la publication au Journal officiel du 22 octobre 2026 valide son éligibilité à l’aide à l’achat d’une voiture électrique en France. De ce fait, elle profite d’une prime pour tous de 3 535 euros, de 5 890 euros si votre revenu fiscal par part est compris entre 11 251 et 16 880 euros et jusqu’à 6 145 euros si votre revenu fiscal de référence par part est inférieur à 11 250 euros.
Une voiture efficiente et relativement bien placée
Rares sont les voitures électriques premium à être éligibles au bonus écologique. Seules les versions d’entrée de gamme de la Mercedes CLA et du GLB électrique arrivent à rester sous les 47 000 euros. Du côté d’Audi, le choix de rester en 400 volts et la plateforme MEB commune avec la Volkswagen ID.3 Neo, permettent d’avoir des tarifs d’accès contenus.
La version de 170 chevaux avec batterie de 52 kWh débute à 38 600 euros au catalogue, pour une autonomie de 423 km WLTP. Ce qui réduit son prix pour tous à 35 065 euros avec l’aide du bonus écologique. Si cette autonomie vous semble trop juste, il est judicieux de s’intéresser à la version de 231 chevaux à propulsion, utilisant une batterie de 84 kWh pour une autonomie allant jusqu’à 646 km WLTP, grâce au très bon travail d’optimisation aérodynamique d’Audi sur l’A2 e-tron. En se contentant du premier niveau de finition, cette version dotée de la plus grande autonomie du catalogue est proposée à partir de 46 900 euros, ce qui la rend éligible au bonus et donc à un tarif de 43 365 euros pour tous.
Une bonne nouvelle pour Audi, qui va avoir fort à faire avec cette Audi A2 e-tron, qui arrive sur un marché très concurrentiel : celui des compactes électriques.

articles.title: Voiture de l'année 2027 : sept finalistes électriques et un duel fratricide chez Volkswagen
articles.text:
Le jury du trophée européen de la Voiture de l’année (COTY) vient de trancher : les sept modèles retenus pour la finale de l’édition 2027 carburent tous exclusivement à l’électricité. La liste des finalistes vient d’être officialisée le 30 octobre 2026 sur le site dédié à l’événement. Ce n’est pas une surprise totale au vu des dernières éditions, mais le symbole est là : le thermique et l’hybride sont restés sur le bas-côté dès le premier tour cette année.
Si les petits gabarits urbains font figure de favoris naturels, le tableau est loin d’être figé. Aucune victoire n’est acquise, d’autant que le groupe Volkswagen se présente avec deux prétendantes : le duel direct entre l’ID. Polo et la Cupra Raval pourrait compliquer les arbitrages du jury et rebattre les cartes face aux outsiders.
Les sept finalistes de l’édition 2027
Sur la ligne de départ pour succéder à la Mercedes CLA titrée l’an dernier, on retrouve :
- BMW iX3 : le premier représentant de la nouvelle plateforme Neue Klasse.
- Cupra Raval : la proposition espagnole, plus affûtée et expressive, de la citadine branchée.
- Hyundai Ioniq 3 : la compacte électrique coréenne au design surprenant.
- Kia EV2 : le petit SUV électrique urbain cubique pensé comme une porte d’entrée abordable vers l’électrique.
- Renault Twingo E-Tech : la grenouille néo-rétro conçue en moins de deux ans.
- Volkswagen ID. Polo : la citadine sobre et pragmatique attendue comme le tournant populaire de Wolfsburg.
- Volvo EX60 : le SUV familial suédois, qui affronte directement le BMW iX3 sur le terrain des SUV haut de gamme.
Si les marques représentent cinq nationalités différentes : Allemagne, Corée du Sud, Espagne, France et Suède, les sept voitures sont toutes produites en Europe élargie. La Turquie, où est produite la Hyundai Ioniq 3, est intégrée à l’union douanière européenne, et donc considérée comme une extension naturelle de l’Europe pour l’industrie automobile. Ne boudons pas notre plaisir.
ID. Polo contre Cupra Raval : le piège du vote partagé
L’élément le plus atypique de cette sélection réside dans la présence conjointe de deux modèles jumeaux : la Volkswagen ID. Polo et la Cupra Raval. Toutes deux partagent la même plateforme technique (traction, formats de batteries identiques) et sortent de la même usine espagnole de Martorell.
Sur le papier, l’ID. Polo coche toutes les cases de la gagnante naturelle. Par sa sobriété, son nom rassurant et sa vocation de voiture du peuple électrique autour des 25 000 euros, elle répond point par point au cahier des charges historique des jurés européens, souvent plus sensibles à l’impact industriel d’un modèle qu’à ses fioritures esthétiques. La raison voudrait qu’elle s’impose.
Mais la présence de la Cupra Raval dans la même finale change la donne. Avec son positionnement plus dynamique et son design plus clivant, la cousine catalane a tout pour séduire une frange plus passionnée du jury. Le groupe Volkswagen risque de voir les points des jurés séduits par cette base technique se partager entre les deux modèles, privant l’ID. Polo du matelas nécessaire pour sécuriser la première place.
En 2025, Renault avait évité cet écueil. La Renault 5 et sa cousine sportive, l’Alpine A290, concouraient sous une seule candidature, et le duo a été sacré ensemble. Volkswagen et Cupra défendent cette fois deux candidatures séparées.
La Twingo en embuscade
Cette division interne chez Volkswagen pourrait faire les affaires de la concurrence, à commencer par Renault. Si l’ID. Polo reste la favorite sur le plan rationnel, la Twingo E-Tech a de solides arguments à faire valoir. Après les précédents succès de Renault dans ce concours, avec le Scénic élu en 2024 puis le duo R5/A290 en 2025, la citadine française joue la carte du prix plancher sous les 20 000 euros et d’une conception particulièrement agile.
Le verdict final sera rendu le 8 janvier 2027 à l’ouverture du Salon de l’automobile de Bruxelles.

articles.title: Disney+ rétablit enfin le HDR en France, mais votre appareil peut-il vraiment l'exploiter ?
articles.text:
Après plusieurs mois de restrictions, Disney+ commence à rétablir le HDR10 en France. Une bonne nouvelle pour les abonnés Premium, mais tous les appareils ne sont pas compatibles avec cette solution. Et le Dolby Vision reste absent.
Le feuilleton de la qualité d'image sur Disney+ connaît un nouveau rebondissement. En août dernier, nous évoquions le retour progressif de la 4K en France, après plusieurs semaines de restrictions liées à un conflit de brevets avec InterDigital, mais le HDR restait absent.
Le service a désormais commencé à rétablir le HDR10 dans les pays européens concernés, dont la France. Une amélioration bienvenue, même si le retour à la normale reste encore lointain.
Disney+ trouve une nouvelle parade pour le HDR10
Pour contourner les restrictions liées au codec HEVC, Disney+ avait commencé à réencoder ses contenus en VP9. Cette solution avait permis de retrouver la 4K sur certains appareils, mais pas le HDR.
La plateforme utilise désormais le VP9 Profile 2, une variante prenant en charge une profondeur de couleur de 10 bits et permettant ainsi de diffuser du HDR10. Selon Disney, cité par FlatpanelsHD, tous les films et séries auparavant proposés en 4K HEVC disposent désormais d'une version VP9. Les contenus HDR10 ont également été réencodés avec ce nouveau profil.
Le catalogue est donc techniquement prêt, mais encore faut-il que les appareils des abonnés puissent exploiter ces flux.
Apple TV, Samsung et Panasonic toujours sur la touche
Le HDR10 est notamment de retour sur certains appareils Android TV et Google TV, dont des téléviseurs Philips, Sony et TCL, ainsi que sur les Fire TV d'Amazon, les téléviseurs LG sous webOS depuis 2020 ou encore les modèles Hisense sous VIDAA depuis 2019.
En revanche, les Apple TV 4K et Nvidia Shield resteraient pour l'heure privées de 4K et de HDR sur Disney+. Les téléviseurs Samsung sous Tizen et Panasonic sous MyHomeScreen ne bénéficient pas non plus de ce rétablissement, pas plus que les plateformes TiVo OS et Titan OS. Cette dernière équipe d'ailleurs certains téléviseurs Philips.
Le cas d'Apple est révélateur : ses puces décodent bien le VP9, mais Apple en réserve l'accès essentiellement à Safari, ce qui empêche pour l'instant Disney+ d'en profiter. Quant à Samsung, ses téléviseurs étaient pourtant les premiers à accueillir le HDR10+ sur Disney+ en octobre 2025. Ils se retrouvent aujourd'hui sans 4K ni HDR dans les pays concernés.
Deux abonnés Premium, qui paient le même prix, peuvent donc regarder le même film avec une qualité d'image très différente. Et pour ceux qui s'estiment lésés, il est déjà possible de demander une compensation à Disney+. Nous avons détaillé les démarches à suivre dans un précédent article.
Et le dossier n'est pas clos. Le Dolby Vision et la 3D restent indisponibles, tandis que le litige avec InterDigital s'est étendu au VP9, sans décision de justice à ce stade. En France, Que Choisir Ensemble avait mis Disney en demeure en septembre de rétablir son offre Premium, facturée 5 € de plus par mois que la formule Standard, ou d'en revoir le prix. Le 26 octobre, l'association est revenue à la charge, déplorant l'absence de réponse circonstanciée de la plateforme.

articles.title: Von Cape Canaveral in den Pazifik: US-Militär testet Raketen-Lieferung mit SpaceX
articles.text:
Rocket Cargo: US-Militär liefert Fracht erstmals per SpaceX-Kapsel aus dem All
Während Otto Normalbürger noch immer darauf wartet, dass seine online eingekauften Waren endlich per Drohne geliefert werden, ist das US-Militär schon einen ganzen Schritt weiter. Mithilfe einer SpaceX-Kapsel ließ es sich Fracht über das Weltall zustellen. Das Ganze war ein Test des „Rocket Cargo“-Projekts des Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL).
Rocket Cargo: Punkt-zu-Punkt-Lieferung per Rakete
Im Fokus des Projekts steht die sogenannte Punkt-zu-Punkt-Lieferung (P2D) mit großer Kapazität mithilfe von Raketen über das All. Das US-Militär untersucht damit, wie taktisch wichtige Ausrüstung punktgenau und schnell an jeden Ort auf der Erde gebracht werden kann.
Laut Pressemitteilung arbeitet das AFRL dafür mit „mehreren kommerziellen Anbietern und kleinen Unternehmen an kurzfristigen Lösungen, darunter SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Sierra Space, Anduril, Inversion Space und Outpost Space.“
Erster Test: Frachtkapsel landete im Pazifik
Der erste erfolgreiche Test fand nun am 20. Oktober an Bord der SpaceX-Frachtkapsel Starfall statt, die mit einer Falcon-9-Rakete von Cape Canaveral aus startete. Am 26. Oktober verkündete das AFRL die Bergung der Frachtkapsel. Sie war im Pazifik gelandet und beinhaltete unter anderem Instrumente zur Messung von Temperatur, Stößen und Vibrationen der Frachtumgebung.
Der übrige Inhalt war vor allem repräsentativer Natur: „Die Forscher legten besonderes Augenmerk auf die Elektronik und die Überlebensausrüstung, darunter ein Satellitenkommunikationsgerät, Batterien, eine Umkehrosmoseanlage zur Entsalzung und medizinische Notfallausrüstung.“ Für spätere Tests hat das AFRL bereits überprüft, ob ein UNI-PAC III-Rettungsfloß in eine der Kapseln passt.
Starfall: Was über die Frachtkapsel von SpaceX bekannt ist
Mehr oder weniger als Randnotiz in diesem Testlauf wird die Starfall-Kapsel von SpaceX erwähnt, über die bisher noch wenig bekannt ist. Starfall wurde erstmals im Juni 2026 mit einer Falcon-9-Rakete ins All befördert. Seitdem hält sich SpaceX weitgehend bedeckt dazu.
Bekannt ist, dass die puckförmige Kapsel rund drei Meter Durchmesser hat und bis zu eine Tonne Fracht transportieren kann. „Die meisten Informationen stammen aus einer Umweltverträglichkeitsprüfung der US-amerikanischen Luftfahrtbehörde FAA, die Anfang des Jahres veröffentlicht wurde“, schreibt Space.com dazu.
Schlussendlich war der Testlauf der AFRL-Frachtkapsel wohl auch eine Erprobung von Starfall. Es bleibt abzuwarten, ob weitere dieser Kapseln gelauncht werden und die (Militär-)Logistik auf der Erde grundlegend verändern können.

articles.title: D2C brands don't need an AI team to get discovered and grow, says Shopflo
articles.text:
D2C brands don't need an AI team to get discovered and grow, says Shopflo
What if your next customer is an AI agent? At TechSparks 2026, Mihir Shah of Shopflo by Pine Labs explained how brands can connect product catalogues to AI shopping platforms and drive conversions.
AI assistants are becoming shopping destinations, but keeping up with them can stretch lean teams.
Shoppers are beginning to turn to AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude to discover products, compare options and make buying decisions. For direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, this raises a new question: how do they stay visible as shopping behaviour changes, without building an in-house AI team?
At TechSparks 2026, Mihir Shah, Chief Business Officer at Shopflo by Pine Labs, presented two ways the company aims to help brands tackle this challenge: agentic commerce, which connects product catalogues to AI-powered discovery and shopping surfaces, and AI agents that help businesses improve growth and operational efficiency.
“You don't need an AI team to figure out growth or efficiency for you. You need Shopflo,” Shah said.
Getting products in front of AI shoppers
Brands have spent years building visibility through search engines, marketplaces, and social media. AI assistants are adding another discovery channel, where shoppers can describe what they need and receive product recommendations.
Shopflo's agentic commerce offering aims to make participating brands' catalogues available across AI-native platforms, including ChatGPT, Claude and other emerging interfaces, said Shah. Through integrations, the company streams product catalogue information to these surfaces, allowing shoppers to discover relevant products and, where supported, proceed towards checkout.
For instance, a shopper looking for festive gifts under Rs 2,000 could discover products from a participating brand through an AI assistant. Shopflo's integration with Pine Labs' payments infrastructure is designed to support transactions through these experiences.
Shah argued that brands will need to look beyond traditional discovery channels as consumer behaviour evolves. However, AI visibility does not replace search engine optimisation (SEO), which continues to contribute to website traffic.
AI agents put growth decisions in context
Discovery is only one part of running a D2C business. Brands must also balance conversion rates, average order value, returns, customer retention and profitability, often using separate tools for each function, said Shah.
Shopflo's Growth Orchestrator, which Shah said was available in beta, aims to bring these decisions together. Brands can define their priorities, whether that means pursuing growth or protecting profitability, and receive recommendations based on their store's performance data.
During the demonstration, Shah showed how the system could identify a drop-off between address entry and payment, suggest a fee-transparency banner and propose an experiment to test whether the change improves conversions.
Brands can review recommendations, set limits and approve experiments before scaling them. They can also decide how much autonomy to give the agents.
“How much or how little to use the agents is under your control,” Shah said.
For D2C businesses working with lean teams, the proposition is less about adopting every new AI tool and more about making existing growth decisions easier to manage. Shopflo's approach combines AI-led discovery with tools that help brands act on their own business goals, while leaving the final decisions in their hands.

articles.title: La metamorfosis de la noche: por qué la Gen Z ya no va (casi) a discotecas
articles.text:
También hay veinteañeros que van a heladerías a escuchar música (con refresco en mano) desde las 10 de la noche en adelante. Por otro lado, están los millennials, que recuerdan las largas noches de discoteca (inicialmente envueltas en humo de tabaco). La Generación Z italiana es más móvil y decide en último momento dónde ir. Prefieren fiestas-evento en entornos con cierto carácter y selección de público (por lo menos un par de palabras con alguien).
¿De dónde viene? En parte de la pandemia.
Los que ahora tienen veinte años fueron confinados justo en la edad de fiestas hasta el amanecer. Los primeros amores. En algunas ciudades se organizaron fiestas clandestinas (fuera de club) en viviendas particulares. Cuando se levantaron las restricciones, no regresaron a la pista habitual. Surgieron colectivos que organizan música (también de artes visuales) y vida social en pisos o lugares recuperados. Cada vez con más personalidad.
En Italia (de donde partimos) pueden ir a ver a un artista emergente colombiano en un club. También pueden ir a una cascina (casa de campo) que queda a media hora de coche de la ciudad y bailar. Existen colectivos que organizan eventos al aire libre. Maratones de música (de día y de noche) en entornos naturales (también en teatro o museo). Incluso se ha hecho cool ir a determinados lugares. Menos excesos. Más selección. Vida social y bienestar.
Sitio con alma (y buena foto)
Hay discotecas que han cerrado. Pero también están las que resisten. Aún hay muchos jóvenes que siguen yendo, solo que ahora es importante el tipo de sitio. Puede ser un sitio retro (como el viejo círculo de barrio que organiza monólogos de humor). También pueden ser lugares nuevos (con muebles de diseño y piscina en el jardín). Hay quien prefiere los sitios que seleccionan en la puerta. Se sale con estilo.
Casi parece una revancha de los meses en casa. A todo esto se le suma la tentación de ponerlo en redes sociales. “Yo también estoy aquí”. O incluso “solo yo estaba aquí”. De hecho, las fotos funcionan mejor en sitios con terraza o en sitios recuperados que con una discoteca en penumbra.
Los horarios también cambian. Ya no hay que esperar a las 11 para ir (con la ropa preparada) y llegar a la medianoche o la una. Y tampoco hay que ir hasta las seis. Se puede empezar por la tarde y acabar a las 22.30. Es el llamado soft clubbing. Bares diurnos en los que se baila en horario razonable, sin sacrificar el sueño (y el bienestar físico y mental).
Incluso existe la fiesta matinal (casi siempre el domingo). Con un capuchino y un cruasán. También se bebe, pero con moderación. Sería falso decir que la Gen Z no bebe.
Otra cosa que ha vuelto es la cena fuera. Puede ser una smash burger (comida de pie) o ir al restaurante de moda (de esos de los que habla todo el mundo). A veces esto eleva el presupuesto, pero el objetivo es mantener el nivel.
Por tanto, la noche es muy diferente a la de nuestros padres y hermanos mayores. Quizás más que un salto hacia delante es un retroceso. Vuelven a cuando bailar era bailar (y conocer gente). Es una especie de nostalgia que esta vez va más allá de los 90. Por ejemplo, surgen iniciativas que promocionan la música electrónica en vinilo.
Qué dicen los datos
¿Es posible medir este cambio? En parte sí. El 5 de junio de 2026, el Ministerio de Sanidad publicaba un informe sobre alcohol. Este se elabora a partir de la Encuesta de Salud de España. Esta encuesta tiene en cuenta a la población residente de 15 años y más.
En el grupo de edad entre 15 - 24 años, el consumo habitual (al menos una vez por semana) ha pasado del 43,8 % al 17,9 % en las dos últimas décadas. Casi un 60 % menos. En el total de la población de 15 años y más, ha pasado del 48,4 % al 31,1 %. Además, en el grupo de los que beben a menudo, la ingesta del fin de semana llega a triplicar la de los días laborables.
En el conjunto de mercados, el panorama es diferente. En la encuesta Bevtrac de IWSR (consultora especializada en bebidas) se analizan 15 mercados (incluyendo España). En marzo de 2025 indicaban que en los últimos dos años (marzo 2023 - marzo 2025) el porcentaje de jóvenes de la Generación Z (en edad legal de beber) que habían consumido alcohol en los últimos seis meses ha pasado del 66 % al 73 %. En el caso de los adultos, en general está en el 78 %.
Además, en esta misma encuesta se observa que aumenta la moderación en todas las edades. Es la generación que más practica la abstinencia intermitente. Cerca del 60 % (frente a algo más del 40 % de los bebedores adultos en general).
Las redes sociales también forman parte del mecanismo. Como explicó Xataka se han convertido en un canal de recomendación de planes para los jóvenes. Aunque en España los bares siguen siendo el centro del ocio. Como resume Esther Clavero (doctora en sociología) en este reportaje, “el ocio juvenil no ha desaparecido, se ha reconfigurado”.

articles.title: Intel Q3 2026 Earnings Data Center Soars While PC Faces Memory Pressure
articles.text:
Intel reported third-quarter 2026 earnings with revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% year-over-year. Non-GAAP gross margin reached 44.1%, and non-GAAP EPS came in at $0.52. Data center demand is surging while the client PC business is struggling (mightily) under memory market conditions. We do not always cover these, but Patrick asked me to do this one because it shows a trend we have seen recently at STH.
Intel Q3 2026 Results Show Contrasting Segments
First off, at an overall level, Intel’s headline numbers are relatively positive. Up almost 21% Y/Y is good, but last year was not great for Intel.
The Data Center and AI (DCAI) group delivered $7.3 billion in revenue, up 78% year-over-year. David Zinsner, Intel’s CFO, called it Intel’s strongest data center revenue growth in 15 years. Segment operating income reached $3.0 billion with a 41.5% margin. One of the interesting bits on why we were covering this announcement is that the demand in the market has shifted towards AMD’s 192-core Turin parts, which Intel does not have a direct competitor for (maybe Clearwater?), but partners tell us that Xeon 6 is selling because basically everything is selling.
Demand is strong across hyperscale, enterprise, and neo cloud customers, with “Purpose Built Silicon” revenue more than doubling year-over-year. Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s CEO, said Intel’s immediate priority is unlocking additional supply to meet extraordinary demand for the Xeon family. On the call, he said that substrate availability is limiting output and it would take some time to ease.
The client side looks very different. Client Computing and Physical AI Group (CCPG) revenue fell 5% year over year to $8.1 billion. Overall inflation is well north of zero depending on the index you use, so revenue falling is not good. On the call Intel cited industry-wide memory shortages impacting the total addressable market. Higher DRAM and NAND prices are pushing system costs up and hurting demand. On the call, it sounded like Intel was looking for 18A supply to be used on the data center side pending substrate availability.
Intel expects the PC slowdown to continue at least through the first half of next year. Memory and NAND pricing pressure is expected to persist into 2027, which means client system costs are likely to stay elevated for a while longer. For those who see today’s memory prices and think they are shocking, the earnings call commentary did nothing to make me think Q1 would see a decline in memory pricing.
Intel Foundry posted $6.7 billion in revenue, up 58% Y/Y, though that figure includes intersegment transactions rather than external customer sales alone. The segment still recorded an operating loss of $1.9 billion with a negative 27.7% margin, but that is narrower than the $2.3 billion loss a year ago.
Improved yields and cycle times are reducing wafer costs. Intel released the Intel 14A 0.9 process design kit in October as committed, and expansion continues across sites including Ohio.
Final Words
We do not cover all earnings calls, but Patrick’s thought was that this was an important one since it also tells a story of STH. Folks wonder why we have been doing a lot of AI desktop and server/ networking coverage, and fewer mini PCs. Intel’s Panther Lake is a cool product, but it is not running larger local models. Right now, DRAM and NAND are being priced for the value they bring attached to AI nodes. Likewise, the NVIDIA-Intel investment and the many NVIDIA GPU-based systems with Intel Xeon CPUs are helping drive Xeon 6 sales and push pricing up. As a result, we are seeing the market demand for non-local AI PCs drop due to higher prices, while the AI-related markets are cooking. We know folks want more mini PC reviews, but this is a fundamental industry challenge. A smaller client-side market also means fewer small companies trying to innovate on form factors, while the data center market is the exact opposite. This came out very clearly in Intel’s earnings.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: Segway Xyber Air : le monstre électrique s’assagit en fatbike de 1 600 W à 45 km/h — Frandroid
articles.text:
Segway a tenté de brouiller les pistes (cyclables) en 2024 avec le Xyber. S’il possédait bien des pédales, il n’avait réellement pas grand-chose du vélo électrique, avec sa puissance maximale de 6 000 W de moto électrique. Pour revenir à la raison, la marque lui adjoint un petit frère, le Segway Xyber Air, présenté le 14 octobre et disponible depuis ce mardi 27 octobre aux États-Unis : il entre cette fois dans les classes légales de vélos électriques américaines, et coûte bien moins cher.
Fini la moto à pédales, bonjour le vélo fatbike électrique
Visuellement, le Xyber Air a suivi une cure de minceur générale, qui le fait passer de l’allure de moto à pédales à celle d’un fatbike. L’architecture est désormais semi-rigide et non plus tout-suspendue, le cadre affine ses tubes, la suspension avant est moins importante (80 mm vs 110 mm), tandis que la batterie migre sous le tube supérieur.
Segway conserve les grandes lignes comme la longue selle, mais on est en présence d’un véritable nouveau modèle, à la manière du MacBook Air face au MacBook Pro. Les roues 20 pouces à bâtons – et non plus à rayons – possèdent également des pneus inédits, de largeur 4 pouces (vs 5 pouces), avec un seul petit garde-boue arrière. Le freinage reste hydraulique, mais l’étrier avant 4 pistons du Xyber laisse place à un 2 pistons.
Les garde-boues complets et le porte-bagages arrière passent d’ailleurs en option : Segway les vend 79,99 dollars chacun (environ 72 euros), le porte-bagages acceptant jusqu’à 10 kg. Avec ces deux accessoires, la facture grimpe à 2 159,97 dollars hors taxes, soit environ 1 930 euros.
Moindres performances, plus d’aisance
Moins visible, le moteur arrière est plus modeste : 80 Nm de couple contre 175 Nm pour le Xyber en version deux batteries (120 Nm avec une seule), et une puissance de crête de 1 600 W (750 W nominaux) contre 6 000 W. Cela reste très élevé pour un VAE européen, plafonné à 250 W. Là où le Xyber d’origine était réservé à un usage hors route, le Xyber Air entre dans les classes 1, 2 et 3 des vélos électriques américains, à choisir dans l’application ; la classe 3 se rapproche de nos speedbikes. Limité à 45 km/h en assistance au pédalage (32 km/h à l’accélérateur), et non débridable à 70 km/h comme le Xyber d’origine, il met environ 6 secondes pour passer de 0 à 32 km/h, contre 2,7 secondes auparavant, et n’accepte plus qu’une batterie. D’une capacité de 717 Wh, elle offre jusqu’à 93 km d’autonomie selon Segway, un chiffre obtenu avec un cycliste de 75 kg sur terrain plat, pour une recharge en 6 h 30.
Ce qui ne change pas, c’est la signature lumineuse en X façon Segway ZT3, certes avec un phare de 600 lumens contre 1 300 lumens sur le Xyber. Le bel écran (proche des trottinettes électriques Segway) est identique, ainsi que la connectivité, avec traceur GPS, alarme et compatibilité Apple Localiser ; le suivi GPS et le mode perte ne sont en revanche gratuits que la première année, avant de passer sur abonnement. Les aides à la conduite telles que le contrôle de traction, l’assistance de démarrage en côte et en descente sont aussi préservées. Enfin, le Xyber Air est bien plus facile à manier avec ses 38 kg, contre 63 kg pour le Xyber en version une batterie, pour une charge maximale de 150 kg et des cyclistes de 1,42 m à 1,83 m.
Un prix réduit d’environ 40 % pour le Segway Xyber Air
Le passage de la moto à pédales au vélo électrique fatbike s’accompagne d’une baisse de prix d’environ 40 %. Le prix public passe ainsi de 3 299,99 à 1 999,99 dollars (environ 2 950 à 1 790 euros, hors taxes). L’écart est toutefois moins net en boutique : Segway affiche actuellement le Xyber d’origine à 2 299,99 dollars (environ 2 060 euros), soit 300 dollars de plus seulement. Plus raisonnable, le Xyber Air resterait tout de même un speedbike chez nous, bien au-delà des 250 W et 25 km/h d’un VAE classique, et Segway n’a annoncé aucune commercialisation en Europe. Il est vendu uniquement aux États-Unis, sur la boutique en ligne de Segway, chez ses revendeurs agréés et dans les magasins Scheels.
