articles.title: Los 10 disfraces más originales y aterradores para Halloween 2026, según la IA
articles.text:
Halloween 2026 se perfila como una edición marcada por el terror conceptual y la fusión entre tecnología y miedo clásico. Dos inteligencias artificiales, Gemini y ChatGPT, fueron consultadas para elaborar listados de disfraces originales pensados para esta celebración, y los resultados combinan referencias a la cultura digital, el folclore de terror tradicional y la experimentación con prótesis y maquillaje de caracterización.
Las propuestas de ambos sistemas muestran un patrón: el miedo ya no se limita a monstruos clásicos como vampiros o zombis genéricos, sino que explora ansiedades contemporáneas vinculadas a la realidad aumentada, los deepfakes y la IA, junto con relecturas de personajes históricos como médicos de la peste o novias fantasmales.
Disfraces de terror tecnológico sugeridos por Gemini
Gemini propuso una serie de personajes que giran en torno a la angustia digital y los avances científicos fallidos. Uno de ellos es el denominado glitch de realidad aumentada, un disfraz que combina ropa urbana con un visor destrozado, cables expuestos y maquillaje facial que simula píxeles desfasados o una pantalla azul de error.
El diseño incluye una luz LED intermitente en un ojo y una pantalla en el pecho con la leyenda “Error del huésped: Conciencia desconectada”.
Otra idea generada por el sistema es el paciente de terapia criogénica fallida, inspirado en la descongelación prematura de un cuerpo. Este disfraz utiliza bata de laboratorio o mono térmico rasgado, escarcha artificial, cristales de hielo y cianosis extrema en labios y dedos. Se complementa con tubos médicos rotos que gotean líquido anticongelante y lentes de contacto blancos que simulan córneas congeladas.
Gemini también describió la entidad de deepfake o rostro robado, un concepto que plantea una criatura que intenta imitar un rostro humano sin lograrlo del todo. El disfraz requiere una máscara de látex o silicona con rasgos hiperrealistas pero asimétricos, cosida de forma burda sobre la cabeza real, con doble conjunto de ojos o una sonrisa demasiado ancha con dientes irregulares superpuestos.
Entre las propuestas más elaboradas figura el cirujano de almas, un personaje con atuendo de quirófano clandestino: delantal manchado de sangre coagulada, guantes quirúrgicos largos, mascarilla antigua y un arnés con frascos de vidrio iluminados por LED que contienen órganos flotantes o rostros diminutos suspendidos en líquido.
Esta idea se suma a otras como el parásito fúngico humanoide, inspirado en el concepto del Cordyceps, y el astronauta de una misión perdida, con un traje espacial desgastado y un casco con el visor teñido de sangre seca.
Personajes clásicos reinterpretados según ChatGPT
El listado elaborado por ChatGPT se orientó hacia una reinterpretación de figuras tradicionales del terror y el folclore de Halloween. Entre sus propuestas aparece el médico de la peste, inspirado en los profesionales medievales que atendían epidemias, con máscara de pico alargado, túnica negra, guantes envejecidos y frascos misteriosos como accesorios.
Otra idea destacada es la muñeca de porcelana rota, que combina un vestido antiguo, peluca peinada, maquillaje blanco y grietas negras que recorren el rostro, con un ojo más abierto que el otro para acentuar el efecto inquietante.
En la misma línea se ubica la novia del cementerio, con vestido de novia deteriorado, velo negro, ramo de flores marchitas y una expresión inexpresiva como rasgo central del personaje.
ChatGPT también propuso el jinete sin cabeza, un disfraz que genera la ilusión óptica de no tener cabeza propia mientras se porta una cabeza falsa bajo el brazo, combinado con ropa oscura de época y maquillaje sangriento. A esto se suma el poseído de ojos negros, descrito como una persona de apariencia normal pero con ojos completamente negros, venas oscuras sobre la piel y movimientos corporales extraños que sugieren pérdida de humanidad.
Entre las ideas con mayor componente de caracterización física aparece la criatura del bosque prohibido, que mezcla elementos humanos y naturales mediante ramas que emergen de la cabeza, musgo sobre el cuerpo y piel agrietada.
El listado se completa con la enfermera del hospital abandonado, el ser de otra dimensión con tentáculos y extremidades deformadas, y la señal maldita, un personaje con una televisión antigua como cabeza que muestra interferencias y rostros inquietantes, en una propuesta que remite al terror analógico.

articles.title: "Estará al fondo del jardín": compraron una casa a las afueras de París y ahora tendrán un centro de datos que consume cuatro veces lo que Disneyland
articles.text:
A las afueras de París, una familia lleva 26 años viviendo en una casa con jardín. Ahora, al otro lado de su valla, todo apunta a que va a levantarse un gigantesco centro de datos de 27 metros de altura, con decenas de sistemas de refrigeración y generadores eléctricos. La instalación tendría capacidad para consumir más de cuatro veces la electricidad anual de Disneyland París. Es la cara más cercana de una transformación que está llevando las infraestructuras de la IA hasta las puertas de barrios residenciales franceses.
Al fondo del jardín. La historia sucede en Ballainvilliers, una localidad de menos de 5.000 habitantes situada al sur de París, junto a Épinay-sur-Orge. Contaba esta semana Le Parisien que allí vive Gilles, un informático que compró su vivienda hace 26 años y que ahora contempla cómo el terreno situado detrás de su propiedad podría convertirse en una enorme instalación industrial.
“Estará al fondo de nuestro jardín”, lamenta en el reportaje publicado. La promotora australiana Goodman pretende transformar una antigua plataforma logística de las editoriales Seuil en un centro de datos sobre una parcela de más de seis hectáreas, con obras previstas a partir de mediados de 2028.
Un vecino de 27 metros. El proyecto contempla un edificio de 22 metros de altura, que alcanzaría los 27 metros en sus chimeneas. Sobre la cubierta se instalarían 84 equipos de refrigeración y el complejo dispondría de 44 grupos electrógenos de emergencia. Dicho de otra forma, los residentes temen convivir con ruido permanente, emisiones contaminantes y riesgos asociados al almacenamiento de combustible.
De ahí que la Asociación de Épinay-sur-Orge para el Medio Ambiente (ASPE) lanzara el 24 de septiembre una petición para reclamar su abandono, que ya había reunido más de 1.200 firmas cuando se publicó la información.
Cuatro veces Disneyland París. La cifra que mejor explica las dimensiones del proyecto es su demanda eléctrica prevista: hasta 883 gigavatios hora anuales funcionando a plena capacidad. Según la comparación recogida por el medio francés a partir de datos de 2025 del complejo turístico, equivale a más de cuatro veces el consumo eléctrico anual de Disneyland París.
Para alimentar los servidores se proyecta una doble conexión eléctrica subterránea de nueve kilómetros hasta una subestación de RTE en Marcoussis. Un inciso: se trata de una estimación de consumo máximo futuro, no de electricidad que la instalación esté utilizando actualmente.
Las dudas sobre la salud. La preocupación vecinal también ha llegado a los organismos ambientales. En un dictamen publicado el pasado 3 de septiembre, la autoridad ambiental regional francesa (MRAe) consideró insuficiente el estudio de los posibles efectos sobre la salud, especialmente por el ruido, las emisiones de los generadores y las eventuales fugas de sustancias refrigerantes.
Goodman sostiene que el proyecto deberá cumplir una normativa estricta y estará sometido a supervisión estatal. Los vecinos preparan alegaciones para la investigación pública prevista para mediados de noviembre, una fase importante antes de que pueda avanzar la autorización de las instalaciones.
París se llena de centros de datos. Ballainvilliers forma parte de una transformación mucho mayor. Según el recuento recogido por Le Parisien, la región de Isla de Francia concentra 213 centros de datos, existentes o proyectados, repartidos en 139 emplazamientos.
Essonne resulta especialmente atractiva por su suelo disponible, la densidad de la fibra óptica y sus conexiones eléctricas de alta tensión. La proximidad a París y a grandes clientes empresariales explica por qué antiguas instalaciones industriales y logísticas están convirtiéndose en infraestructuras digitales de gran escala.
La factura de la IA. Qué duda cabe, el auge de la IA está acelerando esta expansión. En Marcoussis, también en Essonne, Data4 dispone de un campus con 250 MW de potencia, mientras que el futuro Campus IA de Fouju contempla una capacidad superior a 1,4 GW. Son magnitudes que ilustran la creciente presión sobre la red eléctrica francesa y la necesidad de planificar dónde se ubican estas instalaciones.
El debate alcanza también a los terrenos ocupados, la disponibilidad de energía para otros usos y el aprovechamiento del calor que producen los servidores.
Lo que ganaría el municipio. Las autoridades locales han destacado algunas posibles compensaciones del proyecto de Ballainvilliers: cerca de 100 empleos anunciados, la cesión de una parcela para construir un centro sanitario y dependencias municipales, y la posibilidad de reutilizar parte del calor de los servidores en instalaciones agrícolas cercanas.
Los vecinos, por supuesto, cuestionan el alcance de estos beneficios y temen que las molestias recaigan principalmente sobre quienes viven junto al recinto. Por todo ello, la cuestión seguirá abierta durante la tramitación administrativa, una investigación pública que está convocada del 16 de noviembre al 18 de diciembre de 2026 y cuya celebración no equivale a una autorización definitiva.
One more thing. El caso resume una contradicción cada vez más visible en la expansión de la inteligencia artificial: las infraestructuras que sostienen los servicios digitales necesitan enormes cantidades de electricidad y espacio físico, y parece que alguien debe convivir con ellas, o “cargar con el muerto”.
En Ballainvilliers, ese alguien son familias que llevan más de un cuarto de siglo viviendo junto a una parcela donde ahora se proyecta una instalación capaz de consumir nada menos que cuatro veces la electricidad de un monstruo como Disneyland París.
Imagen | Yann Caradec, Andrei Dan Suciu

articles.title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US), providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software.
This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1, where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls.
Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock.
For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements.
This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use.
Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process.
Solution overview
You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways:
- Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result.
- Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests.
The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1. Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used.
Walkthrough
The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment.
Prerequisites
Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files.
Step 1: Set up authentication
Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1. Obtain credentials through your organization’s approved mechanism. This walkthrough uses the named profile codex-il5. Keep credentials, bearer tokens, session tokens, and other secrets out of TOML files.
Protect the profile configuration, credential source, SSO token cache, and any credential helper from ChatGPT desktop app task writes, while allowing approved authentication tools to maintain and refresh credentials.
The ChatGPT desktop app supports two Amazon Bedrock authentication pathways: an Amazon Bedrock API key or the AWS SDK credential chain. AWS SSO through AWS IAM Identity Center is supported within the credential-chain pathway.
The app first checks for AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK in its environment. For desktop use, this variable can be supplied through %USERPROFILE%\.codex\.env on Windows or ~/.codex/.env on Linux and macOS. When present, the bearer token takes precedence over profile-based authentication.
If no bearer token is available, the app falls back to the standard AWS SDK credential chain. The chain can read AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials and related profile settings from ~/.aws/config. On Windows, the corresponding default paths are %USERPROFILE%\.aws\credentials and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\config. The chain also supports SSO profiles. For SSO, it uses the profile settings in the AWS config file and the cached SSO session to obtain temporary role credentials. These credentials don’t need to be manually stored in the AWS credentials file. See OpenAI’s Bedrock authentication documentation and the AWS IAM Identity Center credential provider documentation.
Step 2: Set up ChatGPT desktop app configuration files
You must create two ChatGPT desktop app configuration files: config.toml and requirements.toml.
Important: the configuration files need to be set up before the application is launched. The following table shows the file locations.
| Operating system | User config.toml | Admin requirements.toml | 
| Windows | %USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml | %ProgramData%\OpenAI\Codex\requirements.toml | 
| Linux | ~/.codex/config.toml | /etc/codex/requirements.toml | 
| macOS | ~/.codex/config.toml | /etc/codex/requirements.toml | 
Start from the requirements.toml file. requirements.toml is an administrator-controlled rules file. It sets security limits that users can’t override, for example, restricting which permission levels, tools, or settings the ChatGPT desktop app is allowed to use.
Use the following baseline for the supported AWS GovCloud (US) Amazon Bedrock deployment. The [windows] section applies only to Windows, and sandbox_private_desktop must be supported by the approved runtime.
Next, configure the config.toml file. config.toml tells the ChatGPT desktop app how to operate, including which model provider to use (amazon-bedrock), which model to select, and settings such as permissions or context limits.
Replace the model ID and named profile (for example, codex-il5) with approved values.
Step 3: Launch, initialize, and verify

articles.title: Rocket Report: Winter is coming for Themis; Cowboy Space adds iron to the fire
articles.text:
Baiju Bhatt, founder and CEO of Cowboy Space Corporation, attends an event in Palo Alto, California, to reveal the company's architecture for a new medium-lift rocket and data centers in space.
Credit:
Thos Robinson/Getty Images for Cowboy Space Corporation
Baiju Bhatt, founder and CEO of Cowboy Space Corporation, attends an event in Palo Alto, California, to reveal the company's architecture for a new medium-lift rocket and data centers in space.
Credit:
Thos Robinson/Getty Images for Cowboy Space Corporation
Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It’s been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that’s what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins. I’m a huge fan of the name. Maybe Cowboy Space is striking while the iron is hot as the space industry frets over demand for launch outpacing supply. However, Cowboy Space lags far behind so many other launch providers nearing the launch pad with their medium-class rockets, and the company didn’t have much hardware to show at this week’s big reveal. In other words, don’t mistake style for substance. But we’re rocket fans at Ars, and we wish them luck.
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Virgin’s new rocket plane reaches home port. The first of Virgin Galactic’s new Delta-class rocket planes left its Arizona factory Wednesday for a trip to Spaceport America in neighboring New Mexico, where it will undergo preparations for a test campaign culminating in suborbital flights to the edge of space, Ars reports. Virgin Galactic expects the craft’s first commercial spaceflight to take place “early” in the second quarter of 2027, but like every other projected date in aerospace, this should be taken with a grain of salt. Virgin Galactic halted commercial flights of its previous vehicle, VSS Unity, in 2024.
More to do … The company also revealed the rocket plane’s name: Apeiron. Engineers and technicians at Spaceport America will complete work on the vehicle’s avionics equipment and flight software. Following additional ground tests, Apeiron will be mated again to its carrier aircraft for captive carry tests, followed by a drop test and ultimately a powered test flight above 80 km. With Blue Origin’s retreat from the suborbital spaceflight market and SpaceX’s planned retirement of the orbital-class Dragon spacecraft, Virgin Galactic is the only company with a realistic chance of flying paying commercial passengers to space anytime soon.
ESA’s reusable rocket testbed seems cursed. The European Space Agency’s Director of Space Transportation, Géraldine Naja, said on October 22 that she was uncertain whether the agency would be able to complete the first flight of its Themis reusable rocket demonstrator before the end of the year, European Spaceflight reports. The single-stage rocket hopper has completed two countdown rehearsals at Esrange Space Center in Sweden, but the harsh Scandinavian winter may prevent Themis from taking flight this year.
Missed schedules … ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said in January that the Themis rocket’s first hop test would happen in the first quarter of 2026. Delays are nothing new for Themis. Officials originally expected the rocket’s first low-altitude hop test to occur in 2022. The rocket is powered by a reusable methane-fueled Prometheus engine. ArianeGroup, the company behind Europe’s Ariane rocket family, is the main contractor on Themis, which is supposed to test technologies for an eventual reusable replacement for the expendable Ariane 6.
Rocket Report
Keep up with the latest in space exploration and rocket launches.
Cowboy Space unveils new rocket. Cowboy Space on Monday released the first details about the launcher that it plans to loft before the end of 2028, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports. The rocket, named Big Iron, will be 282 feet (86 meters) tall and about 15 feet (4.7 meters) in diameter. Cowboy Space is developing a methane-fueled engine named Clydesdale. Nine of them will power the first stage, and the second stage will fly a single Clydesdale. Big Iron’s payload capacity will be up to 18 metric tons (39,700 pounds) to low-Earth orbit.
Let the horses run … Baiju Bhatt, the billionaire co-founder of Robinhood, started his space company, originally named Aetherflux, in 2024. He rebranded the company as Cowboy Space earlier this year. Bhatt is chasing the market for space-based AI led by SpaceX. After launching into orbit, the upper stage of the Big Iron rocket will form the core of Cowboy Space’s data center spacecraft, with five racks of GPUs, six inter-satellite laser links, and solar arrays stretching the length of one-and-a-half football fields.
More good news for Stoke Space. The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital announced Monday a conditional commitment to provide a $150 million loan to Stoke Space for construction of a second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, GeekWire reports. Stoke Space is well along in construction of its first launch pad at Cape Canaveral for its reusable medium-lift Nova rocket. The second pad would accommodate an upgraded Nova Block 2 vehicle for heavier payloads.
Swimming in cash … The $150 million government loan is subject to financial, legal, technical, and due diligence requirements. It follows Stoke Space’s $1 billion Series E fundraising round in September, bringing the company’s total amount of capital raised to $2.3 billion. Stoke aims to launch its Nova Pathfinder rocket next year, followed by Block 2 in 2029. The company’s reusable upper stage, the most innovative segment of the rocket, is now undergoing qualification testing at Moses Lake, Washington.
Industry execs forecast launch crunch. The US government may have moved too quickly to conclude that the commercial launch market could support its growing military needs, industry executives warned at a conference this week, Space News reports. The Space Force’s launch strategy, which is designed to broaden competition by tapping commercially developed rockets, has expanded the number of companies eligible to compete for military launches. But executives speaking at the 2026 Silicon Valley Space Week conference questioned whether enough capacity will be available as national security demand rises and SpaceX begins a long-planned transition from its workhorse Falcon 9 to its next-generation Starship rocket.
Pertinent quotes … An executive at Stoke Space, one of the companies seeking to break into the military launch business, said it “may have been a strategic error” for the government to assume the launch problem had been solved. Devin Papandrew, Stoke’s vice president of business development, said the government should consider additional funding, along with relief from regulatory and infrastructure constraints. The head of government relations at United Launch Alliance, the military’s leading launch provider after SpaceX, said the launch supply crunch should ease as new rockets enter service. When might that happen? “2030-ish is the best I would hope for right now,” Hunt said.
SpaceX no longer needs NASA. In a comprehensive feature story this week, Ars reports on the fraying relationship between SpaceX and NASA. For the last decade and a half, NASA has relied upon Elon Musk’s space company to resupply the International Space Station, end US reliance on Russia for crew transport, and develop a critical piece of the puzzle for beating China back to the Moon. But Musk is now all-in on AI, and SpaceX’s clear priority today is focusing on how to rapidly deploy compute on Earth and in space.
The signs are there … SpaceX continues to work on a human-rated lander for NASA’s Artemis Moon program, but there are signs of a partial breakup looming. SpaceX wants to end flights of the Crew Dragon spacecraft by 2030, and is already winding down its remarkably successful Falcon 9 rocket in favor of the company’s much larger but relatively unproven Starship. And Starship’s launch capacity will be filled by SpaceX’s internal demand for Starlink and Starmind, the company’s orbital data center constellation. SpaceX now seems increasingly disinterested in the US government for most contracts outside of data services, such as Starshield for military communications and observations.
ULA to develop upgraded Centaur for SLS. During a lengthy news conference on October 23, NASA provided a detailed overview of how it plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as soon as 2028 as part of its Artemis program, Ars reports. The changes include revised architectures for getting astronauts to the lunar surface on landers provided by SpaceX and Blue Origin. On the launch front, NASA confirmed it will contract with United Launch Alliance to develop an upgraded version of its Centaur V upper stage to fly on the Space Launch System rocket.
LLO or bust … The “extended” Centaur V is a larger version of the upper stage that flies on ULA’s Vulcan rocket. Incorporating the extended Centaur onto the SLS rocket will allow the Orion spacecraft to reach low-lunar orbit, a capability it does not have with the current SLS upper stage. In fact, NASA officials said the extended Centaur will be higher-performing than the costly Exploration Upper Stage the agency originally planned to develop as an SLS enhancement. “Getting Orion to low-lunar orbit means solving propulsion and spacecraft integration problems that were left unaddressed for far too long,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said.
Vulcan’s return-to-flight mission has a launch date. United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company’s 2026 launch schedule into oblivion, Ars reports. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval.
An important mission … The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA’s primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan. It’s also important for the Space Force and Amazon, which have staked much of their future satellite fleets on the success of the Vulcan rocket.
Space Force says America needs a new spaceport. US Space Force leaders want a new spaceport up and running by 2030, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure on bases in Florida and California that have launched rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years, Ars reports. The obvious problem with that ambition is that 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
All options on the table … “We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” said Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities, the Americans that live near it. In many ways, it’s much like an airport, but even louder. So there’s a lot of consideration.” Officials haven’t decided where to put a new spaceport. Garrant later said all options are on the table: a public-private partnership, a new military base, state land, or commercial land.
Next three launches
October 30: GSLV Mk.II | NVS-03 | Satish Dhawan Space Center, India | 18:21 UTC
October 31: Falcon 9 | Starlink 15-18 | Vandenberg Space Force Base, California | 03:48 UTC
November 2: Electron | QPS-SAR-20 | Māhia Peninsula, New Zealand | 08:45 UTC
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: London’s Ares Intelligence raises €2.9 million to turn employee insights into AI adoption plans | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Ares Intelligence, a London-based startup building what it describes as an evidence-based platform for AI transformation, has secured €2.9 million (£2.48 million) in funding.
The round was backed by Creandum and Lakestar, with participation from angels connected to Google DeepMind.
“Enterprise AI today is mostly coding, and that’s only the start. The opportunity across the rest of the business is far bigger and still largely untapped, and we’re at the very beginning of enterprise adoption,” said Richard Keuntje, Vice President, Creandum.
Founded in 2026 by Matt Falconer and 21-year-old Alfie Ranstead, Ares Intelligence was built to solve a problem the founders encountered first-hand while running Instruct, their previous automation company. It says customers ran into the same problem: they wanted to automate parts of their business but had no reliable way of knowing where to begin. Ares Intelligence was to fix this knowledge gap.
The platform deploys an AI interviewer that holds confidential, voice-based conversations with every employee in an organisation, in more than 70 languages. Within weeks, leadership receives a prioritised, evidence-led roadmap identifying where AI can save time and money.
Ares’ platform is GDPR- and SOC 2-compliant, with anonymisation controls that let businesses mask names, redact voices, or strip role metadata before reports reach leadership. Customers can deploy it on their own cloud or use Ares’ infrastructure, in the EU or the US, with data retention windows set by the business.
The founders say the entire process, from training employees on what AI can do to conducting individual interviews, collecting insights and drafting recommendations, takes weeks rather than the months usually taken by a consulting firm.
Ares Intelligence’s approach also flips the script on top-down AI strategy by not relying only on a handful of senior managers to identify AI transformation opportunities. The company’s AI interviewer captures the knowledge of the people closest to the day-to-day work, identifies gaps such as manual workarounds, broken handoffs, and use of unapproved AI tools.
“Businesses across Europe know they need to adopt AI, but many still don’t know where to start. It’s vital that companies begin their AI transformations now to avoid falling behind,” said Falconer, co-founder and CEO, Ares Intelligence.
He added, “The people doing the work every day have a huge amount of knowledge about where AI could make a difference, but they’re rarely asked. Ares gives them a voice across departments, countries and languages, and turns what they share into a practical plan. This funding helps us expand and bring that approach to more businesses.”
Since launch, Ares Intelligence has signed enterprise customers across Europe and the United States in approximately seven months. Tremonia, a Mercedes-Benz spin-out, uncovered more than 400 hours of avoidable manual work per month within four weeks of Ares’ AI interviewer interviewing everyone from senior leadership to the paint shop floor.
“The gap between AI ambition and real-world evidence is the right challenge to back. I’m building a business with AI myself, and there’s a significant difference between an impressive demo and something you can rely on in your actual work. What appeals to me about Ares Intelligence is getting the insight from the people closest to the work,” said Enrico Mellis, Venture Partner, Lakestar.
Ares Intelligence says the fresh capital will help the company expand operations and bring its AI-driven workforce intelligence to more businesses.

articles.title: The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
articles.text:
The iPhone has more screens! The MacBook has a touchscreen! The HomeView does CarPlay apps! For the first time in a long time, Apple is in a period of unabashed gadget experimentation, and while the final results aren’t always perfect, it’s fun to watch the most successful product maker try some new things again. Even when, in this case, “trying” amounts to just slapping a touch panel on a lovely new MacBook Pro — just to see if you might use it.
The delightfully messy state of Apple gadgets
On The Vergecast: MacBooks, Duos, Instagram’s AI problem, and Brendan Carr’s war on the weather.
On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate the merits of a touchscreen laptop, Nilay explains why he is absolutely positively going to buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and David asks, as always, could this have been an iPad?
After that, the hosts discuss Instagram’s foray into long-form content, and Adam Mosseri’s increasingly complicated relationship with AI content. Instagram is at once extraordinarily powerful and under serious threat, and Mosseri’s going to have a hard time making it all work. Finally, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, news about Anthropic’s IPO and Anduril’s laptops, and much more.

articles.title: ¿Estrés o emoción? Por qué tu reloj inteligente no distingue la diferencia
articles.text: Un hombre consulta su ritmo cardíaco en un reloj inteligente. Los relojes inteligentes o smartwatches y las pulseras de actividad se han consolidado como herramientas del sector del bienestar para registrar pasos, ejercicio, sueño y otros indicadores de salud. La Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (CNMC) publicó en noviembre de 2024 que el 34,8 % de las personas con teléfono inteligente en España había utilizado un reloj inteligente o una pulsera de actividad, es decir, aproximadamente una de cada tres. Pero, más allá de su uso para monitorizar la actividad física, las investigaciones estudian ahora hasta qué punto estos dispositivos pueden aportar información sobre el estado de ánimo. ¿Cómo funcionan y qué pueden decirnos realmente sobre nuestras emociones? articles.title: Por qué MrBeast afirmó que tiene su cuenta bancaria “en números rojos” a pesar de su fortuna
articles.text:
Jimmy Donaldson, conocido como MrBeast, tiene 28 años, más de 600 millones de seguidores y una empresa valorada en cerca de 5.000 millones de dólares, según Fortune. Pese a esas cifras, el youtuber afirmó en una entrevista con el The Wall Street Journal que su cuenta bancaria está en negativo
“Tengo dinero en negativo ahora mismo. Pido prestado. Todos los que ven este vídeo tienen más dinero que yo en su cuenta bancaria”, aseguró.
El patrimonio de MrBeast no es efectivo disponible
Según Celebrity Net Worth, la fortuna de Donaldson rondaría los 2.600 millones de dólares en 2026, pero casi la totalidad de ese monto proviene de su participación en Beast Industries, el holding empresarial que controla. El youtuber posee algo más de la mitad de una compañía que vale 5.000 millones sobre el papel, aunque esa valoración corresponde a acciones, no a dinero líquido.
El mismo mecanismo explica por qué figuras como Elon Musk o Jeff Bezos encabezan los listados de las personas más ricas del mundo: su patrimonio incluye participaciones en empresas como Tesla, SpaceX o Amazon que, si se vendieran de golpe, provocarían una caída en el precio de esas acciones. Por esa razón, estos empresarios no necesitan vender sus participaciones para costear sus gastos personales.
Pedir prestado resulta más barato que vender acciones
La clave de la estrategia está en el tratamiento fiscal. Cuando una persona vende acciones y obtiene una ganancia, paga impuestos sobre esa diferencia, conocida como plusvalía. En Estados Unidos, este gravamen puede alcanzar el 20% o más del beneficio obtenido. Por ese motivo, los grandes patrimonios recurren a la venta de acciones únicamente cuando necesitan liquidez para nuevas inversiones, no para gastos corrientes.
La alternativa consiste en utilizar esas acciones como garantía para solicitar un préstamo. El dinero obtenido de esta manera no tributa porque se considera deuda y no ingreso. Los bancos ofrecen a sus clientes más adinerados tasas de interés reducidas a cambio de recibir esas acciones como aval, mientras los dividendos o el crecimiento de la propia empresa permiten pagar el préstamo de forma progresiva. La deuda se renueva periódicamente, pero el pago de impuestos sobre ese capital nunca llega a producirse.
“Compra, pide prestado, muere”, la estrategia con nombre propio
Este esquema financiero se conoce como buy, borrow, die (compra, pide prestado, muere). Consiste en adquirir activos o fundar empresas, solicitar préstamos respaldados por esos activos para financiar el estilo de vida sin venderlos y, al momento del fallecimiento, transferir las acciones a los herederos valoradas al precio vigente en ese instante. De esta forma, los años de ganancias acumuladas dejan de contar para el cálculo fiscal. El Senado de Estados Unidos lleva años intentando cerrar este vacío tributario sin éxito.
Un mecanismo similar aplica al sueldo simbólico que utilizan algunos directores ejecutivos, como fue el caso de Steve Jobs y Larry Ellison, quienes percibieron ingresos mínimos en concepto de salario mientras el valor de sus paquetes accionarios aumentaba cada año sin tributar hasta el momento de su eventual venta.
El relato de “no soy tan rico” cumple una función concreta
Lo singular del caso de MrBeast no radica en la estrategia financiera empleada, utilizada desde hace décadas por grandes fortunas, sino en que la expuso públicamente como si se tratara de una confesión. En junio de 2025, el youtuber escribió en su perfil de X que le había pedido dinero a su madre para costear su boda.
Este tipo de declaraciones proyecta la imagen de una persona que reinvierte sus ingresos y vive con moderación, un mensaje que conecta con una audiencia joven que puede sentirse identificada. Al mismo tiempo, desplaza la atención del dato central: sus participaciones en Beast Industries, valoradas en más de 2.600 millones de dólares, le permiten acceder a crédito a tasas preferenciales en cualquier banco del mundo, una posibilidad fuera del alcance de sus seguidores.
La riqueza real se mide en activos, no en el saldo bancario
El indicador que mide con precisión la riqueza de Donaldson no es su cuenta corriente ni su salario, sino sus activos: la participación que mantiene en Beast Industries, el valor de Feastables y los ingresos generados por el acuerdo con Amazon para Beast Games. La empresa facturó cerca de 500 millones de dólares en 2024 y proyectaba alcanzar los 900 millones en 2025.
Con ese respaldo patrimonial, Donaldson puede sostener gastos de 250 millones de dólares anuales en la producción de sus videos sin necesidad de vender sus participaciones en la compañía. Los bancos le otorgan crédito porque cuenta con el aval más sólido disponible: una empresa cuyo valor aumenta de forma constante. El hecho de que su cuenta corriente registre números rojos responde a una estrategia financiera, una condición distinta a la que enfrenta la mayoría de la población que queda fuera del 1,1% de los ultrarricos.

articles.title: Max-Severity GitLab Vulnerability Exploited Against Alpine Linux
articles.text:
A recent code execution vulnerability in GitLab was exploited one week after disclosure in a failed attack against Alpine Linux’s instance.
Tracked as CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score of 10/10), the flaw stems from insufficient regular expression validation in Onigmo, Ruby’s regular expression engine.
The bug “could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration,” GitLab noted in an October 12 advisory.
According to Alpine Linux, a threat actor targeted its GitLab instance with a CVE-2026-97229 exploit on October 20 and 21. The attack failed, but the Linux distribution rebuilt the instance from scratch.
“Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with,” Alpine Linux notes.
It is still testing the GitLab instance before public release, and has reset all passwords, warning of observed automated login attempts using passwords compromised in other leaks.
As part of the October 20-21 attack, the hackers used a newly registered account to send crafted CI configurations to Alpine Linux’s GitLab instance, crashing the worker process.
“In 4 of those crashes, the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out,” Alpine Linux says.
Because the underlying vulnerability resides in Ruby, not in GitLab, and the Linux distribution’s image runs standard Ruby, the vulnerability was not patched after updating to GitLab 19.3.6.
“If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab’s packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later,” Alpine Linux notes.
On Thursday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it within three days, as mandated by BOD 26-04.

articles.title: Can AI data centers be mass-produced like cars? This startup aims to find out | TechCrunch
articles.text:
AI infrastructure company Runware is making news again, just months after unveiling the Sonic Inference Pod, a modular data center built in a factory and shipped to customers ready to install. Now the company has bigger plans. It told TechCrunch it wants to build a factory that assembles these pods on a production line, as if they were cars.
The idea isn’t entirely new. Companies like Crusoe and Schneider Electric also sell prefabricated pods, but Runware says it can ship its pods faster.
Flaviu Radulescu, co-founder and CEO of Runware, told TechCrunch that the company plans to scale production at its Romania-based factory to 30 megawatts of data center capacity per day by 2028, or nearly 1 gigawatt per month. That’s a whole lot of capacity: At that pace, Runware would produce roughly as much in a year as the entire U.S. was expected to add in data center power this year, about 10 gigawatts. But it also reflects an industrywide push to deploy data centers faster and more efficiently.
Nvidia announced, for example, the Vera Rubin AI factories and the DSX POD earlier this year. Both are also meant to make it faster and easier for companies to build their own AI data centers. The difference with Runware, though, is that it says it has actually built a factory rather than just designed the infrastructure that would let others build one.
Radulescu said Runware will gradually increase production starting next year and that it already has two factories — one it has used for a few years to build the pods, and a second it started building earlier this year. The second is expected to be finished within months and go online early next year.
Runware will manufacture the modular data centers on an assembly line. Customers can provide their own site to assemble them, or Runware can find one for them. Radulescu said Runware aims to bring the pods online within 48 hours. That time covers installation and set-up time, not build time. A pod once took three weeks to build but it will soon take one day as it ramps up production, says the company. Runware will provide spare parts if components fail. Customers can also rent compute from Runware or supply their own GPUs and pay a monthly fee for the pods and operations. Power and internet are charged separately, he said.
The pods can also be customized to customer preferences, he said. The pods have a standard design, but can be configured to meet customer requirements and the latest GPU chips. Chips can take a long time to arrive after they’re ordered, which works in Runware’s favor. “Our pod delivery times are also shorter than current GPU lead times, giving us time to adapt the infrastructure to the hardware being ordered,” he said. “For new GPU generations, our in-house hardware team can design, build, and test components itself, allowing us to adapt quickly.”
Right now, these are all plans — execution is the test. The factory will need a lot of people, inventory, supply-chain logistics, and money. There are cautionary tales about reinventing manufacturing, notably the electric vehicle startup Arrival, once valued at over $13 billion, which struggled to mass-produce electric vehicles cost-effectively compared with traditional plants. Runware, which has raised more than $60 million to date, said it plans to raise a Series B, but for now it is finishing and launching the factory with the $50 million Series A it raised last December.
“Our cost structure is very different,” Radulescu said, explaining how Runware seeks to avoid Arrival’s fate. “We do have headcount and materials cost,” he continued. “But our factory staff is cost-effective relative to the value of deploying compute for AI.” He also said that designing its own systems and buying widely available, affordable parts helps keep costs low. “We’ve brought in a highly experienced plant manager from the automotive industry to work alongside our chief of hardware and help us get that execution right.”
Sourcing components could also be a challenge. Though Runware says it designs and builds its own cooling and other pod systems with standard components, some parts, such as pumps and fans, come from Germany, and it still depends on Nvidia for networking. Still, Runware claims it has received $1 billion in committed interest for its Sonic pods since it began offering them to outside customers a month ago, “representing over 20 megawatts, which we’re now working to deliver,” Radulescu said.
Data centers in the U.S. and abroad have come under fire for how much energy they consume and how that affects the grid and other resources. When pressed, Radulescu said his company’s pods only need power and an internet connection. They’ll use a closed-loop liquid cooling system with air-cooled radiators to release heat, so they don’t really need a water connection. “We’re working with power providers on a site pipeline covering 397 megawatts, with potential to expand to 1.2 gigawatts,” he said, referring to its list of planned sites and adding that the company is deploying its modular data centers on sites that are much smaller than those used by hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google.
The sites, he continued, typically already have power, so they shouldn’t further strain the grid or disrupt the community. The pods also run “completely silent up to temperatures of 86 degrees Fahrenheit. We use energy from renewable sources whenever possible,” he continued. “We are actively working on expanding our network of energy providers and sites. We’re aiming to have renewables as our main energy source.”
Runware will bring its new factory online early next year, then expand to the U.S. and other regions worldwide. Modular systems are the future and will soon become “the standard for large AI deployment,” Radulescu said.
“Customers should be able to plan a hyperscale data center around factory-built pods from the beginning and have it working in months instead of years,” he added.

articles.title: Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
articles.text:
During an hourlong earnings call last night, Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe spent less time talking about the production ramp of the all-important R2 SUV than he did hyping the company’s still-unproven autonomous vehicle ambitions.
Rivian’s autonomy gamble faces its first real test
RJ Scaringe spent nearly half of Rivian’s earnings call hyping self-driving tech. But taking on Tesla’s FSD with custom chips and pricey lidar is an enormous gamble while the mass-market R2 is still scaling up.
But the company faces a crucial test later this year, when it rolls out its point-to-point hands-free driving feature — first to its own employees for testing and validation in 2026, and later to customers in 2027. Following that, Rivian says it will launch its first robotaxi vehicles in partnership with Uber in 2028. In short, the next two years will determine whether Rivian will succeed or fail in its high-stakes quest to become a full-stack autonomy player.
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator,” Derek Mulvey, VP for finance, said during the call.
Success is not guaranteed. Tesla has a huge head start with its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in over 1.7 million active customer cars. But trying to match Tesla’s driver-assist features — while simultaneously designing its own silicon chips, buying pricey sensors, and paying for massive AI computing power — is a huge financial gamble, especially while Rivian is still struggling to build and sell its mass-market R2 vehicles at scale. (The R2 recently became Rivian’s best-selling vehicle by volume, so progress continues.)
“We believe autonomy is a primary product differentiator, market share driver, and long-term value creator.”
— Derek Mulvey
But it’s unclear whether Rivian sees the R2 as its make-or-break vehicle or if solving autonomy will be the true decider. That leaves the company in the middle of a difficult balancing act: launching an ambitious, mass-market electric vehicle while simultaneously reinventing itself as a full-stack autonomous driving powerhouse.
Of course, the feature itself needs to work for Rivian to succeed. During the call, Scaringe revealed that he has been using the new point-to-point driving system in his own commute to the office every day, calling it “a wonderful” experience. He continued:
So, our view is that that is going to become a big driver of demand. And I think it’s unclear how quickly the whole — you know, the whole US market and the whole automotive market — starts to shift to really wanting this, and this being a major purchase criterion. But certainly, we’re at the front end of an inflection point where it’s more and more people exposed to what this could do… We do think it’s a really big driver, in the long term, for market share for us.
But Scaringe was cagey about other details. When asked about Rivian’s take rate for its Autonomy Plus package — in other words, what percentage of Rivian buyers who purchase or subscribe to the software out of the total customer base — the chief executive declined to share the exact number. “The take rate on Autonomy Plus has exceeded our expectations,” he said, “and we’re quite encouraged by it.”
Rivian’s execs are no doubt envious of Tesla’s take rates for FSD: Over 75 percent of new Tesla buyers in North America opted to get FSD in the third quarter of 2026, the company recently reported. Meanwhile, Rivian reported $605 million in revenue from software and subscription services in Q3 2026, a 45 percent increase year over year. And Rivian brought in $256 million in profit in software and services, up $102 million from last year, with a strong 42 percent profit margin.
Rivian will likely spend more money than it brings in as it keeps buying expensive computers and AI systems. On the call, the company pointed out that computer chips, memory, and electronics are getting pricier. It also warned that adding two processors and costly lidar sensors to some R2 models could eat into the profits it hoped to make by building the vehicle in large numbers.
The point-to-point system will face its own hurdles, including edge cases and the complexities of urban driving. A vehicle crash could damage Rivian’s brand and reputation, just as Tesla has experienced many times with FSD. And even though Rivian intends to roll out the feature to require active driver supervision, the company will likely face legal challenges when things inevitably go wrong.
To be sure, Rivian couldn’t afford to sit on the sidelines and concede the autonomous crown to Tesla and Waymo. Self-driving tech could help Rivian post big, software-company-style profits, but paying for expensive AI development while also trying to build the R2 at scale makes the next year or two its riskiest period ever.

articles.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
articles.text:
HBM shortages threaten AI expansion; TSMC weighs price hikes; advanced packaging ramps; domain-specialized AI models; Infineon and UMC boost fab investments; Intel’s quantum move; Lam and imec advance 3D integration; Google expands TPUs; AI-driven earnings; CPU benchmarking methodology for agentic AI.
SK hynix expects memory supply constraints to persist through 2030, with DRAM and HBM volumes effectively sold out through 2029. Samsung expects tight memory supply through 2028, citing lengthy fab construction and equipment lead times, larger dies, and greater process complexity in next-gen HBM, as well as a shift of DRAM capacity toward HBM. Samsung said its 2027 HBM supply is already sold out.
Solidigm, SK hynix’s U.S. subsidiary, reportedly is discussing a proposed $45B NAND flash fab with the U.S. Commerce Department.
China’s CXMT plans to soon begin limited production of HBM3E memory, despite manufacturing yields of just 20% to 30%, per Reuters.
TSMC reportedly is considering a 20% price increase for CoWoS as AI demand continues to strain advanced-packaging capacity.
Applied Materials plans to increase its stake in Besi to ~20%, deepening a strategic partnership that is expanding beyond hybrid bonding into new interconnect architectures and advanced packaging technologies for AI.
Manufacturing
Intel Foundry reported improving manufacturing execution in Q3, citing better yields and cycle times on 18A. The company also released its 14A 0.9 PDK in October and said it continues to engage prospective external customers around 18A-P and 14A, while advancing its EMIB-T advanced-packaging technology.
Infineon plans to invest €1.1B through 2034 at its Villach, Austria facility to establish Europe’s first high-volume manufacturing facility for next-gen GaN power semiconductors on 300mm wafers.
UMC approved an additional $3.2B in capital spending to accelerate its capacity expansion in Singapore and Tainan as demand grows for advanced packaging and silicon photonics.
Lam Research and imec expanded their collaboration on advanced 3D integration, next-gen memory, and high-NA EUV patterning. The work includes deposition, etch, and plasma dicing processes for advanced packaging, along with Lam’s Aether dry resist technology.
AI tools and accelerators
Cadence introduced a portfolio of domain-specialized AI models for agentic chip and system design. Integrated with Cadence’s EDA tools, the portfolio spans multiple model sizes and architectures, combining post-trained LLMs, decision models, and self-improving agent skills.
Arm introduced a new CPU benchmarking methodology for agentic AI. The framework evaluates CPU performance across agentic workloads, including tool execution, orchestration, and reasoning, using repeatable measurements and end-to-end task outcomes.
Google is expanding the reach of its custom AI accelerators, with OpenAI reportedly planning to purchase its TPUs, reports The Information. Separately, Oracle will offer Google’s TPUs through its cloud infrastructure beginning in 2027 and plans to add Arm’s AGI CPUs in fall 2027.
Broadcom‘s XPUs and networking equipment will support Anthropic‘s AI infrastructure expansion, beginning in 2027, under a $63B financing arrangement.
Meta is expanding deployments of Nvidia and AMD AI infrastructure across its data centers, with both chipmakers also taking stakes in the company.
Deals and funding
Intel plans to acquireClassiq, a developer of automated quantum algorithm synthesis software. Intel says the acquisition will give it a full stack of quantum offerings, adding to its silicon spin-qubit technology and manufacturing.
Unconfirmed: Marvell is reportedly in advanced talks to acquire optical components makerLumentum, per Bloomberg. Onsemi reportedly is in talks to acquireFerric, a startup developing integrated voltage regulators for AI processors, for nearly $1B, according to The Information.
Earnings
Quarterly revenue and % growth versus the same quarter in the prior year, unless otherwise indicated:
Advantest: ¥477.7B, up 82%, with robust tester demand for AI.
Workforce | Education— AI in engineering education, VR-based fab training, and expanding university semiconductor workforce programs.
Events and Webinars— Micro 2026, PIC Summit, full-chip curvilinear patterning, and functional verification study.
Global
Asia
Vietnam‘s first semiconductor fab may miss its 2027 trial-production target, according to Reuters. The estimated US$1.3B Viettel project reportedly has yet to begin construction, while negotiations for ASML lithography equipment remain unresolved. Viettel maintains the project is on schedule.
ITIF says the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative has grown to 26 countries, coordinating on semiconductors, critical minerals, energy, advanced manufacturing, and AI infrastructure to reduce dependence on vulnerable supply chains.
Imec and Indiana University formed a semiconductor research partnership focused on advanced electronics, photonics, and workforce development. Initial research will test imec-developed electronic and photonic components in extreme environments, including space.
Cadence will provide U.S. Department of Energy National Laboratories with access to EDA, SDA, multiphysics simulation, digital twins, advanced packaging, and 3D-IC workflows, along with technical expertise.
ChipAgents is expanding its agentic AI platform across digital and analog chip design with a neural engine that combines persistent design knowledge, advanced reasoning and orchestration, dynamic model routing, and physics-aware models. It will also work with Nvidia to fine-tune Nemotron models.
Axiomise and Agnisys teamed up to verify NoCs using formal technologies.
AI power delivery
Infineon introduced new AI power-delivery technologies, including a ±400 V/800 V rack power-distribution reference board, a 5.6 kW M-CRPS reference design, and 900 V monolithic bidirectional GaN switches for solid-state transformers in AI data centers.
Compute, memory and photonics
PsiQuantum demonstrated an 8×8 optical circuit switch built on silicon photonics for AI infrastructure.
TetraMem taped out a 12nm analog in-memory computing SoC based on multi-level RRAM and developed using Synopsys‘ cloud EDA tools.
Fraunhofer IIS integrated permanent micromagnets directly into the silicon substrate of a magnetic sensor chip at wafer level.
Automotive
Infineon introduced a chip-embedding platform for high-voltage power electronics, LinearFET technology for solid-state power distribution in EVs and SDVs, new MOSFETs for 12 V and 48 V vehicle systems, and a high-voltage BMS reference design.
STMicro released an automotive safety sensor platform that combines accelerometers and gyroscopes for ADAS and vehicle-safety applications.
Bosch debuted a new MEMS inertial sensor platform, combining ADAS and vehicle-safety functions up to ASIL D.
Research
TU Munich researchers developed neural-network-based transistor models for 3nm nanosheet devices, accelerating standard-cell library characterization by up to 8× compared with a conventional compact model. The models kept delay-estimation errors below 0.11%.
A Brown University-led team demonstrated ultrathin multiferroic films that retain ferroelectric and magnetic properties at thicknesses of just a few angstroms, overcoming the dead-layer effect in bismuth ferrite. The films also exhibited altermagnetic properties, potentially enabling low-power memory and logic devices.
Chinese Academy of Sciences-led researchers developed a III-nitride-based in-sensor computing device that uses interfacial polarization to separate photogenerated carriers and reduce recombination losses. The sensor-memristor achieved responsivity on the order of 10⁶ A/W, an on/off ratio of 10⁵, and maintained high performance at temperatures up to 300°C.
University of Oxford-led researchers identified a pseudo-direct semiconductor in bismuth sulfide that combines strong light absorption with slower electron–hole recombination. Its unusual electronic structure was estimated to reduce recombination rates by about 75% at room temperature compared with conventional semiconductors with similarly strong absorption, potentially improving solar-cell efficiency.
Security
MITRE’s CWE Program released CWE 5.0, adding new weaknesses, including Hardware Simulation/Synthesis Mismatch. The new hardware weakness covers security-relevant cases where RTL behaves differently after synthesis, potentially exposing data, altering protected state, or bypassing security controls in the resulting hardware.
Alerts and hacks
TianoCore disclosed a critical vulnerability in its widely used EDK II UEFI firmware. The memory-corruption flaw could allow an unauthenticated network attacker to execute code during PXE boot, before the OS loads and before Secure Boot or measured boot can verify any OS component.
Supermicro disclosed nine BMC firmware vulnerabilities across two Oct. 26 advisories, including a critical flaw that could let an unauthenticated network attacker execute arbitrary IPMI commands on an active session. The disclosures also cover privilege-escalation, key-exposure, memory-access, and command-injection flaws.
Keystone said a breach exposed a key used to authenticate its hardware wallets, potentially allowing counterfeit devices to pass authenticity checks. The company is destroying 18,835 unsold devices containing the compromised key.
Government security news
NIST finalized its road map for transitioning to PQC, identifying the quantum-vulnerable standards that federal systems and technology providers will need to replace with quantum-resistant algorithms.
Eclypsium and Nvidia demonstrated how a compromised privileged component in AI compute infrastructure could alter model weights and outputs during live inference without modifying the stored model.
Rowhammer attack on Fil-C’s software capabilities (Independent researcher and U. Sussex)
Trending Video
Why Proof Convergence Matters: Leveraging patterns in formal verification to reach sign-off faster. Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise, talks about the impact of functional interactions involving safety and security, where to look for common patterns to prevent bugs from creeping into these designs, and how this all can be used to reduce time to sign-off with higher coverage.
NVision Quantum demonstrated a single-molecule spin-photon interface and partnered with HyperLight to integrate molecular qubits onto photonic chips using established semiconductor fabrication processes.
FZ Jülich-led researchers demonstrated 6.8-nanosecond single-qubit gates on a superconducting transmon, achieving 99.981% and 99.989% fidelity. Precision pulse shaping suppressed unwanted transitions, keeping leakage below 0.002% per operation.
A Technical University of Denmark team demonstrated integrated quantum light sources using 2D materials, coupling WSe₂ single-photon emitters to WS₂ waveguides on a chip, with an estimated minimum waveguide-coupled rate of 1.68 million photons per second.
Workforce, Education
In a new special report, Semiconductor Engineering examines how AI is changing the skills tomorrow’s engineers will need, with universities placing greater emphasis on strong math and physics fundamentals, critical thinking, and the ability to validate AI-generated results. Semiconductor employers say graduates will need both AI fluency and enough technical depth to recognize when AI gets things wrong.
S. Korea goes All In on AI; new Dresden power fab; Intel expansion; GM secures memory supply; AI power management funding; mature-node foundry capacity; 300mm fab equipment; McKinsey's map of strategic IC supply; security threats; AI burnout.
Lam Research and ASE expansions; data center shifts; CPO system architecture initiative; 2D-transistor interface solution; USENIX HW security; patent suits; image sensors; programmable AI memtransistor; Nvidia's new plan; earnings; Tier IV's L4 auto chip.
